text:
A significant appeal has been submitted to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit concerning federal immigration stops and arrests in Southern California. Formerly known as “Perdomo v. Noem,” the case is now titled “Vasquez Perdomo v. Mullin.” It challenges the methods used by immigration officials in conducting stops and arrests. The Ninth Circuit officially opened the appeal on October 16, 2026, following a notice from the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California regarding the appeal.

“The very fabric of our democracy and the legitimacy of all levels of government come from this premise — that we are all protected against arbitrary, indiscriminate, and widespread surveillance and detention by any governmental agency.” – Almeida-Sanchez v. United States, 413 U.S. 266, 273-274 (1973).

The case is named “Vasquez Perdomo v. Scott” (A short title for the appeal; it does not rename the lawsuit), which refers to Rodney S. Scott, the commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection, one of the federal officials involved in the case. The appeals court has placed this case on its schedule for urgent review. The appellant’s opening brief is due by November 13, 2026, and the appellees have until December 11, 2026, to respond. If the appellant misses these deadlines, the appeal could be dismissed automatically.

The specific ruling that is being challenged has not been publicly disclosed. However, the appeal comes after U.S. District Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong issued a preliminary injunction on September 2, 2026. This order prevented federal agents from making warrantless immigration arrests without examining each case to determine if an individual is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. The judge also mandated that federal agents must officially document the circumstances of these arrests.

Furthermore, the judge issued another injunction prohibiting stops based on whether individuals appear Latino or from working-class backgrounds. This order was initially filed as a sealed document but was made public on October 23, a week after the appeal was submitted.

The history of this case dates back to June 20, 2025, when a petition was filed after several individuals were arrested while waiting for work in Pasadena. These individuals had been detained in a federal building in downtown Los Angeles. The plaintiffs, which include Pedro Vasquez Perdomo, the Los Angeles Worker Center Network, and several labor organizations, expanded their lawsuit shortly after the initial filing.

As the case progressed, U.S. District Judge Frimpong issued temporary orders to prevent stops based solely on race, ethnicity, or language. She also ensured that individuals being detained would have access to legal representation. Although the Ninth Circuit declined to halt one of the orders, the U.S. Supreme Court intervened and stayed it on September 8, 2025.

Significant developments continued in 2026, including the judge denying most of the government’s attempts to dismiss the case and recognizing a new equal protection claim. On July 28, 2026, the judge found the government in civil contempt for not complying with orders related to the case, resulting in a daily financial penalty until it obeyed.

Local governments have also been involved, with Los Angeles County and several cities supporting the effort to challenge these immigration stops. This collaboration highlights ongoing concerns related to immigration enforcement practices in the area.

Fullerton participated only as a friend of the court (amicus curiae), not as a party in the case. It joined Costa Mesa, Goleta, and Santa Paula in submitting an amicus brief in support of the motion for the injunction against the stops. The judge accepted the brief on September 16, 2026, and the cities formally filed it on October 8.

An amicus provides the court with its perspectives and information. In this brief, the cities outlined the impact of the enforcement on their residents, businesses, and police departments.

One excerpt from the court filings states that a report published on July 22, 2026, by the UCLA Latino Policy and Politics Institute highlights that enforcement operations by defendants in Los Angeles had a “chilling effect” on local Latino businesses, significantly disrupting operations in or near enforcement areas. The report, titled “The Cost of Fear: The Impacts of Immigration Enforcement on Small Businesses and Latino Entrepreneurs in LA County,” indicates that Los Angeles County, with a population of 4.76 million, is comprised of nearly half Latinos, who own more than a quarter of local businesses. Additionally, the report found that negative impacts on businesses persisted even a year later due to ongoing enforcement and community fear.

Furthermore, amici have received reports that some community members are afraid to leave their homes, even to take their children to school. This fear has extended its impact to educational institutions. Studies show that immigration sweeps lead to increased school absences and negatively affect children’s educational outcomes. For instance, a Stanford study found that school absences increased by 22% in California’s Central Valley, where enforcement activities were taking place.

“Amici are all cities that pride themselves on being homes for everybody, including immigrants, and on providing safe, secure, and thriving communities for residents, visitors, workers, and businesses. Defendants’ unlawful operations have directly undermined these goals. As well as being unconstitutionally implemented, Defendants’ operations have had significant negative impacts on some of Amici’s communities.”

Key Dates:

– December 11, 2026 – Deadline for appellees’ answering brief

– November 13, 2026 – Deadline for appellant’s opening brief

– October 23, 2026 – Amended injunction made public

– October 16, 2026 – Appeal officially opened

– September 2, 2026 – Preliminary injunction issued

– July 28, 2026 – Government found in civil contempt

– July 22, 2026 – Case renamed “Vasquez Perdomo v. Mullin“

– January 9, 2026 – Government appeals previous injunction

– November 13, 2025 – Attorney-access order granted

– September 8, 2025 – Supreme Court stays earlier restraining order

– July 11, 2025 – Temporary restraining orders issued

– July 2, 2025** – Amended complaint filed

– June 20, 2025 – Case originally filed

– June 18, 2025 – The arrests took place in Pasadena and started the lawsuit. Three of the named plaintiffs were detained that morning: Pedro Vasquez Perdomo, Carlos Alexander Osorto and Isaac Villegas Molina.

What happened, according to court records

Where they were: All three are Latino day laborers. They were at a bus stop, waiting for work. One news account places it across from a Winchell’s Donuts on Orange Grove Boulevard, but that detail comes from a secondary source (VisaVerge), not the court records.

The operation: Agents in unmarked vehicles detained them during what the government called a “targeted operation.” The judge’s October 23 order says the stop was blocks away from the address of the person agents were actually looking for. It also says officers never asked the three men about that person and never went back to search for him after the arrests. An ICE deportation officer involved, Corey Clement, testified that his supervisor knew how the operation was conducted and had no concerns.

The men’s accounts: In sworn declarations, Osorto said at least four men in masks and civilian clothes, carrying guns, ran at them without identifying themselves or showing badges. Villegas Molina said an armed, masked man yelled: “Don’t run.” He said the man asked for ID, which he showed (a California driver’s license), then handcuffed him and put him in an unmarked vehicle without saying he was an immigration agent.

Detention: The men were taken to B-18, the basement holding area in the downtown Los Angeles federal building. They described it as crowded and unsanitary, with limited access to necessities and medical care, and said they were denied phone calls.

The government’s position: At the September 24, 2026 hearing, government lawyers argued that Vasquez Perdomo and Osorto fled when agents appeared. The judge wasn’t persuaded. She said any attempt to move away came only after unidentified armed men ran at them. She also found no evidence that Villegas Molina fled at all.

Afterward: The habeas petition was filed two days later, on June 20, 2025. Osorto, who had serious health problems, was released on July 30, 2025, on a $5,000 bond with an ankle monitor.

NEW YORK, United States (CMC) – Caribbean immigration advocates have welcomed a United States (US) federal judge’s ruling in favour of a New York ban on local law enforcement officers working with agencies such as Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), being able to make civil arrests.

Judge Mae A. D’Agostino also rejected the injunction on another law giving New York Attorney General Letitia James the authority to investigate sheriffs who cooperate with ICE.

Both measures were signed into law by New York Governor Kathy Hochul in May as part of a sweeping budget package that places limits on local law enforcement’s ability to engage in or assist with President Donald Trump’s civil immigration enforcement or otherwise perform the functions of federal immigration officers.

“The New York Immigration Coalition (NYIC) thanks Albany-based Judge Mae A. D’Agostino for rejecting a preliminary injunction request from a coalition of more than 15 county sheriffs claiming that the ban violates federal and state constitutions,” NYIC President and CEO Murad Awawdeh told the Caribbean Media Corporation (CMC).

NYIC is an umbrella organisation of over 200 immigrant and refugee groups in New York and Awawdeh said the ruling ensures that neither federal financial incentives to local law enforcement agencies nor politics can undermine the public safety needs and priorities of all New Yorkers.

“In an environment where ICE agents are brutally attacking immigrant New Yorkers at home, on our streets, and in other public spaces, the ban prioritises the public trust that is needed to keep all New Yorkers safe,” he added.

Governor Hochul has defended her policy in opposing ICE attacks in New York, particularly in the Haitian community in Brooklyn, New York.

“ICE is prohibited from going to sensitive locations. We’re very focused when it comes to ICE and its devastating impact on the community. People are terrified, and it seems very un-American (ICE’s tactics),” Hochul added.

Caribbean immigration advocates in New York have also welcomed a lawsuit by the governor and James against the Rensselaer County Sheriff’s Office in Upstate New York for failing to comply with the state’s Local Cops, Local Crimes Act that prevents collusion with ICE agents.

The legislation prohibits New York State and local law enforcement agencies and local governments from entering into or maintaining 287(g) agreements with ICE for federal civil immigration enforcement and requires any agreements in place to have been terminated by August 25, 2026.

Rensselaer County Sheriff Kyle Bourgault has refused to terminate its 287(g) agreement.

“We applaud Attorney General Letitia James and Governor Hochul for taking every step necessary to ensure that New York’s law enforcement agencies remain accountable to the communities they serve and focused on keeping all New Yorkers safe, not carrying out ICE and the Trump administration’s deportation agenda,” Awawdeh said.

“Every law enforcement agency in New York has a duty to serve and protect every resident, while upholding state and local law”.

text:
The morning after Tuesday's midterms was gloomy and rainy in Minneapolis, but people still gathered at the place where Border Patrol agents shot and killed Alex Pretti, a VA nurse and U.S. citizen, last January. All week, community members have come here to place their "I Voted" stickers at the memorial.

Nicki Adams, who dated Pretti and was his close friend for nearly 17 years, watched quietly as a woman added her sticker to a street lamp completely covered in the red decals.

"I wanted to see all the stickers. I just wanted to be here," she says. "It just means a lot to me. I think it would mean a lot to Alex, too."

A few blocks away, people left their stickers where an ICE officer killed Renee Good, a mom of three and a U.S. citizen, just a few weeks before Pretti's death. In Houston, they left them where an ICE officer killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a father of three and a Mexican immigrant, in July.

Adams says these stickers, and the election results this week, send a clear message to Congress: "You work for us, and please carry on these values that we care about … We want to be seen and heard and taken care of and have our neighbors taken care of."

The deaths of Pretti and Good during the ICE surge in Minneapolis marked a pivotal moment for the country, sparking intense public backlash to President Trump's aggressive deportation efforts. But federal law enforcement officials have given little indication they're progressing in investigating their deaths, or the deaths of at least seven other people killed by federal immigration agents since Trump took office again last year. DHS did not respond to an NPR request for the status of those investigations.

Now, after Democrats' sweeping wins this week, their deaths at the hands of immigration agents will likely be the targets of renewed investigations. With a majority in Congress, Democrats can issue subpoenas to the major players in Trump's mass deportation plan, compelling them to testify under oath before the legislature.

That could include White House Border Czar Tom Homan, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, former Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino, and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, among others.

Congress can also demand internal documents like use-of-force reports.

"They can dissect these individual shootings, and really unravel the story of what happened," says Naureen Shah, who leads the ACLU's immigration policy work.

Democrats have already held shadow hearings on the ICE shootings, during which they've called in family members and witnesses to testify.

But Shah says now Congress can ask key questions of top decision makers: What orders were given to immigration officers in the field? What was training like for these officers?

Who made the decision to paint Good and Pretti as threats, including calling Pretti a "would-be assassin" and a domestic terrorist, when video showed otherwise?

"It's like we can turn the faucet on and actually find out so much more," Shah says. "There's an aspect of this that is really about a kind of reckoning with how it's possible that things that seemed unthinkable could happen on American streets. How do you have that reckoning if you don't actually have the ability to force people to explain themselves?"

Democratic leaders have already said that's the plan.

Maryland Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, who is expected to lead the House Judiciary Committee, told NPR in a statement that Congress will use "every tool" at its disposal to investigate ICE and that it is time for the agency to "start answering to the American people."

California Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia, expected to lead the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, vowed to take on DHS and ICE abuses in a two-word statement: "Lawyer Up."

Mississippi Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson, expected to lead the House Committee on Homeland Security, sent a letter on Wednesday to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, demanding the agency "comply with all document preservation requirements."

Illinois Democratic Rep. Delia Ramirez wrote on social media that Noem, Miller, Homan, Bovino and Mullin should "clear" their schedules.

In response to that, DHS general counsel James Percival said Democrats are "more interested in political shenanigans than in governing" but said the agency is prepared to "deal with this nonsense."

There are key limitations to what Democrats in Congress can do with their majority when it comes to ICE accountability, says Rachel Moran, a professor at the University of St. Thomas School of Law.

Major changes, like clawing back funding for the agency, would require a veto-proof majority, something the Democrats don't have.

"You still have a president who has shown a complete lack of interest in accountability for federal agents and in fact, a great deal of knee jerk defensiveness about their conduct," Moran says.

In a statement, a White House spokesperson told NPR "if Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."

Democrats, the statement added, "should be reminded that we still control the federal government and all of its powers."

But that's not true. Congress has its own powers, one of them being the ability to compel testimony. Moran says a deeper probe into the shootings could still serve important purposes, like making evidence available for states to use in their own criminal investigations.

Minnesota officials, for instance, have been fighting with the federal government to get evidence related to the Pretti and Good killings.

Brent Ganger, Renee Good's brother, says learning more information about his sister's death will be hard to hear, "but I think it's also super important for us to understand what happened that day. I don't want history to keep repeating itself."

It was painful, he says, to watch immigration agents kill more people after his sister. He thought her death would be a turning point. In a way, it might have been the start of one. After the surge in Minneapolis, most Americans said ICE had gone too far.

Ganger, who considers himself a moderate, was happy to see the Blue Wave this week. On election night, he was scrolling Instagram when he saw a photo of his sister's memorial site, with all the "I Voted" stickers.

"I was very grateful to see the repudiation of this administration from the country. It felt very supportive of my entire family," he says.

The next morning, in his home in Colorado, he got up and made biscuits and gravy, his sister's favorite breakfast.

Maryland’s senior senator wants answers from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement surrounding the death of a Laurel, Maryland, man.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen said ICE has until Nov. 16 to turn over information about the death of the man in its custody and why his wife is now facing deportation after speaking out.

“If they’ve got nothing to hide, they should have nothing to fear from an independent investigation,” Van Hollen said.

On June 27, 47-year-old Julián Curo-Churata was arrested by ICE agents at a Home Depot in Laurel less than a week after he had attended an immigration court hearing. ICE later transferred him to the Richwood Correctional Center in Monroe, Louisiana.

Eleven days after a judge denied Curo-Churata’s request to voluntarily return to his home country, Peru, he died at a hospital while in ICE custody on Sept. 29.

In an Oct. 1 news release, ICE said Curo-Churata received proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals while in custody.

But in a letter to the Department of Homeland Security and ICE, Van Hollen questions that account. He points out that correctional officers reportedly said Curo-Churata had been lethargic and unresponsive throughout the day but wasn’t taken to the hospital until later that evening.

Van Hollen is also concerned about the timeline. ICE said Curo-Churata was taken to the hospital at 8:14 p.m., but hospital records show he didn’t arrive until 10:26 p.m., even though the hospital was a seven-minute drive away.

The senator wants to know what happened during that time, why it took so long to get him medical attention, and why detention center staff took him to the hospital instead of calling an ambulance.

“While U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement claims that he had proper medical care, this is the same operation that called Renee Good and Alex Pretti domestic terrorists after they’ve been shot and killed by federal agents,” Van Hollen said. “So we’ve learned we can’t trust what the Trump administration tells us about these cases.”

Van Hollen’s letter also raises questions about the treatment of Curo-Churata’s wife, Verónica Ramírez, after she spoke to The Washington Post about her husband’s death.

“It was soon after she asked questions about why her husband had died in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody that she was contacted and swept up in deportation proceedings,” Van Hollen said. “It appears to be a clear case of retaliation against her.”

Van Hollen told WTOP that his office has spoken to Ramírez.

“She’s now very worried about her own deportation, especially the impact that will have on their child,” Van Hollen said. “She’s obviously traumatized by everything that’s happened to herself and her husband.”

Van Hollen believes the results from Tuesday’s elections, which gave Democrats control of both houses of Congress, will help get answers.

“We’re dealing with an U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operation that thinks it’s an accountability-free zone,” Van Hollen said. “They have tried time and again to stonewall investigations, to refuse to answer questions. So, we’ll have to use all the tools at our disposal to demand accountability.”

When asked about Stephen Miller replacing Susie Wiles as President Donald Trump’s chief of staff, Van Hollen said Trump was “doubling down on cruelty in his administration.”

“What Donald Trump just did was give voters all over the country a big back of his hand. I mean, this was like a kick in the teeth,” Van Hollen said. “Stephen Miller has been the architect of the worst abuses coming out of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.”

text:
(The Center Square) – The U.S. Supreme Court will hear arguments on Tuesday in a case to determine whether presidential administrations can issue financial damages against immigrant employers.

Justices on the high court will hear arguments in U.S. Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, a case centered around a New Jersey farm that was found liable for more than $550,0000 in damages. The Labor Department conducted an investigation against the family-owned farm for not providing adequate housing and work conditions for H-2A farmworkers.

The H-2A visa program allows migrant farm workers to temporarily reside in the United States while employed in the country. Farms that recruit workers are required to comply with regulations that ensure U.S. citizens are not disadvantaged in the recruitment process.

Lawyers for the farm argued that officials in the executive branch should not be allowed to assess damages against family-owned farms. Sun Valley Orchards went out of business following the assessed damages.

“There is no precedent or history supporting agency adjudication of such employment-related issues," lawyers for the farm wrote. "The government’s contrary argument would vastly expand the public rights exception for immigration-related claims to encompass myriad issues involving temporary workers."

Lawyers for the government disagreed with Sun Valley Orchards. The lawyers argued that Congress has given authority to administrative agencies like the Department of Labor to adjudicate worker issues.

"Administrative adjudications provide an efficient mechanism for ensuring that employers who participate in that vast program comply with those terms and conditions," the lawyers for the government wrote in a brief to the court.

Alex MacDonald, co-chair of the law firm Littler Mendelson’s Workplace Policy Institute, said the dispute represents a unique case where the Trump administration is defending a policy that argues for more government regulation, likely because it falls into the category of immigration policy.

Justices on the high court will decide whether the federal courts are equipped to step in with workplace disputes or if administrative bureaucracy has the say. MacDonald said the court’s opinion on administrative authority will have broad influence for migrant worker disputes moving forward.

“Depending on the way the court decides this case, yeah, it could have implications for those other [migrant worker] statutes,” MacDonald said.

The case balances a unique blend of public and private rights, MacDonald said. He said the right to equal housing and fair employment would often be settled in a courtroom under Article III of the Constitution. However, the government has leeway to handle any of these issues when immigration is involved because it poses a national security issue.

Thomas Berry, director of the Cato Institute’s Center for Constitutional Studies, said migrant worker programs are discretionary and provide for different legal processes.

“If you participate in a discretionary privilege program, you also do not get an article 3 court right,” Berry said.

MacDonald said legal precedent provides for a gray area in adjudication of migrant labor disputes. He predicted justices will deal with definitions of the word “impose” in federal laws that give executive agencies the power to handle migrant worker disputes.

“We're looking at one word in a statute that just says 'impose,'” MacDonald said about the high court’s potential thought process. “That's not obvious to us that that should be an administrative hearing with what we've said about cases that should go to article three courts.”

Berry raised the possibility that a high court ruling in favor of Sun Valley Orchards could allow for deportation proceedings to be handled differently, a critical issue for the Trump administration.

However, MacDonald said the statutes for deportation proceedings provide requirements for a specific hearing to take place, unlike when adjudicating migrant worker disputes.

“[A] removal proceeding is not about a dispute between an employer and a worker involving employment law,” he said. “So, there's not that same private rights element to it.”

However, lower courts could alter other work visa proceedings with similar statutory language at issue. This could mark a significant shift for the Trump administration while it attempts to restrict foreign workers in other visa programs.

“A lot of the statutes, at least the ones I'm familiar with, are similarly unclear about the department's authority or how it is supposed to go about enforcing the relevant statutes,” MacDonald said.

Justices on the high court will hear arguments in the case on Tuesday and are expected to issue a decision by June 2027.

A 21-year-old Wisconsin state trooper was detained by ICE after federal agents detained him at a Madison airport Thursday.

In an update Friday night, Carel Van Der Merwe's lawyer said he was released on supervision after Rep. Derrick Van Orden reportedly "got involved and requested his release."

Trooper's asylum case and career

Van Der Merwe was going to board a flight to visit his parents in New Mexico. He has served in the Wisconsin State Patrol since July 2025, WisDOT said Friday. He has no criminal record.

Timeline:

FOX 9 found video of Van Der Merwe graduating from the academy in 2025. In the video his father pins his uniform.

"Carel very much loves the United States, and he is very much into service," his attorney, Marc Christopher, said.

Christopher said Van Der Merwe fled South Africa with his parents at 14. After first settling in Florida, the family applied for asylum in 2019 and is still waiting for their asylum interview while the case moves through the courts.

Local perspective:

Immigration attorneys have said asylum cases can sometimes take upward of 10 years to complete, and because of that, asylum seekers often get work authorization while they wait.

"Because it takes so long, individuals are allowed to obtain work authorizations. So Carel's parents got work authorizations and then when he wanted to work, he obtained a work authorization," said Christopher.

Christopher said the family followed the legal process. He also said they fear going back to South Africa. "They have indicated that they fear they're going to be jailed or tortured should they be returned back to their home country," said Christopher.

Detention fight now underway

On Thursday, as Van Der Merwe tried to board a flight to visit his parents, ICE agents stopped him and arrested him, according to Christopher. He was being held at the Dodge County Detention Facility waiting a hearing date, when he was released on supervision after Rep. Derrick Van Orden requested it.

What they're saying:

Christopher said Van Der Merwe told agents he was a state trooper and had gone through training and a background process.

"He told him he was an active-duty officer. He told them he's gone through training, that he's going through background. And ICE's response was, 'we don't care,'" said Christopher.

DHS said in a statement, "In defiance of our nation's laws, he overstayed his admission. This illegal alien will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings. To be clear: work authorization does not confer legal status in the United States."

What's next:

Christopher said he does not see Van Der Merwe as someone who would run or put anyone at risk.

"I don't know how anybody could reasonably look at this case and, in any way, find that this young man is a flight risk or a danger to community," said Christopher. "In fact, he's the exact opposite. He's someone who's sworn to uphold and protect our laws and to protect our citizens."

Immigration attorneys have said that asylum seekers with pending applications and no criminal record can no longer count on the longstanding practice of staying out of custody. DHS also said the Trump administration is working to stop people without green cards from getting on any flight unless they are to self-deport.

Christopher said it could take one to three weeks for Van Der Merwe to get a bond hearing.

text:
Donald Trump just gave the middle finger to millions of American voters.

Any other president who suffered the kind of drubbing at the polls that Trump did this week might have felt at least a sliver of humility – and perhaps even an obligation to work with the new opposition in Congress.

But not for the first time in his political career, Trump veered in the opposite direction. On Friday he made Stephen Miller, condemned by Democrats and civil rights groups as a white nationalist, one of the most powerful unelected officials in Washington by naming him White House chief of staff.

Miller is the architect of Trump’s far-right, nativist immigration agenda. He is, therefore, arguably the architect of the blue wave that engulfed Republicans in Tuesday’s midterm elections as voters – including many Latinos – expressed their disgust. Yet instead of firing Miller, Trump promoted him.

It was a declaration of war. Miller, 41, is a longtime proponent of the presidential authority that Trump has spent the past two years expanding at the expense of Congress. In 2017 he declared: “The powers of the president to protect our country are very substantial and will not be questioned.”

Now Republicans’ catastrophic defeat is likely to leave Trump more reliant on unilateral executive action than ever to advance his domestic agenda.

“In a lot of ways Stephen Miller has been the id to Trump’s authoritarian impulses and machinations,” Kurt Bardella, an adviser to Democrats in Texas, said. “I have to imagine that anointing this person chief of staff – the most powerful non-elected position in all of government – is a signal that they intend to double down on that authoritarianism.

“You’re going to see a lot of executive orders, unilateral action and stress testing of the checks and balances system continue for the final two years of his presidency.”

Trump’s second term has presented a concerted effort to dismantle those checks and balances that have traditionally constrained the occupant of the White House. He has signed 292 executive orders in less than two years, more than in his entire first term and a record pace for a modern presidency.

He has bypassed Congress on military action and tariffs, withheld congressionally approved spending, deployed the National Guard against the will of state authorities, politicised the justice department, punished critics and challenged judicial independence. Congress, dominated by Republicans reluctant to confront him, offered little resistance.

But this week’s landslide, the biggest in a midterm election since Watergate, puts Democrats back in charge of the House of Representatives and Senate. That the elections were free and fair, and that Trump did not dispute the result, was itself a victory for democracy.

Democrats will now seek to rein in the president and block his legislative agenda, bringing them into direct conflict with Miller, who was already a hugely powerful deputy chief of staff at the White House and now takes over from Susie Wiles.

Miller has been a champion of the Iran war and prominent voice on many of the president’s other priorities, including countering diversity initiatives and targeting transgender rights. He is reportedly one of a small group of White House staffers who approve all executive orders.

He is best known for driving the ‌immigration crackdown in Trump’s second term, setting ‌a target of 3,000 arrests per day – far above levels under previous administrations. He has pushed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to target anybody in ‌the country illegally, not just those with criminal records.

There are limits on what Democrats can do to stop the immigration drive since the One Big Beautiful Bill Act included major increases for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) that will keep it funded for the rest of Trump’s term.

Even so, they will now chair House committees with the ability to launch investigations, issue subpoenas and hold high profile hearings. Along with ICE, they might scrutinise Jeffrey Epstein files and the department of government efficiency (Doge). They have also vowed to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office.

The appointment of the pugnacious Miller as Trump’s consigliere suggests that the White House is moving to a war footing. He is likely to marshal a team of lawyers and attack Democrats by accusing them of weaponising the deep state against the president. As a frequent guest on the conservative Fox News network, he will also wage war in the court of public opinion.

“Trump’s decision to elevate Stephen Miller means that he’s spoiling for a fight with Democrats and they’re going to just rely on executive action to try and push their agenda through,” said David Cohen, a political science professor at the University of Akron in Ohio, who studies the American presidency and White House staffing.

Cohen added: “It’s a White House that doesn’t seek out cooperation with Congress. It’s their way or the highway, essentially, and it’s possible Stephen Miller is relishing this because he’s a believer in the unitary presidency and executive presidential action and he views this as a way where he can expand the powers of the presidency.”

Trump is not the first president to seek to consolidate authority. Arthur Schlesinger Jr’s 1973 book The Imperial Presidency warned that an accumulation of presidential power threatened the constitutional separation of powers.

In 1989 the American Enterprise Institute thinktank published The Fettered Presidency, a counterpoint arguing that legal and congressional constraints had unduly weakened the executive. It helped inspire a modern conservative drive to expand presidential authority, which accelerated under George W Bush and was subsequently exploited by Barack Obama as congressional gridlock made legislating increasingly difficult.

The combination of Trump and Miller, however, takes the concept of an American Caesar to a new extreme – and flies in the face of the verdict delivered by the electorate on Tuesday.

“It’s a step that I find hard to fathom except as the president giving the middle finger to the American public,” said Bill Galston, a senior fellow in governance studies at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington.

“In the same way that he ransacked the state of Texas for the very worst senatorial nominee imaginable, now he’s done the same thing with the chief of staff position. This is simply outrageous.”

The mayor of Houston, the most populous city in the US state of Texas, has ordered the city’s police force to sharply limit its cooperation with the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

John Whitmire’s executive order came on Friday, days after Democrats swept statewide offices in the traditionally Republican state.

According to the order, Houston police will contact ICE only when a person is being arrested for a jailable offence, according to the Reuters news agency.

Whitmire said he had consulted Texas’s newly elected governor, lieutenant governor and comptroller before acting, and that the move was meant to reduce fear and anxiety across the city.

“Elections matter,” Whitmire told reporters. “I do this to begin a healing process,” he said, adding he hoped his executive order would become a model for other Texas cities.

Joining Whitmire at the news conference, Houston Police ⁠Chief J Noe Diaz said he supported the change and that his department had already begun to implement the new policy.

Under the new rules, people stopped for minor traffic violations will no longer be referred to ICE simply because they have an administrative immigration warrant.

The decision reverses a policy Whitmire put in place in April under pressure from outgoing Republican Governor Greg Abbott.

Abbott had threatened to withdraw about $110m in state public safety grants, arguing that a city council ordinance limiting police contact with ICE breached Senate Bill 4, a 2017 state law that bars local police from restricting cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton also sued the mayor, the city council and the police chief over the ordinance.

“We’re taking an interpretation of the law today, working with the newly elected members of the state leadership, in implementing this policy,” Whitmire told reporters. “We don’t want people to worry about ⁠their workers, their family members, their students.”

The issue has drawn intense scrutiny in Houston. The Houston Chronicle found that city police contacted ICE at least 107 times in the first eight months of 2025, compared with nine times in the whole of 2024.

In July, an ICE agent shot dead Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a longtime Houston resident.

FIEL Houston, an immigrant rights group, called the order a victory for the city but said it was long overdue. “Today Houston won. Today our community can breathe easier,” FIEL Executive Director Cesar Espinosa said in a statement to KPRC.

Whitmire said he expected Houston’s approach to become a model for other cities. In Austin, Mayor Kirk Watson asked city officials on Friday to revise their own policy on ICE warrants.

Nithya Raman, mayor-elect of Los Angeles, held back tears as the enormity of her victory began to sink in.

“This city has given me and my family so much,” Raman, an Indian-born urban planner who came to the United States at the age of six, told supporters in Los Angeles on Thursday night, after projections showed her winning the mayoral race.

“The idea that Angelenos voted for an immigrant to be their next mayor at this moment in American history is so deeply moving to me,” the 45-year-old said.

Raman’s victory means that three of the world’s most influential cities – New York, Los Angeles and London – will now be led by individuals of South Asian descent.

A democratic socialist, she also gives the progressive movement another leader in a major US city, after New York and Washington, DC.

The result came amid a dominant showing by Democrats in US midterm elections, in which the party wrested control of both chambers of Congress and scored its biggest landslide victory in half a century. Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), which backed Raman’s campaign, also claimed an impressive series of wins, with 105 of its endorsed candidates on track to secure elected office, according to the group.

For Raman, the victory provides a bigger platform to address central planks of her political vision for the US’s second-largest city, including tackling its longstanding homelessness crisis and expanding affordable housing.

The Asian Democrats of Los Angeles County (ADLAC) congratulated Raman on becoming the first Asian-American elected to lead Los Angeles and said it looked forward to working with her to “deliver for our communities”.

“We saw a wave of change across the country this election, and Los Angeles was no exception,” ADLAC President Zahra Hajee said. “The political establishment should take note: Voters want real solutions and a government that actually works for them.”

From southern India to LA City Hall

Raman was born in the state of Keralam, in southern India, and moved to the US with her family at the age of six.

She studied at Harvard University before earning a master’s degree in urban planning from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

After completing her studies, Raman moved back to India and launched an initiative to improve urban governance in the southern city of Chennai.

In 2013, she moved to Los Angeles, where she co-founded a nonprofit organisation to support people experiencing homelessness. The organisation, SELAH Neighborhood Homeless Coalition, stresses that unhoused people are “fellow members of our community worthy of the same dignity, respect and representation afforded to any housed person”.

Raman also spent a year as entertainment director of Time’s Up, an organisation founded by Hollywood figures to raise money for legal support for victims of sexual harassment.

Her foray into politics came in 2019, when she shocked Los Angeles’s political establishment by defeating incumbent city councilman David Ryu and becoming the first DSA-backed candidate elected to the council. She credited a major grassroots organising drive for that victory.

Raman’s run for mayor this year came as another surprise to the local political scene, as most Democratic Party leadership stuck with incumbent mayor Karen Bass. Raman entered the race at the 11th hour, reversing her earlier endorsement of one-time ally Bass. She said Los Angeles had reached a “breaking point” and was “no longer a place of opportunity for too many”.

Bass was endorsed by prominent Democrats such as California Governor Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi.

In the end, none of that mattered.

Homelessness ‘a moral failing’

Raman’s mayoral campaign focused on expanding affordable housing, addressing the city’s decades-old homelessness crisis and protecting immigrants.

Her campaign described the city’s housing crisis as “the compounding moral crisis of our time”. Growing desensitisation to homelessness, it added, “is a moral failing”.

“Every time we see one of our neighbors living and dying on the streets, we should be shocked,” a campaign policy statement said. “Instead, in Los Angeles, it has become routine.”

Raman envisions a new approach to addressing homelessness, including expanding medical teams for people living in encampments or on the streets, alongside huge new investment in housing.

She estimates her policies will halve the number of people sleeping in tents and encampments throughout the city by 2028, when the Olympic Games will come to Los Angeles. As of 2025, the city had some 44,000 homeless people, including 27,000 staying on the streets, in vehicles or encampments, according to the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority.

Raman has also pledged to replace the city’s police chief, whom she says has “lost the confidence” of residents by failing to curb federal immigration raids carried out by the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency.

“Federal raids have left Angelenos afraid to live in the city they call home – where they work and raise their families,” said Raman’s campaign. “That has to stop.”

While Raman was championed by many progressive voices, she initially faced a rift with the DSA over not making the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement against Israel an official part of her policy platform.

Raman has said she believes Israel is committing genocide in Gaza. In an October statement to DSA clarifying her position on BDS, Raman said she believes the best way for Los Angeles residents to express solidarity with Palestinians is through “non-violent protest, legislative action, and diplomatic pressure, including BDS”.

In a close vote, the DSA decided against revoking the endorsement granted to Raman by its local Los Angeles chapter, and ultimately celebrated her election victory.

In her victory speech, Raman promised to restore what she called an ambitious, creative and entrepreneurial Los Angeles.

“For too long our broken and unjust status quo has convinced Angelenos that this is the best that we can do,” she said.

‘I am myself’

Raman joins a growing number of leaders with immigrant backgrounds in global metropolises.

In New York last year, Zohran Mamdani was elected as the city’s first South Asian and Africa-born mayor. Like Raman, he has Indian roots; Mamdani’s father is a leading scholar and his mother an internationally renowned filmmaker.

Overseas, Sadiq Khan, the son of Pakistani immigrants, has been the mayor of London since 2016. And in Toronto, Olivia Chow, who moved to Canada from Hong Kong at the age of 13, has served as mayor since 2023.

Raman’s rise has drawn comparisons with Mamdani’s. Both have immigrant backgrounds, belong to the DSA, have advocated major changes to urban policy, including on housing, and sought protections for immigrant communities.

Ana Oaxaca Carrasco, assistant professor of political science at the University of Wisconsin – Madison, said Mamdani and Raman both connect to immigrant communities through their policies and personal experiences.

“These leaders embody the multicultural realities of the cities they represent,” Carrasco told Al Jazeera. “Their names, identities, lived experiences and immigration stories have been visible parts of their political appeals.”

“By openly identifying as immigrants, they have broken barriers in political representation in ways that may resonate with immigrant communities across national origins,” Carrasco added.

Raman has said she is flattered by comparisons to Mamdani but is careful to distinguish herself.

“Mamdani is one of the most popular politicians in America right now, and I’m very grateful to be compared to someone who is that skilled as a communicator and a leader,” she said in an October interview with Vanity Fair.

“But I am different. I am myself.”

text:
The mayor of Houston, Texas, has directed the city's police to limit co-operation with federal immigration officials.

The move by John Whitmire, a Democrat, comes on the heels of stunning victories by the party in Texas during this week's midterm elections. It breaks with policy set by Republican Governor Greg Abbott, who lost his re-election bid.

"I do this to begin a healing process," Whitmire said on Friday, and to "reduce fear and anxiety across our community". He added: "I also do this knowing that elections matter."

There has been months of public outcry in Houston after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man who was driving to work.

Houston police chief Noe Diaz said on Friday that officers will now only contact ICE if someone they arrest for a jailable offence also has an administrative ICE warrant, which are issued internally by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), within which ICE operates.

"For example, if our police officers pull someone over for a minor traffic infraction and they write a citation, that person receives a citation and goes about their day," Diaz said.

Under the previous rules, Houston police officers were required to inform ICE if anyone they were dealing with came up as having one of these warrants attached to their name when they were searched on the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) - a digital database that includes records on wanted persons, stolen property, certain missing people and those arrested and fingerprinted for serious offences.

Whitmire said on Friday that he had directed the Houston Police Department to make the changes through an executive order.

He also called on Congress to change federal immigration rules, saying "ICE needs better training. They need body cameras. They need to be trained in de-escalation."

He added, "But this can only be done in Washington. I can only control what I can control."

In response, a spokesperson for the DHS told Houston's NBC affiliate, KPRC 2, in a statement: "We remain disappointed that sanctuary politicians seek to limit cooperation with ICE, as our law enforcement are simply fulfilling their sworn duties to serve and protect our communities."

"Partnerships with law enforcement are critical to having the resources we need to arrest criminal illegal aliens across the country," the spokesperson added.

Another Texas city, Austin, has also begun implementing a similar policy change.

Democrats won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.

Texas, a long-time Republican stronghold, was the site of one of the most stunning upsets in the vote, with the state electing its first Latina governor, Gina Hinojosa, as the first Democrat governor since 1995. It also elected its first Democratic senator since 1988.

text:
WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump's new White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, is behind many of the administration's signature domestic policy initiatives — especially its sweeping crackdown on immigration.

An outspoken defender of Trump's most far-reaching goals to remake government going back to his 2016 run for president, Miller is known for his harsh language and unapologetic bombast, attracting outsized attention from supporters and critics alike. His record is likely to be scrutinized by Democrats in his powerful new role as he leads Trump's White House through a difficult lame duck period after the Republican Party lost both houses of Congress.

Here are some memorable things Miller has said through the years:

On immigration: 'We are being conquered'

During a 2023 spike in illegal border crossings, Miller described migrants as invaders, even though many were escaping poverty and violence in their home countries.

"We are being conquered," he told Fox News Channel in December 2023, commenting on the sharp rise. "We have millions of people coming in from different cultures and different ways of living and different belief systems."

Miler also warned that "a generation from now," people "will not know the country that they are living in. These consequences are permanent. Unless there's massive large-scale deportations by the millions, it will be irrevocable."

He called a Minneapolis man killed by ICE a 'domestic terrorist'

After federal agents shot and killed Alex Pretti during protests against the Trump's administration's hardline immigration policies in January, Miller posted on social media that the 37-year-old Minneapolis resident was a "domestic terrorist" and an "assassin" who had "tried to murder federal agents."

Later, Miller said in a statement that the federal officers in Minneapolis "may not have been following" protocol.

America 'created' Venezuela's oil industry and Greenland 'obviously' should be part of the US

In January, after a daring U.S. military operation captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, Miller used a lengthy post on X to decry "reverse colonization" in which he suggested that Western nations were sacrificing too much for the developing world and that such practice "has been a long self-punishment of the places and peoples that built the modern world."

In another post, he defended the right of the U.S. to take over Venezuela's vast oil reserves, writing: "American sweat, ingenuity and toil created the oil industry in Venezuela. Its tyrannical expropriation was the largest recorded theft of American wealth and property. These pillaged assets were then used to fund terrorism and flood our streets with killers, mercenaries and drugs."

He defended Trump's assertion that the U.S. was now running Venezuela, by telling CNN's Jake Tapper: "You can talk all you want about international niceties and everything else. But we live in a world, in the real world, Jake, that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power. These are the iron laws of the world."

In the same interview, Miller also argued that the U.S. could seize Greenland by military force from NATO ally Denmark. "Obviously, Greenland should be part of the United States," he said.

"Nobody's going to fight the United States militarily over the future of Greenland," Miller said.

Speeding up deportations by suspending habeas corpus

In May of 2025, Miller suggested that the Trump administration was looking for ways to expand its power to deport migrants who are in the United States illegally. To achieve that, he said officials were "actively looking at" suspending habeas corpus — the constitutional right for people to legally challenge their detention by the government.

"The Constitution is clear — and that of course is the supreme law of the land — that the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus can be suspended in a time of invasion," Miller said.

"So, I would say that's an option we're actively looking at," Miller said. "Look, a lot of it depends on whether the courts do the right thing or not."

In the nearly 18 months since, the idea has not been publicly pursued by Trump and his administration.

Family separation: 'No one is exempt from immigration law'

During Trump's first term, Miller championed a strict immigration deterrence policy that previous administrations had been hesitant to adopt: family separation. It called for routinely having federal agents separate children from their parents if families were apprehended illegally crossing the border.

Miller defended the policy to The New York Times in 2018, saying it "was a simple decision by the administration to have a zero tolerance policy for illegal entry, period."

"The message is that no one is exempt from immigration law," he added.

The tactic sparked widespread outcry, and the Trump administration did not revive it in its second term. Still, Miller has helped promote mass deportations of people already living illegally in the U.S. that has divided families according to legal status.

Arguing about the true meaning of the Statue of Liberty

During Trump's first term in 2017, Miller appeared in the White House briefing room to detail for reporters plans to cut back on the number of green cards issued, while prioritizing English speakers and skilled workers.

Asked if doing so might violate the spirit of the poem on the Statue of Liberty, that reads in part, "Give me your tired, your poor, Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free," Miller responded, "I don't want to get off into a whole thing about history here." He then did just that.

"The poem that you're referring to, that was added later, is not actually a part of the original Statue of Liberty," Miller said.

Birthright citizenship is 'suicide'

When the U.S. Supreme Court blocked Trump's attempt to throw out birthright citizenship — which grants citizenship to any child born on U.S. soil — Miller said immigrants and their children pose an existential threat to the nation.

"This is absolutely a deep knife wound in the heart of the American republic," he told Fox News Channel in June. "If your ruling requires you to suicide your civilization, your reading of the Constitution is wrong."

On vaccines: 'Nobody has studied it'

Miller is one of many members of the administration who has expressed skepticism about childhood vaccines. In August, he praised the president for signing an executive order aimed at curtailing the vaccine schedule for children.

"Millions and millions of parents feel they've been pressured when their children are just weeks out of the hospital to take five shots, six shots, seven shots all at once," said Miller, a father of four, including an infant born in June. "Nobody has studied it. Nobody's looked at it. Nobody's thought about it."

His comments contradict what the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has said, which is that research shows getting several vaccines simultaneously "does not cause any chronic health problems."

The Democratic Party 'does not care' about US citizens

In August 2025, Miller appeared on Fox News Channel to respond to criticism from Democrats over Trump's deployment of the National Guard in Washington and other U.S. cities — brushing aside concerns that the presence of troops was frightening residents, while having only a questionable impact on crime.

Miller used the occasion to take aim at Democrats more broadly.

"The Democrat Party does not fight for, care about or represent American citizens," he said. "It is an entity devoted exclusively to the defense of hardened criminals, gang bangers and illegal alien killers and terrorists."

Miller added: "The Democrat Party is not a political party. It is a domestic extremist organization."

text:
A Wisconsin state trooper originally from South Africa is set to be released from custody after he was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials Thursday at an airport while trying to visit his parents.

Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe entered the country in 2019 at 14 years old and attended high school in New Mexico, according to his attorney.

According to Attorney Mark Christopher, Van Der Merwe's parents applied for asylum, and he was granted work authorization because the process can take years. Van Der Merwe attended the New Mexico Military Institute for college and wanted to serve in the U.S. military, but was not permitted because of his immigration status.

Van Der Merwe started working as a Wisconsin state trooper in July 2025. He is authorized to work in the country, according to Christopher.

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that Van Der Merwe had legal permission to stay in the country until September 2019 but "in defiance of our nation's laws ... overstayed his admission."

WKBT in La Crosse, Wisconsin, said Friday afternoon that Van Der Merwe had a conversation with Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and will be released.

"It's one of the more egregious and ridiculous cases I've ever come across," said Christopher. "I can't think of any public utility or benefit of detaining him."

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — After Democrats' overwhelming midterm victories this week, winning candidates spoke of the need, once they are sworn in, to rein in President Donald Trump's mass deportation machine. Some suggested putting forward a new vision for immigration reform while both houses of Congress are in Democratic control.

The lofty goals come after two years in which Democrats, while in the minority, were limited in how much they could counter Trump's supercharged and, at times, chaotic immigration enforcement. But there are clear limits to what they can achieve even after Democrats' epic win, with Trump — who rode into power in part on a promise to curb immigration — in office for another two years and wielding his veto power.

What's more, Republicans have frontloaded billions of dollars for immigration enforcement. And the key architect of the president's hard-line immigration agenda, Stephen Miller, was elevated Friday to become Trump's chief of staff — suggesting immigration enforcement may not slow down any time soon.

Here's a look at what might come next for immigration after Election Day:

Investigating alleged corruption and ICE policies

Democrats appear ready to use the power of congressional oversight to investigate Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security. That strategy will likely resonate with voters angry aboutt how enforcement operations were carried out in places like Minneapolis or ICE arrests of longtime immigrants integrated into American society.

The administration ramped up immigration enforcement during the first two years of Trump's second term, launching major operations in multiple cities and sending arrests soaring. DHS also came under criticism for alleged corruption and misuse of funds it was granted to carry out Trump's immigration agenda.

Nationally, about 6 in 10 voters said the Trump administration's actions on immigration enforcement had "gone too far," according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters. A similar share disapproved of how ICE was doing its job. And about 6 in 10 voters said immigrants to the U.S. today do more to "help the country," while less than half, about 4 in 10, said they do more to "hurt the country."

Rep. Robert Garcia, a Los Angeles-area Democrat who will take over the House Oversight Committee and is a prominent critic of Trump's immigration agenda, warned the administration to "lawyer up," adding that investigating alleged abuses at DHS was one of his priorities.

The next Congress will "address the Trump administration's assault on the rule of law and hold those responsible accountable," said Mississippi Rep. Bennie Thompson, the ranking Democrat on the House Homeland Security committee.

Those investigations could delve into issues like DHS purchases of massive warehouses to hold arrested immigrants; whether ICE cut corners when hiring thousands of new deportation officers; or deaths in ICE detention facilities.

Garcia and Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut held shadow hearings featuring family members of people killed during immigration enforcement operations, a whistleblower exposing problems with ICE training, and American citizens caught up in immigration enforcement operations.

No Republicans attended and Democrats couldn't subpoena witnesses. Now they can, opening up a new level of scrutiny of the administration's actions.

Calls to put forward a Democratic vision for immigration

The last time Congress even came close to passing comprehensive immigration reform was in 2013. That proposal cleared the Senate but died in the House.

Border crossings that surged under the Biden administration further served to dampen any Democratic enthusiasm to talk about legalization for any immigrants.

Sarah Pierce, director of social policy for Third Way, a Washington, D.C., think tank, said Democrats need to show voters their own vision for immigration and border security and not just focus on oversight hearings of what happened during the last two years.

"They should lean into oversight, but I think that they also need to couple that with a proactive vision for what immigration should look like in the United States," said Pierce.

At least one of the party's new senators is ready for the discussion. During an interview with Fox News after the election, Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas discussed the need to pass comprehensive immigration reform, including a pathway to citizenship for immigrants living and working illegally in the country for years.

In the House, Rep. Gabe Vasquez of New Mexico pointed to the Democratic gains made with Latino voters and the higher numbers of Latino lawmakers who will take office next year as reasons for Democrats to not shy away from talking about immigration issues.

He said Democrats should find ways to address immigration through a lens of affordability, a central issue for voters. For example, they could tackle staffing shortages by creating a new visa class for workers who provide care for children or the elderly.

"This cannot be a third-rail issue for Democrats," said Vasquez. "We can actually reform our immigration system to bring costs down for all Americans and at the same time give people who are either here undocumented or want to come to this country an opportunity to have legal status."

Democrats' power to curb Trump's immigration agenda is limited

Trump, shortly after the election, said he was prepared to work with Democrats on certain issues, highlighting immigration as one of them. But that collaborative tone may not bear out in practice.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin vowed on social media, "Deportations will continue." A few days later, Trump promoted Miller to become his chief of staff.

Immigration and Latino activists lambasted Miller's promotion, calling it an act of defiance after voters spoke clearly at the polls and a sign the president would continue his immigration policies. California's Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla, who's been a key critic of Trump's immigration agenda, said Trump was choosing to double down by picking Miller and vowed, "So will we."

It's unclear if Democrats and the White House will find a middle ground to successfully pass immigration legislation. With Trump in office for another two years, he can veto any Democratic legislation, and Republicans have the money and the personnel to pursue Trump's immigration agenda regardless of Tuesday's results.

Republicans during the summer of 2025 supercharged immigration enforcement with $150 billion intended to expand immigration detention capacity, finish the border wall and hire thousands more deportation officers. Earlier this year they frontloaded routine funding for ICE and Border Patrol for the next three years.

"My fear is that enforcement will get worse. And the country will also see that Congress does not have many tools to stop the executive branch because the executive branch power on immigration has grown so vast," said Andrea Flores, who was a policy adviser in the Obama and Biden administrations.

Conservatives want action from lame duck Congress

Many administration supporters want this current Congress — in the little time it has left — to pass laws solidifying the gains the Trump administration says it has made on border security and immigration. Without codifying changes to asylum law or tightening requirements on employers to verify workers' immigration status, they warn, a different administration could quickly reverse the new immigration landscape Trump has shaped.

NumbersUSA, an advocacy group that seeks to restrict immigration, has a timer on its website counting down the days until this Congress is over with a warning to "make border security permanent."

"If this Congress in the lame duck does not secure the border with lasting legislation," said the organization's co-president, Jeremy Beck, "then this Congress will have failed to meet the moment."

___

Associated Press reporter Linley Sanders contributed to this report.

ICE investigators determined that detention staff “deviated from safe limits of practice,” or “did not provide medical care within safe limits of practice” for the 23 detainees.

In at least eight of the cases, medical staff failed to perform CPR correctly, or at all. In only three of the cases, investigators determined that the deficient medical care did not directly contribute to the person’s death.

The agency continues to insist that there has been no spike in detainee deaths, though 2025 saw the most immigrant detainee deaths since 2003. So far in 2026, 31 immigrants have died in ICE detention.

During President Donald Trump’s second term, ICE has subjected tens of thousands of people—including U.S. citizens, lawful immigrants, and immigrants with no criminal convictions—to overcrowded rooms, unsanitary conditions, and insufficient food and water.

In many cases, immigrants report having been denied adequate medical care. Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff released a report in October 2025 documenting at least “85 credible reports of medical neglect” at U.S. detention centers. In January, ICE announced that it had stopped paying for immigrant detainees to receive health care—and wasn’t planning on paying again for months.

For the Trump administration, the cruelty is part of the point. The Department of Homeland Security even rejected plans to construct immigration detention facilities that were more humane.

Stephen Miller will be taking over as White House chief of staff beginning Monday.

Trump made the announcement on Truth Social Friday afternoon, saying that “Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job! President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

Miller, previously the White House deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, is receiving the promotion after serving in both Trump administrations. He is well-known for his hardline, xenophobic, and racist views on immigration, which led to violent and deadly mass deportation policies in Trump’s second term.

Trump’s decision to elevate Miller suggests that he is unrepentant about much of the negative attention brought by ICE’s violence even after Republicans were dealt historic losses in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Earlier this week, Miller was the target of leaks from Republicans and Trump administration officials over how his deportation plans were going too far, with even one anecdote about First Lady Melania Trump complaining to the president about people she knew being deported. Wiles reportedly tried for months to steer Trump away from Miller’s approach, according to The New York Times.

Ultimately, though, Wiles is the one on her way out. She tendered her resignation Thursday night, as Trump has partly blamed her for the GOP’s devastating election losses, Wired journalist Hugo Lowell reported. Rumors that she would be made into a scapegoat for the elections had been floating around for weeks.

In a statement posted on X, Wiles said, “Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First. More than anything, I’m grateful for the extraordinary people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside. While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will.”

Promoting Miller now is a clear message to Democrats after their massive election victory.

The death of nurse Alex Pretti at the hands of ICE agents in January caused a sea change in Americans’ thoughts on immigration, and gave Democrats the edge this November. ICE heavy-handed tactics continued, though. ICE agents have shot at least 25 people in Trump’s second term, according to the Times. On top of that, dozens of immigration detainees have died in ICE custody due to inhumane conditions encouraged by Miller.

But Trump clearly doesn’t care about any of that, and wants to double down on the most brutal part of his second term by elevating his most vile staffer, giving Miller the run of the White House. Any thoughts of Trump moderating or working with Democrats in the final two years of his presidency have been dashed by this move, and Democrats should receive the message loud and clear.

In response to Miller’s appointment, Democratic Representative Robert Garcia, who will be taking over the House Oversight Committee next year, said “Stephen Miller should lawyer up.”

Measles hasn’t been a national concern since 2000, when the long-term use of a vaccine proved so effective at minimizing risk and exposure to the disease that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention declared measles eradicated from the United States. That status is up for reassessment this month. If it’s determined that a singular viral strain has circulated the country for 12 months, the U.S. will no longer qualify for the label.

The virus’s dormancy has been challenged by anti-vaxers, who have opted against medicating their children in fear that vaccinations could cause autism (a thoroughly debunked conspiracy). One such conspiracist, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has refused to combat the ensuing measles outbreak with vetted science—instead, he has issued guidance that the illness can be treated by simple vitamins.

In April, Kennedy fell short of offering a full-throated endorsement of the MMR vaccine that has historically been used to treat measles, telling CBS News that his agency was focused on finding treatments for unvaccinated individuals while falsely claiming that the jab had not been “safety tested” and was not effective for long-term prevention. As of 2025, there are no known effective treatments or cures for measles other than vaccine prevention.

The return of historically eradicated diseases is thanks to a growing movement of anti-vax parents who refuse to provide their children with the same public health advantages that they received in their youth, mostly in fear of giving their children autism. The researcher who sparked that myth with a fraudulent paper lost his medical license and eventually rescinded his opinion. Since then, dozens of studies have proven there’s no correlation between autism and vaccines, including one study that surveyed more than 660,000 children over the course of 11 years.

But America’s is not the first measles response that Kennedy has bungled. Under Kennedy’s stewardship, the anti-vax nonprofit Children’s Health Defense had its own questionable history with the disease. Preceding a deadly measles outbreak on Samoa in 2019, the organization spread rampant misinformation about the efficacy of vaccines throughout the nation, sending the island’s vaccination rate plummeting from the 60–70 percent range to just 31 percent, according to Mother Jones. That year, the country reported 5,707 cases of measles as well as 83 measles-related deaths, the majority of which were children under the age of five.

The Washington Post reports that now that Democrats won back control of Congress, they are planning to probe powerful entities in Wall Street and Silicon Valley, and the first targets could be Apple, Meta, and Elon Musk and all of his companies.

The House is already preparing to investigate how President Trump used Musk’s artificial intelligence chatbot Grok in the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, according to the Post. House Democrats are also looking at Apple’s hosting of tracking apps used by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and at Meta for demanding that local governments sign nondisclosure agreements regarding data centers.

Corporate lawyers in Washington, D.C., are scrambling to meet with corporate executives to offer advice on the impending high-profile public investigations. Many firms are preparing pitches to attract Musk as a client, as he is not only the world’s richest man, but also holds billions in government contracts, has a close relationship with Trump, and led the disastrous Department of Government Efficiency initiative.

One lawyer at a major D.C. firm told executives in a private online meeting Thursday that “this is a new era.”

“If your company is caught up in this oversight, it’s likely to be much more highly publicized,” the lawyer said, according to the Post.

Dozens of corporations and CEOs donated to Trump’s transition fund, his inauguration fund, and his White House ballroom project. Where that once may have protected them from regulations and investigations from the Trump administration, with this new Congress, the opposite is true. Trump also made millions investing in many companies and publicly praised companies that did him favors.
