text:
Drone and missile attacks struck across Ukraine on Saturday, wounding at least nine people, as Kyiv and Moscow prepared for new talks next week with the United States.

Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the US are to meet on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war. The new round of negotiations would be the fourth brokered by the Trump administration, the most recent having been in Geneva in February.

Western governments backing the peace initiative are seeking a new formula to break the impasse while acknowledging that territorial and security questions remain unresolved.

The Russian missiles that hit overnight across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, damaged homes and commercial properties, triggering new power and water outages, national and city authorities said.

Kateryna Korniichuk, 64, was at home with her granddaughter when an attack hit.

“The first blast wave threw us against that wall and then against the other wall, because we were in the corridor. It’s very hard. No sleep, no peace — nothing. The children aren’t sleeping, and neither are we," she told The Associated Press. “I’m old, I can handle it, but what have the children done wrong?”

Strikes also prompted officials to close Kyiv's 816-meter-long (892-yard-long) Northern Bridge, a major route connecting the city with large residential areas on the east bank of the Dnipro River.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that work was already underway to repair the city's Northern Bridge and that water pressure in Kyiv had been stabilized.

Earlier Saturday, he had described the city's energy situation as "extremely difficult, affecting the city’s heating and water supply systems.”

In a statement Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia was preparing for trilateral talks by “launching ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s critical infrastructure.”

Later, he said that Moscow was stepping up strikes to build pressure on Ukraine ahead of the Abu Dhabi talks. “Russia perceives diplomacy in its own peculiar way – as a form of aggression,” he wrote in an online post.

The Ukrainian leader said that Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight, of which only four were shot down due to a lack of Patriot interceptors.

Zelenskyy also said that Russia had used North Korean-made ballistic missiles to strike energy facilities, citing preliminary findings from investigations at impact sites.

The barrage involved 172 drones over Kyiv and 12 other regions, wounding nine people, including a child, he said.

“When Russia tries to plunge Kyiv — a city of millions — and the entire country into a blackout, Ukraine must not be left to face this alone,” Zelenskyy said. He urged greater US support and attention from Congress, calling for bipartisan backing for Ukraine and stronger sanctions on Russia.

Ukraine’s Energy Ministry said Saturday’s missile attacks damaged networks that carry electricity from nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central regions, as well as multiple other power facilities. It said outages were most widespread in the Kyiv and central Zhytomyr regions, as well as in the eastern regions of Kharkiv, Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk.

The outages were separate from scheduled rolling blackouts imposed to protect the grid, which remain in effect across much of Ukraine.

Russia’s Ministry of Defense confirmed Saturday that it had targeted the Northern Bridge, saying that it facilitated the transport of weaponry, military hardware and specialist equipment for Ukraine’s armed forces.

It also said that it had targeted an industrial facility in the capital producing Flamingo missiles, as well as a power station, an electrical substation, and a plant producing ammunition, explosives and gunpowder in the wider Kyiv region. It also confirmed striking an electrical substation in the Zhytomyr region.

Meanwhile, in southern Ukraine, a recovery operation continued into its sixth day in the village of Komyshuvakha, devastated on Monday when multiple Russian guided bombs slammed into a former school and nearby shelter as residents waited for humanitarian aid.

Emergency services said they had recovered nine more bodies in the previous 24 hours, bringing the death toll early Saturday morning to 55. Dozens of people remain missing.

Village resident Mykola Krasnov, 72, said he was still looking for his wife but had heard no word from rescuers.

“She went to get humanitarian aid, and a three-ton bomb was dropped there. Where is she?” he said. “She didn’t come home, and they didn’t find her body there. She isn’t in the morgue, and she isn’t here alive.”

The village of Komyshuvakha is located near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region.

A Ukrainian attack killed one person in Russia’s Belgorod region when a drone hit a private home in the town of Grayvoron, local officials said Saturday.

Russia’s Ministry of Defense said its forces shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight over 10 Russian regions, including Belgorod. Drones were also destroyed over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black and Azov Seas, it said.

The head of Russia’s southwestern Saratov region, Gov. Roman Busargin, wrote on social media that a drone attack damaged “civilian infrastructure” and several residential buildings in the area. Russian media outlets later reported that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and shared images of plumes of smoke over the city.

The head of Russia’s Oryol region, Gov. Andrey Klychkov, also said Saturday that a Ukrainian attack had damaged commercial warehouse and production sites in the regional capital, as cited by state media.

Russian media outlets reported that a Ukrainian attack sparked a blaze at Oryol’s Proton-Electrotex plant, which produces components for military equipment.

Syrian authorities' announcement late Friday that they had foiled a major drug-smuggling operation from Lebanon in the Serghaya area of rural Damascus drew attention for one particular reason: the operation was handled by Defense Ministry troops rather than internal security forces, security expert Diaa Qaddour told Asharq Al-Awsat.

Another military analyst linked the growing tensions along Syria's borders with Lebanon and Iraq to Iran's dissatisfaction with the Syrian government.

The Defense Ministry's Media and Communications Department said border guards had intercepted an attempt to smuggle narcotics into Syria from Lebanon near Serghaya, along the border in the Damascus countryside.

The smugglers opened fire on the patrol, prompting troops to return fire and forcing the gunmen to retreat into Lebanese territory, the ministry said.

According to Syria's Internal Security Forces, the authorities seized 280 kilograms of hashish and 28,000 Captagon pills.

The incident followed extensive raids carried out by the Lebanese Army on November 4 in the rugged outskirts of Arsal, which led to the arrest of suspected smugglers and the interception of vehicles attempting to cross the border illegally.

It also came days after Syrian authorities arrested members of a cell allegedly plotting an attack on the Homs oil refinery. Damascus accused the cell of having ties to Lebanon's Hezbollah, an allegation the group denied.

Speaking to Asharq Al-Awsat, Qaddour accused Hezbollah of stepping up what he described as terrorist activities inside Syria, including attacks targeting sensitive sites.

He warned that the border region had become extremely volatile, with tensions liable to escalate at any moment, requiring Syrian security forces to remain on constant alert.

Damascus has been working to strengthen security cooperation with neighboring countries in an effort to close illegal border crossings and dismantle cross-border smuggling networks.

Security coordination topped the agenda during Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi's visit to Damascus on October 28, when he led a high-level ministerial delegation.

Border control was also a priority in talks between the Syrian government and a Lebanese delegation headed by Deputy Prime Minister Tarek Mitri, which visited Damascus on November 2.

Since the start of the country's liberation, Damascus has sought to reassure its neighbors by tightening border controls and reopening crossings in ways that benefit both sides economically.

Military affairs analyst Rashid Hourani described the approach as "border-crossing diplomacy."

Speaking to Asharq Al-Awsat, Hourani said Damascus had sought to resolve its disputes with neighboring countries by securing its borders and ensuring they posed no threat to Syria or its neighbors.

But developments along the Syrian-Lebanese and Syrian-Iraqi borders, he argued, point to growing Iranian frustration with Damascus.

He attributed Tehran's displeasure partly to Syria's success in tightening border security and partly to recent discussions about its possible participation in the Makkah Agreement, alongside an announcement that Damascus would provide Saudi Arabia with military expertise to confront the Houthis, Iran's ally in Yemen.

"Iran therefore sought to cause trouble for Syria and instructed Hezbollah, whose regional influence has diminished, to stir up tensions along the Syrian border," Hourani said.

He argued that a similar dynamic was at play along the Iraqi border, where Iranian-backed militias exert considerable influence over decision-making within the country's military and security institutions.

Securing Syria's borders remains one of the most pressing security challenges facing Damascus.

Qaddour assessed the threat entering Syria across its borders as "moderate to high in the near term," although he said it could still be contained if current security efforts were sustained.

He identified the border with Lebanon as particularly vulnerable because of its rugged terrain and numerous illegal crossings.

The Iraqi border, by contrast, has seen substantial fortification through the construction of walls and trenches, while active security coordination with Jordan has helped authorities intercept major smuggling shipments.

Hourani also pointed to Syria and Jordan's participation in an anti-ISIS alliance established in March 2025 alongside Türkiye, Iraq and Lebanon.

He said their membership in the coalition made it likely that the two countries would overcome the fallout from a Jordanian military operation in Syria's Daraa Governorate, where an operational error resulted in civilian casualties.

Meanwhile, recent developments have underscored the growing security threat along the Syrian-Lebanese border, with successive operations exposing what analysts describe as coordinated attempts to destabilize Syria.

Qaddour said drug trafficking remained the most serious threat, with evidence pointing to longstanding links between smuggling networks, elements of Syria's former regime and Hezbollah.

He also warned of an increasingly troubling development: smuggling cartels resorting to armed resistance against security forces.

The latest incident, in which smugglers exchanged fire with Syrian troops before fleeing into Lebanon, illustrated the growing danger, he said.

Qaddour argued that the situation demanded more than routine security coordination.

He called for tighter joint control over illegal crossings, expanded intelligence sharing and a systematic crackdown on cross-border criminal networks.

He also raised the possibility of urgent operations at particularly vulnerable points along the Lebanese border, warning that failure to close these security gaps could turn them into a persistent source of instability for both countries.

text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, mere days after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections.

Miller, long a key member of Trump’s inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies. He is one of Trump’s closest and longest-serving advisers, joining his long-shot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He currently serves as White House deputy chief of staff for policy and oversees a broad portfolio, though he is best known for his role in Trump’s immigration policy.

The staff shuffle signals that Trump, now staring down a combative Congress that will soon be controlled by Democrats, is resisting a conciliatory approach after the GOP’s midterm thrashing on Tuesday. Miller is a dogged defender of Trump and his “America First” principles, and has built a deep and sophisticated understanding of a president’s executive power and how the federal government operates, portending a potential burst of executive actions in the final two years of Trump’s presidency.

Wiles gave Trump her resignation on Thursday night, a person familiar with the events said, speaking on condition of anonymity to describe the private conversation. Trump praised Wiles in a Truth Social post and said she’d continue to work for his political organization.

“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” Wiles said in a social media post shortly after Trump’s announcement. She added that her commitment to “the President and the mission” will not change.

Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post and the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.

The departure also came months after Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026.

Miller is a longtime Trump aide

During the midterm campaign, Miller took frequent partisan swipes at Democrats, calling them “extremists, freaks and America-hating lunatics” on social media and promoted unfounded theories about election fraud in California and Alaska.

He has been a major part of the Trump administration’s anti-fraud task force targeting benefit programs and a decision to suspend Microsoft and others from a green card program. He also served as homeland security adviser at the White House, giving him a perch from which to coordinate with other agencies across the government.

Miller was a veteran Senate aide who worked for former Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., before he joined Trump’s nascent presidential campaign in 2016. Sessions was the first senator to endorse Trump in his first run and later served as his attorney general.

But the immigration policies that Miller is so closely allied with were a major liability for Republicans during the just-wrapped election. The midterm AP Voter Poll found that most voters, about 6 in 10, said the administration’s immigration enforcement actions had gone too far and that they “somewhat” or “strongly” disapproved of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement had handled its responsibilities.

“Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down,” said Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is set to become chairman of the powerful House Oversight Committee. “Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families.”

In a statement, Garcia added: “Stephen Miller should lawyer up.”

Wiles brought order to Trump’s campaign

The veteran Florida operative joined Trump’s team during his 2016 presidential bid to run the campaign in his adopted home state. She performed the same role again in 2020 before overseeing the entire 50-state effort in 2024. She is the second woman to lead Trump’s presidential campaign to victory, although she never embraced the formal title of campaign manager.

Wiles, 69, has been credited with steering the most disciplined of his three presidential bids, and Trump himself has said he was often told that Wiles led his “best-run campaign.” Often called the “ice maiden” by the president, she was seen as the no-brainer choice to serve as White House chief of staff at the start of his second term.

She cut her reputation as someone who brought discipline to the president’s chaotic style and shunned the spotlight, so much so that at Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd.

Wiles showed unusual candor in an interview

But in December 2025, nearing the end of Trump’s first year back as president, Wiles became the headline when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials conducted by the author Chris Whipple, an expert on White House chiefs of staff.

The Wiles interviews stuck out for their candor, which is unusual for a sitting White House chief of staff. She said Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality,” although the president does not drink, and said then-Attorney General Pam Bondi had “whiffed” in her handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files while remarking that Vice President JD Vance has been a “conspiracy theorist for about a decade.”

Trump and other administration aides rushed to defend Wiles, who, in turn, disparaged Vanity Fair for publishing what she called a “disingenuously framed hit piece,” though she did not deny making the comments.

In the interviews, which were conducted over a period of several months, Wiles also revealed a bit of her management style, saying she was “not an enabler.”

“I try to be thoughtful about what I even engage in,” Wiles said. “I guess time will tell whether I’ve been effective.”

Trump went through four chiefs of staff in his first term: Reince Priebus, who Trump fired after just six months; John Kelly, who served the longest at 17 months; Mick Mulvaney, who held the role for a little over a year in an “acting” capacity; and Mark Meadows, who served as gatekeeper for the 10 months before Trump left office.

Wiles overcomes personal health struggle

Six months after her diagnosis, Wiles revealed she was “cancer-free,” indicating she no longer showed evidence of cancer after her pathology results came back clear. She thanked her family, friends, doctors, and gave special thanks to Trump for his “unwavering support” in a statement.

“She’s tough,” Trump said at a White House event in October. “She’s a tremendous fighter.”

In a rare interview, Wiles told Fox News Digital last month that she hadn’t been planning on getting the mammogram that ultimately detected her cancer. Her doctor suggested she do the exam anyway, because a mammogram machine was available that day and her schedule was too busy and unpredictable.

“Had he not encouraged me to do it that day, I would have gone back to work and probably not thought about it again until July,” Wiles told the outlet. “We would be having a very different conversation in that case. Four months may not sound like a long time, but with cancer, early detection matters. I will always be grateful to my doctor for knowing me well enough to insist.”

Wiles is a seasoned political operative

In addition to Trump, Wiles also ran incumbent Sen. Rick Scott’s 2010 campaign for Florida governor and briefly served as manager of former Utah Gov. Jon Huntsman’s 2012 presidential campaign. She spearheaded Ron DeSantis ' successful run for governor in 2018, but DeSantis would eventually urge the Trump campaign in 2020 to cut ties with Wiles, creating a rift that led to a particularly vicious effort by those in Trump’s orbit to mock DeSantis throughout his failed run for the Republican presidential nomination against Trump in 2024.

Wiles, the daughter of the late NFL player-turned-broadcaster Pat Summerall, also worked in the offices of former Jacksonville mayors John Delaney and John Peyton. Her first White House job was as a scheduler for President Ronald Reagan.

In addition to her government and campaign positions, Wiles has worked as a lobbyist. She was a partner at Florida-based Ballard Partners, which rose to prominence in Washington during Trump’s time in the White House. Her clients included General Motors, a trade group for children’s hospitals, homebuilders, and the city of Jacksonville.

She was also registered as a lobbyist for the Venezuelan television network Globovisión, which was owned by businessperson Raúl Gorrín, who was charged in Miami with money laundering. The firm later called its work for Gorrín a mistake and said Wiles had almost no role in managing the relationship with Gorrín.

“Ronald Reagan did something very smart in supporting immigration reform,” says Raúl Hinojosa, professor of Chicano studies at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA).

In the first year of Trump’s second term alone, nearly 400,000 people were detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
“One of my core causes has been the fight for immigration reform, because I believe that, just as I was able to legalize my status in this country, many other people should have that opportunity and be able to live peacefully with their families,” says Moreno.
text:
Unprepared for the bluenami — the label for the Democrats’ sweeping midterm victory — U.S. President Donald Trump spent weeks ramping up his anti-immigrant rhetoric at dozens of campaign rallies in support of Republican candidates. “There will be no amnesty for illegals,” he repeated over and over, while blaming undocumented immigrants for crime in U.S. cities and a host of other problems, claims that have been contradicted by numerous studies and reports.

But Trump’s tone began to soften as he watched, like millions of Americans, a new political landscape take shape on television screens: Democrats were storming the polls, heading toward control of Congress and winning governorships in key states such as Texas. One of the president’s first reactions was to strike a more conciliatory note on the issue he had long demonized, saying he was willing to sit down and negotiate with Democrats.

“We can work with them [the Democrats] on Immigration. I’ve always felt like we should be able to work on immigration,” he said in an interview with FOX News the day after those adverse elections.

Activists who have spent decades marching and advocating for immigration reform see the Democrats’ control of Congress as a golden opportunity to reopen that debate. In meetings and discussions since Tuesday’s elections, they have begun talking about returning to the streets to demand an end to immigration raids and the legalization of more than 10 million undocumented immigrants whom the Trump administration has relentlessly targeted since mid-2025. They believe the president, weakened by the election results and facing reduced support in both chambers, may now be willing to compromise.

“The blue wave won — what’s next for migrants? Don’t let the Democrats leave us behind and don’t let what happened with president Barack Obama repeat itself, when he said he would leave immigration reform for his second term and didn’t pass it,” says Francisco Moreno, 66, executive director of the Council of Mexican Federations in North America (COFEM). “I don’t see a Trump determined to do it, but maybe it can be achieved.”

The Democrats’ blue wave has shaken Trump’s administration just as the United States approaches the 40th anniversary of a milestone event for the country’s immigrant community: the amnesty granted by Republican president Ronald Reagan to millions of undocumented immigrants in 1986.

Over the past four decades, much has changed both in the way Republican presidents govern and in the recognition of a population that contributes $1.6 trillion to the country’s gross domestic product. The country has gone from opening the door to the legalization of nearly three million people so they could live and work in peace to a dark era of immigration raids and mass deportations, one marked even by the deaths of migrants and U.S. citizens during violent federal enforcement operations.

The benefits of the 1986 amnesty

On November 6, 1986, when a very different political climate prevailed in the White House, Reagan signed the Immigration Reform and Control Act (IRCA), granting legal status and opening a pathway to permanent residency, and eventually citizenship, for undocumented immigrants who had lived continuously in the United States since before January 1, 1982. Migrants of Mexican origin, who remain the country’s largest immigrant group, were the main beneficiaries.

During a presidential debate in 1984, Reagan had already signaled his position, defending the regularization of people living in the shadows. “I believe in the idea of amnesty for those who have put down roots and lived here, even though sometime back they may have entered illegally,” he said at the time.

“Ronald Reagan did something very smart in supporting immigration reform,” says Raúl Hinojosa, professor of Chicano studies at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA). “Because he was from California and at that time he understood that his political base there was the farmers, who needed migrant labor.”

Various studies have found that immigrants who benefited from Reagan’s amnesty saw improvements in both their earnings and educational attainment. One such analysis found that, by 1992, six years after the immigration reform, the incomes of workers who had obtained legal status had risen by an average of 15%. Women benefited the most, with earnings increasing by 21%. In addition, four out of 10 Mexicans who obtained permanent residency, or a green card, moved into better-paying jobs.

“That initiative helped the U.S. economy more than any other policy decision in the last 40 years. Because it made it possible for millions of people to produce more, earn more, buy homes, start businesses, send their children to college. It was a revolution in those families’ lives,” Hinojosa says. “The problem is that today Donald Trump decided to use the anti-immigrant issue for his own political gain. Not because it benefited the country, nor because it helped the people who voted for him.”

What began as a campaign talking point in 2015, when Trump claimed that Mexico was sending drug traffickers, rapists and criminals to the United States, escalated into a second term defined by relentless efforts to make life so difficult for immigrants that they would effectively deport themselves. In many cases, that strategy has proven effective through a sustained campaign of aggressive immigration enforcement operations. In the first year of Trump’s second term alone, nearly 400,000 people were detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The crackdown continues despite the damage it has inflicted on sectors that depend heavily on immigrant labor, including agriculture, construction and hospitality.

“They’re coming in from the Congo. They interviewed some people last night. ‘Where are you from?’ ‘Congo.’ ‘Where did you live?’ ‘Prison.’ They’re emptying out their prisons into our country,” Trump said at a rally in Ohio last week, repeating another false claim that was met with applause from his supporters.

In a sign of the Trump administration’s unpredictability, one of its officials made clear, the day after the midterms, that the hard-line approach would continue. “Deportations will continue,” Markwayne Mullin, the secretary of Homeland Security responsible for carrying out the administration’s immigration agenda, warned in a post on X.

Juan José Gutiérrez, head of the Full Rights for Immigrants Coalition, also laments the direction U.S. immigration policy has taken when comparing the approaches of the Reagan and Trump administrations. “The contrast shows us that this country, which was admired and served as an example of how a democracy should work, has regressed and is now closed to migration,” he says.

‘There are grounds for another amnesty’

Moreno believes the case for a new form of immigration relief could build on H.R. 4393, better known as the Dignity Act, introduced in July 2025 by Representative María Elvira Salazar, a Florida Republican, and Representative Veronica Escobar, a Texas Democrat. Escobar was reelected in Tuesday’s elections, while Salazar is still awaiting the outcome of a closely contested race in Miami.

The bill would allow undocumented immigrants who have lived in the United States since before December 31, 2020, to apply for protection from deportation, a work permit and travel authorization. The status would be valid for seven years and renewable indefinitely, but it would cost $7,000 and would not provide a pathway to permanent residency. It would also exclude people convicted of certain crimes, including some misdemeanors.

“There are grounds for another amnesty,” Moreno says. “Regardless of how fickle the president may be, I believe this is the time to start taking action. It’s one thing that the country has turned blue and that, in theory, Democrats are more progressive in their views on migrants and are our allies; but we can ensure that this support has an impact in Congress. The ideal moment is now.”

Moreno is himself a beneficiary of Reagan’s amnesty. Born in the Mexican state of Michoacán, he was 20 in 1980, when he arrived in the United States on a visit and decided to stay. He put his legal studies on hold and began working for a cleaning company in Los Angeles. He had come chasing the dream of becoming a Hollywood actor, but ended up building a different career: one in activism.

In his office, he keeps a collection of mementos from the marches he has taken part in. Among them is a banner from the historic demonstration of March 25, 2006, when an estimated one million people took to the streets of downtown Los Angeles to demand the withdrawal of legislation that would have criminalized undocumented immigrants and those who assisted them. The bill in question was the controversial H.R. 4437, introduced by Republican Congressman James Sensenbrenner, which sparked one of the largest waves of public outrage and protest in recent U.S. history. “Yes to families united! No to criminalization!” reads the banner, now yellowed with age.

“One of my core causes has been the fight for immigration reform, because I believe that, just as I was able to legalize my status in this country, many other people should have that opportunity and be able to live peacefully with their families,” says Moreno. “The worst part of it all is the fear. ‘Let’s see how this president turns out,’ ‘let’s see how this governor turns out,’ ‘let’s see if he starts attacking us.’ Because there have been all kinds of politicians over the last 40 years, but nothing has happened.”

title: US Justice Department drops bid to force California to set aside disputed ballots
description:
California had processed roughly 9 million ballots as of early Friday, with nearly 5 million still left to be counted, according to state election officials.
California prosecutors in recent weeks have arrested over 30 noncitizens who are accused of illegally registering to vote.
Elections clerks around California in the week before the election were sent subpoenas to testify before grand juries slated to convene in November.
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter appointed the special master in late October, shortly after allowing California to proceed with elections as planned.
The special master would have also considered whether or not California election officials did in fact have a mechanism for separating the ballots.
text:
The U.S. Department of Justice on Friday moved to dismiss its own lawsuit that sought to stop California from counting roughly 20,000 ballots it alleged went to noncitizens until their immigration status could be verified.

The request to dismiss the case comes days after Republicans' significant losses in the midterm elections and about a week before a scheduled hearing where a special master was slated to evaluate the accuracy of the list. California officials have previously said the list is out of date and includes legitimate voters — a sentiment that the federal judge presiding over the case echoed in his blistering order denying the federal government's request.

The case was at the forefront of President Donald Trump's administration's effort to assert control over state-run elections across the country, which Trump has said are rife with illegal voting without providing evidence.

The Department of Justice remains enmeshed in litigation with multiple immigrant and voting rights groups seeking to limit its use of the list of what is says are suspected noncitizens. Another controversial suit it filed in Alaska at Trump's direction before the election to block the victory of the Democrat in that state's Senate race was swiftly dismissed by a federal judge. The administration is appealing that ruling but has yet to file a full brief at the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.

California had processed roughly 9 million ballots as of early Friday, with nearly 5 million still left to be counted, according to state election officials. The motion to dismiss the lawsuit said that, by the time of the upcoming hearing, the state will have already irreparably "commingled the challenged ballots with lawful ones."

"The relief the United States sought and needed is no longer available—rendering voluntary dismissal necessary," the motion said.

Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, previously argued in court that the lawsuit would be irrelevant after election day, because there would be no way to sequester the ones allegedly belonging to noncitizens. The lawsuit was filed in mid-October, when ballots had been sent to all of the state's 23 million registered voters, and after hundreds of thousands of ballots were already processed. Once a ballot is processed, it is completely anonymized.

Essayli said at the time the lawsuit was filed that his goal was to "safeguard the integrity of the election so it doesn't have an effect on the upcoming election."

"We want to stop the illegal voting. We don't want to chase it later," he said outside of court the week before the election.

California prosecutors in recent weeks have arrested over 30 noncitizens who are accused of illegally registering to vote. Some who were arrested were also accused of voting in previous elections. Elections clerks around California in the week before the election were sent subpoenas to testify before grand juries slated to convene in November. It's not clear who is being criminally charged in those cases, but the department does not typically subpoena people whom it regards as targets of a criminal investigation to appear before a grand jury.

U.S. District Judge David O. Carter appointed the special master in late October, shortly after allowing California to proceed with elections as planned. Carter, who was appointed by former President Bill Clinton, argued in his blistering order that separating ballots at that late stage would risk disenfranchising citizens and warned it would "wreak havoc" on the midterm elections.

The special master would have also considered whether or not California election officials did in fact have a mechanism for separating the ballots.

text:
US President Donald Trump announced Friday that White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles will step down, naming his longtime adviser Stephen Miller as her successor, effective Monday, November 9.

The move comes just three days after Republicans suffered a sweeping defeat in the midterm elections, losing control of both chambers of Congress.

The announcement marks a striking reversal for Trump, who categorically denied reports of a possible leadership change on October 16.

“There is zero chance,” Trump told CNN at the time, calling the reports false and insisting that Wiles would remain in her position for a long time.

Wiles, first female White House chief of staff, managed Trump's 2024 campaign

Wiles, 69, one of Trump’s closest and most trusted advisers, managed his successful 2024 presidential campaign and became the first woman in American history to serve as White House chief of staff. In September, she announced that she was cancer-free after undergoing treatment for breast cancer diagnosed earlier this year. She continued working throughout her treatment.

US officials told The Jerusalem Post that Wiles submitted her resignation on Thursday.

The 41-year-old Miller is the grandson of Jewish refugees and has been among Trump’s most influential advisers for nearly a decade. Currently serving as deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, he is widely regarded as the chief architect of the administration’s aggressive immigration crackdown, including mass deportations and tighter border enforcement. His influence has also extended into national security and foreign policy.

Miller is a trusted advisor to the US president, and his appointment suggests the White House is "preparing for a confrontation" with the Democrats, who are expected to take control of Congress.

He is also an uncompromising factor in the harsh and negative sense of the word, and it is estimated that this will make Trump's ability to work with the Democrats non-existent.

Far-right Americans celebrated Miller’s appointment, and US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth marked the occasion with a three-word X/Twitter post, saying "Patriots in control."

Trump praises Wiles' 'outstanding job,' says she is to transition to political operation

Trump praised Wiles for having done an “outstanding job” and said she would transition to his political operation, keeping her within his broader political orbit.

In an X post later on Friday, Wiles said she was "proud" of what she and Trump had "accomplished together" during her time as chief of staff.

"More than anything, I’m grateful for the extraordinary people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside," she wrote. "While my role may be changing, my commitment to the president and the mission never will."

Trump addressed the move in remarks to the press on Friday, saying he "wanted to make a change," and that Wiles had done "a great job."

"Stephen has been excellent, and sometimes in life, you have to make moves," Trump told reporters at the White House as he departed for Florida. "Stephen has been with me from the beginning. He understands politics very well and is a very good manager. He will do a great job."

Democrats threaten Miller: 'You’d better get a lawyer'

Democratic Congressman Robert Garcia, poised to become chair of the House Oversight Committee following the Democratic victory in the midterm elections, launched a sharp attack on Miller's appointment later on Friday, warning of impending investigations.

"Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is only doubling down on his policies," Garcia stated. "Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that terrorized our communities and led to the abduction and death of American citizens and immigrant families."

"Democrats on the Oversight Committee will continue to investigate Miller for his misconduct, and we will fight his policies of hate in Congress and in the courts," he added. "Stephen Miller had better get himself a lawyer."

As early as election night, once it became clear that the Democrats were on track to take control of Congress, Garcia issued a two-word warning to Trump administration officials: "Lawyer up" - alluding to the investigations expected to target senior administration figures once the new Congress takes office in January.

Miller, Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought and White House lawyers have worked since April to identify executive actions Trump could take without new legislation, including measures on immigration, tariffs, housing costs and federal spending, Reuters reported Sunday, citing three people familiar with the planning.

TRUMP TOUTS 'ULTIMATE POWER' OF VETO IF DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF HOUSE AND SENATE

text:
Federal

Democrats Win Control of House and Senate in Midterm Elections

Democrats won control of the House and Senate in the November 3 midterm elections and will lead both chambers when the new Congress convenes in January 2027. Republicans’ share of the Latino vote fell from roughly 44 percent in 2024 to approximately 30 percent, although voting patterns varied by state and district. Voters interviewed about their choices cited living costs and immigration enforcement as some of the factors that influenced their vote. In Texas, Democrats won the gubernatorial and U.S. Senate races, while several predominantly Latino border counties that supported Trump in 2024 backed Democratic candidates.

The change in congressional control will give Democrats responsibility for committee leadership and oversight, including the ability to hold hearings and request information about the administration’s immigration policies. Potential areas of scrutiny include ICE enforcement and detention practices, due process protections, and delays in legal immigration processing. Congressional oversight does not itself change immigration law or halt executive actions. Legislation would require passage through both chambers and the president’s signature, or sufficient votes to override a veto, and many Senate measures would need enough support to overcome a filibuster. The administration will retain authority to implement and enforce immigration policy within existing law while Congress considers any legislative or funding changes.

ICE Rapidly Re-Arrests Immigrants Freed by Courts, Drawing Judicial Pushback

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is re-arresting some immigrants minutes after their court-ordered release, prompting legal challenges over whether the agency is complying with judges’ decisions. Reporters found seven such cases in Minnesota, though attorneys suspect there are more. The cases involve immigrants who won habeas corpus petitions challenging the legality of their detention. In one case, Nicaraguan immigrant Yader Cortez was re-arrested approximately three minutes after leaving a federal building on October 2, following a judge’s determination that his initial warrantless arrest was unlawful.

In another Minnesota case, a judge ordered ICE to immediately release Ecuadorian asylum seeker Milton Saltos Velasquez after agents re-arrested him on October 19 before he could leave the federal building. The judge found that ICE had violated his release order and warned that the government could face sanctions, prompting agents transporting Saltos to jail to turn around. In an earlier case, the same judge wrote that treating an immediate re-arrest as compliance “would render habeas relief meaningless.”

President Trump Names Stephen Miller White House Chief of Staff

On November 6, President Trump announced that Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, effective November 9. Miller, currently deputy chief of staff, has played a central role in developing the administration’s immigration enforcement and deportation policies. His appointment places him in charge of coordinating White House staff and advancing the president’s broader agenda. Wiles, who has served as chief of staff since January 2025, will move to Trump’s political operation. The transition will take effect as the White House prepares to work with Democratic majorities in both chambers of Congress.

Legal

Ninth Circuit Temporarily Pauses Restoration of TPS for Venezuelans

On November 3, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit issued a 14-day administrative stay delaying the restoration of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for more than 627,000 Venezuelans. The pause begins November 6, when protections were expected to resume. Days earlier, a three-judge panel had unanimously rejected the Trump administration’s request to continue blocking a district court ruling that found its actions ending the protections unlawful.

The dispute centers on former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem’s effort to cancel Venezuela’s 2023 TPS designation, which the district court found exceeded her statutory authority. The Supreme Court paused that ruling in October 2025, allowing the administration’s actions to take effect during the appeal. Following a separate Supreme Court decision in June 2026, the case returned to the Ninth Circuit for reconsideration. TPS holders argued that courts retained authority to determine whether the secretary had acted beyond the powers Congress granted. The ongoing litigation leaves their protection from deportation and eligibility for work authorization under TPS uncertain.

Federal Judge Blocks Policies Fast-Tracking Unaccompanied Children’s Asylum Cases

A federal judge on October 30 temporarily blocked Trump administration policies that sharply reduced notice for unaccompanied children’s asylum interviews and restricted their ability to reschedule. The judge ordered U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to reinstate its prior procedures, including a requirement to provide at least 21 days’ advance notice. Under policies adopted in August and September, some children received fewer than 24 hours’ notice, while requests to reschedule required a showing of “exceptional circumstances.” The temporary restraining order remains in effect through November 13 while the judge considers whether to issue a longer-term injunction.

The ruling follows an October 15 lawsuit by six legal service providers arguing that the accelerated process prevented attorneys from adequately preparing children to present their asylum claims. The organizations reported receiving more than 600 interview notices since August 1, sometimes requiring attorneys to represent multiple children in interviews scheduled for the same time. The judge found that the shortened notice was inconsistent with the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act, which requires asylum procedures to account for unaccompanied children’s specialized needs, and that the stricter rescheduling standard violated the Administrative Procedure Act.

State and Local

Judge Temporarily Restores Tennessee Driver’s License Access for DACA Recipients and Other Immigrants

A Tennessee judge temporarily blocked restrictions preventing Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipients and other immigrants with federal work authorization from obtaining or renewing driver’s licenses. On November 2, the judge issued a temporary restraining order after the Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition (TIRRC) and six individual plaintiffs challenged the state’s documentation requirements. The order prevents the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security from refusing valid employment authorization documents and other federal documents for verification through the federal Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) system. It also blocks the state from requiring a foreign passport, visa and approved arrival record as the only acceptable documentation. The ruling provides temporary relief while the lawsuit proceeds and does not permanently invalidate the policy. A hearing is scheduled for November 16.

The lawsuit follows reports that longtime license holders, including DACA recipients, people with Temporary Protected Status and individuals with pending asylum applications, were being denied renewals under the state’s revised interpretation of a 2025 law. Plaintiffs argue that the state abruptly changed its longstanding practice of accepting work permits without following required rulemaking procedures. Affected residents described losing access to jobs, medical appointments and transportation for their children, with one registered nurse saying she was considering leaving Tennessee because she could no longer drive to work. Gov. Bill Lee acknowledged that the policy may have created “unintended consequences” and said his office was reviewing the issue. TIRRC has since received reports of successful renewals but cautioned that implementation of the court order may vary across Driver Services Centers and is tracking continued denials.

Colorado Voters Reject Amendment Requiring Law Enforcement Cooperation With ICE

Colorado voters rejected Amendment 81, a proposed constitutional amendment that would have required state and local law enforcement to notify federal immigration authorities in certain criminal cases. The measure would have applied when a person in custody was charged with a violent crime or, for those with a prior felony conviction, any crime, and law enforcement determined that the person was unlawfully present or could not verify their status after a “reasonable effort.” Agencies would have had 72 hours after charges were filed to notify the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Because the proposal would have amended the Colorado Constitution, it needed at least 55 percent support to pass.

Amendment 81 would have overridden state laws limiting local participation in civil immigration enforcement. Federal immigration authorities can already access public information about people held in Colorado jails, including their charges and upcoming court dates, but state and local agencies generally cannot share personally identifying information without a court order. Supporters, including the advocacy group Advance Colorado, argued that the measure would promote cooperation between local and federal authorities and improve public safety. Opponents warned that its undefined “reasonable effort” standard could lead to racial profiling, weaken trust between immigrant communities and police, and place additional responsibilities on local agencies. The amendment’s rejection leaves Colorado’s existing limits on cooperation with federal civil immigration enforcement in place.

Immigration Operation Targeting Truckers Expands to 14 States

An Oklahoma-led immigration enforcement operation has expanded across 14 states, with officials reporting more than 230 arrests during a coordinated 72-hour effort, including more than 40 people driving commercial vehicles. Oklahoma Public Safety Commissioner Tim Tipton said the operation brought together state agencies and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after truckers began sharing information about enforcement locations and rerouting to avoid Oklahoma. Officials identified participating states stretching from North Dakota to Florida but did not disclose the operation’s dates. The effort builds on Operation Guardian and expanded use of 287(g) agreements, which authorize participating state and local officers to perform certain immigration enforcement functions. Oklahoma agencies had entered 136 such agreements as of October, including 109 signed this year.

The expansion comes amid reports that routine traffic stops and mandatory inspections are leading to the detention of immigrant truckers, including people with federal permission to live and work in the United States. Ukrainian drivers who fled Russia’s invasion have been caught in the crackdown, with a Ukrainian representative reporting that at least a dozen were detained in Oklahoma and Indiana over the summer. Attorneys warn that the enforcement is prompting drivers to leave the industry and raising concerns about racial profiling and prolonged detention. Indiana State Police denies targeting immigrant truckers, while supporters argue that increased enforcement improves road safety and compliance with commercial driving standards.

LEGISLATIVE FLOOR CALENDAR

The U.S. Senate is scheduled to be in session from Monday, November 9, through Tuesday, November 10. The U.S. House is scheduled to be in session from Monday, November 9, through Thursday, November 12.

text:
A federal judge in Colorado probed representatives of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the U.S. Attorney’s Office on Friday about breakdowns that led both entities to violate her orders.

The hourlong hearing before U.S. District Court Judge Nina Y. Wang also included discussion of a previously undisclosed memorandum of agreement between the federal court and the U.S. Attorney’s Office signed last month. While the document permits the U.S. Attorney’s Office to generally refrain from filing responses to immigration detention challenges, it does not excuse the government from ignoring specific orders for information.

Recommended Stories

▶

“I think you would agree with me that when the court orders a response,” Wang said, “that is not covered by the memorandum.”

“I would certainly agree,” said Assistant U.S. Attorney Andrew Soler.

Wang also learned that ICE disobeyed her order to release a man from immigration custody without further restrictions because the agency’s lawyers allegedly withheld the order from an ICE supervisor until the day Wang ordered a representative into court.

“Can you tell me why ICE did not receive notice of the explicit Oct. 30, 2026, order that required no conditions of release that was issued by the court at 9:30 a.m.?” Wang asked.

“I cannot tell you,” responded Nichole Black, the assistant Denver field office director.

Soler and Black made their third appearance in three days after Wang and U.S. District Court Judge Charlotte N. Sweeney directed them to explain their conduct. Sweeney has also summoned the Denver field office director into her courtroom on Monday to discuss ICE’s practice of re-arresting people on the spot who have obtained an order of release from a federal judge.

For more than a year, Colorado’s federal trial court has faced a flood of “habeas corpus” petitions from those in immigration detention, pushing court filings to unprecedented levels. The most common allegation is that the government is improperly denying bond hearings to people who are eligible by law to be released while their immigration proceedings unfold. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit recently rebuked the government’s interpretation of its authority.

On Oct. 8, the district court’s clerk, Jeffrey P. Colwell, and U.S. Attorney Peter McNeilly entered into a memorandum over the handling of habeas cases. Colwell declined to disclose the agreement with Colorado Politics, describing it as “simply an internal document.” Instead, McNeilly’s office provided the agreement.

The document describes how habeas cases will proceed after filing, with the clerk’s office providing petitions to the U.S. Attorney’s Office by email directly, instead of petitioners having to serve the government. Within seven days, the U.S. Attorney’s Office will respond to the petition, unless the presiding judge orders otherwise.

For several months, the U.S. Attorney’s Office has largely filed brief, boilerplate responses declining to contest petitioners’ allegations of unlawful detention. The memorandum, in contrast, allows the office to refrain from filing any response. In those instances, “the petitioner shall be released from custody no later than 24 hours after the response deadline, and the respondents shall file, no later than seven days after the response deadline, a status report informing the Court that the petitioner has been released.”

The agreement was intended “to allow the government to assess, really, the merits of a petition or the lack thereof and respond accordingly,” said Sweeney during her hearing on Wednesday. She noted that her practice was to give the government a much shorter timeline to respond, but “in the spirit of cooperation, I agreed with the seven-day response time.”

Attorneys who litigate habeas petitions and who had not seen the memorandum reacted positively to the attempt at handling the deluge of habeas filings, now numbering roughly 100 per week in Colorado.

“I know courts across the country have been struggling to process the cases. I’m not surprised that they are working to put a process in place, given the high volume of cases and the significant liberty interests at stake,” said Monique Sherman of the Rocky Mountain Immigrant Advocacy Network.

Ciara Fernandez Faber said the agreement offers a streamlined, predictable process. With the task of serving the government electronically now placed upon the court’s clerk, the result is a cost savings to represented and unrepresented petitioners.

“The dam seems to have broken. This new system speeds up the inevitable,” she said. “I am not familiar with other agreements like this.”

However, Wang, a Joe Biden appointee, pointed out during her hearing that the U.S. Attorney’s Office continued to drop the ball after the agreement.

Andres Lopez Juan filed a habeas petition on Oct. 20, which the court assigned to Wang that same day. She issued an order tracking the language of the memorandum, and the government did not file a response. On Oct. 30, she confirmed that Lopez Juan was to be released that same day, and that he “SHALL NOT be subject to any conditions beyond Petitioner’s prior conditions of supervision or release, if any.”

Quickly, Lopez Juan’s attorney filed a motion informing Wang that ICE had imposed GPS monitoring and additional conditions of release that did not exist for him before. Wang ordered the U.S. Attorney’s Office to respond by Nov. 4. It did not.

“That was my responsibility and that was my fault,” Soler told her on Friday. “I want to apologize.”

Wang interjected that shortly before the hearing, she encountered two more cases where the U.S. Attorney’s Office ignored her orders to respond.

“So, what process is the United States’ civil division using to try to avoid these situations and to comply with unequivocal court orders to respond?” she asked.

Jane Bobet Rejko, a deputy chief of the civil division, said her office has hired more people to exclusively work on immigration habeas cases, and they intend to hire more. Their job entails tracking when materials are due in court.

“What we’ve recognized was that there was a gap in that process for the situation that happened in this case,” Rejko said, where a judge requires a follow-up response after an order of release. “We did not have an established way to deal with that situation.”

She added that the office has done a “complete audit” of habeas cases that Soler handled recently, and said the office takes Wang’s concerns “very seriously.”

“You can imagine, counsel, that it is incredibly disruptive to the court’s ability to clearly adjudicate these petitions when we are spending our time chasing down things that should be effectuated without our interaction,” said Wang.

She told Rejko that, “until this issue is resolved,” she is requiring the government to give her updates about petitioners’ releases within hours, not the seven days laid out in the memorandum.

“I am significantly concerned that these petitioners are being released contrary to the orders of release and it is taking days for the court to understand that,” Wang said. Even though the memorandum was intended to foster efficiency, “the actual practice right now is creating even more work.”

As for ICE, Wang established in a separate hearing on Thursday that the agency’s policy is to impose monitoring conditions on all released habeas petitioners unless they have a medical condition or a judge’s order explicitly prohibits it. However, Black testified that she did not learn of Wang’s Oct. 30 order specifying no conditions of release on Lopez Juan until Nov. 5, the day Wang ordered her into court to explain Lopez Juan’s ongoing GPS monitoring.

“We rely on our legal counsel to update us on those types of actions,” said Black.

“Are (judicial orders) provided as they’re issued?” asked Wang.

“In this case, obviously not,” said Black.

Soler clarified that he forwarded Wang’s order to ICE within minutes of her releasing it.

Wang directed the government to explain why she should not hold it in contempt for violating her order. Although she doubted whether she had the authority to order the government to pay Lopez Juan’s attorney’s costs, she held off on a definitive answer.

text:
On November 6, 2026, President Trump announced a major shake-up in his White House. Susie Wiles is leaving her post as Chief of Staff, and longtime adviser Stephen Miller will take her place, effective Monday, November 9. The move comes days after Republicans suffered a devastating midterm election in which Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress.

Many of us hoped the midterm results would push the administration toward a more measured and lawful approach to immigration. Instead, the voters asked for moderation, and the White House answered by handing the keys to the most anti-immigration official in modern American history.

Who Is Stephen Miller?

Stephen N. Miller has served as White House Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy and Homeland Security Advisor since 2025. He began his career as an aide to then-Senator Jeff Sessions and is widely described as the architect of Trump’s immigration policy. The Southern Poverty Law Center lists him among its extremists. He has praised the Immigration Act of 1924, which severely curtailed legal immigration for four decades.

Miller’s focus has never been limited to the southern border. Reducing legal immigration has long been his explicit and documented goal. His own words make that clear.

In Stephen Miller’s Own Words

On a leaked call about restricting legal immigration, Miller said the first priority was to “turn off the faucet” of new arrivals.

In a 2023 Fox News interview, he told host Jesse Watters, “We are being conquered.”

When Stephen Miller talks about a faucet, he is talking about our doctors, our engineers, our researchers, our students, and their children. These are people who pay taxes, build companies, create American jobs, and follow every rule the system asks of them. Labeling them as conquerors is not policy; it is fear dressed up as governance.

His Record on Legal Immigration

Our clients lived through Miller’s influence in the first Trump term. USCIS denied 24% of first-time H-1B petitions through the third quarter of fiscal year 2019, compared with 6% in 2015. The National Foundation for American Policy found that the administration adopted 52 policies restricting visas and green cards for highly skilled workers and none easing their access.

The second term has gone further. In September 2025, the administration imposed a $100,000 fee on employers sponsoring H-1B workers coming newly from outside the United States, and USCIS changed how the annual H-1B lottery is run. In January 2026, the State Department suspended immigrant visa issuance for 75 countries. As Chief of Staff, Miller will now control the flow of policy across the entire White House, not just the immigration portfolio.

What We Expect Over the Next Two Years

With Democrats controlling Congress, new restrictive immigration legislation is unlikely. That makes executive action the more likely tool: policy memos, USCIS guidance, stricter adjudication standards, higher fees, expanded vetting, and slower processing. None of these require a vote in Congress, and they can affect pending cases overnight.

Since Congress can no longer pass his agenda, expect it to arrive through memos, fees, and delays. The battlefield is now the USCIS adjudicator’s desk, and preparation is the best defense.

We expect more Requests for Evidence, closer scrutiny of H-1B wage levels and job duties, more FDNS site visits, tougher review of extensions and amendments, and longer delays for adjustment of status applicants, especially Indian nationals already waiting years in the green card backlog.

How to Protect Yourself

Maintain valid status at all times and file extensions well before deadlines. Keep complete copies of every petition, approval notice, I-94 record, and pay stub. Consult your attorney before any international travel. Respond to every RFE or NOID with thorough, well-documented evidence. Employers should review their H-1B public access files and compliance records now, before an FDNS officer knocks on the door.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — After Democrats' overwhelming midterm victories this week, winning candidates spoke of the need, once they are sworn in, to rein in President Donald Trump's mass deportation machine. Some suggested putting forward a new vision for immigration reform while both houses of Congress are in Democratic control.

The lofty goals come after two years in which Democrats, while in the minority, were limited in how much they could counter Trump's supercharged and, at times, chaotic immigration enforcement. But there are clear limits to what they can achieve even after Democrats' epic win, with Trump — who rode into power in part on a promise to curb immigration — in office for another two years and wielding his veto power.

What's more, Republicans have frontloaded billions of dollars for immigration enforcement. And the key architect of the president’s hard-line immigration agenda, Stephen Miller, was elevated Friday to become Trump's chief of staff — suggesting immigration enforcement may not slow down any time soon.

Here's a look at what might come next for immigration after Election Day:

Investigating alleged corruption and ICE policies

Democrats appear ready to use the power of congressional oversight to investigate Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security. That strategy will likely resonate with voters angry aboutt how enforcement operations were carried out in places like Minneapolis or ICE arrests of longtime immigrants integrated into American society.

The administration ramped up immigration enforcement during the first two years of Trump's second term, launching major operations in multiple cities and sending arrests soaring. DHS also came under criticism for alleged corruption and misuse of funds it was granted to carry out Trump's immigration agenda.

Nationally, about 6 in 10 voters said the Trump administration’s actions on immigration enforcement had “gone too far,” according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters. A similar share disapproved of how ICE was doing its job. And about 6 in 10 voters said immigrants to the U.S. today do more to “help the country," while less than half, about 4 in 10, said they do more to “hurt the country."

Rep. Robert Garcia, a Los Angeles-area Democrat who will take over the House Oversight Committee and is a prominent critic of Trump's immigration agenda, warned the administration to “lawyer up,” adding that investigating alleged abuses at DHS was one of his priorities.

The next Congress will “address the Trump administration’s assault on the rule of law and hold those responsible accountable,” said Mississippi Rep. Bennie Thompson, the ranking Democrat on the House Homeland Security committee.

Those investigations could delve into issues like DHS purchases of massive warehouses to hold arrested immigrants; whether ICE cut corners when hiring thousands of new deportation officers; or deaths in ICE detention facilities.

Garcia and Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut held shadow hearings featuring family members of people killed during immigration enforcement operations, a whistleblower exposing problems with ICE training, and American citizens caught up in immigration enforcement operations.

No Republicans attended and Democrats couldn’t subpoena witnesses. Now they can, opening up a new level of scrutiny of the administration's actions.

Calls to put forward a Democratic vision for immigration

The last time Congress even came close to passing comprehensive immigration reform was in 2013. That proposal cleared the Senate but died in the House.

Border crossings that surged under the Biden administration further served to dampen any Democratic enthusiasm to talk about legalization for any immigrants.

Sarah Pierce, director of social policy for Third Way, a Washington, D.C., think tank, said Democrats need to show voters their own vision for immigration and border security and not just focus on oversight hearings of what happened during the last two years.

“They should lean into oversight, but I think that they also need to couple that with a proactive vision for what immigration should look like in the United States,” said Pierce.

At least one of the party's new senators is ready for the discussion. During an interview with Fox News after the election, Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas discussed the need to pass comprehensive immigration reform, including a pathway to citizenship for immigrants living and working illegally in the country for years.

In the House, Rep. Gabe Vasquez of New Mexico pointed to the Democratic gains made with Latino voters and the higher numbers of Latino lawmakers who will take office next year as reasons for Democrats to not shy away from talking about immigration issues.

He said Democrats should find ways to address immigration through a lens of affordability, a central issue for voters. For example, they could tackle staffing shortages by creating a new visa class for workers who provide care for children or the elderly.

“This cannot be a third-rail issue for Democrats,” said Vasquez. “We can actually reform our immigration system to bring costs down for all Americans and at the same time give people who are either here undocumented or want to come to this country an opportunity to have legal status.”

Democrats' power to curb Trump's immigration agenda is limited

Trump, shortly after the election, said he was prepared to work with Democrats on certain issues, highlighting immigration as one of them. But that collaborative tone may not bear out in practice.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin vowed on social media, “Deportations will continue.” A few days later, Trump promoted Miller to become his chief of staff.

Immigration and Latino activists lambasted Miller's promotion, calling it an act of defiance after voters spoke clearly at the polls and a sign the president would continue his immigration policies. California’s Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla, who’s been a key critic of Trump’s immigration agenda, said Trump was choosing to double down by picking Miller and vowed, “So will we.”

It's unclear if Democrats and the White House will find a middle ground to successfully pass immigration legislation. With Trump in office for another two years, he can veto any Democratic legislation, and Republicans have the money and the personnel to pursue Trump’s immigration agenda regardless of Tuesday’s results.

Republicans during the summer of 2025 supercharged immigration enforcement with $150 billion intended to expand immigration detention capacity, finish the border wall and hire thousands more deportation officers. Earlier this year they frontloaded routine funding for ICE and Border Patrol for the next three years.

“My fear is that enforcement will get worse. And the country will also see that Congress does not have many tools to stop the executive branch because the executive branch power on immigration has grown so vast,” said Andrea Flores, who was a policy adviser in the Obama and Biden administrations.

Conservatives want action from lame duck Congress

Many administration supporters want this current Congress — in the little time it has left — to pass laws solidifying the gains the Trump administration says it has made on border security and immigration. Without codifying changes to asylum law or tightening requirements on employers to verify workers' immigration status, they warn, a different administration could quickly reverse the new immigration landscape Trump has shaped.

NumbersUSA, an advocacy group that seeks to restrict immigration, has a timer on its website counting down the days until this Congress is over with a warning to “make border security permanent.”

“If this Congress in the lame duck does not secure the border with lasting legislation," said the organization's co-president, Jeremy Beck, “then this Congress will have failed to meet the moment.”

___

Associated Press reporter Linley Sanders contributed to this report.

text:
Members of San Diego’s congressional delegation on Friday demanded answers from the Trump administration regarding the death of an immigrant detainee at Otay Mesa Detention Center.

Guillermo Pascual Verganza, 42, was found unconscious and unresponsive in his single-occupant cell at the Department of Homeland Security facility near the border on Oct. 24, according to the San Diego County Medical Examiner’s Office.

Prison staff members and paramedics tried in vain to revive the man before pronouncing him dead at the scene shortly before 12:30 p.m., the county agency reported.

San Diego Democratic Reps. Juan Vargas, Scott Peters, Sara Jacobs, along with Rep. Mike Levin, who represents part of North County and south Orange County, joined in writing a letter with California’s senators, Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff, expressed their “grave concern” over Pascual’s death.

They called for an inquiry into his death and for regular updates on its progress because “without complete and accurate information, Congress cannot fully assess whether existing policies, procedures and safeguards are sufficient to protect individuals in federal custody.

“A thorough investigation is all the more important in light of previously documented concerns regarding delayed access to medical care, subpar detention conditions and compliance with public health reporting requirements,” the lawmakers wrote to the letter, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and Acting Immigration and Customs Enforcement Director David Venturella.

In the week following Varganza’s death, officials with CoreCivic, the Tennessee-based firm that runs the facility, said in a statement that they had immediately informed their “government partners at U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement” of his loss.

ICE did not respond to a request for comment about the death.

The Guatemalan national had been taken into custody in Escondido in early October, according to news accounts.

County actions

During a news conference last month, San Diego County Supervisors Paloma Aguirre and Terra Lawson-Remer called on the Trump administration and CoreCivic to cooperate with county investigators and clear the way for ongoing inspections of the Otay Mesa Detention Center.

After ICE denied supervisors access to the detention center, the county sued and secured a federal court order allowing an inspection in June.

That scrutiny identified failures to promptly report suspected tuberculosis cases, a lack of vaccines in stock and delays in providing necessary medical equipment, according to the supervisors. In September, the county issued another notice of noncompliance after a suspected tuberculosis case allegedly went unreported for about three weeks.

The county’s public health officer is evaluating additional oversight measures, including follow-up inspections. Litigation over the county’s ongoing inspection authority remains unresolved.

While exact numbers of detention center fatalities are elusive, the ACLU reported last month that at least 57 people had died while in U.S. immigration detention since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term. That’s more than double the number of deaths recorded from the previous four years combined.

According to a Human Rights Watch report released in June, the mortality rate of ICE detainees, based on 52 known deaths at the time – had reached its highest level in over a decade.

“Urgent action is needed to address this crisis and prevent further deaths,” the report concluded.
