text:
A UC Berkeley student was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement at San Francisco International Airport Friday while waiting to board a flight to Portland for a vacation with her boyfriend.

Related video above: House passes immigration enforcement bill amid partisan divide in June

Paula Valentina Albornoz Hernandez, 23, is currently being held at ICE’s California City Detention Center, agency records show, while UC Berkeley students and administration mobilize to support her. Attorneys at Centro Legal de la Raza have filed a habeas corpus petition challenging her detention.

The arrest likely represents the first ICE detention of an active UC Berkeley student since the Trump administration began its mass deportation push last year, said both Niko De Bremaeker, a managing attorney at Centro Legal de la Raza, and university spokesperson Aileen Zerrudo.

The business administration student arrived in the U.S. from Colombia in 2022, De Bremaeker said. He said she overstayed her visa and applied for asylum based on experiencing “severe gender-based violence” in her home country, an application that is still pending. She had a valid work permit, De Bremaeker said, and had attended San Jose City College before transferring to Berkeley where she was conducting research on artificial intelligence.

On Friday night, her boyfriend Anthony said, the couple had arrived early at the airport for a weekend getaway that he hoped would help take Albornoz Hernandez’s mind off her heavy course load. They were waiting in the gate area, he said, when an ICE agent in plain clothes approached Albornoz Hernandez and asked her name, saying she looked familiar. Without identifying himself as working for ICE, the agent guessed a couple of different names, Anthony said, to which Albornoz Hernandez said no.

The third time, Anthony said, he guessed right. Once Albornoz Hernandez confirmed her name, ICE agents separated the couple, then told Albornoz Hernandez that her visa was expired and they were going to detain her, Anthony said. (Berkeleyside agreed to identify him by his first name only due to the sensitivity of his girlfriend’s case.)

“It was scary seeing that my partner was getting ripped apart from me and there’s nothing I can do about it,” Anthony said.

Albornoz Hernandez spent most of the weekend at Stockton Detention Center, De Bremaeker said, before being taken to California City, a facility northeast of Los Angeles where earlier this year, a court-ordered investigation found major flaws in the medical care provided to people detained there.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security confirmed by email that ICE agents had detained Albornoz Hernandez at SFO.

“She entered the country on September 6, 2022, with legal permission to stay until March 6, 2023. In defiance of our nation’s laws, she did not depart,” wrote the spokesperson, who did not give their name. “She will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.”

The DHS spokesperson denied that ICE agents had failed to identify themselves when approaching Albornoz Hernandez, saying agents “clearly identify themselves as law enforcement in accordance with agency policy.”

Asked why agents had detained someone with a pending asylum application and valid work permit, the spokesperson replied that “work authorization or a pending application does NOT confer legal status in the United States.”

ICE has stepped up arrests at San Francisco International Airport and other airports since the summer, especially targeting people who had overstayed visas in the past. Immigration agents have also held green card holders in a windowless room in the airport for days at a time, a San Francisco Chronicle investigation found.

De Bremaeker said Albornoz Hernandez had no criminal record or previous arrests; a Berkeleyside search of Alameda County and federal court records did not turn up any criminal history.

“This is somebody who was very much known with the government, she had been complying at every step, she was doing everything she was supposed to do and obviously excelling within the community,” De Bremaeker said.

Her arrest “demonstrates the arbitrary nature in which the government is arresting folks and how deeply it cuts into our communities,” he said.

UC Berkeley chancellor asks for student to be allowed to resume studies

In a petition filed in U.S. District Court Monday, attorneys with Centro Legal de la Raza argued that ICE’s arrest of Albornoz Hernandez violated federal law and the U.S. Constitution because officers did not present a warrant and did not interview her to determine whether she was a flight risk before taking her into custody. Berkeleyside has asked DHS for a response to those claims.

The petition asks the court to order Albornoz Hernandez’s release and prevent the government from detaining her again unless it can prove in a court hearing that she poses a flight risk or is a danger to the community.

In a letter of support attached to the petition, UC Berkeley Chancellor Rich Lyons called Albornoz Hernandez “one of our outstanding students.”

“It takes remarkable dedication and perseverance to complete a degree at UC Berkeley,” he wrote. “I am deeply concerned that her current situation will unnecessarily interfere with the opportunity that she has earned, potentially impacting her academic progress.”

“I respectfully request that you make it possible for Paula to resume her studies with us,” he added.

Student was headed to Oregon with her boyfriend for trip hiking in the outdoors

Anthony described his girlfriend as hyper-responsible and studious and said she had long dreamed of attending UC Berkeley. The two met in school, he said: He was working towards his high school diploma and Albornoz Hernandez toward her GED.

“She always talked about Berkeley and how she wanted to get in,” he said. “I just admired how confident she was — she knew what she wanted and was going for it.”

They kept in touch as Albornoz Hernandez went on to San Jose City College, and started dating last summer. After transferring to UC Berkeley, he said, Albornoz Hernandez studied harder as she adapted to a more competitive environment. “She’s always working, day and night,” he said.

Anthony hoped the trip to Portland, which neither of them had visited before, could give her a chance to relax. They both love the outdoors, he said, and looked forward to going hiking, maybe seeing some waterfalls.

He has always been protective of Albornoz Hernandez’s safety, he said, taking time from his own studies and job as a welder to drive her from evening church services in Hayward back to Berkeley, then trekking home to San Jose. Now, he said he is plagued by guilt that the trip he planned unexpectedly led to her arrest, but tries to stay focused on getting her released soon.

Albornoz Hernandez’s friends at UC Berkeley have also helped out, he said, informing professors about her absence so she doesn’t fall too far behind.

“We want her to not miss out on her schooling because this is her dream,” he said.

The Alameda County Immigration Legal Education Partnership is advising anyone with an uncertain immigration status to avoid traveling by plane without consulting an attorney first. They have also urged anyone who is detained or witnesses an ICE arrest to call their hotline.

Albornoz Hernandez is scheduled for a hearing in immigration court on Nov. 17, De Bremaeker said. The immigration case is separate from the federal case challenging her detention.

We were moving smartly, and I underscore we were moving smartly, and then things, you know, got where they got.”

The investigation focused initially on the 2016 Russia investigation and then on the FBI's search of Mar-a-Lago, which led to the federal indictment of Trump by then-special counsel Jack Smith's office in the classified documents case.

The U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs in October, a surprisingly strong number that includes what appear to be some AI-related construction and manufacturing jobs.

American workers have so far seen relatively few benefits from the AI boom that has driven the stock market higher and fueled trillions of dollars in spending by the world’s top tech giants.

As global tech stocks have plunged over fears about the midterm election's effect on AI development, Trump said this morning that he's "100% in favor" of the technology.

"As President, I am 100% in favor of Super Intelligence (SI), and will work with the many States in the U.S. that want to become RICH by having them. They are GOLD, and only foolish leadership will say 'NO' to the riches they bring!" he wrote in a post on Truth Social.

John D. “Jay” Rockefeller IV, the progeny of one of America’s most famous and wealthiest families who during three decades in the Senate sought expanded healthcare for the poor and excoriated President George W. Bush’s handling of the Iraq War, died today at his home in Washington, The Washington Post reported. He was 89.

His family did not ​provide a cause, the newspaper added.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., last night dismissed concerns about whether he's a good fit to lead his caucus as majority leader in the new Congress.

In an interview on MS Now, he was asked for his response to people who feel like he's not the right person for that role.

"The bottom line is: first ... we’ve had a very, very strong finish here, and I have worked really hard to get the results we got. But second, the issue is not me, Lawrence. The issue is unity, fighting together. We still have a big job to do," he said.

Global market rout deepens after midterms intensify AI fears

An intensifying rout of tech stocks hit global markets today, with a surge of red tickers spreading from Wall Street to Asia and Europe after the blue wave of the U.S. midterm elections fueled fears over AI development.

The steep losses in Asia — Japan’s Nikkei suffered its worst week since 2020 — came after a dramatic plunge in U.S. tech stocks following the success of anti-AI candidates, which deepened concerns about the durability of the artificial intelligence boom.

In a video on social media, Hegseth said, “A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice.”

Judge blocks construction on Trump’s D.C.-area arch after commission’s approval

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan granted a temporary restraining order blocking the administration from “initiating, making, or otherwise effectuating any construction, excavation” or other steps in the arch project for 14 days.

text:
Happy Friday! A blue wave could be good news for litigation funders.

Funders have battled a series of Republican-introduced federal bills that would enact disclosure requirements or set parameters on outside investment in US litigation. Victoria Sahani, a Boston University School of Law professor, says those bills will be “dead on arrival when the Democrats take over.”

On the state level, efforts to regulate the industry have been more bipartisan and have had more success. Ed Gehres, managing partner at Invenio LLP, a law firm focused on litigation finance transactions, says funders have to remain vigilant.

“This is the time to build a moat,” he said. “The important thing is to build this political capital when you don’t need it as much.” Read More

Bloomberg Law subscribers can get this Litigation Finance newsletter in their inbox on Fridays. Sign up here.

Burford YPF Update

A Republican senator and attorneys generals from 14 states and one territory submitted amicus briefs asking the US Supreme Court to review the YPF ruling. The YPF case is famously backed by litigation funder Burford Capital.

After the court decision that ordered Argentina to pay $16.1 billion to investors was reversed earlier this year, the claimants had a few different options. One was to seek a US Supreme Court review.

Burford Capital published its unaudited financial results for the third quarter on Wednesday, and during the earnings call CEO Christopher Bogart said the briefs were “a pretty significant development in the process of that case.”

The funder reported it had total revenue of $135 million, achieved $100 million of de-leveraging, and closed the quarter with more than half a billion dollars of cash on hand.

What I’m Reading

Michael Di Gennaro, chief growth officer at the Law Practice Exchange, wrote for Bloomberg Law Perspectives about MSOs and how companies looking to invest in multiple legal practices will need to consider economies of scale and cross-marketing opportunities. He cites Charlesbank Capital Partners’ investment in an MSO supporting Wood Smith Henning & Berman as an example of private capital pursuing legal practice areas outside of personal injury.

Disputes between litigation funders and the law firms they finance are surfacing in federal courts across the country, The Wall Street Journal reported this week. Texas-based Galindo Law Firm filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy after rapidly scaling into a high-volume mass tort practice with the support of tens of millions from private lenders.

Litigation funder Loopa Finance announced the appointments of Raquel Assis and Roberto Gassmann as investment managers, reinforcing its commitment to expanding its presence across Latin America, Europe and the United Kingdom. Assis will focus on consolidating Loopa’s growth in Brazil and Gassmann will focus on further strengthening its presence in Europe and the UK.

Leading the News

House Democrats Plot Trump Probes to Prioritize in Majority

Democrats are leaving open the possibility of impeaching or subpoenaing President Donald Trump, saying nothing is off the table as they prepare for two years of investigations in the House majority.

Musk DOGE Probe Competes With Democrats’ Oversight Priorities

Resurgent Democrats are wrestling with how best to investigate Elon Musk and the Department of Government Efficiency against a long list of priority targets, including alleged conflicts of interest involving President Donald Trump’s family and the extent of Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes.

PR Nightmare Threatens Companies Called for Congressional Probes

Congressional investigations may evoke a courtroom feeling, but companies facing potential Democratic probes should address them as more of a public relations campaign.

Law Firm Deals to Face New Hill Scrutiny

Democrats pledging to put heat on law firms that made deals with President Donald Trump now have more tools at their disposal thanks to majorities in both chambers of Congress. The question is: How hard will lawmakers press for answers?

Nine large firms last year pledged $940 million in free legal services in the pacts with Trump. The deals came as the president lobbed executive orders against firms because of their ties to lawyers he sees as enemies.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, poised to lead the powerful House Judiciary Committee next Congress, is among the Democrats who have been asking firms for more information on the Trump deals. They say at least two firms — Kirkland & Ellis and Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom — are stonewalling those efforts.

Democrats will enter the new Congress with a long list of oversight targets, including Trump immigration enforcement, Justice Department misconduct allegations, and funding for the White House ballroom project. It remains to be seen where the Trump deal firms figure into the priorities, Ryan Tarinelli reports.

Commentary & Opinion

Weil Gotshal’s Closest Relationship Cost the Firm Everything

A law firm, even one with 1,200 lawyers, is simply a collection of relationships: partners deciding to work together. It thrives when those relationships are strong. And it can die if they wither.

At Weil Gotshal & Manges, there was no relationship more important than that between Mike Aiello, its highest paid partner and most prodigious business generator, and Barry Wolf, its longtime executive partner. Their story is the story of Weil’s final decade. Their relationship dictated the firm’s strategy and decisions. It decided who stayed at the firm and who left. And when it shattered, the firm did too.

NOAA Review Sends California Coastal Program Into Troubled Waters

Alston & Bird attorneys examine the review and renewal of California’s registration under the Coastal Zone Management Act. The results could have broader implications for coastal governance and environmental policy nationwide.

Weil Shows What Happens When Any Partner Could Leave at Any Time

The lesson from the sudden collapse of Weil is that the largest law firms are now businesses in every sense, and they can fail the way businesses fail, Major, Lindsey & Africa president John Cashman says.

Exercise Your Constitutional Rights to Protect the Rule of Law

Ten retired US judges ask what can citizens do when federal officials charged with protecting their legal rights disregard them? The very essence of citizenship is to exercise the constitutional rights of free speech and peaceful assembly in these circumstances, they say.

Partners Who Stay Through Firm Collapse Need Defined Protections

When a firm closes, what happens to the partner who stays? Fidelium Advisors’ James Dixon says firm leaders should confront those questions before the first serious wave of departures.

text:
This is a guest post by David Leopold, America’s Voice Legal Advisor and former president of the American Immigration Lawyers Association.

On Tuesday, Nov. 3, the American people spoke loud and clear with one voice: Enough. Enough violence. Enough cruelty. Enough chaos. Mass deportation must end.

Voters handed Democrats the House and the Senate in an election where Trump’s war on immigrants was on the ballot. For nearly two years, this administration promised to go after dangerous criminals. Instead, it turned its fury on the very immigrants who embody America’s core values: family, community, and hard work. Trump didn’t send ICE after “the worst of the worst.” He sent masked agents in military gear to seize parents and children at immigration court, disappear longtime neighbors into a maze of prisons, banish people to foreign gulags, and terrorize immigrants and U.S. citizens all over the country.

Americans saw the violence first-hand in their communities or beamed into their home night after night. They watched children torn from parents, neighbors dragged from their cars, U.S. citizens murdered in the streets, and a government at war with its own people. The rights under our Constitution were ripped apart. The American people did not need a lawyer to tell them this was wrong, lawless and unjust. Their intuition and conscience told them. And when they voted they answered with a thunderous “No!”

This election was a demand to restore due process, fairness, and humanity. And Americans reset the table. From deep-red Texas to blue-state Maine, Republicans lost their seats because voters refused to keep feeding a vicious, out-of-control machine. Voters saw the Trump administration’s bad governance. The message could not have been louder or clearer.

So now that the country has spoken, will Trump’s assault on immigration finally end?

Not by itself. Ballots alone do not unlock a single ICE prison cell. Families are still behind bars tonight. The voters have done their part; now the Democratic Congress must do its part. It must act boldly and without apology, knowing it carries a clear mandate to hold Trump accountable, not to enable his lawlessness.

On day one, it should take three steps.

First, wield the power of the purse. It is Congress’s strongest weapon. Republicans have already poured roughly $145 billion into ICE, much of it to cage human beings. But the annual spending bills that fund most of Homeland Security are now in Democratic hands. Not one more dollar should flow without basic guardrails the public already supports: visible identification of ICE agents, body cameras, and judicial warrants.

Second, use subpoena power to drag the truth into the light. Americans deserve to know where ICE is holding people; more than 16,000 have vanished from its online locator, as if they never existed. The American people deserve answers for millions of immigration status revocations and a collapse in citizenship approvals. And Congress must hold accountable everyone responsible, including the ICE and Border Patrol agents who carried out unlawful, cruel, and deadly actions across America. The people have demanded that it stop.

Third, reclaim Congress’s Article I authority as a co-equal branch of government. For too long, Congress looked away and let Trump rule by executive order and social media posts. Those days must end. Trump may keep abusing executive power. But if he does, he will do so in open defiance of the clear will of the American people who have demanded that Congress end Trump’s chaos and restore the rule of law.

Due process is not a Democratic value or a Republican value. It is an American value: the promise that no government stands above the law and no person falls beneath its protection. Everyone facing arrest, detention, or deportation deserves a fair hearing before a judge and a real chance of getting a lawyer. Without that, no one should be locked away or banished to a country they barely remember or have never seen.

On Tuesday, the American people threw out the enablers of a vicious out of control anti-immigrant ICE machine. Congress’s job now is simple and urgent: end Trump’s lawlessness and restore accountability, order, and, above all, human decency; make sure the Constitution still means something for everyone within our borders, and that cruelty ends now.

The American people have spoken.

text:
An 8-year-old Haitian boy is in federal custody after showing up for a scheduled immigration appointment earlier this week.

The incident was documented on video Wednesday by Karen Pohl, a volunteer immigration court observer with the group Detention Resistance. She said she’s never seen someone that young being detained before.

“It was just — I couldn't believe what I was seeing because I had never watched a child by himself get detained in that manner,” Pohl said.

The incident was upsetting to watch, she said.

“This is kind of like war,” Pohl, a retired Navy veteran, said. “And you just do what you got to do and deal with the emotion later because these people need us. There’s nobody else that’s witnessing how they’re being targeted and abused.”

The boy had been living with his uncle in City Heights after his father was deported in March 2025.

According to a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson, the uncle did not have legal custody.

In accordance with the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act, the spokesperson said the boy was considered an unaccompanied minor.

“Out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety, ICE determined it was best to remove the child from the household and place him in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement,” the spokesperson said.

Cody Petterson, a board trustee with the San Diego Unified School District (SDUSD), said the uncle was designated on school records as an authorized caregiver.

“I am not surprised ICE would say just about anything to justify their actions,” he said.

While he does not know the full details on who has legal custody of the boy, he said the uncle was someone the father entrusted his child to.

“This is a classic case of legalized lawlessness, where these agencies will attempt to use the law to actually further what is essentially a lawless activity,” Petterson said. “There is no question that the best place for this child was with the uncle that their father had designated as the guardian.”

In a three-page letter to Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., SDUSD and other local officials are demanding the federal government release the boy back to his uncle’s custody so that he could continue his education with familiar “schools, teachers, classmates and support systems.”

“We demand the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) and the ORR change its policies and procedures affecting school-aged children who enter government custody or placement,” the letter said. “At a minimum, greater consideration should be given to the educational continuity of these students.”

Wister Gaetan, the co-founder of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, said the boy should be doing what boys his age are doing, going to school and playing with other kids. He said the boy should be returned to his family.

“This kid was in a setting that provided him with love, (brought) him to school and a path to education,” Gaetan said. “Sitting behind bars with the U.S. government is purely unacceptable, a violation of his due process rights and civil liberty.”

San Diego City Councilmember Sean Elo-Rivera, who also posted the information on Instagram on Thursday, is calling for the restoration of temporary protected status for Haitians.

“We're in this situation because of a decision to end a program that did not need to be ended, that should not have been ended,” he said.

The family is working on resolving the custody issue.

Meanwhile, the district said it will provide crisis counselors for students at Fay Elementary School, where the boy attended.

California officials have previously said the list is out of date and includes legitimate voters — a sentiment that the federal judge presiding over the case echoed in his blistering order denying the federal government's request.[br /][br /]The case was at the forefront of President Donald Trump's administration's effort to assert control over state-run elections across the country, which Trump has said are rife with illegal voting without providing evidence.[br /][br /]The Department of Justice remains enmeshed in litigation with immigrant and voting rights groups seeking to limit its use of the list of what is says are suspected noncitizens. The motion to dismiss the lawsuit said that, by the time of the upcoming hearing, the state will have already irreparably "commingled the challenged ballots with lawful ones."[br /][br /]"The relief the United States sought and needed is no longer available—rendering voluntary dismissal necessary," the motion said.[br /][br /]Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, previously argued in court that the lawsuit would be irrelevant after election day, because there would be no way to sequester the ones allegedly belonging to noncitizens. The lawsuit was filed in mid-October, when ballots had been sent to all of the state's 23 million registered voters, and after hundreds of thousands of ballots were already processed. Once a ballot is processed, it is completely anonymized.[br /][br /]Essayli said at the time the lawsuit was filed that his goal was to "safeguard the integrity of the election so it doesn't have an effect on the upcoming election."[br /][br /]"We want to stop the illegal voting. We don't want to chase it later," he said outside of court the week before the election.[br /][br /]The United States Attorney's Office for the Central District of California referred all questions to the Department of Justice in Washington, D.C., which did not respond to an emailed request for comment on Friday evening.[br /][br /]California prosecutors in recent weeks have arrested over 30 noncitizens who are accused of illegally registering to vote. Some who were arrested were also accused of voting in previous elections. Elections clerks around California in the week before the election were sent subpoenas to testify before grand juries slated to convene in November. It's not clear who is being criminally charged in those cases, but the department does not typically subpoena people whom it regards as targets of a criminal investigation to appear before a grand jury.[br /][br /]U.S. District Judge David O. Carter appointed the special master in late October, shortly after allowing California to proceed with elections as planned. Carter, who was appointed by former President Bill Clinton, argued in his blistering order that separating ballots at that late stage would risk disenfranchising citizens and warned it would "wreak havoc" on the midterm elections.[br /][br /]The special master would have also considered whether or not California election officials did in fact have a mechanism for separating the ballots.[br /]

text:
By Gabrielle Caumon

Reporting Texas

Rafael, a former Austin middle school theater teacher, heard last year that some of his students from first-generation immigrant families had seen Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids at their apartment complex.

Fear, Rafael told them, should not stand in the way of their future. So he shared his story.

Rafael, 33, told the students that he is a Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipient who came to Texas from Mexico at age 6. The DACA program, created in 2012 by the Obama administration, provides eligible immigrants who came to the U.S. as children with temporary protection from deportation and allows them to obtain work authorization.

“I wanted to show my students: Look, if I did, you can do it,” said Rafael, who spoke on the condition that only his first name be published. “That was something really special; they were able to see someone like them teaching them, going through this entire path and being able to work because of DACA.”

But Rafael, like other DACA recipients and immigration lawyers, is fearful in the current immigration climate. Recipients are navigating a precarious legal status in the U.S. immigration system as court rulings reshape the legal landscape and deepen uncertainty.

Austin immigration attorney Jason Finkelman said DACA continues to face legal challenges. Texas and other states have argued that the DACA program conflicts with federal immigration law, he said, and that the Obama administration exceeded its authority when it created the program.

Courts have upheld parts of those challenges, Finkelman said, but current DACA recipients can still renew their status and work authorization every two years. However, the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has been barred from approving new DACA applications since July 16, 2021.

In January 2025, the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found parts of DACA to be illegal but allowed it to remain in place while the litigation continues. The court upheld DACA’s protections against deportation of DACA recipients, but the ruling could prevent DACA recipients from obtaining work permits.

The constant changes affect more than recipients’ immigration status. It can also shape the decisions about careers, finances and families.

“If you don’t know if you’re going to be able to work and make a living, are you going to buy a home? Are you going to save for retirement? Can you support your children?” Finkelman said. “So when this work authorization is temporary, and these renewals are unpredictable, that uncertainty can impact a family’s financial security in this country.”

Criminal defense attorney Pedro Villalobos, the first DACA recipient licensed to practice law in Texas, said DACA recipients must keep moving forward despite the instability of their status.

“You’ve got to keep trying to achieve your goals, try to get an education, try to advance your career professionally, and do your best because you can’t view that as an impediment,” Villalobos said. “It’s a hurdle, but not an impediment.”

Born in Mexico, Villalobos arrived in Texas at 3 and graduated from the University of Texas School of Law in 2016.

Villalobos, now a lawful permanent resident, has more comfort and security than he did under DACA, when renewal issues could upend his life at any moment. He said, however, that he remains vigilant given the current climate.

Rafael, meanwhile, said he has always been confused about where his status stands and how much longer he has in the country.

“As soon as DACA gets cancelled or stopped, obviously my name is now on a list,” Rafael said. “They have my address. They have all my information. They can just come pick me up. It’s one of those things where the future is just so blurry.”

The risks are real. In January 2025, the Department of Homeland Security rescinded restrictions on immigration enforcement in sensitive locations, including schools.

The fear Rafael sees in his students is one he remembers from his own childhood, when he worried whether his parents would still be home when he returned from school.

“Seeing my own students living with that is a really heartbreaking experience,” Rafael said. “At the end of the day, as teachers, we are supposed to be protecting these kids, and it’s really hard when both the students and the faculty are scared because you never know what’s gonna happen.”

Rafael has since moved to a different school district, where he teaches students from more privileged backgrounds. He has not shared his immigration status with those students.

When Rafael’s family arrived in Texas, his father hoped he and his sister would have opportunities beyond working in construction or at a fast-food restaurant. Their parents emptied their savings account to help Rafael and his sister obtain their DACA status.

“With my dad giving us this opportunity, I get to have a car, travel, teach; I get to do what I love; my sister gets to buy a car, a house and create a family — and it’s all because of DACA.”

But even after building a career, Rafael said he does not know how long that stability will last.

“DACA doesn’t prevent anyone from entering a career, but what its effect is, is on the ability to maintain that work authorization,” Finkelman said.

Filing a renewal application on time does not automatically extend work authorization. If a work permit expires before a new one arrives, recipients generally must stop working, Finkelman said, even if their DACA status remains valid.

“Someone may have a college degree and experience and a great employment record, but if they don’t have that work permit or they have to plan around getting a work permit every two years, that creates a lot of uncertainty,” Finkelman said.

Recent renewal delays have added to those concerns. Some recipients are waiting more than six months for their renewal, compared with an average of 15 days in fiscal 2025. Finkelman said the reason for the longer delays remains unclear.

Rafael said he was “lucky” with his latest renewal. After seeing warnings about delays on TikTok and Reddit, he applied earlier than planned, moving up his renewal from its January 2027 expiration date. He submitted his application on Aug. 16 and received approval on Sept. 15.

One of his friends, however, had to start a GoFundMe in April after a delay in his renewal application, which he had submitted Dec. 5, cost him his job. His application was approved at the end of July, and his employer rehired him.

For Rafael, the risks extend beyond his ability to work. Last year, before going to work, he said he stopped at a Circle K near his school, in a predominantly Latino community in Austin. An ICE agent came in.

“My heart is beating at a thousand miles an hour, but I’m making sure that I have my teacher’s ID on me, that I have my wallet with me, that I have my work permit with me,” Rafael said. “Just making sure that I have a way to actually show them like, ‘Hey, I am here, I can legally be here.’”

He has stopped going to that convenience store.

“We have to be the perfect model citizens,” Rafael said. “We have to respect everything and be careful — because one mistake, and our entire life goes away.”

Lasting security for DACA recipients would require congressional action, Finkelman said, including legislation that creates a pathway to permanent residence for people brought to the U.S. as children.

“We’re not asking for a free ride; we’re not asking for special privileges,” Villalobos said. “We’re only asking to give us a chance to prove ourselves and show you that we can succeed, that we can make something of ourselves.”

Rafael said he wants to live somewhere where he no longer has to worry about his future because of his immigration status.

“I need to move to a place where I know I’m going to be safe, where I am no longer going to be treated like a pawn,” Rafael said — “like Texas treats DACA recipients.”

text:
The Justice Department on Friday moved to dismiss its own lawsuit that sought to stop California from counting roughly 20,000 ballots it alleged went to noncitizens until their immigration status could be verified.

The request to dismiss the case comes days after Republicans' significant losses in the midterm elections and about a week before a scheduled hearing where a special master was slated to evaluate the accuracy of the list. California officials have previously said the list is out of date and includes legitimate voters — a sentiment that the federal judge presiding over the case echoed in his blistering order denying the federal government's request.

The case was at the forefront of the Trump administration's effort to assert control over state-run elections across the country, which Mr. Trump has said are rife with illegal voting without providing evidence.

On Monday, on the eve of Election Day, the Supreme Court rejected an emergency appeal from the Justice Department to require California to separate mail ballots received from the approximately 20,000 people it alleged were noncitizens.

The Supreme Court rejected the appeal in a one-line, unsigned order.

The Justice Department remains enmeshed in litigation with immigrant and voting rights groups seeking to limit its use of the list of what it says are suspected noncitizens. Another controversial lawsuit it filed in Alaska at Mr. Trump's direction before the election to block the victory of the Democrat in that state's Senate race was swiftly dismissed by a federal judge. The administration is appealing that ruling but has yet to file a full brief at the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals.

California had processed roughly 9 million ballots as of early Friday, with nearly 5 million still left to be counted, according to state election officials. The motion to dismiss the lawsuit said that, by the time of the upcoming hearing, the state will have already irreparably "commingled the challenged ballots with lawful ones."

"The relief the United States sought and needed is no longer available—rendering voluntary dismissal necessary," the motion said.

Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, previously argued in court that the lawsuit would be irrelevant after Election Day, because there would be no way to sequester the ones allegedly belonging to noncitizens. The lawsuit was filed in mid-October, when ballots had been sent to all of the state's 23 million registered voters, and after hundreds of thousands of ballots were already processed. Once a ballot is processed, it is completely anonymized.

Essayli said at the time the lawsuit was filed that his goal was to "safeguard the integrity of the election so it doesn't have an effect on the upcoming election."

"We want to stop the illegal voting. We don't want to chase it later," he said outside of court the week before the election.

The United States Attorney's Office for the Central District of California referred all questions to the Department of Justice in Washington, D.C., which did not respond to an emailed request for comment on Friday evening.

California prosecutors in recent weeks have arrested over 30 noncitizens who are accused of illegally registering to vote. Some who were arrested were also accused of voting in previous elections. Elections clerks around California in the week before the election were sent subpoenas to testify before grand juries slated to convene in November. It's not clear who is being criminally charged in those cases, but the department does not typically subpoena people whom it regards as targets of a criminal investigation to appear before a grand jury.

U.S. District Judge David O. Carter appointed the special master in late October, shortly after allowing California to proceed with elections as planned. Carter, who was appointed by former President Bill Clinton, argued in his blistering order that separating ballots at that late stage would risk disenfranchising citizens and warned it would "wreak havoc" on the midterm elections.

The special master would have also considered whether or not California election officials did in fact have a mechanism for separating the ballots.

text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, installing as his closest adviser a loyal, combative bulldog for his “America First” agenda as the president prepares to stare down a newly empowered Democratic Congress next year.

Miller, long a member of Trump’s tight inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies. He is one of Trump’s longest-serving aides, joining his long-shot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He most recently has served as White House deputy chief of staff for policy and oversees a broad portfolio, though he is best known for his role in Trump’s immigration policy.

The staff shuffle signals that Trump, whose Republican Party was handed monumental defeats in Tuesday's midterm elections, is resisting a conciliatory approach to Democratic lawmakers who are eager to investigate the administration — including Miller himself as a top target. Miller, 41, is a dogged defender of Trump and has built a deep and sophisticated understanding of a president's executive power and how the federal government operates, portending a potential burst of executive actions in the final two years of Trump's presidency.

Wiles gave Trump her resignation Thursday night, a person familiar with the events told The Associated Press, speaking on condition of anonymity to describe the private conversation. Trump praised Wiles and said she’d continue to work for his political organization.

Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post and the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.

“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” Wiles said in a social media post shortly after Trump’s announcement.

The departure also came months after Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026.

Miller is tied to immigration policies that voters said went too far

During the midterm campaign, Miller took frequent partisan swipes at Democrats, calling them “extremists, freaks and America-hating lunatics” on social media and promoting unfounded theories about election fraud in California and Alaska.

He has been a major part of the Trump administration’s anti-fraud task force targeting benefit programs and a decision to suspend Microsoft and others from a green card program. He also served as homeland security adviser at the White House, giving him a perch from which to coordinate with other agencies across the government.

He joined Trump on Friday for his trip to Florida, and the president noted to reporters that "Stephen has been with me from the beginning.

"He gets it; very good politically," Trump said as he departed the White House. "He’ll do a great job. Great manager.”

But the immigration policies that Miller is so closely associated with were a major liability for Republicans during the just-wrapped election. The midterm AP Voter Poll found that most voters, about 6 in 10, said the administration’s immigration enforcement actions had gone too far and they “somewhat” or “strongly” disapproved of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement had handled its responsibilities.

“Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down,” said Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is set to become chairman of the powerful House Oversight Committee. “Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families.”

In a statement, Garcia added, “Stephen Miller should lawyer up.”

Wiles brought order to Trump’s campaign

Trump on Friday praised Wiles, the veteran Florida operative who joined Trump’s team during his 2016 presidential bid, as having done a “very good job, great job.”

But he added, “Sometimes in life, you have to make moves.”

Wiles, 69, is the second woman to lead Trump’s presidential campaign to victory, although she never embraced the formal title of campaign manager.

She has been credited with steering the most disciplined of his three presidential bids, and Trump himself has said he was often told that Wiles led his “best-run campaign.” Often called the “ice maiden” by the president, she was seen as the no-brainer choice to serve as White House chief of staff at the start of his second term.

Wiles stuck with the job even after her breast cancer diagnosis. Deep into the midterm campaign, six months after having revealed her diagnosis, she said she was “cancer-free,” indicating she no longer showed evidence of cancer after her pathology results came back clear.

In a rare interview, Wiles told Fox News Digital last month that she hadn’t been planning on getting the mammogram that ultimately detected her cancer. Her doctor suggested she do the exam anyway, because a mammogram machine was available that day and her schedule was too busy and unpredictable.

Wiles, the daughter of the late NFL player-turned-broadcaster Pat Summerall, cut her reputation as someone who brought discipline to the president’s chaotic style and shunned the spotlight, so much so that at Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd.

In addition to Trump, Wiles also ran incumbent Sen. Rick Scott’s 2010 campaign for Florida governor and briefly served as manager of former Utah Gov. Jon Huntsman’s 2012 presidential campaign. She spearheaded Ron DeSantis ’ successful run for Florida governor in 2018, but DeSantis would eventually urge the Trump campaign in 2020 to cut ties with Wiles, creating a rift that led to a particularly vicious effort by those in Trump’s orbit to mock DeSantis throughout his failed run for the Republican presidential nomination against Trump in 2024.

Wiles once said Trump had ‘an alcoholic’s personality'

But in December 2025, nearing the end of Trump’s first year back as president, Wiles became the headline when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials conducted by the author Chris Whipple, an expert on White House chiefs of staff.

The Wiles interviews stuck out for their candor, which is unusual for a sitting White House chief of staff. She said Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality,” although the president does not drink, and said then-Attorney General Pam Bondi had “whiffed” in her handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files while remarking that Vice President JD Vance has been a “conspiracy theorist for about a decade.”

Trump and other administration aides rushed to defend Wiles, who, in turn, disparaged Vanity Fair for publishing what she called a “disingenuously framed hit piece,” though she did not deny making the comments.

In the interviews, which were conducted over a period of several months, Wiles also revealed a bit of her management style, saying she was “not an enabler.”

“I try to be thoughtful about what I even engage in,” Wiles said. “I guess time will tell whether I’ve been effective.”

Democrats will hold at least 54 seats in the 100-member Senate next year and as many as 56 depending on final results in Alaska and Mississippi — where contests remain narrow with votes still outstanding.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who is likely to return as majority leader next year, promised in an interview with the AP that Democrats will prevent the Republican president from installing a “right-winger” on the Supreme Court or “crappy nominees” elsewhere in the federal judiciary or in Trump’s Cabinet.

The Latest:

Trump says he expects ‘very little’ staffing changes to his administration

Speaking to reporters on the tarmac after he landed in Palm Beach, Trump was asked if he expected more departures in coming months after Wiles left as chief of staff.

“Very little,” he said, adding “We have a great cabinet.”

In an interview with CBS’ “60 Minutes” taped before he left for Florida, Trump suggested at least some staff turnover, saying of his Cabinet, “I think they’re good. But I’ll do — be doin’ maybe a few changes.”

He declined to say who, while also defending Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Hegseth could face impeachment by the incoming Democrat-controlled Congress.

The U.S. Department of Justice has moved to dismiss its own lawsuit that aimed to stop California from processing up to 20,000 ballots it suspected were mailed to noncitizens.

The lawsuit was part of the Trump administration’s effort to stop alleged illegal voting.

The defense secretary could face impeachment after Democrats take control of Congress in January, following their big midterm election wins on Tuesday.

Democrat Nancy Lacore wins election to US House in South Carolina’s 1st Congressional District

Lacore is a former Navy vice admiral who served as chief of the Navy Reserve before Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired her last year without explanation, part of a series of steps targeting military leaders during President Donald Trump’s second term.

She defeated Republican Jenny Costa Honeycutt. Honeycutt is an attorney and a member of the Charleston County Council.

After Democrats flip Texas House, state’s longest-serving Black lawmaker says she has support for speaker

Rep. Senfronia Thompson would be the first Black lawmaker and first woman elevated to Texas House speaker in the state’s history. The 87-year-old Democrat was first elected in 1972.

Democrats won a majority in the state House for the first time since 2002 as part of their sweeping victories in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

The next House speaker will be elected by majority vote of the 150-member chamber next January. Thompson will have to hold together the coalition she claims until then.

US coordinates with Canada to target Iranian digital asset providers

The Treasury Department on Friday targeted several firms exchanging Iranian rials and other currencies for allegedly helping Tehran evade sanctions and fund its proxies.

Some of the providers dealt with Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges already sanctioned by Washington.

The latest targets were coordinated with the Canadian government as several of the individuals and entities named are based in Vancouver and Toronto.

“Anyone, anywhere in the world, who helps Tehran evade sanctions risks being held accountable,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a statement.

The actions are part of the Trump administration’s economic campaign to cripple the various financial networks that help sustain Iran as the longtime adversaries struggle to find a diplomatic resolution to a more than eight-month long conflict.

Ukraine welcomes more help from Melania Trump in the future

Ukrainian officials have praised first lady Melania Trump for her role in a humanitarian ceasefire in the besieged Ukrainian city of Oleshky and hope for more of her help going forward.

Davyd Arakhamia, head of the parliamentary faction of Zelenskyy’s party, and Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, spoke to reporters in Washington a day after a White House event recognizing the recent six-day truce between Russia and Ukraine in Oleshky.

Lubinets says he thinks of the first lady “as a heavyweight” in negotiations, saying her office was instrumental in getting the Russians to open negotiations.

Asked about a greater role for Melania Trump in talks between Russia and Ukraine, Arakhamia said, “we would appreciate it.” He says he wants to expand the ability to get truces in other parts of the war-torn country.

Ukraine expects to see more support from US after midterms

A Ukrainian official says with Democrats winning control of Congress in the midterm elections, they expect American support to surge next year.

Davyd Arakhamia, head of the parliamentary faction of Zelenskyy’s party, told reporters in Washington that he sees “the chances for us to get better U.S. support” financially and generally is “at least double” with the new Congress.

Arakhamia said he and other Ukrainian officials know newly appointed White House chief of staff Stephen Miller “well” and were broadly optimistic about his new role.

But before the congressional changes, “we have the hardest winter ever,” Arakhamia said.

Russia has been targeting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. He said the country’s supply of missile interceptors is all but depleted.

Congressional Hispanic Caucus chair says promoting Miller is ‘putting lipstick on a pig’

Democratic Rep. Adriano Espaillat of New York said Trump’s decision to name Miller the White House chief of staff “is a desperate and irresponsible cry for attention.”

He said Miller has been the architect of Trump’s immigration policies and voters have “rejected mass deportations, the targeting of Latino communities.”

To give Miller “a fancier title is just putting lipstick on a pig,” he said.

‘I wanted to make a change,’ Trump says, explaining chief of staff shakeup

Trump praised both Wiles and Miller to reporters but said it was time for a change.

“Susie has done a very good job. Great job,” Trump said as he left the White House to travel to Florida. But he said, “We’ve got to make moves sometimes.”

Trump said Miller is great.

“He gets it” and is “very good politically. And he’s a very good man. He’ll do a great job, great manager,” Trump said.

Wiles steered Trump’s 2024 comeback campaign. She has long been seen as a check on some of his most destructive impulses.

description:

During the first Trump administration, it was Miller who devised the “Muslim ban” restricting travel from Muslim-majority countries.

text:
On Tuesday, voters resoundingly rebuked Donald Trump and his brutal mass deportation campaign that sent military tanks and masked agents though residential streets.

But on Friday, the president doubled down. He named Stephen Miller – the architect of the administration’s most aggressive immigration policies – as his chief of staff.

It was never likely that Trump – who rose to political prominence on the promise that he would expel immigrants en masse from the US – would dampen his agenda, even after voters rejected Republican candidates up and down the ballot, near and far from the southern border, in blue and deep-red states.

But the elevation of Miller – a zealous, anti-immigrant crusader who has been by Trump’s side since the president’s first term – is an ominous signal that the deportation machine that Trump has built up over the past two years will be driving ahead at full speed.

Miller more than any single other person is responsible for unleashing a series of violent immigration raids across US cities this year and last, for sending hordes of masked agents in military gear through residential streets to round up undocumented immigrants. He has pushed the administration to all but shut down legal immigration as well. In his previous roles – as a deputy chief of staff and policy adviser – he has stuck close to Trump’s side and stoked the president’s most extreme instincts.

“The elevation of Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff signals a doubling down on the administration’s cruelest impulses,” said Faisal Al-Juburi, the co-chief executive of Raíces, a Texas-based humanitarian aid and immigration services non-profit. “Miller’s promotion guarantees an acceleration of mass deportations and of brute force unleashed within our neighborhoods.”

After immigration agents shot and killed Alex Pretti, a nurse, amid immigration raids in Minneapolis, it was Miller, according to the Wall Street Journal, who raised the idea that Trump could invoke the Insurrection Act to send in military troops.

It was Miller who came up with the legal framework of using the Alien Enemies Act to cast Venezuelan immigrants – including asylum seekers – as foreign terrorists associated with the Tren de Aragua cartel, and using that reasoning to expel them to a Salvadorian megaprison and to strike small Venezuelan boats.

During the first Trump administration, it was Miller who devised the “Muslim ban” restricting travel from Muslim-majority countries. It was he who designed the now-notorious zero tolerance policy of the first Trump administration – which separated more than 5,600 children from their parents and caregivers at the US-Mexico border. More recently, he’s pushed the administration to accelerate the deportation of undocumented children.

Miller, 41, who is himself the descendant of Jewish immigrants to the US and grew up in liberal Santa Monica, California, came to reject his home town, viewing California as a failed state that had been perverted by mass immigration. Eventually, he came to see immigration as a leftwing plot to undermine his vision of a traditional United States.

In more than a decade by Trump’s side, Miller has worked with the president to wrest extreme executive authority, to undermine Congress and the judiciary and defy oversight – in large part to advance his anti-immigrant campaign.

“He never backs down,” said Trump’s defense secretary Pete Hegseth in a congratulatory social media post, calling Miller a true patriot.

Democratic lawmakers who’ve re-taken control of Congress, governor’s offices and statehouses may have to spend much of the next two years bringing Miller’s ambitions to heel. Human rights activists and advocates on behalf of immigrants are immediately calling on congressmembers to do everything they can to stop Miller.

US representative Robert Garcia, the California Democrat who is poised to lead the House oversight committee next year, warned that Miller “should lawyer up” – promising to investigate him and his involvement in the administration’s mass deportation scheme.

Senator Alex Padilla said that if Trump was doubling down, “so will we”, promising to use “every tool at our disposal – oversight, investigations, subpoenas, and our leverage over federal funding – to expose this administration’s abuse of power and hold those responsible accountable”.

But even with full control of Congress, Democrats will likely have a limited ability to rein in the administration’s immigration enforcement agencies – which are bloated with $70bn in funding through 2029. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is poised to massively expand its workforce. Immigration arrests and detentions are already at an all-time high.

Miller, meanwhile, has shown a unique unwillingness to concede – in 2018, he reportedly sank a deal that would have gotten Trump $25bn funding for a border wall in exchange for a provision that would have provided permanent protection for undocumented immigrants who had come to the US as children.

It hasn’t seemed to faze him that the administration’s policies have alienated the coalition of voters who elected Trump into office in 2024 – including a large contingency of Latino voters. And he is unlikely to be moved by voters’ backlash against the Trump administration’s most extreme policies.

“This puts him in a position of greater power to wreak havoc,” Al-Juburi said.

text:
The Montana Supreme Court sided unanimously with Gallatin County Attorney Audrey Cromwell in her case against Attorney General Austin Knudsen on Friday, ruling that Knudsen exceeded his authority when he attempted to take control of Cromwell’s local responsibilities. The court did not decide the question underlying Knudsen’s attempted takeover of Cromwell’s office, which relates to how much county governments must cooperate with U.S Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The conflict began in October 2025 when Gallatin County records personnel sought Cromwell’s legal advice about an ICE request for confidential criminal justice information. Law enforcement agencies generally exchange such information with one another, but members of the public, including the media, must go through an onerous process to obtain it. (The information sought in this instance, for example, remains publicly unavailable.) Cromwell’s office advised county records personnel that ICE was not entitled to the information without a court order.

In April, Knudsen exercised supervisory powers — “the power to order and direct county attorneys in all matters pertaining to the duties of their office,” according to Montana code — over the Gallatin County Attorney’s Office. Exercising that control of Cromwell’s office, Knudsen ordered Cromwell to fulfill ICE requests.

Cromwell issued the memorandum that Knudsen demanded, but noted to her staff that she could not “vouch for the accuracy of the legal analysis underlying the directive.”

She also filed a petition with the Montana Supreme Court arguing that ICE shouldn’t have automatic access to confidential criminal justice information for civil immigration purposes and that Knudsen had overstepped his authority by exercising supervisory powers over her office.

On Friday, the court ruled that Knudsen did not have legal authority to take supervisory control of Cromwell’s office. Justice James Shea wrote the unanimous opinion.

Shea wrote that a county attorney has responsibility to two entities: the state and the county. Montana’s attorney general, Shea ruled, can exercise supervisory control only over a county attorney’s state-related responsibilities, like “prosecuting criminal laws and on occasion instituting or defending a civil suit in the name of the state.”

In this situation, because Cromwell was acting in her capacity as a legal adviser to Gallatin County, Shea ruled that Knudsen can’t force her to change course.

“The AG does not have supervisory authority over a county attorney when the county attorney acts as legal advisor to the county and its subdivisions,” Shea wrote.

Knudsen’s Supreme Court filings also argued that the case was beyond judicial review, positing that the dispute was an internal executive-branch matter to which Cromwell was a subordinate party. Shea rejected that argument, ruling that Cromwell had independent responsibility as a county official and a right to dispute Knudsen’s interference with her duties. Shea’s opinion, and a concurring opinion by Chief Justice Cory Swanson, rejected that argument.

The state Supreme Court also made plans to hear additional arguments about two underlying questions: Does ICE qualify as a criminal justice agency under Montana law? And does a criminal justice designation alone entitle an entity to confidential information, regardless of whether the request was for civil or criminal purposes?

The court asked both Knudsen and Cromwell to file briefs by Dec. 7, 2026.

------

text:
President Donald Trump on Friday announced White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller will be promoted to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.

Trump revealed the stunning shake-up just three days after Democrats won a landslide victory in the midterm elections, gaining majority control in the House and Senate and scrambling the trajectory of Trump’s last two years in office.

Elevating Miller, an architect of Trump’s controversial mass-deportation efforts, is bound to raise the hackles of the incoming class of congressional Democrats, who have already vowed to investigate the government’s immigration policies.

“It has been the privilege of my lifetime to have served on his team from Day One, and I am honored beyond words to serve as his White House Chief of Staff,” Miller said on X later Friday.

“The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic,” he said.

Miller will take over starting Monday, Trump said in a Truth Social post, praising his longtime aide as “one of my most trusted advisors.”

Wiles, “who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation,” the president wrote.

Asked about the move later Friday afternoon, Trump said, “I wanted to make a change.”

“I think Susie’s done a very good job, great job. But I just wanted to make it,” Trump told reporters as he left the White House for an event in Cape Canaveral, Florida.

“Stephen’s been great,” Trump said, adding, “Sometimes in life you have to make moves.”

Wiles resigned Thursday night, a senior White House source told MS NOW. Wiles told Trump, who was said to be angry with her following the GOP’s huge election losses, “let me make this easy on you — I am going to resign,” MS NOW reported.

“Today is my last day as White House Chief of Staff,” Wiles said in an X post Friday afternoon. “Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime.”

“While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will,” she wrote.

Senior administration officials were quick to congratulate Miller.

“Patriots in control,” read an X post from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, whose job security has come into question after some Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, blamed the midterm results on the Iran war.

Vance also praised Miller on X, saying he “will do great things.”

The official X account for Trump’s political operation celebrated the announcement by posting a black-and-white photo of Miller under the caption, “It’s Miller time.”

Democrats and other critics, meanwhile, filed in to denounce the pick.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who could be elected House speaker next year, called Miller “a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands.”

“His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today,” Jeffries wrote on X.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., wrote that Trump “learned nothing from his historic defeat.”

“Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn’t have made a worse choice. Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way,” Schumer wrote.

Others took Miller’s promotion as a sign that Trump, who seemed to express some willingness to negotiate with a blue Congress, will instead remain combative.

“For those who hoped the @POTUS might pivot to work with the incoming Congress, the appointment of Miller is a bucket of ICE cold water,” wrote David Axelrod, a former senior advisor to President Barack Obama.

The White House reshuffle follows multiple resignations of senior staff in the Department of Justice since Election Day. They include Harmeet Dhillon, a leader in the DOJ’s civil rights division, John Eisenberg, who headed the national security division, and Jason Reding Quiñones, who had been in charge of conspiracy investigations related to Trump’s foes.

Wiles oversaw Trump’s winning 2024 presidential campaign and has wielded major influence in his second administration, while largely staying out of the spotlight. She drew focus in late 2025, when Vanity Fair reported that Wiles admitted that Trump had pursued “retribution” as president and that he had an “alcoholic’s personality.”

Trump, and many other top administration officials, defended Wiles at the time, underscoring her status in the White House.

While Wiles is not fully leaving Trump’s orbit, her resignation follows a pattern of other top female officials who have left or been fired from Trump’s second administration, and then replaced by men.

text:
Members of San Diego's congressional delegation and California's senators Friday demanded answers from the Trump Administration in the death of an immigrant detainee who died last month at Otay Mesa Detention Center.

Guillermo Pascual Verganza, 42, was found unconscious and unresponsive in his single-occupant cell at the Department of Homeland Security penitentiary near the U.S.-Mexico border on Saturday, according to the San Diego County Medical Examiner's Office.

Prison staff members and paramedics tried in vain to revive Pascual Verganza before pronouncing him dead at the scene shortly before 12:30 p.m., the county agency reported.

Democrat representatives from San Diego including Juan Vargas, Scott Peters, Sara Jacobs and from San Juan Capistrano Mike Levin, and Democrat senators Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff wrote a letter to demand an investigation into the death.

The letter, addressed to Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and Acting Immigration and Customs Enforcement Director David Venturella, read:

As members of the San Diego Congressional delegation, we write to express our grave concern following the latest death of an individual in ICE custody at Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego, California, operated by the for-profit prison corporation CoreCivic.

Any death in federal custody is a tragic reminder of the serious responsibility entrusted to DHS, ICE and their contracted detention facilities to safeguard the lives of those in their care.

A thorough investigation is all the more important in light of previously documented concerns regarding delayed access to medical care, subpar detention conditions and compliance with public health reporting requirements.

We further request that the department regularly update members of Congress as the investigation progresses. Without complete and accurate information, Congress cannot fully assess whether existing policies, procedures and safeguards are sufficient to protect individuals in federal custody.

In the week following Varganza's death, CoreCivic, the Tennessee-based firm that runs the facility in the 7400 block of Calzada De La Fuente, released a statement confirming the in-custody death.

"We are deeply saddened by the loss of anyone in our care," the company stated. "Our government partners at U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement ... were notified immediately."

ICE did not respond to a request for comment about the death.

Pascual Verganza, a Guatemalan national, had been taken into custody in Escondido in early October, according to news accounts.

During a news conference on Tuesday afternoon, San Diego County Supervisors Paloma Aguirre and Terra Lawson-Remer called on the Trump administration and CoreCivic to cooperate with county investigators and clear the way for ongoing inspections.

"Earlier this year, we took ICE to federal court for blocking public health inspections amid disturbing reports of unsafe conditions at Otay Mesa (Detention Center)," Lawson-Remer said. "Now a man has died inside that facility. When the federal government flouts due process and shuts the door on independent health inspectors, we cannot look away. We need answers, accountability and the ability to protect the health and safety of everyone held inside."

The lawsuit "wasn't a political exercise - it was a necessary step to protect human lives," Aguirre said.

"Ensuring basic human rights, medical oversight and safety within our borders is non-negotiable," she said. "ICE and CoreCivic must be held accountable for these failures right now, before another family is forced to suffer this same unimaginable grief."

After ICE denied supervisors access to the detention center, the county sued and secured a federal court order allowing an inspection in June.

That scrutiny identified failures to promptly report suspected tuberculosis cases, a lack of vaccines in stock and delays in providing necessary medical equipment, according to the supervisors. In September, the county issued another notice of noncompliance after a suspected tuberculosis case allegedly went unreported for about three weeks.

The county's public health officer is evaluating additional oversight measures, including follow-up inspections. Litigation over the county's ongoing inspection authority remains unresolved.

While exact numbers of such fatalities are elusive, the ACLU reported last month that at least 57 people had died while in U.S. immigration detention since the start of President Donald Trump's second term - more than double the number of deaths recorded from the previous four years combined.

According to a Human Rights Watch report released in June, the mortality rate of ICE detainees - based on 52 known deaths at the time - had reached its highest level in over a decade and more than doubled since Trump's current term began. The rate at that time was nearly four times that of the Biden administration, and more than 2.5 times as high as that of the first Trump administration, the watchdog organization reported.

"Urgent action is needed to address this crisis and prevent further deaths," the report concluded.

The Democratic mayor of America's fourth-largest city is reversing course on cooperation with federal immigration authorities despite an executive order from defeated Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott that threatened the loss of millions in state funding for noncompliance.

The Lone Star State swung blue for the first time since its new senator-elect, James Talarico, was born, and Houston Mayor John Whitmire wasted no time Friday announcing new restrictions on cooperation with ICE.

Whitmire told The New York Times that city police are not permitted to notify ICE if they encounter an illegal immigrant in "nonviolent contacts" like traffic stops or minor offenses.

'WE DIDN'T EXPECT THIS': TEXAS DEMOCRATS STUNNED AS BLUE WAVE TOPPLES GOP STRONGHOLD

"If they’re charged with a new crime, we’ll let ICE know as we get them to the jailhouse," he told the paper Friday.

Abbott lost his bid for a fourth term Tuesday, and Talarico flipped one of the state’s Senate seats blue for the first time since Clinton Treasury Secretary Lloyd Bentsen won his final re-election bid in 1988 — seven months before the current senator-elect was born.

Texas’ most recent Democratic governor, Ann Richards, the mother of former longtime Planned Parenthood president Cecile Richards, was elected shortly thereafter in 1990.

Whitmire did not respond to a request for comment but signaled to the Times that he made the decision at least in part because Abbott’s order requiring DHS contact caused "anxiety" among Houstonians.

In a statement put out Friday afternoon, Whitmire said, "I have signed an executive order directing HPD to no longer contact ICE for nonviolent offenses, helping reduce fear in our communities. Thank you to Chief Diaz, our state and local leaders for their collaboration. A step toward building a stronger Houston. Let’s Go to Work."

He also acknowledged Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa won’t take office until January but characterized his decision as "responsible" and "more effective policy."

A DHS spokesperson responded to Whitmire's move in comments to Fox News Digital.

"We remain disappointed that sanctuary politicians seek to limit cooperation with ICE, as our law enforcement are simply fulfilling their sworn duties to serve and protect our communities," the spokesperson said.

"Partnerships with law enforcement are critical to having the resources we need to arrest criminal illegal aliens across the country. Seven of the top 10 safest cities in the United States cooperate with ICE.
