text:
Stephen Miller, Donald Trump’s most controversial aide and the architect of his sweeping immigration crackdown, will become his new White House chief of staff days after Republicans lost control of the US Congress in US midterm elections.

The president announced the extraordinary appointment on Friday, confirming that Susie Wiles – his current chief of staff, and the first woman to serve in the role – had been ousted.

In a social media ‌post, Trump called Miller, 41, “one of ​my most trusted advisors” and praised Wiles for doing “an ⁠outstanding job”. Miller will begin on Monday.

Wiles, 69, reportedly handed in her resignation on Thursday night and said in a social media post that serving Trump “has been the honor of a lifetime”.

Holding an umbrella, Trump emerged from the White House South Portico on Friday for a trip to Florida. “I wanted to make a change,” he said. “I think Susie’s done a very good job ... Stephen’s been great, and we’ve got to make moves.”

“Stephen’s been with me from the beginning. He gets it,” the president said. “Very good politically and he’s a very good man. He’ll do a great job. Great manager.”

Trump then boarded the Marine One helicopter, followed by Miller, secretary of state Marco Rubio and close aide Natalie Harp.

In a statement, Wiles added: “I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.”

She said her commitment to “the President and the mission” will not change.

Miller’s appointment is the first sign of a shake-up at the White House following Republicans’ catastrophic defeat in the midterms. His record as a far-right firebrand implies that Trump is preparing for an aggressive fight against congressional Democrats’ oversight and investigations.

Chris Whipple, author of The Gatekeepers: How the White House Chiefs of Staff Define Every Presidency, told CNN: “It’s almost a declaration of war by Trump … He [Miller] only knows one gear and that’s full-throttle, full steam ahead over the cliff.”

David Axelrod, a veteran Democratic strategist, added on X: “For those who hoped the @POTUS might pivot to work with the incoming Congress, the appointment of Miller is a bucket of ICE cold water.”

Miller is one of the most polarising figures in the administration and one of Trump’s closest and longest-serving advisers, having joined his 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He is a former aide to the former senator Jeff Sessions of Alabama, who would go on to serve as Trump’s first attorney general.

In Trump’s first term, Miller was the driving force behind policies such as family separation and a travel ban on Muslim-majority countries. More than a hundred Democrats in Congress signed a letter to Trump calling Miller a “documented white nationalist” and demanding his removal.

A biography of Miller, written by journalist Jean Guerrero in 2020, was entitled Hatemonger.

Miller has served as deputy chief of staff since Trump’s return to the presidency in January 2025. He had been hugely influential in hardline immigration policies and demanding an end to birthright citizenship. He is also one Trump’s most ardent, outspoken and pugnacious defenders.

Appearing on Sean Hannity’s Fox News show on Monday, just before the midterms, Miller said of the president: “He saved America from a corrupt political class. He saved America from open borders. He saved America from countries that want the American way of life to end, from foreign adversaries, from domestic adversaries.”

Miller added: “President Trump took a bullet for you, he bled for you, he faced life in prison for you. And what he needs from you tomorrow is your vote.”

Wiles is the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.

Wiles led Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign to victory and was credited with bringing discipline to a chaotic effort and clamping down on leaks from his second administration.

The Florida operative generally shunned the limelight. At Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd.

But Wiles made headlines last year when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials. Her comments stood out for their candour, including her observation that Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality”.

Her departure came months after she indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease. She went public with the diagnosis in March.

Critics said Miller’s appointment showed that Trump had learned the wrong lessons from Tuesday’s electoral reckoning.

Becca Balint, a Democratic congresswoman from Vermont, posted on X: “On Tuesday, the American people rose up and overwhelmingly voted in opposition to the disgusting and inhumane policies of this second Trump administration. What does Trump do? He promotes Stephen Miller – the architect of some of this administration’s worst decisions. Sickening.”

title: Rights on the Ballot Alongside US Congressional Elections
description:
Alongside the high-profile congressional and gubernatorial races decided during the United States midterm elections on November 3, human rights were at issue in several state and local ballot measures across the country.
Vermont voters approved an amendment providing equal protection to individuals regardless of their race, ethnicity, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or national origin.
Ballot measures on transgender rights also showed mixed results.
Colorado voters rejected a measure that would have required state and local law enforcement to coordinate with federal immigration authorities in some circumstances.
The US Congressional elections may be the biggest story of the week, but voters took up some important human rights issues directly in these initiatives and the impacts will be felt for years to come.
text:
Alongside the high-profile congressional and gubernatorial races decided during the United States midterm elections on November 3, human rights were at issue in several state and local ballot measures across the country.

In Virginia, voters adopted a measure to automatically restore voting rights to people with felony convictions upon release from prison, ending a lifetime ban that had been in place since the Jim Crow era.

Arizona voters rejected and Wisconsin voters approved measures to end diversity, equity, and inclusion practices in education, employment, contracts, and administration, mirroring Trump administration initiatives to dismantle programs to address ongoing impacts of historical discrimination based on race and ethnicity. Vermont voters approved an amendment providing equal protection to individuals regardless of their race, ethnicity, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or national origin.

Meanwhile, Missouri voters rejected an effort to restrict the right to abortion care and measures to safeguard abortion rights were successful in Nevada and Virginia but failed in Idaho.

Ballot measures on transgender rights also showed mixed results. In Colorado, voters adopted a measure to ban gender-affirming surgeries for youth under 18. In Missouri, one of 27 US states to have a ban on gender-affirming care for youth, voters opted to keep the ban out of the state’s constitution.

Virginia voters approved an amendment formally lifting the state’s obsolete ban on same-sex marriage and affirming that two adults may marry regardless of sex, gender, and race.

Immigration-related measures were also on several ballots. Colorado voters rejected a measure that would have required state and local law enforcement to coordinate with federal immigration authorities in some circumstances. Voters in Honolulu, Hawaii were consulted on a measure requiring their police department to ensure the constitutional rights of all persons regardless of immigration or citizenship status, and work with federal agents only when required by statute or a court order, though the results are still to be decided. And voters in Chicago, Illinois, said they agreed that the city should seek financial compensation from the federal government for harm caused by immigration enforcement operations.

The US Congressional elections may be the biggest story of the week, but voters took up some important human rights issues directly in these initiatives and the impacts will be felt for years to come.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, installing as his closest adviser a loyal, combative bulldog for his “America First” agenda as the president prepares to stare down a newly empowered Democratic Congress next year.

Miller, long a key member of Trump’s inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies. He is one of Trump’s longest-serving aides, joining his long-shot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He most recently has served as White House deputy chief of staff for policy and oversees a broad portfolio, though he is best known for his role in Trump’s immigration policy.

The staff shuffle signals that Trump, whose Republican Party was handed monumental defeats in Tuesday's midterm elections, is resisting a conciliatory approach to Democratic lawmakers who are eager to investigate the administration — including Miller himself as a top target. Miller, 41, is a dogged defender of Trump and has built a deep and sophisticated understanding of a president's executive power and how the federal government operates, portending a potential burst of executive actions in the final two years of Trump's presidency.

Wiles gave Trump her resignation on Thursday night, a person familiar with the events told the Associated Press, speaking on condition of anonymity to describe the private conversation. Trump praised Wiles and said she’d continue to work for his political organization.

Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post and the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.

“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” Wiles said in a social media post shortly after Trump’s announcement.

The departure also came months after Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026.

Miller is tied to immigration policies that voters said went too far

During the midterm campaign, Miller took frequent partisan swipes at Democrats, calling them “extremists, freaks and America-hating lunatics” on social media and promoting unfounded theories about election fraud in California and Alaska.

He has been a major part of the Trump administration’s anti-fraud task force targeting benefit programs and a decision to suspend Microsoft and others from a green card program. He also served as homeland security adviser at the White House, giving him a perch from which to coordinate with other agencies across the government.

He joined Trump on Friday for his trip to Florida, and the president noted to reporters that "Stephen has been with me from the beginning.

"He gets it; very good politically," Trump said as he departed the White House. "He’ll do a great job. Great manager.”

But the immigration policies that Miller is so closely associated with were a major liability for Republicans during the just-wrapped election. The midterm AP Voter Poll found that most voters, about 6 in 10, said the administration’s immigration enforcement actions had gone too far and that they “somewhat” or “strongly” disapproved of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement had handled its responsibilities.

“Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down,” said Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is set to become chairman of the powerful House Oversight Committee. “Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families.”

In a statement, Garcia added: “Stephen Miller should lawyer up.”

Wiles brought order to Trump’s campaign

Trump on Friday praised Wiles, the veteran Florida operative who joined Trump’s team during his 2016 presidential bid, as having done a “very good job, great job.”

But he added, “Sometimes in life, you have to make moves.”

Wiles, 69, is the second woman to lead Trump’s presidential campaign to victory, although she never embraced the formal title of campaign manager.

She has been credited with steering the most disciplined of his three presidential bids, and Trump himself has said he was often told that Wiles led his “best-run campaign.” Often called the “ice maiden” by the president, she was seen as the no-brainer choice to serve as White House chief of staff at the start of his second term.

Wiles stuck with the job even after her breast cancer diagnosis. Deep into the midterm campaign, six months after having revealed her diagnosis, she said she was “cancer-free,” indicating she no longer showed evidence of cancer after her pathology results came back clear.

In a rare interview, Wiles told Fox News Digital last month that she hadn’t been planning on getting the mammogram that ultimately detected her cancer. Her doctor suggested she do the exam anyway, because a mammogram machine was available that day and her schedule was too busy and unpredictable.

Wiles, the daughter of the late NFL player-turned-broadcaster Pat Summerall, cut her reputation as someone who brought discipline to the president’s chaotic style and shunned the spotlight, so much so that at Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd.

In addition to Trump, Wiles also ran incumbent Sen. Rick Scott’s 2010 campaign for Florida governor and briefly served as manager of former Utah Gov. Jon Huntsman’s 2012 presidential campaign. She spearheaded Ron DeSantis ’ successful run for governor in 2018, but DeSantis would eventually urge the Trump campaign in 2020 to cut ties with Wiles, creating a rift that led to a particularly vicious effort by those in Trump’s orbit to mock DeSantis throughout his failed run for the Republican presidential nomination against Trump in 2024.

Wiles once said Trump had ‘an alcoholic’s personality'

But in December 2025, nearing the end of Trump’s first year back as president, Wiles became the headline when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials conducted by the author Chris Whipple, an expert on White House chiefs of staff.

The Wiles interviews stuck out for their candor, which is unusual for a sitting White House chief of staff. She said Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality,” although the president does not drink, and said then-Attorney General Pam Bondi had “whiffed” in her handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files while remarking that Vice President JD Vance has been a “conspiracy theorist for about a decade.”

Trump and other administration aides rushed to defend Wiles, who, in turn, disparaged Vanity Fair for publishing what she called a “disingenuously framed hit piece,” though she did not deny making the comments.

In the interviews, which were conducted over a period of several months, Wiles also revealed a bit of her management style, saying she was “not an enabler.”

“I try to be thoughtful about what I even engage in,” Wiles said. “I guess time will tell whether I’ve been effective.”

___

Associated Press writers Michelle L. Price in Washington and Jill Colvin in New York contributed to this report.

A Wisconsin state trooper has been detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and is facing deportation to South Africa, according to his lawyer.

Aaron Van Der Merwe, 21, was detained Thursday as he was waiting to board a domestic flight, according to a statement issued by law firm Christopher & De León.

Van Der Merwe told ICE officers he had a work permit and a pending asylum application.

“According to Van Der Merwe, the officers said they did not care, placed him in handcuffs and shackles, and transported him to immigration detention in Dodge County,” the law firm said.

An ICE database shows Van Der Merwe is currently being held at a detention facility in Juneau, Wisconsin.

“In defiance of our nation’s laws, he overstayed his admission. This illegal alien will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement.

“DHS reversed the horrendous Biden-era policy that allowed aliens in our country illegally to jet around our country. Under President Trump, DHS will no longer tolerate this. This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport,” the spokesperson said.

Attorney Marc Christopher said he will seek his client's release on bond.

“This is inhumane and despicable,” Christopher said in a statement. “Putting a Wisconsin State Trooper behind bars while his asylum case sits unresolved does not make our communities safer. Wisconsin’s congressional delegation should demand his release and demand answers.”

text:
HOUSTON, Texas -- The mayor of Houston on Friday said the city would limit cooperation with federal immigration authorities, heralding "a new model" of immigration enforcement after Democrats won power in Texas for the first time in decades.

Mayor John Whitmire said the city would go after immigrants "that pose a danger, not those that are going about their family business, work and education."

A traffic incident "will not even ... you write a citation or you warn them and they go about their way. No contact with (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement) over nonviolent, non-jailable offenses. It reduces the fear and anxiety."

Details of the change were to be spelled out in an executive order, but the move by the nation's fourth-largest city is one of the first steps to curb ICE's powers since Tuesday's election.

The Trump administration's immigration crackdown in Houston has sparked protests after an ICE officer fatally shot a Mexican homebuilder this summer and another struck a man with a car.

RELATED: Lorenzo Salgado Araujo shot and killed by ICE agent in Houston, authorities confirm

A grand jury last week indicted ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Prosecutors say Morales intentionally rammed his car into Miguel Parra Hernandez, whose leg was broken. ICE has asserted that Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle, an account that prosecutors say is contradicted by video.

READ MORE: ICE agent indicted for running over man turns himself in, posts bond, DA's office says

Despite a one-time $75 billion infusion from Congress, ICE remains heavily dependent on local police to find people subject to deportation and turn them over. It has done so partly by signing about 2,600 agreements — many in Texas — to deputize local police and other state and local agencies to enforce immigration laws. Texas has been a primary target for ICE arrests.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has closely aligned the state with the Trump administration to collaborate on enforcing federal immigration laws. He lost his bid for a fourth term to Democrat Gina Hinojosa.

title: She should be celebrating Senior Night. Instead, this El Paso teen is in Dilley ICE detention.
description:
Michell planned to participate in Senior Night festivities Friday, a celebration honoring senior student-athletes, performers and participants in extracurricular programs.
LEARN MORE: ‘Why are you taking her?’ ICE arrests surge in El Paso region as families feel the impact ICE arrests continue to surge across the country – including in El Paso – as President Donald Trump’s administration enforces its mass detention and deportation agenda.
She also said she hadn’t seen her dad because the family had been separated at the detention center, Ximena added.
Michell and her family, originally from Venezuela, were taken to the ICE El Paso Service Processing Center on Montana Avenue near the airport after being arrested.
The next day, they were at the controversial family immigration detention facility in Dilley, Texas, south of San Antonio.
text:
Two months ago during homecoming celebrations, Michell Germán was crowned Lady-in -Waiting at El Paso High School, donning a white “Hoco Court” sash over her Tigerettes dance team uniform. Her mother and 11-year-old sister stood proudly beside her, holding small cellophane-wrapped flower bouquets.

Michell planned to participate in Senior Night festivities Friday, a celebration honoring senior student-athletes, performers and participants in extracurricular programs.

Instead, the 17-year-old and her father, mother and sister are sitting in the South Texas Family Residential Center near Austin after being detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on their way to school two weeks ago.

“She’s missing memories she’ll never get back,” Congressman Joaquin Castro, D-San Antonio, said in an Instagram post Thursday. Castro noted the school and dance team had planned a special recognition of Michell for Senior Night, but two of her friends on Friday told El Paso Matters that she asked that not happen. Castro in the post said he met with the family at the detention center last week and called Michell “a bright young student.”

Those who know her say that might be an understatement.

“She and her family are incredible people, they’re good people with good hearts,” 17-year-old Ximena Terrazas said about her friend and dance troupe colleague. They often talked about teenage girl stuff, she said, including boyfriends, teachers, homework, music and dance routines. And whether it was offering an ear or a shoulder or hands-on help, Michell has been trustworthy and reliable, she noted. “She has always been there for me and our other friends. She always offers to help with whatever we need.”

Michell is enrolled at El Paso High’s Center for Career and Technology Education program, where she’s studying cosmetology and working toward her state license. She aspires to be a cosmetic surgeon, according to her school’s social media posts. Besides spending hours practicing and performing with the Tigerretes, she worked part time at a smoothie shop and regularly volunteered with seniors.

“She has dreams, she has the potential, character and drive to accomplish them and become a productive member of society. You have a young lady doing everything right – studying hard, taking on extracurricular activities, working, volunteering, helping her community,” said El Paso attorney Veronica Vallejo, an El Paso High School booster and volunteer who has known Michell for at least a year.

“Everything is getting ripped away from her. … This is wrong.. This is bigger than immigration, it’s about a young woman’s life,” Vallejo said, adding that she’s concerned about Michell’s well-being.

The family’s status is unclear, including how long they’ve been in the United States, whether they are seeking asylum or have authorization to be in the country. An Austin law firm reportedly representing the family didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment and information.

The Department of Homeland Security and ICE also didn’t respond to requests for comment.

LEARN MORE: ‘Why are you taking her?’ ICE arrests surge in El Paso region as families feel the impact

ICE arrests continue to surge across the country – including in El Paso – as President Donald Trump’s administration enforces its mass detention and deportation agenda. The administration has moved to end programs such as temporary protected status and humanitarian parole, at the same time expanding arrests to include people with pending asylum claims or other immigration applications.

Ximena said her friend’s detention brought home the reality of that enforcement.

“She sent me a photo of her in the patrol car and said she was afraid,” Ximena said about when Michell was first arrested, adding she and her teammates cried for hours after hearing about the detention.

PODCAST: Inside El Paso’s ICE arrest surge and the families caught in deportation proceedings

“Since this happened, we see how hurtful this all is. I know a lot of people around school are paying more attention to the news and information about immigration and raids and ICE,” Ximena said. She added that she’s realized how many people are “ignorant and lack empathy because of the hate comments we see online and how they’re happy these things happen. It’s really sad.”

Ximena said she recently had a 30-second call with Michell from Dilley before the call dropped. Michell sounded calm but different, she said, and told her she missed her and her dance team. She also said she hadn’t seen her dad because the family had been separated at the detention center, Ximena added.

Michell and her family, originally from Venezuela, were taken to the ICE El Paso Service Processing Center on Montana Avenue near the airport after being arrested. The next day, they were at the controversial family immigration detention facility in Dilley, Texas, south of San Antonio.

The 2,400-bed center, operated by CoreCivic under a $160 million a year federal contract, has faced intense scrutiny, public protests and calls for closure over numerous allegations of human rights violations, including poor water and food quality, unsanitary conditions, medical neglect and limited communication access between detainees and their attorneys or family members.

The prolonged detention of children at Dilley has also come into question as many detainees have surpassed the 20-day limit established by the 1997 federal court ruling known as the Flores Settlement Agreement, which set standards for the detention, treatment, placement and release of children in U.S. immigration custody.

In August, a California federal judge appointed a master and independent monitor at Dilley to oversee compliance with the Flores settlement.

Castro called for ICE to release the family immediately, and called on Democrats to get to work to “shut down the Dilley Trailer Prison and end family detention once and for all.”

Congresswoman Veronica Escobar, D-El Paso, echoed a similar sentiment, citing this week’s midterm election that returned control of Congress to Democrats as a way forward. On Facebook, she said a constituent reached out to her for help with the family and in turn she reached out to Castro.

“The election results give us an opportunity to end the cruelty and we intend to do everything possible (to) bring it to an end,” she said.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

text:
RICHMOND, Va. — Attorney General Jones and a multistate coalition of 23 states secured an important victory in court that stops the federal government’s imposition of illegal immigration-enforcement conditions on Congressionally-authorized public safety grants, including grants intended to keep law enforcement officers safe and fight crime.

District of Rhode Island Chief Judge John J. McConnell, Jr. declared the Trump Administration’s actions unlawful and permanently enjoined any implementation or enforcement of these illegal conditions.

“The Trump Administration continues to play games with federal funding, this time jeopardizing critical public safety funds that state and local law enforcement agencies rely on to protect their communities,” said Attorney General Jones. “Our dedicated law enforcement professionals work every day to keep their communities safe, and the court’s decision today will ensure they have the resources they need to carry out this important mission.”

Last year, the Trump Administration, disregarding the clear letter of the law and intent of Congress, declared that states would be unable to access Victims of Crime Act (VOCA) funds unless they agreed to the Administration’s extreme immigration demands. State attorneys general succeeded in getting the federal government to remove those conditions on over $1.3 billion of VOCA funds.”

However, this year, the U.S. Department of Justice (USDOJ) has applied these illegal conditions to new grants, including funds dedicated to law enforcement and juvenile justice.

Among the affected programs is the Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Formula Grants (known as the Byrne JAG Program). For decades, regardless of which political party held power, the Byrne JAG Program has been the leading federal source of criminal justice funding to state and local governments.

Civil immigration enforcement is a federal responsibility and not a state government responsibility. The Trump Administration’s unlawful attempts to coerce states into doing their bidding conflict with core principles of American governance – the separation of powers and federalism. The Administration’s actions violated laws passed by Congress as well as the Spending Clause of the U.S. Constitution.

This lawsuit was co-led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta, Delaware Attorney General Kathy Jennings, New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport, Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul, and Rhode Island Attorney General Peter F. Neronha. text:
During the final years of the first Trump Administration, even as polls showed he would lose his 2020 re-election campaign, the Immigrant Legal Resource Center (ILRC) began implementing a long-term strategy to defend Texas from anti-immigrant attacks, maintain California’s pro-immigration policies and develop strong federal anti-criminalization champions.

The ILRC understood that Texas would be the testing ground for racist and hateful policies that would lay the groundwork for Trump should he become president again.

Days after President Biden was sworn into office in 2021, Texas Governor Greg Abbott launched Operation Lone Star (OLS), an unconstitutional and deadly Texas law enforcement scheme that has wasted billions of dollars to target migrants for arrest, jail, and deportation. Abbott proved he was willing to sacrifice Texas’s Black and Brown communities to test how far he could push OLS as Trump and his cronies took notes as they planned for his comeback.

The ILRC, along with our partners across Texas, began educating local, state and federal lawmakers and alerting communities to be prepared for anti-immigrant attacks. This work was critical when Trump won the presidency again in 2024 and immediately set out to effectuate his mass deportation agenda, using Texas as his blueprint.

The Texas Legislature continued passing hateful laws aimed at targeting anyone suspected of being undocumented for detention and deportation. Another law required most counties to enter into 287(g) agreements with ICE, making local police officers de facto ICE agents. ICE enforcement actions began taking place across the state, causing widespread fear and driving immigrant communities underground.

The ILRC and our partners never wavered and continued to grow the opposition to the mass deportation agenda across the state, working to create positive change to defeat anti-immigrant policies. Communities learned the power of their collective voices to stand up and fight back. This work was tedious and arduous but has contributed to the effort that has ushered in new leadership for Texas that we hope will lead to compassionate and meaningful change for the state’s diverse communities and become a blueprint for positive immigration policies across states still governed by hateful and racist laws.

Meanwhile in California, the ILRC worked with state lawmakers to ensure funding remained in place to protect immigrant communities. The work of ILRC and our partners led to the creation of the Immigration Legal Fellowship Project to develop the organizational capacity of legal service providers in underserved rural and regional areas of California. We continue to find creative ways to push back on plans to repurpose warehouses and other facilities for immigration detention.

The ILRC along with so many movement partners around the country continues to conduct in-person and virtual Know Your Rights trainings to groups, lawmakers and advocates nationwide, making sure our communities are prepared if they are stopped by federal enforcement agents.

The ILRC’s webinars, trainings, briefings and publications have continued to ensure legal practitioners and community advocates are kept up to date on the ever-changing policy landscape, both federally and in California and Texas.

We demand our leaders–local, state and federal–be bold in their demands and call on them to use the powers they currently have: federal lawmakers must use their oversight capabilities to hold those who have enacted harsh and hateful laws to account; state lawmakers must undo punitive policies currently in place; and, local leaders must step up since change always starts at the grassroots level.

Elected leaders must push for legislation that repeals harmful laws that have strengthened ICE’s current authority to detain, deport, and remove our immigrant community members.

Elected leaders must end policies that have blocked access to immigration benefits for low-income communities or color, and they must strengthen policies that protect immigrant community members from racial profiling, criminalization, and deportation.

title: It Wasn't Just Gas Prices. Anti-ICE Sentiment Fueled Republican Midterm Losses. | Truthout
authors: Shireen Akram-Boshar, Chris Walker, Austin C. McCoy, Marianne Lavelle, Dan Gearino, Mitch Perry, Sharon Zhang, Amy Goodman, Juan González, Mark Olalde
description:
Polls show 6 in 10 Latino voters supporting Talarico over Republican Ken Paxton — and in South Texas, Talarico performed better than Democrats have since the 1930s.
ACLU Texas polling prior to the midterm elections showed that 53 percent of residents in Texas border regions feel that immigration enforcement has made life harder, rather than making their communities safer.
Residents asked why Collins had not done more to stop ICE’s violent raids — and why she instead voted for more funding for the agency.
Pew also found that Americans across racial and ethnic groups view ICE more unfavorably today than they did a year ago, with 56 percent of Americans saying they have a negative view of the agency overall.
Only 35 percent say they view the agency favorably.
text:
While President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance blame Republicans’ losses in the midterm elections on their war on Iran — with Trump flippantly saying that the war “drove the gasoline up a little bit short term” — Tuesday’s results also represent a rejection of the Trump administration’s deportation campaign.

In Texas, where Trump won a Latino majority in the presidential election in 2024, the midterms saw a reversal, with Latino votes playing a role in the victories of Democrats James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa. Polls show 6 in 10 Latino voters supporting Talarico over Republican Ken Paxton — and in South Texas, Talarico performed better than Democrats have since the 1930s.

Rep. Joaquin Castro (D-Texas) said that “we haven’t seen this huge a Latino voter surge before,” and stated that “the difference is ICE and the mass deportation campaign.” Talarico had spoken against the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) killing of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, and against ICE’s tactics.

ACLU Texas polling prior to the midterm elections showed that 53 percent of residents in Texas border regions feel that immigration enforcement has made life harder, rather than making their communities safer. The polls also showed that 63 percent of those residents believe that ICE tactics “have gone too far.”

One resident surveyed in the poll — which spoke to 1,031 adults in El Paso and Rio Grande Valley counties — said that “ICE isn’t helping by deporting our hardworking immigrants regardless of their status. This whole region and country has been built on the backs of immigrants.” The resident had voted for Trump in the 2024 presidential election.

In Maine, too, voters expressed that the ICE crackdown over the past year had pushed them to vote against Republican Sen. Susan Collins, with the ICE killing of Johan Sebastian Guerrero in July as a particular flashpoint. Residents asked why Collins had not done more to stop ICE’s violent raids — and why she instead voted for more funding for the agency.

Democrat Troy Jackson, on the other hand, has said that he will “fight to abolish ICE.” In his victory speech on Wednesday, he said: “Masked agents terrorizing our neighbors and ripping families apart should never be accepted in the United States of America.”

And in Minnesota, the site of ICE’s “Operation Metro Surge” at the beginning of the year, which saw federal agents murder Renee Good and Alex Pretti, the early Latino vote increased by 217 percent compared to 2022.

Polling by Pew Research Center in September and October found that a majority of Black (69 percent), Latino (67 percent), and Asian (66 percent) adults in the U.S. have a negative opinion of ICE, while 49 percent of white adults have an unfavorable view of the agency. Pew also found that Americans across racial and ethnic groups view ICE more unfavorably today than they did a year ago, with 56 percent of Americans saying they have a negative view of the agency overall. Only 35 percent say they view the agency favorably.

text:
By Gerald Imray

October 5, 2026

A Laotian citizen deported by the United States to Eswatini under the Trump administration's immigration crackdown was released from a maximum-security prison in the African nation on Sunday after being held there for more than a year, his lawyer said.

Phone Chomsavanh was among five immigrants deported to Eswatini — where he has no ties — in July 2025 in the early days of the Trump administration's secretive and highly contentious third-country deportation program.

Chomsavanh's U.S.-based lawyer, Tin Thanh Nguyen, said in a statement announcing his release that he had only been informed that he was being deported to Eswatini shortly before a military cargo plane carrying him and other deportees landed there more than 14 months ago.

Chomsavanh was now being deported to Laos, Nguyen said.

Chomsavanh and the four other immigrants he was deported to Eswatini with were convicted of serious crimes in the U.S., but had served their sentences by the time they were sent to the Matsapha Correctional Complex near Eswatini's administrative capital, Mbabane.

"He had already served his time. Instead they put him on a plane without telling him where it was headed and left him in a prison in a country he had never heard of, where nobody ever accused him of anything," Nguyen said. "He sat there for more than a year. No notice, no hearing, no chance to object. That is not due process by any definition."

He said in separate messages to The Associated Press that Chomsavanh had left Eswatini and landed in Johannesburg en route to Laos.

An Eswatini government spokesperson didn't immediately acknowledge Chomsavanh's release.

Chomsavanh was born in a refugee camp in Thailand after his parents fled Laos, and his family moved to the United States when he was 7, his lawyer said.

Chomsavanh is one of around 500 immigrants who have been deported from the United States to African countries that aren't their home nations since the third-country program began last year, according to advocacy groups Human Rights First and Refugees International, which have been monitoring the deportations.

Around a dozen African countries have accepted third-country deportees from the U.S., some in exchange for millions of dollars in payments. Eswatini, which is Africa's last absolute monarchy and is ruled by a king, was paid $5.1 million by the Trump administration to take deportees, according to the agreement between the countries. Eswatini has received around 30 deportees so far.

The program, which results in immigrants being held in countries they have no ties to and where they haven't been charged with any crime, has been fiercely criticized by rights groups and lawyers. It has been the subject of legal challenges in the U.S. and in some of the countries where immigrants have been sent.

The Trump administration has defended the policy as a way to quickly remove immigrants who have final deportation orders from the U.S. when their home countries might not immediately take them back.

Last month, a U.S. appeals court upheld a judge's ruling to halt the program, because it didn't give immigrants facing removal from the U.S. time to challenge their deportation to a third country if they fear persecution or torture there.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled last week to temporarily allow U.S. President Donald Trump's administration to continue swiftly removing immigrants to third countries, though it will hear arguments in the case in December.

The program has largely been carried out in secrecy, with little transparency over how many immigrants have been deported to third countries, and where and in what conditions they are being held.

authors: LEKAN OYEKANMI, ANNA WILDER and VALERIE GONAZLEZ
description:
HOUSTON (AP) — Houston's mayor on Friday directed police to limit cooperation with federal immigration authorities, signing an order that he called a result of Democrats reclaiming power in Texas for the first time in decades.
Abbott, a Trump ally, has threatened Texas cities over attempts to curtail immigration enforcement.
Houston has been a recurring scene of protests to Trump's immigration crackdown in the wake of one ICE officer fatally shooting a Mexican homebuilder and another striking a man with a car.
Last week, a grand jury in Houston indicted the ICE officer who was inside the vehicle on charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

text:
HOUSTON (AP) — Houston's mayor on Friday directed police to limit cooperation with federal immigration authorities, signing an order that he called a result of Democrats reclaiming power in Texas for the first time in decades.

The shift in the nation's fourth-largest city is one of the first actions to restrict U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations in response to Democrats' rout in Tuesday's midterm elections. It is also a sign the results are already having an impact in Texas, where Republican leaders have enthusiastically embraced President Donald Trump's mass deportation agenda.

The stunning victories included Democrat Gina Hinojosa ousting Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, which will make her Texas' first Latina governor and the first member of her party to hold the office in more than 30 years. Abbott, a Trump ally, has threatened Texas cities over attempts to curtail immigration enforcement.

"I've said many times, elections matter," Mayor John Whitmire said.

ICE would only be contacted for jailable offenses

Whitmire, a Democrat, said the city would go after immigrants "that pose a danger, not those that are going about their family business, work and education." In the case of a traffic incident, "you write a citation or you warn them and they go about their way," he said.

Under the mayor's directive, Houston police should contact ICE only if the person it stops is arrested on a charge that is subject to jailing or if ICE issues an administrative warrant, meaning that the person is wanted by immigration officials.

Houston has been a recurring scene of protests to Trump's immigration crackdown in the wake of one ICE officer fatally shooting a Mexican homebuilder and another striking a man with a car. Last week, a grand jury in Houston indicted the ICE officer who was inside the vehicle on charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

ICE has denied that the officer intentionally struck Miguel Parra Hernandez, whose leg was broken, and criticized Whitmire over making the policy change.

"We remain disappointed that sanctuary politicians seek to limit cooperation with ICE, as our law enforcement are simply fulfilling their sworn duties to serve and protect our communities," the agency said in a statement.

Texas has closely aligned with Trump on immigration

Despite a one-time $75 billion infusion from Congress, ICE remains heavily dependent on local police to find people subject to deportation and turn them over. It has done so partly by signing about 2,600 agreements — many in Texas — to deputize local police and other state and local agencies to enforce immigration laws. Texas has been a primary target for ICE arrests.

Abbott has closely aligned the state with the Trump administration to collaborate on enforcing federal immigration laws. In April, he had threatened to take away nearly $200 million in public safety grants from Austin, Dallas and Houston after city officials in Houston tried to limit police officers' cooperation with ICE.

At the time, Hinojosa called Abbott's threat to withhold funds from cities "shameful." She and Democratic Sen.-elect James Talarico took a moderate approach to immigration during their breakout campaigns, standing for robust border security but frequently criticizing Trump's crackdown, particularly over ICE officer shootings in Texas.

Spokespersons for Hinojosa and Talarico did not immediately respond to requests for comment Friday.

Though Trump's promise to arrest and deport immigrants living in the country illegally was popular during his campaign, Americans now disapprove of his approach to immigration enforcement.

In Texas, more than half of voters in the state's Senate race said the Trump administration's actions on immigration enforcement had "gone too far," according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 5,000 voters in Texas. About 2 in 10 voters said it had "not gone far enough," and a similar share said it's "been about right." That was roughly in line with what voters said nationally.

Advocate calls the change a 'sigh of relief' for immigrant communities

The change was celebrated by immigrants' rights activists in Houston who have been critical of Whitmire. Collaboration between local police and federal agents has made people afraid of getting stopped for a traffic ticket or calling for help, said Cesar Espinosa, executive director at FIEL, an immigrant rights group in Houston.

"It means that the mom taking her kid to school is not going to have a panic attack every time she sees HPD," Espinosa said.

Ruby Powers, a Houston immigration attorney, said trust won't be restored right away.

"It will probably take some time for the Houston immigrant community to truly feel a little bit safer than they did before this executive order took place," Powers said.

—-

Wilder reported from Austin, Texas, and Gonzalez reported from McAllen, Texas. Associated Press reporters Elliot Spagat in San Diego, Jesse Bedayn in Austin and Linley Sanders in Washington contributed to this report.

PUTNAM COUNTY, Fla. – After video showed law enforcement officers detaining multiple workers Thursday at the construction site of the future Palatka Primary School, the Putnam County Sheriff’s Office confirmed an Immigration and Customs Enforcement operation at the site.

The incident unfolded at the former Kelley Smith Elementary School site, now under construction as the Palatka Primary School project.

The Sheriff’s Office said the law enforcement presence near Round Lake Park Silver Lake was lifted Thursday afternoon following the ICE operation in which multiple people fled the construction site.

According top the Sheriff’s Office, the incident began before 7:30 a.m. when a traffic stop on State Road 19 prompted several people to run from law enforcement and flee into the woods. Deputies say due to the proximity to a nearby school and the possibility that one person may have been armed, Palatka Intermediate School was placed on a modified lockdown for several hours as a precaution.

By 3:30 p.m., the Sheriff’s Office announced on social media that the law enforcement presence had downgraded.

The Putnam County Sheriff’s Office says its deputies, along with the Palatka Police Department and Florida Fish Wildlife Conservation Commission responded to a mutual aid request to assist in locating the people who fled.

“This was not a sheriff’s office investigation and our role was supporting another agency as we do with other organizations,” the Putnam County Sheriff’s Office said in a statement.

The sheriff’s office noted that any additional information regarding the operation would be at the discretion of the Department of Justice.

What neighbors say they saw

Video shared with News4JAX by a nearby resident shows law enforcement officers — some wearing masks — taking multiple workers into custody at the construction site. The neighbor, who said he regularly speaks with the workers and brings them water, captured the footage.

Residents who live in the area who spoke with News4JAX off camera wondered if this may have involved Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

School district responds

Putnam County Superintendent Rick Surrency released a statement about the incident. It reads in part:

“There was a law enforcement operation that took place at the construction site of Palatka Primary School. The AJAX construction company cooperated with officers and kept the district informed about the situation.”

The statement also noted that construction at the school was delayed by several hours as a result of the operation.

The construction company had yet to respond as of Friday afternoon.

text:
A federal judge in Minnesota ordered the Trump administration to release a former Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipient, finding he was improperly arrested without a warrant in a North Dakota traffic stop and unlawfully detained.

U.S. District Judge John R. Tunheim on November 2 ordered the release of Ivan De Haro Villagrana, a Mexican citizen who came to the United States in 2002 when he was 5 years old. Villagrana obtained deferred action under the DACA program in 2016. His DACA was not renewed around 2021 following a conviction for driving under the influence, according to the court order.

DACA was created under the Obama administration in 2012 to protect certain immigrants brought to the U.S. as children from deportation and allow them to work legally. The program does not provide lawful immigration status or a pathway to citizenship.

Read More on News

The ruling comes amid the government's nationwide immigration crackdown and a historic rise in legal challenges to detention. More than 93,000 immigration-related habeas cases have been filed since January 2025, according to a ProPublica tracker, with cases recently surging in Minnesota.

Newsweek has contacted Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and the Department of Homeland Security for comment via email and is awaiting responses. The man's legal team confirmed his release but declined to comment further.

Federal judges have emerged as a key check against the Trump administration’s deportation machine. They have ordered the release of immigration detainees and called out immigration officials for disregarding due process rights and, in some cases, flouting court orders.

McKenzie County Sheriff's Deputy Brady Gustafson stopped Villagrana in Watford City, North Dakota, on September 22 for driving without headlights, according to court filings.

Villagrana was unable to provide identification, according to the ruling. Gustafson contacted ICE Officer Johnston, who interviewed the man by telephone to establish his identity and check his immigration status.

After checking government records, Johnston determined Villagrana did not have immigration documentation allowing him to remain in the United States. Authorities also identified an address for him in Mitchell, Nebraska.

Johnston determined that a warrantless arrest was justified because of what he described as "geographic challenges" and the distance between the nearest ICE office and Villagrana's residence, according to the order.

Johnston instructed Gustafson to arrest Villagrana for immigration violations, and the deputy took him to the McKenzie County Correctional Facility in Watford City.

At the time of his arrest, Villagrana had never previously been in immigration custody or placed in removal proceedings, according to his habeas petition.

Villagrana was transferred to ICE custody on September 23, per the filings. He was issued an I-200 administrative warrant and a Notice to Appear, both dated that day. ICE transported him to the Sherburne County Jail in Elk River, Minnesota, where he remained detained at the time of the ruling.

The federal government argued that Villagrana's detention was lawful and mandatory under federal immigration law and that officials had complied with the law governing warrantless immigration arrests.

Under federal law, immigration officers may arrest a noncitizen without a warrant if they have reason to believe the person is violating immigration law and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. The Eighth Circuit has interpreted "reason to believe" as requiring probable cause.

Tunheim found ICE had reason to believe Villagrana was in the U.S. without legal status after he confirmed it during the phone interview. But the judge said his failure to provide identification alone was not enough. The key question was whether ICE had reason to believe he would flee before it could obtain a warrant.

The government argued he might flee because he was in a working vehicle, lived far from the nearest ICE office, and had not regularized his immigration status.

Tunheim rejected those arguments. Villagrana stopped for the deputy, answered questions that allowed authorities to identify him, and stayed during his phone interview with ICE, the judge said.

Authorities also already had Villagrana's home address, and the government did not argue that ICE would have been unable to find him after getting a warrant.

"The warrantless arrest exceptions of § 1357(a) were not enacted for and should not be used to promote the convenience of an arresting officer," Tunheim wrote.

The judge also rejected the argument that Villagrana's immigration status showed he was likely to flee.

"Removability alone is not a reason to believe that a noncitizen is likely to escape," the judge wrote.

Tunheim pointed to Villagrana's previous participation in DACA. He had received several DACA approvals and, according to his petition, had previously given the Department of Homeland Security his fingerprints, photograph, and home address.

"These actions are not consistent with a noncitizen intending to evade detection," Tunheim wrote.

The judge found the government had not shown that Villagrana was likely to flee before authorities could get a warrant or that ICE would have been unable to find him afterward.

Tunheim wrote that authorities had "improperly arrested and detained" Villagrana and that his detention was unlawful.

He ordered Villagrana released within 48 hours of the November 2 order.

Authorities were required to give his lawyers at least 12 hours' notice of his release and return his personal belongings, including any driver's licenses, passports, or immigration documents. The judge also ordered that he be released without conditions such as a location-tracking device.

The parties were ordered to update the court on his release by November 5 and say by November 9 whether any further court proceedings were needed.

Update, 11/06/26 10:01 a.m. ET: this article was updated with a comment from Villagrana's legal team.

Topline:

The 31st Conference of Parties, or COP31, starts Monday with speeches from world leaders and will later dig into how to follow through on past climate pledges.

Why it matters: A key issue this year is the implementation of promises to transition away from fossil fuels. Co-host Turkey is also pushing a separate plan that would help do that by shifting more global energy use — including transportation — to electricity generated from solar and wind power. Negotiators also will hash out how to provide promised funds to poor countries to switch to renewables, adapt to a warmer world and recover from climate-induced damage.

The backstory: Eleven years ago, the world was on track to hit 4 C (7.2 F) of warming above preindustrial levels by the end of the century. In 2015, nations set the goal of keeping warming to below 2 C (3.6 F), but with a preferred limit of 1.5 C (2.7 F), as measured over a multi-year period. Now, the world is at 1.4 C (2.5 F) of warming and is hurtling toward 2.6 C (4.7 F), the U.N. found.

Three stories about climate change are playing out like popular movie genres as United Nations climate negotiations begin in Antalya, Turkey.

There’s the horror story. Many scientists believe global warming is accelerating. Two months ago, the U.N. readjusted its decade-old goal of limiting global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) because the world is blowing past that threshold. The fallout from rising temperatures is felt globally, with Europe’s deadly summer heat waves and Nepal’s devastating flooding as stark examples.

There’s the love triangle. For more than a century, the world has been powered by coal, oil and gas. This love affair spurred economic development, as well as the emissions warming the planet. But renewable energy is capturing some of the world’s attention because it’s cheaper and cleaner than fossil fuels. Instead of switching from one to the other, the world is using both to meet demand from power-hungry artificial intelligence and ever-growing economic development. This isn’t helping curb climate change.

Then there’s the war movie. Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine triggered a European energy shock. This year the United States and Israel bombed Iran. The conflict closed the Strait of Hormuz and sent fossil fuel prices skyrocketing, forcing nations to rethink their energy systems.

These stories are colliding as the 31st Conference of Parties, or COP31, starts Monday with speeches from world leaders and will later dig into how to follow through on past climate pledges.

A key issue this year is the implementation of promises to transition away from fossil fuels. Co-host Turkey is also pushing a separate plan that would help do that by shifting more global energy use — including transportation — to electricity generated from solar and wind power. Negotiators also will hash out how to provide promised funds to poor countries to switch to renewables, adapt to a warmer world and recover from climate-induced damage.

“It’s really the moment that we place a magnifying lens on what’s happening in the world on climate change, both good and bad,” David Waskow, international climate chief at the World Resources Institute, said.

While the U.S. is the world’s largest historic carbon polluter, it skipped last year’s COP and isn’t expected to participate this year.

“There’s always two topics in the climate negotiations that are relevant and difficult,” said Niklas Höhne, co-founder of Germany’s NewClimate Institute. “The first one is who produces emissions (and) how much. That is difficult enough. But what is even more complicated is the other issue, and that is who pays. And on this one, we are particularly in a difficult situation because the U.S., as the largest contributor, has dropped out. And there’s no other player who can jump in.”

Global climate efforts are off track

Eleven years ago, the world was on track to hit 4 C (7.2 F) of warming above preindustrial levels by the end of the century. In 2015, nations set the goal of keeping warming to below 2 C (3.6 F), but with a preferred limit of 1.5 C (2.7 F), as measured over a multi-year period.

Now, the world is at 1.4 C (2.5 F) of warming and is hurtling toward 2.6 C (4.7 F), the U.N. found.

October 2026 was the hottest October on record, and 2026 is virtually certain to end up as the second year to exceed the 1.5 degree Celsius level, behind 2024, the European climate agency Copernicus announced Friday.

“We have failed so far,” said Johan Rockström, director of Germany’s Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research.

Rockström said Earth will likely experience more extreme weather, such as floods, droughts and storms, and may soon reach “tipping points,” such as ocean currents changing and the Amazon rainforest collapsing.

It comes down to fossil fuels

Even though burning fossil fuels is the main cause of warming, it has rarely been targeted in final documents agreed upon at the conference, mostly because those decisions require consensus.

“The reason we are seeing the breach of 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming is because we avoided the absolutely fundamental question of how climate change happened and what’s responsible, the source of the problem and that’s fossil fuels,” said Harjeet Singh, founding director of Satat Sampada Climate Foundation. “Unless and until we resolve the issue of fossil fuel phase out, we will not be able to deal with the problem.”

Brazil, which hosted COP30 last year, this month released a detailed voluntary roadmap for how countries could transition away from fossil fuels.

The roadmap is meant to turn the “big problem” of reducing fossil fuels into “smaller actionable solutions,” Ana Toni, who served as CEO of last year’s climate talks, said. One key thing nations must do is stop subsidizing fossil fuels, she said. The U.N. estimates fossil fuel subsidies globally hit $1.1 trillion this year.

“What’s standing in the way is not so much technology as governments and incumbent industries,” said Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics. “One cannot underestimate the power and influence of the fossil fuel industry in slowing down action.”

Climate talks bring hope and frustration

Barbados youth activist Ashley Lashley’s first COP was five years ago. She was frustrated by the lack of progress then, but hopeful because there was urgency to keep the 1.5-degree goal alive.

Lashley still attends negotiations with some hope, but she is more frustrated than ever. She said “the science has become more alarming, but yet politically we seem to be negotiating how much failure we are prepared to tolerate.”

Qiyun Woo, a Singaporean youth environmentalist, said her generation is tired of “seeing their present and futures blanketed in wildfire smoke, in devastating floods (and) landslides.”

What gives most experts hope is how cheap solar and wind energy are, along with electric car growth, strengthening the economic argument for transitioning away from fossil fuels.

“It has never been as easy to reduce emissions as it is today because, again, this year, renewable energy has been developing faster than before,” Höhne said.

Hope for progress on the sidelines

Much of the work at climate negotiations happens on the sidelines, where not everyone has to agree and some nations do more than others.

One important sideline initiative this year is Turkey’s goal of increasing electricity’s share of global energy use from 21% to 35% by 2035, preferably by using renewable power.

Mohamed Adow, a veteran COP observer and director of Power Shift Africa, said the conference is taking place at a time when the world is deeply fragmented.

“The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has intensified economic and energy security pressures,” he said. “We don’t expect this particular conference to be able to sufficiently respond to the present day challenge ... that is affecting livelihoods and economies.”

The climate talks are hindered by the continued absence of the U.S., Adow said, adding that it wasn’t fair to nations like Nepal, which have to face catastrophic destruction alone while the world’s wealthiest country and biggest polluter sits on the fence.

“A time will come when we will have to hold the U.S. accountable for the climate harms that it’s caused,” he said.

___

Borenstein reported from Washington, Delgado from Bangkok and Arasu from Bengaluru, India.

This is the Nov. 6 issue of Make It Make Sense, LAist's elections newsletter breaking down the results of the 2026 general election. You can sign up here to receive issues in your inbox through the end of November.

Good morning! We’re beginning to feel the drag of Election Month. Cue the 🎶 Jeopardy music 🎶. We’re still waiting for an outcome on a lot of our statewide propositions, but we’ve got some juicy tax updates (if you can call them that) and another key race call.

First, now that Nithya Raman will be L.A.’s next mayor, what happens to her current council seat that stretches from the San Fernando Valley to the Santa Monica Mountains?

LAist asked L.A. City Council President Marqueece Harris-Dawson’s office: “We look forward to working with Mayor-elect Raman and will discuss with her an appointment who best serves the residents of the Fourth District,” Martin Schlageter, a senior adviser to Harris-Dawson, said in a statement.

That indicates the district could avoid a special election, but who could be appointed is still very much up in the air.

Meanwhile, Raman will have to work closely with a City Council that didn’t back her bid for mayor. LAist asked the 12 members who will be working alongside her about how they plan to work with her — read what they said here.

🌴 L.A. city attorney: Marissa Roy takes the win with a commanding lead

What happened: Marissa Roy will be the next L.A. city attorney. Her opponent, John McKinney, conceded the race, saying in a statement, “While the results are not what we hoped for, I accept the outcome and congratulate Marissa Roy on her victory. I wish her well as she prepares to serve as Los Angeles City Attorney. Her success in protecting our residents and serving the public interest will be important to the future of our city.”

How we got here: Roy held onto a strong lead over McKinney ever since polls closed, and currently has more than twice as many votes. Roy will be a fresh face in the role after incumbent city attorney Hydee Feldstein Soto was ousted in the June primary in a rare defeat of an elected city official.

What the candidates had to say:

Roy said on social media Wednesday that election night was “a really good night for the people who believe that we should take care of one another, that we can stand up for our rights — even in what feels like an increasingly lawless world — and that we will achieve justice when we fight for it.”

McKinney added that he is deeply grateful for everyone who supported his campaign, including voters, volunteers and supporters.

What’s at stake: The city attorney runs an office of more than 550 lawyers representing L.A. in all legal matters, including filing lawsuits and defending against them. Roy, backed by powerful progressives like U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, has vowed to take on the Trump administration in court.

💸 L.A. and O.C. voters are saying yes to dozens of tax measures

What happened: By LAist’s count, more than 30 cities or districts in L.A. and Orange counties asked voters to approve tax measures this election. They include sales taxes — like Measure FD in the city of Los Angeles — hotel taxes, business taxes and utility taxes. So far, all but six seem likely to pass.

🌴Measure FD is passing: L.A. city voters are steadily approving (53.68%) another half-cent sales tax, this time to bolster L.A. Fire Department resources. The sales tax will go up to 10.75%, although residents likely won’t start paying the higher rate until spring. And it still won’t be the highest in the county — Palmdale and Lancaster pay 11.75%, and San Gabriel's newly passed Measure PS brings its combined rate to 12%.

🌴 South Gate utility users tax is failing: The L.A. County city is asking residents to approve an 8% tax that would be added to bills for utilities such as electricity, water, cable and phone services. Voters are resoundingly rejecting Measure SG, with nearly 70% saying “no.”

🌴🍊 Transient occupancy taxes: Nearly a dozen of these proposals, which tax overnight hotel guests or short-term rentals, are passing in cities from Burbank in L.A. County to Los Alamitos in O.C. You can see more details in our roundup here.

Check out the vote count charts for these too-close-to-call races

🌴 L.A. City Council District 3

What’s happening: This San Fernando Valley race to replace Bob Blumenfield is getting spicy as more results roll in. Tim Gaspar, an entrepreneur who has said the city needs someone coming from the outside, is losing his early lead. He’s fallen 875 votes behind Barri Worth Girvan, a Valley community advocate with experience in various government offices.

Worth Girvan said in a social media post Thursday that she is encouraged by the trend so far. “While many ballots remain to be counted and results will continue to shift, we expect this trend to continue as more mail-in ballots are tallied, and we remain cautiously optimistic that when all the votes are counted, we will prevail.”

🌴 L.A. City Council District 9

What’s happening: The race to succeed Curren Price has been narrowing each day. Jose Ugarte had more than a 14-point lead over Estuardo Mazariegos when polls closed, but it has since shrunk to about four. Ugarte, a community outreach director, is endorsed by Price and a few other members of the City Council. Mazariegos leans more to the left and is supported by the local chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, as well as L.A. City Controller Kenneth Mejia.

Ugarte said on social media Thursday that while ballots are still being counted, “we remain optimistic.”

🍊 O.C. Supervisors District 4

In the race for the Fourth District, Democrat and Buena Park mayor Connor Traut is leading with 50.80% of the vote over Republican Tim Shaw, a member of the O.C. Board of Education.

🍊 O.C. Supervisors District 5

Democratic incumbent Katrina Foley is still on track to keep her Fifth District seat against Republican Assemblymember Diane Dixon, with a gap that’s widened to 7,600 votes. If either Republican wins, it will change the balance of power on the Board of Supervisors.

What else got called

🥑 State superintendent: Republican Sonja Shaw is conceding the race to Democrat Richard Barrera, who is more than a million votes ahead. In a social media post Wednesday, Shaw wrote, “Last night, voters made their choice. I would be lying if I said my heart wasn’t heavy.” Barrera is a labor leader and union organizer in San Diego, and has served on the board of San Diego Unified for nearly two decades.

🌴 L.A. County Superior Court judge: Office No. 87 is settled. Attorney David DeJute has conceded the race to Anthony "A.J." Bayne, a deputy public defender with over 30 years of courtroom experience. Bayne ran without a long roster of Democratic endorsements, which were a common fixture this cycle for judicial candidates. He was rated “well qualified” by the L.A. County Bar Association.

👀 We’re still watching 👀

🥑 Insurance commissioner: We’re still holding our breath on the race to lead the nation’s largest property and casualty insurance market. Two Democrats are trying to take on the role: State Sen. Ben Allen and attorney Jane Kim. Allen (47.3%) has been steadily trailing Kim (52.7%), who slightly bumped up her lead in the last few days.

🥑 The remaining props:

Prop 4: This proposal would lift the ban that keeps California and many local governments from using tax dollars to fund political campaigns. It could reshape how elections are funded, but so far, it’s failing by a few percentage points.

Prop 5: Should California change how it replaces elected state officials being recalled? The Legislature put it on the ballot, and it’s succeeding by 2 percentage points. If it holds on to the lead, voters would no longer vote on a recall and a replacement in the same election, instead punting a successor to a separate ballot.

Prop 38: This proposition is passing by a decently wide margin (55.1%). It would pave the way for the state to borrow $8.4 billion in bonds for immunology research. Supporters argued that the research could lead to treatments that help people living with cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's, but opponents say half the funds would go to just one research group.

Props 40, 41, 42: This is the billionaire’s tax and the two countermeasures designed to kill it. So far, it’s looking like Prop 40, the wealth tax, is failing (54.5% “no”), as well as Prop 41 (53.4% “no”), which would prohibit new tax revenue from being excluded from the state spending limit. The other, Prop 42, may pass (53.3% “yes”), which would ban new wealth taxes on personal property.

Prop 43: Speaking of taxes … this would make it harder to pass and raise some local taxes by bumping up the threshold of votes to a two-thirds majority. It would specifically apply to special tax measures put up by voters. It’s currently failing by about a million votes.

Prop 45: This is designed to limit environmental reviews for certain projects, such as housing and infrastructure, by cutting the time it takes to go through the state’s evaluation process. It’s opposed by groups like the National Wildlife Federation, and it's failing by about a 10-point margin.

🌴 L.A. County’s judicial seats: The races for offices 64 and 65 are still up in the air, but there are clear leaders. Maria Ghobadi, a deputy district attorney running for seat 64, has nearly 53% of the vote, while Justin Allen Clayton, a deputy public defender running in 65, has 56%. Neither of their competitors has conceded yet. Meanwhile, the fight for Office No. 131 between two public defenders is narrowing. David Ross trails Donna Tryfman, but he picked up more votes in this morning’s drop.

😰 Is it over yet? 😰

These results are based on about 8.9 million votes counted so far statewide — more than 2.5 million in L.A. County and nearly 892,000 in Orange County.

We still have a ways to go! The California secretary of state estimates there are 4.8 million ballots left to count overall, which includes 642,000 in L.A. County and 298,270 in O.C.

This election is turning out to be a banner year for voter turnout — we’re on track to far exceed the 2022 midterms. But we won’t know the full picture until after Nov. 10, the deadline for mail-in ballots to arrive. You can check on the status of your ballot via the state’s BallotTrax system.

The next local ballot counts drop this afternoon starting around 4 p.m., but hey, we’re going into the weekend! From here on out, we’ll only be back in your inboxes when there’s major news to share — like a call on the billionaire’s tax — and we’ll focus on understanding what these results mean for your life in Southern California.

text:
Prompted by the midterm election results, Houston Mayor John Whitmire said Friday he’s directing the Houston Police Department to reduce contact with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers.

Whitmire issued a new executive order directing HPD officers to contact ICE officers only when a person with an administrative ICE warrant is charged with a jailable offense, Whitmire said.

“Department personnel shall contact ICE regarding a person only if that person is already going to jail on new charges or other warrants and has a positive National Crime Information Center (NCIC) hit for an ICE administrative warrant,” Whitmire said in the order.

“The fact that a person is, or is suspected to be, subject to immigration enforcement shall not, by itself, be a basis to contact ICE, to prolong any detention, or to take any person into or hold any person in custody,” the order stated. “If a person is not otherwise going to jail on new charges or other warrants, Department personnel shall not contact ICE regarding that person.”

Sign up for the Hello, Houston! daily newsletter to get local reports like this delivered directly to your inbox.

HPD’s interactions with ICE posed a political conundrum to Whitmire over the past year.

In April, he joined a group of Houston City Council members in an effort to curtail the department's coordination with federal immigration agents — by giving officers discretion over whether or not to contact ICE about civil immigration warrants, and prohibiting them from detaining people for those warrants.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott intervened, threatening to revoke more than $110 million in public safety funding. Whitmire and the city council capitulated, reversing the measure and requiring officers to detain immigrants for a "reasonable" amount of time while waiting for ICE agents to respond to warrants.

Before the city council meeting in which officials walked back the ordinance, Whitmire's staff passed out a memo to city council members detailing more than $260 million in direct appropriations to Houston from the Republican-controlled Texas Legislature in 2025. Whitmire said a battle with the state would cost the city funding in the future.

The original ordinance required HPD to provide regular reports on those interactions, and that measure survived. According to the department's first two reports, officers contacted ICE nearly 200 times from April through September, including at least 36 instances in which HPD officers handed people directly to ICE.

Related: Houston police responded to a man in a mental health crisis. ICE arrested him

According to records obtained by Houston Public Media, some of those incidents came after people called emergency services for help — including for a suicide attempt and domestic violence.

Abbott nor the Texas Attorney General’s Office immediately responded to a request to comment regarding Whitmire’s announcement.

This is a developing story.
