text:
Over nearly 12 years as governor, Greg Abbott transformed Texas into a national model for state-led immigration enforcement, spending billions of dollars to deploy National Guard soldiers, arrest migrants and build border barriers while repeatedly testing the limits of state authority.

But on Election Day, voters ousted Abbott and elected two Democrats who have criticized his immigration policies: Gina Hinojosa, the first Mexican American elected governor of Texas, and Nathan Johnson, the first Democrat elected attorney general since 1994.

Johnson will succeed Attorney General Ken Paxton, whose office defended the governor’s immigration policies in federal court.

The historic Democratic wins across the country, including Texas, were a rebuke of the Trump administration’s economic policies and its immigration crackdown that has led to federal agents killing U.S. citizens and immigrants alike.

In Houston, where an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in July, people placed their “I voted” stickers at Salgado’s memorial.

Democrats also reclaimed support from voters in border counties, particularly the Rio Grande Valley, that had swung toward Trump just two years earlier when he campaigned on mass deportations of criminals. Leading up to the election, business owners said the arrests and deportations of undocumented people left some construction companies short of workers.

The election gives Democrats an opportunity to reshape Texas’ approach to immigration enforcement after years of Republican leadership. But Hinojosa and Johnson will inherit a system built through billions in spending, state laws, federal partnerships and court rulings that could limit how quickly they can change course.

“Obviously, a new state governor can’t rewrite immigration laws, but Texas can make a difference in terms of the choices they make about how it uses its state resources,” said Kristin Etter, director of policy and legal services at the Texas Immigration Law Council, a statewide nonprofit that advocates for immigrants’ rights.

Both Hinojosa and Johnson have been critical of Abbott’s approach to immigration. But on the campaign trail, they didn’t commit to fully dismantling the immigration framework the governor and Paxton have built for the past decade.

Abbott announced Operation Lone Star in March 2021, describing it as a collaboration between Texas Department of Public Safety troopers and National Guard members to combat human and drug smuggling into Texas. They deployed aircraft, boats and other personnel to assist in the mission. He said this was necessary because the Biden administration was implementing what he described as open-border policies.

Later that spring, he issued — and would later renew — disaster declarations that allowed the governor to mobilize resources and impose harsher criminal penalties on immigrants who crossed the border into the areas declared a disaster. Eventually, Abbott issued an executive order saying the state was being invaded and the federal government failed to defend the state, ordering troopers and National Guard members to apprehend migrants crossing the Rio Grande and return them to ports of entry so they would return to Mexico.

So far, Operation Lone Star has cost Texas $11 billion.

Later that summer in 2021, Abbott announced the state would fund and erect its own barriers along the Texas-Mexico border. Earlier this year, the Texas Facilities Commission, the state agency in charge of the building project, declared mission accomplished after the state installed about 82.2 miles of barrier. The state Legislature allocated $3.1 billion for the project as part of Operation Lone Star costs.

Hinojosa, who didn’t respond to questions from The Texas Tribune and didn’t bring up any policy issues during a news conference on Thursday, has previously said she would review the effectiveness of Operation Lone Star.

“Operation Lone Star needs to only exist to make us safer,” she said in an interview with KRGV-TV last month. “What has happened is we’ve spent billions of dollars in this state, billions of dollars to detain immigrants, to police for immigrants. That was not a plan to keep us safe. We need a review of Operation Lone Star.”

She has also described Operation Lone Star as “political theatre.”

“Public safety shouldn’t be a political stunt,” she said. “I will spend the money it takes to keep our community safe.”

The money behind Operation Lone Star isn’t permanent. The GOP-controlled Legislature last year approved nearly $3.4 billion for border security in the current state budget. Any funding to continue the operation into the next two-year budget cycle, which starts in the fall, would have to be renewed by lawmakers next session.

When the Legislature reconvenes in January, the House will be controlled by Democrats, many of whom, like Hinojosa, have condemned — and voted against — the state’s border security spending.

Hinojosa criticized Abbott for allowing state police to cooperate with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportation officers to find, arrest and deport undocumented Texans. She has also said that she supports having a secure border with Mexico.

“We need secure borders, absolutely, but targeting hard-working long-standing members of our community is not making us more secure,” she told CNN on Sept. 8.

Texas immigration lawsuits

Johnson has expressed similar sentiments while also blasting Abbott’s immigration policies. His campaign statements say that he supports cracking down on drug smuggling, human trafficking and “all forms of cross-border criminal enterprise,” and add that Texans “should reject policy and tactics that damage our sense of decency and fracture our communities.”

“We should not divert vital resources away from public safety to score political points. The attorney general has a role to play in assuring all of this: assisting with federal enforcement as appropriate, and blocking federal actions when they go too far.”

Etter said that one practical thing Hinojosa can do is stop renewing Abbott’s border security disaster proclamation, which has greatly expanded his powers without going through the state legislature.

Abbott has renewed it 69 times since first issuing the proclamation in 2021. It allowed him to justify sending National Guard members and state troopers to different parts of the Texas-Mexico border to apprehend people crossing the Rio Grande as part of Operation Lone Star.

Johnson didn’t respond to emailed questions from The Texas Tribune. As the state’s chief legal officer, Johnson will inherit decisions about whether to continue legal fights championed by Paxton or change the state’s position.

Paxton’s office helped shape national immigration policy by filing lawsuits challenging federal programs such as Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals — an Obama-era program that allows some immigrants with no criminal records to be temporarily protected from deportation.

Under Paxton’s leadership, the attorney general’s office also defended state enforcement measures such as Senate Bill 4, which allows police to arrest people suspected of crossing the Texas-Mexico border illegally.

Paxton filed more than 20 immigration-related lawsuits against the federal government that undermined the Obama and Biden administrations’ policies aimed at helping immigrants temporarily defer deportation or enter the country legally. Critics said Paxton was initially successful because he strategically filed the lawsuits in courts where judges were appointed by President Trump.

“Texas has led all of the major lawsuits attempting to end protections for immigrants in the entire country,” said Kathleen Martinez, an immigration attorney with an office in Dallas. “I think without Texas filing and leading the charge on these ridiculous federal lawsuits, it’ll help protect our programs on a federal scale.”

César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández, an immigration attorney from the Rio Grande Valley and law professor at Ohio State University, said Texas voters electing Johnson as attorney general is just as consequential as Hinojosa.

“Ken Paxton has been at the forefront of working hand-in-hand with Republican leaders of other states, and more recently with the Trump administration, to make Texas the model of harsh immigration policies,” he said.

Many of the court rulings didn’t give clear wins to Paxton, he said. In April 2026, the 5th Circuit Court of Appeals, which has a conservative majority reinforced by President Trump in his first term, ruled that Texas can enforce a law, known as SB 4, that allows police to arrest people suspected of crossing the Rio Grande.

The law says a magistrate judge can order people deported if they’re convicted of the state’s illegal entry statute. Still, the appeals court didn’t rule the law is constitutional, only that Texas can enforce it while the case is being litigated.

“The victories that Texas has won have basically allowed it to chart its own course using its own taxpayer funding to take a more aggressive approach,” García Hernández said. “But to say Texas has the permission to chart its own course is very different from saying that Texas is required to adopt that approach. So, the next batch of statewide leaders will have the opportunity to revisit how it is Texas taxpayers use their financial resources.”

Operation Lone Star arrests

Amrutha Jindal, who oversees indigent defense appointments for Operation Lone Star arrests as the director of Lone Star Defenders, expects Hinojosa to scale back Operation Lone Star but said the effects of the mission will be felt for years.

She said her organization has represented about 20,000 people who have been arrested on charges of trespassing, smuggling and a few illegal entry cases as part of Operation Lone Star. She said there are currently about 1,000 cases pending in state criminal courts.

“The program could end in name, but it wouldn’t end in practice in terms of the cases playing out,” Jindal said.

Advocates say the election results are a referendum on not just Trump’s immigration policies but Texas’ treatment of immigrants.

“Voters along the border and throughout the state sent a resounding message to Texas leaders: We have had enough, get ICE out of our communities,” said Osvaldo Grimaldo, policy strategist on border and immigrants’ rights at the ACLU of Texas.

Edna Yang, co-executive director of American Gateways, an Austin-based immigrant rights advocacy organization, said she interprets the Texas election results as a reaction to people being angry after “witnessing the cruelty towards immigrants that has been going on for the last two or so years.”

Yang added that regardless of the results, she wants to continue to put the focus on the immigrants who have been impacted by state and federal immigration policies. She hopes that with new leadership, policymakers can come up with a less punitive and more humane approach toward immigrants.

“There are still people in detention, families who are separated, asylum seekers who need representation, who are being denied access to due process,” Yang said.

text:
Dozens of people charged in connection to January's protest inside a Twin Cities church during the height of Operation Metro Surge returned to federal court on Thursday.

The group was protesting David Easterwood, a pastor who serves at Cities Church on St. Paul's Summit Avenue. Easterwood also leads the St. Paul field office of Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Thirty-nine people were charged with violating the FACE Act, which restricts "violence and intimidations targeting religious worship sites."

Among those arrested for the Jan. 18 protest were journalists Don Lemon and Georgia Fort, as well as lawyer and activist Nekima Levy Armstrong.

Defendants say they were peaceful and protected by the constitution. Inside the federal courthouse in downtown St. Paul Thursday, the judge heard from those who were involved.

For nearly an hour, lawyers spoke on behalf of two of the defendants, a couple who were arrested at their apartment a month after the protest by Homeland Security Investigation agents.

Lawyers pressed the HSI agent who arrested them about his process, specifically about why their phones were taken when only an arrest warrant — not a search warrant — was administered.

The agent said he was assigned to help HSI here for 30 days during Operation Metro Surge, and that he had probable cause to take the phones.

"The feeling among the defendants is positivity. We have hope," said defendant William Kelly. "We're going to win and I think the judge is going to give us a fair trial, if we get to trial. But he'll give us options on these motions. I think he'll make a fair ruling."

In a statement Thursday afternoon on social media, the head pastor of the church said "I saw these people scream in the faces of innocent worshipers, shut down our service, and terrorize children," adding that he wants a "fair ruling."

Later, in a statement to WCCO, lead pastor Jonathan Parnell said "The dangerous and unlawful invasion of our worship service on January 18 has harmed our church, and continues to negatively affect families and children."

"It was a shameful event that should never happen in any place of worship. We remain hopeful that common sense and justice will prevail," he continued.

This summer, St. Paul's city attorney dismissed the state level charges.

The next hearings are scheduled for Nov. 9 and 10.

When Huabing Xie told detention staff at an ICE facility in California that his chest hurt, neither of the supervising medical providers on site evaluated or treated him. Nearly two hours later, he died of a heart attack.

Delvin Rodriguez hanged himself with a bedsheet, a day after telling a guard at an ICE facility in Mississippi he didn’t want “to be on the earth anymore.” A correctional officer had removed the sheet from his cell, but another guard returned it.

At a federal detention facility in Philadelphia, medical staff diagnosed Parady La with drug withdrawal. They said he had vomited and was in a stupor. Yet they didn’t send him to the emergency room until guards discovered he had no pulse and his lips and hands had turned blue. He was later pronounced dead.

The failures that preceded the deaths of these three immigrant detainees in the first year of President Donald Trump’s second administration are described not in civil lawsuits but in scathing and blunt reports written by ICE’s internal investigators.

The Chronicle obtained 29 mortality reviews of immigration detainees who died from January 2025 through January 2026. Twenty-three of those immigrants died after receiving medical care that the agency itself determined was deficient. The others received care that fell within safe limits, the reports found.

The records, obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request, provide stark evidence of what immigration advocates have called a “crisis” since Trump and his administration launched an aggressive deportation push. Immigrants without permanent legal status — a majority of whom have no criminal convictions — have been subjected to dangerous lockups run by the government or private prison contractors around the country.

The documents represent the first official acknowledgement by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement of widespread failures in the healthcare provided to people who died in custody, even as the administration has repeatedly and publicly claimed immigrants receive “comprehensive medical care,” which the Department of Homeland Security has described as the “best healthcare that many aliens have received in their entire lives.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

To the contrary, ICE’s investigators found that detention staff “deviated from safe limits of practice” or “did not provide medical care within safe limits of practice” for the 23 detainees.

The reviews determined that medical staff repeatedly fell short of an array of detention standards, including failing to provide emergency care. At least eight times, medical staff failed to perform CPR correctly or at all on immigrant detainees who then died. In only three of the 23 cases, investigators concluded that deviations from safe limits of practice did not directly contribute to a person’s death.

A Chronicle investigation published in April found that at least 17 people died in ICE custody over the same period after medical staff delayed or failed to provide critical care that might have saved their lives. Nearly all of those people are among the 23 whom ICE found to have received deficient care.

“These records are from ICE’s own review, and the data are damning,” said Chioma Chukwu, executive director of the nonpartisan watchdog American Oversight, which previously sued the federal government to obtain mortality reviews of deaths during the first Trump administration and in 2021. “When an administration knows the consequences and keeps dismantling the safeguards, cruelty is a choice.”

Loading...

Overall, at least 62 people have died in ICE custody since Trump returned to office in 2025, including three people in eight days in late October.

In a statement to the Chronicle, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said that “all in-custody deaths are tragic, taken seriously, and are thoroughly investigated by law enforcement.” The department said there had been “NO spike in deaths,” despite federal data showing that the 33 deaths in ICE detention in 2025 were the most in any year since the agency’s creation in 2003.

The record number of fatalities was not solely due to the surge in people being detained, a Chronicle analysis found. The deaths have occurred at the highest rate per average daily population of people in detention since at least 2009, with the exception of 2020, when death rates soared due to COVID-19.

The Chronicle’s findings, shared with lawmakers, spurred immediate calls for accountability from congressional Democrats, who won control of the House and Senate on Tuesday.

Rep. Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, the ranking Democratic member of the House Homeland Security Committee, said detention contractors must not only face financial penalties, but ICE should cancel the contracts of those that don’t meet federal standards and put the health of detainees at risk. He said he plans to hold hearings on the issue next year.

“This investigation found proof that ICE’s detention contractors have not been providing proper medical care to detainees — and that lack of care has tragically contributed to deaths,” Thompson said. “ICE has not held these contractors responsible, and that must change.”

ICE Health Service Corps, which administers and provides healthcare for people in ICE detention, performed the mortality reviews by examining medical records, conducting on-site staff interviews and watching available surveillance video. The investigations are intended to “determine the appropriateness of clinical care” prior to a person’s death in detention and whether policy changes are needed. They are much more detailed than the briefer “detainee death reports” that ICE is legally required to publish within 90 days of an individual’s death in its custody.

Joseph Nwadiuko, an assistant professor of medicine at the University of Pennsylvania and internal medicine doctor who researches healthcare in detention, read the documents at the Chronicle’s request. He said that they “show a lot of tragedy.”

“They show a lot of people who are in distress and who are not getting the help they need when they need it,” Nwadiuko said. “And it’s due to systemic failures on ICE’s part.”

A majority of the deaths occurred in facilities operated by private prison contractors, the largest of which are GEO Group and CoreCivic. Two deaths of ICE detainees occurred in facilities run by the Federal Bureau of Prisons.

Emery Nelson, a spokesperson for the Federal Bureau of Prisons, said individuals in custody have access to “community-standard, patient-centered treatment … as clinically indicated.” He said, “We take seriously our duty to protect the individuals entrusted in our custody, as well as maintain the safety of correctional employees and the community.”

CoreCivic, which was faulted by ICE investigators for substandard medical care provided to three detainees who died in its facilities, said its leadership team closely reads ICE’s mortality reviews “to assist us in providing safe, humane and respectful care at all our facilities.” The company posted $116.5 million in profits last year and earned record revenue amid a surge in people detained.

GEO Group, which boasted of record new business last year as it secured federal contracts, did not respond to a detailed request for comment about the mortality reviews. ICE faulted the company’s staff for substandard medical care provided to 10 people who died under the company’s watch during the same time period.

The internal reviews call for ICE to ensure implementation of a “correction action plan, if applicable.” But they do not describe any disciplinary actions or sanctions against companies or staff providing substandard medical care leading to a death.

ICE did not respond to the Chronicle’s questions about what discipline, if any, is meted out to those whose actions are linked to a person’s death in custody.

The release of the mortality reviews to the Chronicle came amid more than a dozen pending lawsuits seeking these records that had been filed by government watchdogs, journalists and relatives of the deceased. In late September, ICE posted some of the mortality reviews on its FOIA webpage, then quickly deleted them.

“In the past, it has been exceedingly difficult to obtain records related to deaths of people in ICE detention under FOIA absent protracted litigation,” said Eunice Cho, associate litigation director at the National Immigrant Justice Center, who advised American Oversight on its lawsuit for past mortality reviews.

David Loy, legal director for the First Amendment Coalition, said the disclosure to the Chronicle could make it more difficult for ICE to withhold similar documents in the future. Congress, he noted, has authorized billions in spending for immigration enforcement as the Trump administration has intensified its crackdown.

“If a human being dies in government custody, the public has a compelling interest in knowing what goes into providing such medical care,” Loy said. “The public has a right to know, how is the government executing this massive ramp-up in immigration detention?”

In facility after facility across the country, the mortality reviews show, ICE medical staff failed to administer lifesaving measures as patients were in crisis, failed to perform CPR correctly or took too long to try to intervene in major emergencies.

Jean Wilson Brutus, a Haitian migrant, had just been brought to GEO Group’s Delaney Hall Detention Facility in Newark, N.J., on Dec. 12, 2025, when he began struggling to breathe. As he walked with a guard to his cellblock, he abruptly stopped and lowered himself to the floor. The guard radioed for medical help.

Three members of the medical staff arrived, but none recognized Brutus’ irregular breathing, inconsistent pulse and unresponsiveness as symptoms of cardiac arrest, ICE investigators concluded.

As a result, they did not treat Brutus with an automated external defibrillator, a standard device that shocks the heart to restore normal rhythms. They were also slow to perform CPR, and then did so wrongly, applying chest compressions at an angle, away from the chest, the investigators noted after reviewing surveillance video. Further, medical personnel failed to provide supplemental oxygen for nearly 10 minutes.

The mortality review team faulted the facility for not having required lifesaving devices including a defibrillator or oxygen tank immediately available at the scene.

Brutus’ cousin, Evans Belony, said in an interview that Brutus had worked as a security guard in Haiti and at a chicken slaughterhouse in Brazil before arriving at the U.S. border in Texas in 2023. There, Border Patrol allowed him into the country but placed him in removal proceedings.

“He was a very handy person,” Belony said. “Even though he was big in stature, he was so soft on the inside.”

Oliver Barry, an attorney representing Brutus’ relatives, said the report, which the Chronicle shared with him, “differs wildly” from previous statements ICE made about Brutus’ death. In the previously released, congressionally mandated death report, ICE laid out a chronological account of the medical emergency but did not note any of the shortcomings in his treatment.

“This is the most factual report or information thus far,” he said.

On April 25, 2025, at the Broward Transitional Center in Pompano Beach, Fla., Marie Ange Blaise was found unresponsive inside her dormitory. A responding nurse administered an ammonia inhalant — used to revive people who faint — and detected a pulse, but did not do CPR or take any basic life-support interventions. She was pronounced dead within 20 minutes.

“They did not appropriately treat Ms. Blaise’s presenting symptoms during the medical emergency,” the investigators wrote, concluding that staff at the GEO Group-run facility failed to provide appropriate emergency care and did not provide medical care within safe limits of practice.

In another case, ICE investigators found that detention staff at GEO Group’s Moshannon Valley Processing Center in Clearfield County, Pa., failed to provide up-to-standard care for a 46-year-old Eritrean man who should have been sent to an emergency room.

Fouad Saeed Abdulkadir, a former green card holder, was placed in deportation proceedings after being convicted of welfare fraud in 2024. He told medical staff he had chest pain and difficulty breathing, and his pulse was measured at 132 bpm, but staff didn’t send him to the ER or arrange a follow-up. Investigators also concluded that detention medical staff did not provide proper treatment for his asthma, diabetes and high cholesterol.

Six days later, at 2 a.m. on Dec. 14, detention staff found Abdulkadir in his cell struggling to breathe and called 911. Emergency medical service workers arrived, but had to wait eight minutes outside before staff escorted them in, which ICE investigators said amounted to “inappropriate emergency care.”

In the meantime, Abdulkadir lost his pulse. His oxygen levels fell. By the time EMS technicians got in and took over lifesaving efforts, it was too late. Abdulkadir died within the hour from a pulmonary embolism, a blood clot in a lung artery.

Dr. Nwadiuko, who examined Abdulkadir’s mortality review, said it was as if medical staff “slept-walked for six days” while Abdulkadir deteriorated. Still, if EMS had not been kept waiting outside the facility, they could have saved his life, he said.

“Time is of the essence in cases like this,” he said. “There should be a protocol so an EMS provider rolls up and doesn’t have any difficulty walking through the front doors to take care of a patient who is coding.”

The mortality reviews obtained by the Chronicle documented failures beyond emergency response. In the cases of 11 people who died, ICE investigators criticized choices in their medical care, including inadequate treatment of chronic conditions and missed follow-up on warning signs.

One of these was Nenko Stanev Gantchev, a 56-year-old Bulgarian man who came to the U.S. in 1995 on a temporary exchange visa. When ICE arrested him in September 2025 on an outstanding removal order, he was taking medications for high blood pressure and Type 2 diabetes.

Though staff recognized he was at risk for a life-threatening condition in which plaque builds up on the walls of the heart, ICE investigators found that medical staff at a GEO Group facility, North Lake Processing Center in Baldwin, Mich., did not provide him with adequate chronic disease management nor the necessary medication to lower cholesterol and reduce his risk of heart attack and stroke.

ICE’s investigators also found that medical staff prescribed him with medication that was inadequate to control his diabetes, and another drug that is considered dangerous for people like him who are showing signs of possible heart failure.

After discovering abnormalities in Gantchev’s heart’s electrical activity on an electrocardiogram and detecting a murmur, and given his dizziness and low blood pressure, staff should have sent him to the emergency room and ordered an immediate echocardiogram to check how well his heart was functioning, said Nwadiuko, who reviewed his mortality report.

Instead, medical staff scheduled him for a cardiology appointment on Dec. 19, a month out. He would not survive for that long. On Dec. 15, he was found unresponsive on his cell floor with a faint pulse.

ICE investigators criticized staff members for delaying lifesaving care by transporting Gantchev to the medical department before starting those procedures, instead of doing it on the spot. Once there, they delayed connecting him to supplemental oxygen. He died that evening. His cause of death was listed as hypertensive and atherosclerotic heart disease.

ICE investigators concluded that staff at the GEO Group-operated North Lake Processing Center failed to provide care “within safe limits of practice.”

Another theme emerges in the reports obtained by the Chronicle. Repeatedly, ICE investigators found, staff at detention facilities failed to recognize, supervise or protect detainees suffering from serious mental illness who later died by suicide.

Reviewers concluded that, in several deaths, staff lacked or misplaced the required “cutdown” tools, delaying efforts to free people who had hanged themselves.

At Adams County Correctional Center, a CoreCivic facility in Mississippi, Delvin Rodriguez demonstrated a choking gesture and pointed to a sheet in his cell. He told a correctional officer, crying, that he didn’t want “to be on earth anymore.” Yet staff did not communicate his suicidal gestures and behaviors to medical staff or incoming custody staff, ICE investigators found.

The 39-year-old man had been on his way to a construction job site in the resort town of Breckenridge, Colo., when he was arrested by ICE in September 2025, alongside other Latino workers, said his attorney Alex Sanchez. Rodriguez had no criminal convictions.

An only son in a family of sisters, he came to the U.S. to find work to support his parents, children and siblings in Nicaragua. Sanchez said he was the “pillar of his family.” His relatives, who declined to be interviewed, said he didn’t have a history of mental illness or suicidal ideation prior to being detained.

“This report confirms that the system failed Delvin,” Sanchez said.

Trump administration officials have repeatedly responded to claims of medical failures within ICE detention by arguing that detainees can choose to “self-deport.” An agency spokesperson, Jason Sweeney, previously told the Chronicle in response to inquiries about delays in medical care that “being in detention is a choice,” and said ICE offers $2,600 and a free flight to those who voluntarily leave the country.

But Rodriguez had agreed to “self-deport” within a day or two of arriving at the facility, Sanchez said. He wanted to return to his family in Nicaragua. But for reasons that are unclear, he was kept locked up for almost three months, awaiting deportation. ICE records state he was scheduled for a deportation flight home on Dec. 13, 2025.

On Dec. 3, after Rodriguez told two guards he wanted to die, they did not alert medical staff or the incoming shift, investigators found, only removing a sheet from his cell. The next day, an unknown staff member placed a sheet back in Rodriguez’s cell, which he used to hang himself.

Such communication failures were common, according to the reports: In 13 cases, ICE investigators found, staff failed to relay warning signs to providers.

When Maksym Chernyak, a 44-year-old Ukrainian war refugee, experienced a seizure on Feb. 18, 2025, while detailed at Krome Processing Center in Miami, Fla., medical staff didn’t call 911 for about an hour, during which time staff witnessed him suffering several more seizures, ICE records show.

Agency investigators found numerous failures in his care, but said they “did not directly contribute to his death,” without elaborating.

Katie Blankenship, an attorney representing Chernyak’s family in a wrongful death claim, questioned that conclusion.

“What we have known from the beginning and what we’ve known today from the report is that ICE’s medical neglect killed Maksym Chernyak,” she said. “This is a government that will never take accountability.”

Chaofeng Ge, a 32-year-old Chinese man, died by hanging in ICE detention on Aug. 5, 2025, days after being detained. He had been taken into immigration custody from a jail, where he’d served time for credit card fraud.

When he was booked into Moshannon Valley Processing Center, the facility in Pennsylvania, his medical paperwork showed he had attempted suicide in the past and used antidepressants. ICE investigators wrote that medical staff “did not take appropriate action” and kept him in the general population.

Four days later, two officers found Ge hanging in a handicapped shower stall, bound at his hands and feet. “Custody staff who found Mr. Ge did not immediately relieve the pressure off his neck and cut him down, activate an emergency response, or call emergency medical services,” ICE investigators wrote.

Yanfeng Ge said in an emailed statement that his brother died “cast aside, isolated and ignored.”

“There were so many opportunities to save him, but no one at Moshannon Valley cared enough about him to pay attention,” Ge said. “It did not have to be this way.”

description:

Instead, agents have to try and apprehend migrants on city streets.
The Brooklyn arrests came amid a wider enforcement push, with ICE arresting nearly 2,200 illegal migrants during a statewide crackdown in August, known as Operation Rotten Apple.
The stark warnings offered a glimpse into the dangers agents face as they head onto the streets to carry out arrests.
He also rejected accusations that ICE agents abduct or disappear people, defending the speed of the arrests as a safety precaution.
text:
BROOKLYN, N.Y. — With New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani escalating his opposition to ICE, federal agents continue to carry out high-stakes street arrests that one of the agency's top officials says could be avoided if the city cooperated with federal authorities instead of enforcing its sanctuary policies.

Fox News Digital embedded with ICE agents last Thursday, getting a rare, firsthand look at the surveillance, tense stakeouts and split-second decisions behind arrests on Brooklyn streets — while riding along with the agency's top local enforcement official as he blasted city and state leaders over policies he says put officers and the public at risk.

The early-morning operation saw agents move in on two men, handcuffing them and rushing them into unmarked SUVs. The first arrest was over in seconds. The second turned into a tense struggle.

MAMDANI CALLS ICE A 'ROGUE' AGENCY AFTER NYC SHOOTING, CLAIMS AGENTS VIEW LAW AS 'MERELY A SUGGESTION'

Behind the wheel was Ken Genalo, head of ICE's Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) in New York City, who accused Mamdani, Gov. Kathy Hochul and the City Council of keeping dangerous offenders on the streets.

"100% all of this is about politics. It is not about public safety," Genalo said as he sat in his vehicle while his team staked out a Georgian illegal migrant charged with sexual abuse.

He argued that sanctuary laws force ICE to track down suspects who should have been handed over to agents at local jails. Instead, agents have to try and apprehend migrants on city streets.

"They don't acknowledge the victims, they don't acknowledge the angel families, those that unfortunately have suffered severe loss due to illegal alien crime," he said.

The operation came less than a week after Mamdani released a Spanish-language video advising New Yorkers on how to respond to ICE agents, as tensions flared following the shooting of a Dominican migrant who authorities say tried to ram officers with his vehicle. The migrant had been in the U.S. for just three years but had already racked up a lengthy rap sheet for theft, robbery, assault, drug and weapons offenses, according to DHS.

The Brooklyn arrests came amid a wider enforcement push, with ICE arresting nearly 2,200 illegal migrants during a statewide crackdown in August, known as Operation Rotten Apple.

But the ride-along with ICE revealed what those figures cannot: hours of painstaking surveillance, careful planning and tense waiting — all for arrests that can be over in seconds and quickly escalate.

WATCH: NYC ICE official rips Mamdani, sanctuary laws after tense street arrests

DHS BOSS REVEALS OVAL OFFICE PLAN TO 'WITHHOLD FUNDING' FROM SANCTUARY CITIES AFTER AGGRESSIVE NEW YORK BUST

Inside ICE's predawn raids

Before dawn Thursday, more than a dozen armed ICE agents gathered at a secret Brooklyn location, wearing protective vests marked "ERO."

Commanders briefed them on several targets and the potential risks: one might be armed, another was an amateur boxer. The stark warnings offered a glimpse into the dangers agents face as they head onto the streets to carry out arrests.

Agents checked their gear, attached body cameras to their vests and hit the streets around 5:50 a.m.

Genalo drove an unmarked SUV, monitoring radio chatter and explaining how agents tracked their targets, what could go wrong and why timing was critical.

The first target was Nika Tkeshelashvili, 40, a Georgian national who ICE said entered the United States illegally through the southern border in January 2023 and was arrested in September on a first-degree sexual abuse charge. The charge remains pending.

His next immigration court hearing wasn't until October 2028 — a five-year wait that drew disbelief from Genalo.

As the SUV rolled through Brooklyn, Genalo explained how agents establish a "pattern of life" — studying a suspect's routine to determine when and where to make an arrest.

In Tkeshelashvili's case, the intelligence was surprisingly mundane. Agents believed he regularly emerged between 7 a.m. and 7:30 a.m. to move his car and avoid a parking ticket.

Unmarked ICE vehicles took up positions along nearby streets while Fox News Digital waited with Genalo roughly half a block away, with a clear view of the apartment building where the Georgian national was expected to emerge.

But as the minutes ticked by, he was nowhere to be seen. Genalo remained unfazed.

Meanwhile, daylight crept across the neighborhood, bringing commuters, schoolchildren and growing traffic. Genalo explained that darkness was an ally during these operations, but as the streets filled, a discreet arrest became harder.

MAMDANI DEMANDS TRUMP RELEASE ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SHOT BY ICE AGENT AS PROTESTS ERUPT IN THE BRONX

Even weeks of surveillance could not guarantee Tkeshelashvili would appear, Genalo explained. If he stayed inside, agents might have to return another day.

Then, at 7:57 a.m., a voice broke over the radio.

"Target one just stepped out with a cigarette going towards the car if I'm not mistaken," an agent reported.

Genalo raised his hand and pointed toward the radio. "I think that's ours," he said as more chatter crackled through the SUV.

"He's wearing a black vest, red shirt, red hat," another agent radioed.

"Team two, that's Tango. That's Tango," an agent called out.

Within moments, agents converged on Tkeshelashvili in the middle of the street. Genalo accelerated toward the scene, the arrest unfolding through the SUV's windshield.

By the time Fox News Digital pulled up, officers had already handcuffed Tkeshelashvili and were moving him into a waiting vehicle. He remained calm and said little. Within moments, the team was moving on toward Target 2.

Genalo hailed the arrest as "textbook" and "flawless," praising the intelligence, timing and surprise that allowed agents to secure their target without a struggle.

Speed, he explained, was critical.

Minutes earlier, we heard over Genalo’s radio that another ICE team had encountered agitators blowing whistles, shouting and warning locals that federal agents were nearby.

The team was pursuing an Ecuadorian migrant who faced sexual misconduct charges involving a child, Genalo said, but the agitators disrupted the operation.

"Why would you protest that we're trying to arrest this individual?" Genalo said.

A tense struggle on Brooklyn streets

As we pulled away from the first arrest scene, Genalo briefed us on the next target: Yves Frantz Augustine, 45, a Haitian national who ICE said entered the U.S. legally in 1997 but overstayed his visa. Ordered deported in 2006, he remained in the country, later amassing a criminal record that included an assault conviction for which he served seven years in prison, along with weapons offenses and a terroristic threat case, according to ICE.

Augustine previously served seven years in prison for assault, but ICE's attempt to deport him in 2011 during the Obama administration failed because Haiti would not issue the necessary travel documents, Genalo said.

ICE tried to take him into custody after further arrests, but New York authorities refused to hand him over despite three detainer requests, according to Genalo.

Agents faced a major concern during this operation: Augustine was taking a child to school.

Genalo explained that agents would wait until Augustine drops off the child before moving in, saying ICE policy is to avoid making arrests near schools or in the presence of children.

Another team of agents was tracking Augustine from cars and on foot, relaying updates over the radio as Brooklyn's morning rush gathered pace.

Genalo pulled up alongside the curb, explaining that Augustine was expected to walk straight toward our SUV. We waited as traffic rolled past and officers closed in on his position.

At approximately 8:26 a.m., the go-ahead came over the radio.

Agents quickly surrounded Augustine just ahead of our SUV, grabbing his arms as they tried to handcuff him.

"Don't move! Police! Let me see your hands!" an officer shouted, drawing his weapon.

"We have a warrant for your arrest!" another announced.

But Augustine refused to put his hands behind his back, prompting the agents to press him against the metal shutters of a closed storefront as they struggled to cuff him.

"No, no, no, no," Augustine shouted.

"Sir, don't fight," an officer warned, while a third appeared and tried to calm him.

"Just put your hands behind your back, sir," the third agent said, placing his hand on his shoulder.

As agents led Augustine away in handcuffs, his jacket slipped down, revealing the words "it's all a trap" emblazoned across the back of his shirt. The front read "NOCOMP."

He continued pulling back as agents moved him toward a waiting SUV, pleading for his children.

"Think about my kids," he cried out, according to footage recorded by Fox News Digital.

Appearing stunned, he continued questioning the arrest.

"A warrant for what?" he shouted and asked to call his wife before claiming he was now a U.S. citizen. An officer showed him the warrant and gave him time to read it before placing him in the SUV.

Genalo disputed the citizenship claim, citing Augustine's 2006 deportation order.

The arrest took roughly four minutes, far longer than the first, before agents secured Augustine and cleared the street.

Back in the SUV, Genalo said Augustine's resistance forced officers to use additional restraint techniques, explaining that agents typically move detainees to a secure location before transferring them to an ICE processing facility.

"We want to get in, make the arrest, and get out as fast as possible," Genalo said.

He also rejected accusations that ICE agents abduct or disappear people, defending the speed of the arrests as a safety precaution.

"We don't kidnap people, we don't disappear people. We arrest people," he said.

ICE vs. City Hall

For Genalo, the arrests reflected a wider battle over law and order — with ICE trying to remove dangerous offenders while city leaders refuse to cooperate and protesters work to disrupt operations.

"You have murderers on the street. I mean, that by itself is absolutely amazing that you can say you're keeping the community safe by releasing murderers back on the streets," he said.

Genalo said both Brooklyn suspects had previously been in local custody, but authorities ignored ICE requests to hand them over. The refusals, he argued, wasted taxpayer money and put officers, suspects and the public at risk.

During the stakeout for Tkeshelashvili, agents feared their cover was blown when an NYPD patrol car appeared, adding another hurdle amid limited cooperation with local police. Genalo suggested a resident may have called police, but the concern was quickly resolved.

Genalo laid much of the blame on Mamdani, Hochul and the City Council, accusing them of putting political ideology ahead of public safety while allowing offenders to return to the communities they claim to protect.

"They're criminals that committed heinous crimes. And they should not be in the community," Genalo said of many of the migrants ICE has been apprehending.

For Genalo, a Brooklyn native and 34-year law enforcement veteran deployed to Ground Zero with a special response team after 9/11, the breakdown in cooperation is personal. He recalled when ICE worked closely with local police and had its own unit at Rikers Island, taking more than 100 people a week into custody directly from the jail. Today there is no cooperation.

Genalo blamed former Mayor Bill de Blasio for ending the arrangement and said former Mayor Eric Adams tried to restore cooperation but was hamstrung by the City Council. Mamdani, meanwhile, has called for ICE to be abolished and publicly opposed its enforcement operations.

Genalo repeatedly fumed over New York City's sanctuary policies throughout the ride-along, challenging city leaders to put the issue on the ballot and let New Yorkers decide whether police should cooperate with ICE.

"Let the residents decide," he said.

A bipartisan push for a public vote in 2024 and 2025 went nowhere. Genalo suggested council members feared the result.

Genalo also criticized anti-ICE protest networks that monitor federal vehicles, alert residents and mobilize protesters when officers are spotted.

Even before Thursday's operation began, a car carrying civilians circled the agents' secret meeting point and parked nearby, raising suspicions that its occupants might be spotters. Officers kept watch until the car drove away.

"I give a lot of kudos to the men and women of ICE in New York City and nationwide staying professional in spite of the agitation that they're facing," he said.

Despite his blistering criticism of Mamdani and the city's sanctuary policies, Genalo said he was willing to talk with the mayor.

"I just wish we could sit down and collaborate and come to an agreement because we have the same job to do, and that's to keep the people of the community of New York City safe," Genalo said.

"The men and women of ICE in New York City will not waver," he said.

text:
The United States is scheduled to appear in Geneva on November 10 for its Universal Periodic Review, the United Nations’ peer review process of every member state’s rights record. But the US is unlikely to show: the Trump administration declared in 2025 that the US would not participate.

After the US failed to turn up in November 2025, the review was rescheduled. Should the US again fail to appear next week, it should not be given another extension and should not be exempt from this process which, as the name suggests, applies to every UN member country.

As part of the process, US and international rights groups, including Human Rights Watch, made 192 submissions highlighting a range of human rights issues. The civil society submissions paint a worrying picture, with a dramatic worsening of the US government’s rights record over the past year.

At President Trump’s direction, the US government dismantled its civil rights enforcement apparatus. It has also violated the prohibition on non-refoulement and sent Venezuelan men to torture in El Salvador’s prisons. The Trump administration also continues to retaliate against opponents, restrict the rights of transgender people, and eliminate regulations that curb climate warming pollutants, among other things. In an unprecedented assault on the rule of law, the administration escalated its sanctions against the ICC, targeting the court as a whole.

State legislation and targeted federal funding cuts have dramatically reduced access to safe abortion care and other reproductive health care in many states, curtailing women’s rights. During the immigration crackdown, authorities have separated breastfeeding and other parents from their children and have detained pregnant women despite a longstanding government policy that directs agencies to avoid this except in limited circumstances.

The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights has highlighted concerns about deaths in immigration detention; harmful migration policies and enforcement; and sanctions against the ICC and Palestinian rights groups. The UN Special Procedures mandate holders have also raised concerns regarding: unlawful killings at sea; allegedly arbitrary removal of immigration judges and politicization of immigration courts; and unlawful use of lethal force by immigration enforcement agents.

text:
By all accounts, Tuesday’s election went off with few complications, but for the immigrant communities, there was fear of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents showing up at polling places.

In response, two community organizations stepped up to host voting centers at their offices, providing safe spaces for people to cast their ballots.

“Especially the members of our community that have been historically marginalized, underserved, that feel that they have not been included or fear has been used as a tactic against them to not engage in our election process,” said Jimmy Figueroa, the senior director of youth and community programs at Chicano Federation of San Diego.

In front of Barrio Station in Logan Heights, the lines stretched out the door on Election Day, but the wait time was minimal.

“For the people that I saw at the back of the line, coming 20 minutes later, I would already see them at the front of the line,” Figueroa said.

Barrio Station hasn’t been a polling place since 2020, when San Diego switched from the precinct format to the vote center format.

Figueroa said it was important for the Federation to reestablish the location as a polling place to ensure the community felt safe and knew the staff.

“It was pivotal to have the voting center here at Barrio Station, specifically accessible to the Barrio Logan community,” he said.

This comes amid the Trump administration's surge in immigration crackdowns in recent weeks. There were some reports of ICE agents at vote centers in Northern California. That spooked some San Diego residents.

“We've sensed that many of our immigrant communities have expressed some level of fear regarding the increased immigration enforcement and the horrific kidnapping of our community members,” said Homayra Yusufi with Partnership for the Advancement of New Americans (PANA). “So we want to make sure that folks had a safe space that they could cast their vote.”

Yusufi, a senior policy strategist at PANA, said it was the first year the organization hosted a vote center.

“We had a grandma come here,” she said. “She had lived in San Diego and City Heights for decades and had never voted before, and this was her first time coming in here. And because she knew where PANA was, she felt safe here.”

The fear was not unfounded. A recent ProPublica investigation found that more than 500 U.S. citizens have been detained by ICE since the start of the second Trump administration.

“It was great to see us prioritizing our neighbors over hate,” Yusufi said. “And so I am just really excited to see the record number of turnout that happened yesterday at the elections.”

She said Tuesday's high voter turnout gave her hope.

title: Belgium to allow home searches for suspected illegal migrants | The Daily Star
description:
Belgium's parliament early on Friday approved a controversial law allowing police to enter the homes of suspected undocumented migrants who have ignored orders to leave the country.
Around 3,000 people formed a human chain around Brussels' Palace of Justice on Wednesday evening to protest the bill.
Searches will be limited to the homes of people who have been denied asylum in Belgium, have ignored orders to leave and are seen to be a threat to public security.
Home searches must be agreed to by an investigative judge and can only occur between 5am and 9am, with immigration officials present.
Ahead of the vote, Amnesty International urged lawmakers to reject the legislation, which it said could also affect people who help undocumented migrants.
text:
Belgium's parliament early on Friday approved a controversial law allowing police to enter the homes of suspected undocumented migrants who have ignored orders to leave the country.

The measure is part of a broader push by Prime Minister Bart De Wever's right-leaning coalition to limit migration and increase expulsions of those who have been denied the right to stay in the country.

The legislation has drawn strong opposition from human rights groups and lawyers, who argue that allowing police to enter private homes for immigration enforcement risks undermining constitutional rights and privacy laws.

Around 3,000 people formed a human chain around Brussels' Palace of Justice on Wednesday evening to protest the bill. More than 50 other demonstrations and gatherings were organised in towns and cities across the country, Belgian media reported.

The law was finally approved by a majority of lawmakers around 5am local time (0400 GMT), following a lengthy debate that lasted throughout the night.

Searches will be limited to the homes of people who have been denied asylum in Belgium, have ignored orders to leave and are seen to be a threat to public security.

Home searches must be agreed to by an investigative judge and can only occur between 5am and 9am, with immigration officials present.

Ahead of the vote, Amnesty International urged lawmakers to reject the legislation, which it said could also affect people who help undocumented migrants.

The government has defended the measure as a tool to enforce deportation orders for people who are considered a danger to public order or national security.

text:
Paula Valentina Albornoz Hernandez.

A 23-year-old UC Berkeley student from Colombia was arrested by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents at San Francisco International Airport while waiting to board a flight to Portland for a vacation with her boyfriend, the Associated Press reported. Paula Valentina Albornoz Hernandez is currently being held at ICE's California City Detention Center. Her arrest has prompted protests and support efforts from fellow students and university officials, while immigration lawyers have filed a habeas corpus petition challenging her detention. Albornoz Hernandez arrived in the US in September 2022 and overstayed her visa, but subsequently applied for asylum, citing severe gender-based violence in Colombia. Her application is still pending, and she had a valid work permit, according to her attorney Niko De Bremaeker of Centro Legal de la Raza. She was travelling to Portland with her boyfriend on Friday when an ICE agent in plain clothes approached her in the airport's departure area and asked her name. The agent reportedly guessed her identity three times before she confirmed it. ICE agents then separated the couple and informed her that she was being detained because her visa had expired. Her boyfriend, identified only as Anthony, described the arrest as frightening, saying he felt helpless as agents separated them.

DHS defends arrest

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) confirmed that ICE agents had detained Albornoz Hernandez at the airport. It said she had entered the country legally on September 6, 2022, with permission to stay until March 6, 2023, but had failed to leave after her authorised period expired. The department said she would receive due process and remain in ICE custody while removal proceedings were underway. It also maintained that having a work permit or a pending asylum application did not grant her legal immigration status. Her lawyers, however, have challenged the detention in a federal court, arguing that ICE officers did not present a warrant or assess whether she posed a flight risk before taking her into custody. The petition seeks her release and asks the court to prevent further detention unless the government establishes that she poses a flight risk or a danger to the community.

University seeks her release

UC Berkeley Chancellor Rich Lyons also expressed concern over the detention, describing Albornoz Hernandez as an outstanding student and asking authorities to allow her to resume her studies. The arrest could be the first detention of an active UC Berkeley student by ICE since the Trump administration began its mass deportation drive last year, according to the university and her attorney. Albornoz Hernandez, who previously attended San Jose City College, was studying business administration at Berkeley and conducting research on artificial intelligence. She is scheduled to appear before an immigration court on November 17. Her lawyers' federal challenge to the detention is a separate legal proceeding. text:
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

LOS ANGELES — Long before the Trump administration started deporting hundreds of thousands of immigrants, many with school-age children, public schools nationwide faced a massive and accelerating drop in student enrollment caused mostly by shrinking families.

"Birth rates here in Los Angeles County have been declining for decades, which means fewer children enrolled in our schools," said Kelly Gonez, a board member in the LA Unified School District (LAUSD), the second largest in the country, which lost more than 300,000 students over the last two decades.

LA isn't alone. The population of children under age 18 began to fall nationwide after 2010, according to U.S. Census data, dropping by roughly 2.1 million kids through 2025.

With public schools in much of the country facing a demographic cliff, the Trump administration last year began detaining and expelling large numbers of foreign residents. A study by the Migration Policy Institute found as many as 1.9 million people left the U.S. during the first 18 months of Trump's second term.

As part of the crackdown effort, federal officials weakened restrictions that prevented ICE agents from operating near public schools. "Many of our families immediately went into hiding," Gonez said. "We were predicting a 2% drop in enrollment. It was double that."

Researchers who study education and population trends aren't surprised. This is the first time in nearly a century, since the era of the Great Depression, that birth rates and immigration levels are low at the same time. Large-scale deportations mean even bigger and more rapid changes in areas with large immigrant communities.

"The U.S. isn't alone in facing the challenges of demographic decline," said Thomas Dee, an economist who specializes in education policy at Stanford University. "To stop or slow immigration really exacerbates those problems. Communities are now confronting very painful decisions about closing schools."

The scale of decline is daunting. According to the U.S Department of Education, the number of kids in public schools nationwide peaked in 2019 and fell by roughly 1.5 million students as of the 2024 school year.

Based on data gathered before Trump's immigration crackdown began, federal researchers project enrollment will decline by at least another 2 million students by 2030. That would mean a 7% national decline in roughly a decade.

40 states see public school enrollment declines

It's unclear how large or sustained the impact of Trump-era immigration policies will be on enrollment trends. Dee and other researchers say that depends on how long ICE crackdowns and other restrictions remain in place.

In the short term, the blow to many districts could be severe. When Dee studied public schools in communities hit by ICE raids in California's Central Valley in 2025, he found student daily absences spiked more than 20%.

Texas, meanwhile, saw the number of kids in classrooms plunge statewide last year by more than 76,000 students. The vast majority of that drop came among Hispanic kids and the children of immigrant families, according to a study by the Texas Education Agency.

Florida, home to a large community of Haitian refugees who were stripped of temporary protected status by the Trump administration in July, saw a big drop in enrollment this year. The state's two largest public school districts, Miami-Dade and Broward County, lost roughly 30,000 children combined in a single year.

"It's really the effect of both the exodus of the existing families and stopping the inflow [of foreign migrants and children] that normally would have occurred," Dee said.

A report published in June by two education think tanks, Bellwether and WestEd, warned that public schools have entered an era of "sustained" enrollment declines which are already reshaping districts in 40 states.

The analysis found the "primary overall driver of declining enrollment is a sustained drop in birth rates" followed by a "national slowdown in immigration."

"At the local level, enrollment decline may permanently reduce available resources and will significantly reshape public education systems for years to come," the study concluded, while predicting a loss of $11 billion a year in public school funding linked to falling enrollment.

Other factors have spurred public school enrollment losses, including the COVID-19 pandemic and the shift of more students to private and homeschool learning. But the U.S. Department of Education projects private schools, too, will lose more than a million students by the end of this decade.

"We had over 200 students that didn't show up"

While debates over immigration policy play out in Washington, D.C., teachers, parents and students say ICE crackdowns already mean more empty classrooms and less vibrant neighborhoods around schools.

"This street right here is actually where the ICE standoff happened. It was right before school," said teacher Guadalupe Cardona, who stood recently outside Santee Education Complex, a high school in South Los Angeles as school buses rumbled past.

In October 2025, an ICE agent opened fire here. No children or school employees were injured, but a man from Mexico without legal status and an ICE agent were struck by bullets. Cardona believes fear following that clash and other raids caused enrollment to plummet.

"In my school alone, we had over 200 students that didn't show up on the first day of school," she said.

"We found that a lot of them were just [gone], no longer living where they had put their address down. We lost two teachers at the beginning of the school year because of it. It is something that hurts beyond just, like, putting your job at risk."

Guadalupe Pineda, a parent, works in a shop just down the street from Santee High. She says dread of ICE, combined with fewer students coming and going, have hurt her community. "There's definitely less sales, less traffic, less everything."

After growing up in LA and attending public school here without legal status, Pineda told NPR she was able to secure U.S. citizenship a few years ago. She said she understands why people are pulling their kids out of school and in many cases leaving the U.S. altogether.

"People are still scared, very much scared to go out to do everyday things. I feel like if I didn't have everything set [with my immigration status], I would probably leave. I would be afraid of being separated from my family."

White House celebrates deportation campaign

NPR asked White House officials about the impact on public schools of ICE crackdowns and other federal immigration policies, including the revocation of temporary refugee status for hundreds of thousands of people living in the U.S. legally.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis sent a brief email response saying deportations "make American classrooms less crowded." Bis also pointed to a September post on the social media platform X, where administration officials celebrated the overall drop in the number of legal and undocumented immigrants living in the U.S.

"The total foreign-born population declined 2.9 million from January 2025 to July 2026," the statement said. "The huge recent decline in the foreign-born population indicates that net migration to the United States was negative in the last year and a half for the first time since the 1930s."

Advocacy groups that support sharply reduced immigration view these trends as a necessary correction after years of what they describe as lax border security. Ira Mehlman with the Federation for American Immigration Reform said he's not troubled by the prospect that many public school districts will have to downsize.

"We don't guarantee the school system X number of kids," Mehlman said. "That is not the job of our immigration system, that you're going to have X number of kids every single year and if you don't, we're going to go find some for you."

But research suggests it's not only foreign-born children disappearing from classrooms. According to Brookings Institution estimates, as many as 4.6 million school-age kids including many U.S. citizens live in homes with family members vulnerable to deportation.

Vanessa Salazar was one of them. She was 18 years old, a U.S.-born senior in LAUSD last year, when her mother was detained and deported to Mexico. "It really threw me off balance," she said. "Coming home without my mother there to be my anchor, really affected my performance in school."

Salazar dropped out to cope with what she describes as her family's trauma and now lives in Mexico with her mother. "It's like, why am I going to be in this country that doesn't really want my people, my community or my culture?" she said.

With birth rates hitting another record low last year and ICE now arresting as many as 50,000 people each month, future school district losses could soar.

A study released in August by state officials predicted public schools in California alone could lose another 710,000 students over the next decade "if current trends in fertility and migration hold."

With LAUSD now facing a second school year in a row with 4% enrollment declines, the district announced a citywide effort in September aimed at identifying buildings and campuses that will close.

Kelly Gonez, the school board member, told NPR she expects cuts to be deep and painful. "When your district is roughly half the size of student population it was 20 years ago, it's hard to find a sustainable path to keep campuses open," she said.

title: Trump wooed Latino voters, but his ICE tactics sent them back to the polls - The Guardian
authors: Guardian staff, Ed Pilkington in Anchorage
description:
It speaks to how Trump first wooed, and then alienated, the backing of many Latino voters, effectively shooting himself in the foot.
In the closing days of the 2024 presidential race, Trump made a special pitch to Hispanic voters.
But on Tuesday night, Latino voters delivered Trump a resounding message of a very different sort.
If Trump and the Republican party had assumed they had forged a new alignment with Hispanic voters, they must now think again.
In key battleground states, Latino voters flexed their electoral muscle in this midterm cycle to a degree arguably never seen before.
text:
Tuesday night’s explosive rout of the Republican party was supercharged by the fury of Hispanic Americans who turned out in record numbers in key battlegrounds to protest the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant assault on their communities.

“Trump went against us,” said Benny Melendez from Weslaco, Texas. “He made us the target of ICE operations, so we decided to punish him by voting against his party. That’s what happened.”

Melendez, the owner of a small housebuilding company in south Texas, voted for Donald Trump in the presidential election two years ago, attracted by his promise to secure the Mexican border and improve the economy. But on Tuesday, he cast his vote for the Democrats in a display of pure anger.

Two of his cousins and up to 15 of his building workers have been picked up and deported to Mexico by ICE. When Melendez voted for Trump in 2024 he expected the immigration raids would focus on those with criminal records, he said, not his relatives and employees.

“They’re taking our neighbors. They’re taking our friends. They’re they’re taking our workers, and they’re taking our family members. This is an attack against our community.”

Melendez’s rage, replicated in the millions across Texas, Florida and other critical swing states, itself tells a story. It speaks to how Trump first wooed, and then alienated, the backing of many Latino voters, effectively shooting himself in the foot.

In the closing days of the 2024 presidential race, Trump made a special pitch to Hispanic voters. “I love Hispanics,” he told them, “and Hispanics love Trump.”

To some extent, that audacious appeal worked: in 2024 Trump garnered 48% of the Latino vote, according to Pew Research, 12 points up from four years previously.

But on Tuesday night, Latino voters delivered Trump a resounding message of a very different sort. In a dizzying switch in affiliation, Hispanic American support for Republicans plummeted from the almost half who backed Trump just two years ago to 30% today.

According to the New York Times analysis of voter trends, election night marked a 28 point shift from 2024 in Latino allegiance toward Democrats nationwide. The dramatic turn was more notable than any other demographic voting group, with the next largest shift of 17% coming from Asian Americans.

The shift helped propel Democratic wins in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, as well as governor’s seats in states like Texas, Georgia, Arizona and Nevada.

If Trump and the Republican party had assumed they had forged a new alignment with Hispanic voters, they must now think again. Any such alliance was abruptly and spectacularly uncoupled on Tuesday.

“People have called us the sleeping giant for a long time, and now we’re really the swinging giant,” said Stephanie Valencia, co-founder of the Latino polling experts, Equis Research.

“The vociferous message that voters sent last night was an F-U to Trump and Republicans and their misplaced priorities and broken promises.”

It was a night of stunning surprises, and of firsts. Texas, the state with the second largest Hispanic populace after California, elected its first Latino governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, a native of the Rio Grande Valley whose mother is an immigrant from Mexico, in an astounding rebuke to decades of largely white Republican rule.

Democrat Xavier Becerra, the son of immigrants from Mexico, will become the first elected Latino governor in California, the world’s fourth largest economy.

Here too the same voters’ fury was powerfully vented. “We’ve known better than anybody what these last two years have been like,” California senator Alex Padilla, the son of Mexican immigrants, told the crowd at Becerra’s closing campaign stop at the Palladium in Los Angeles on Sunday. “We have endured relentless attacks on our communities by Donald Trump and his rogue ICE agents.”

Angelica Salas, an immigration activist who leads the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights of Los Angeles, called Becerra “familia”.

“Xavier Becerra dreams the way we dream,” she said.

In key battleground states, Latino voters flexed their electoral muscle in this midterm cycle to a degree arguably never seen before. Texas took the prize for the seismic jolt that shot across the state.

In Hispanic-dominated south Texas where Trump made some of his greatest gains two years ago, Democrats won all four congressional districts along the border with Mexico. That included the three districts that Republicans had gerrymandered in an attempt to bolster their control of the US House – a move that backfired.

Two of those districts were held by their Democratic incumbents, Henry Cuellar in Texas 28 and Vicente Gonzalez in Texas 34. The third gerrymandered district, 81% Hispanic Texas 15, was flipped by the Democratic candidate, the Tejano music star Bobby Pulido.

Pulido always looked to be doing well against the Republican incumbent, Monica De La Cruz, even though Trump had prevailed here in 2024. In the end, Pulido’s victory was overwhelming, by an astonishing 24 percentage points with 95% of the ballots counted.

“Not bad for a quinceañera singer,” Pulido said at his victory event.

Pulido’s campaign manager Abel Prado told the Guardian that the outstanding result was in part a reflection of Trump’s mass deportation drive that has seen thousands of undocumented Hispanic people detained and deported by ICE in Texas. “When you implement policies with such cruelty and malice, then this is what you get,” Prado said.

Among the 48,000 individuals that the Pulido campaign assembled in its voter database, almost 40% they found were members of mixed-status families. “These are people whose parents couldn’t vote, but they could, and so when my dad got deported, or my mom got deported, that became a crystallizing moment.”

Prado said that many people in the district who had voted for Trump in 2024 “came to their senses and realized the consequences of their previous vote. Tuesday night was a correction to what happens when one party is allowed to run rampant and do whatever they want without fear of consequences.”

The 30 million registered Latino voters are as diverse politically, culturally and economically as any other group. Talk of a Latino monolith has for years led analysts to reach simplistic and inaccurate conclusions about their voting patterns.

Yet Tuesday’s results showed a surprisingly similar rejection of Trump’s policies across very different Hispanic communities. In Florida, Latino voters swung powerfully toward Democratic candidates in the Cuban and Venezuelan communities of Miami-Dade, and equally in the heavily Puerto Rican areas around Orlando.

In Miami-Dade, which Trump won by a whopping 15 points in 2024, the Republican incumbent Maria Elvira Salazar was fighting a neck-and-neck battle with her fellow Cuban American newscaster, the Democratic candidate Eliott Rodriguez.

That the race was so tight amounted to the realisation of Salazar’s worst fears. In September she was blasted over news headlines when she warned Trump in a campaign advert that his mass deportation of Hispanic immigrants had “gone too far” and that the very people who had put him back in the White House now “feel betrayed”.

Trump’s response was indicative. He accused Salazar of backstabbing him, claiming that his “Latino support hasn’t wavered.” The voters disagreed.

Tuesday’s results will reverberate for some time. Democratic leaders, as they prepare to take control of Congress and begin the search for a presidential nominee, should be mindful that Hispanic voters are hungry for policies that reflect their needs, Valencia said.

“This was a cry for help from voters to focus on the right things: the economy and inflation, immigration, and wars abroad. Democrats are entering a probationary period with voters, they should not make the mistake of thinking that this swing is permanent.”

The election has also ushered in a new generation of young, ambitious Hispanic politicians and organizers determined to be heard. Pulido’s entire campaign staff was aged under 25.

“These are people who have never had a seat at the table who can now become a new voice in how we do things,” Prado said. “We absolutely rejected anybody parachuting into the district, out-of-towners telling us how to do things.”

He added: “If there’s a gringo operative out there trying to take credit for what happened to the Latino vote in Texas on Tuesday night, please shut the fuck up.”
