text:
A traveling memorial honoring immigrants who died in immigration custody or enforcement actions was installed on Loyola’s Lake Shore Campus Nov. 4, displaying 128 crosses on the West Quad. Each cross represented an individual from one of more than 40 countries.

The Migrant Crosses Project was organized by the School of Social Work Student Organization’s (SSWSO) social justice committee in collaboration with Priests for Justice for Immigrants (PJI) and Sisters and Brothers of Immigrants, two Catholic-led advocacy groups working to promote justice for immigrants.

The memorial was on display 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. as part of a traveling memorial, Director for the Center for Immigrant and Refugee Accompaniment (CIRA) María Vidal de Haymes said in an email to The Phoenix. Each week, a parish, campus or school displays the crosses as a visible act of remembrance for the over 100 people who have died in immigration custody or enforcement actions since 2020.

Vidal de Haymes said the project aims to make sure the people who died are seen and remembered. It also invites communities to work to protect others.

She said she was contacted by Sister Bernadine Karge, a religious sister and member of Sisters and Brothers of Immigrants. She is also a good friend of the School of Social Work, according to Vidal de Haymes.

Twenty years ago, Karge traveled with Vidal de Haymes, students and alumni to Veracruz, Mexico, after they were invited by the founder of Jesuit Migrant Services in Mexico to participate in a certificate program for lay pastoral leaders in communities heavily impacted by migration.

The group helped develop a curriculum to prepare parish members to respond to what they were seeing in their communities.

“In some communities, they saw mental health issues because of separation, because of family members going north to work in other communities” Vidal de Haymes said. “They wanted to have a sort of program to feed and support the migrants that were in transit from Central America through their communities. So each parish kind of designed their own project.”

Vidal de Haymes said she then reached out to Rachel Moore, president of SSWSO and an advanced-standing master’s in social work student, to help organize the memorial through the organization. She also submitted a request to Assistant Vice President and Dean of Students Will Rodriguez to bring the project to Loyola.

Loyola is the first university to host the event, according to Moore.

Along with the crosses, a sign reading “Justice for Sheridan Gorman,” was placed in front of the memorial sometime in the early afternoon Nov. 4. It’s unclear who placed the sign at the exhibit.

Gorman was shot and killed March 19 at Tobey Prinz Beach. The shooting sparked anti-immigrant backlash, led by the Trump administration, after suspect Jose Medina, a Venezuelan immigrant, was arrested and charged with murder, The Phoenix previously reported.

Moore said she believes the way immigration enforcement has been handled is “atrocious and absolutely a violation of human rights and human dignity.”

“I think that as a social work student, being passionate about human dignity and human rights is so important, and it’s important to honor people who have been lost so that their names are not forgotten and they’re not just another statistic,” Moore said. “They’re a name — they are a person who meant something to someone.”

Vidal de Haymes said the purpose of the project was to remember the individuals who’ve been harmed by ICE in detention and ICE operations.

“[We want] to memorialize their lives and their loss, and really work towards non-repetition — ending this broken immigration system that’s harming individuals and families, and leaves many people who are here seeking protection vulnerable,” Vidal de Haymes said.

Although Moore couldn’t attend the event, she said she hopes students can take away the importance of remembering the people represented by the crosses.

“I think when you look at someone’s name, it makes it much more real and much more important, and I hope that it instilled that importance in people,” Moore said.

Moore said she also worked with three undergraduate social work students — Miquela Omosowon, Ally Byrom and Vivian Kayye, who helped install the crosses and shared information about the project on social media.

Vidal de Haymes said she helped the students set up the event, who were then able to reflect on what they helped organize.

“The students in the class were able to visit the exhibit, and they spent some time reflecting on it,” she said. “They talked about how moving it was, and how for them it helped them see beyond just the numbers of, you know, statistics regarding immigration.”

Moore said the memorial serves to advocate for social justice and a commitment to social justice in students.

“Service is a huge principle of social work, and I see in those three students huge amounts of service being done from them,” Moore said. “So the service that they put forth is huge and inspiring as well for me.”

title: Trump administration coordinated with Iran on deportations for asylum seekers in middle of war – AP
description:

At least a dozen Iranians held in Immigration and Customs Enforcement facilities were notified over the past week that they would be deported to Iran, the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund said.
According to the AP and the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund, some of them were told they could be deported as soon as Sunday.
The Iranian American Legal Defense Fund said that the detainees were contacted by an Iranian representative office in the Pakistani Embassy in Washington about an upcoming deportation flight to Iran through Pakistan.

text:
The Trump administration held talks with Iran about deporting Iranians in the midst of Operation Epic Fury, the Associated Press reported on Friday.

Court documents obtained by the AP show that the administration intended to deport Iranian nationals through a third country as recently as mid-October. The documents did not note when the Iranians would be deported, or through which country.

At least a dozen Iranians held in Immigration and Customs Enforcement facilities were notified over the past week that they would be deported to Iran, the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund said. According to the AP and the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund, some of them were told they could be deported as soon as Sunday.

The judge in the case ordered the administration to give the court 24 hours' notice of any finalized plans to deport the Iranians, and five days’ written notice before such a deportation is carried out.

The administration had conversations with Iranian leaders about the deportations as early as last year before the war began. The court documents show that the administration maintained contact with Iran during the war to figure out “possible avenues for removal.”

Trump administration maintained contact with Iran over deportations, despite icy diplomatic relations

The AP noted that the news that the US continued those talks during the war with Iran illustrates the lengths to which the administration will go to carry out its immigration policy.

“We are at war with a country where the President of the United States has said, as recently as two or three days ago, if not yesterday, that it is essentially lawless... A country that is an enemy of the United States, according to the current president. A country that, according to our president, murdered tens of thousands of protesters,” Judge Ana Reyes said, according to the Oct. 15 transcript provided by the AP.

“And what you’re telling me is that the United States of America is going to send individuals back to that region, facing what you and I and everyone who would ever look at this would know would be, at a minimum, a serious threat of certain death.”

“Yes, your honor. The government is executing lawful orders of removal.” Justice Department Attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel said, according to the transcript.

Georgiev-Remmel noted to the court there was no specific date set to deport any individuals.

The State Department did not respond to the AP’s request for comment.

The Iranian American Legal Defense Fund said that the detainees were contacted by an Iranian representative office in the Pakistani Embassy in Washington about an upcoming deportation flight to Iran through Pakistan. Some were also notified by Department of Homeland Security officials of the flight. None were provided any written information about their deportation.

One of the detainees attempted suicide once he learned he could be deported to Iran, according to the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund’s executive director Yasmine Chubin.

“Some of those same asylum applicants, and others who could face the same death, are being sent back, all against a backdrop of further and intensifying US bombing of Iran. This flight must be stopped,” Chubin said, according to the AP.

The lawsuit on the asylum seekers, which the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund filed, alleges that the administration shared confidential information with the Islamic regime, thus violating national immigration laws and endangering scores of Iranian nationals. It alleges that the US and Iranian governments coordinated a campaign to pressure Iranian nationals detained by ICE to return to Iran. Notably, this would come after decades of hostile relations between the US and the Islamic Republic.

DHS denied sharing asylum application records with the regime.

The judge overseeing the case noted that the DHS may have shared confidential information with regime leadership, but appeared skeptical of the plaintiff’s allegations that the DHS has a policy of sharing private records.

Reyes warned the DOJ attorney that she would initiate contempt proceedings if the government did not follow her orders to give the court advance notice of planned removal flights.

“We are talking about sending individuals in our care and custody to a country that we have bombed, and we may continue bombing, and is a declared enemy of this country,” she said, according to the transcript.

Notably, the report comes as Iran has killed hundreds of protesters from January 2026 demonstrations. Iranians are rarely deported in the US because of the lack of relations between the US and Iran, in addition to fears of persecution or death for those who are forced to return.

text:
Legal service organizations, represented by the American Civil Liberties Union of Massachusetts, filed a lawsuit Oct. 28 challenging a new federal policy allowing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to hide the locations of thousands of detainees through its Online Detainee Locator System, which went into effect Sept. 15.

The lawsuit was filed by Greater Boston Legal Services, Rian Immigrant Center, Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project and Amica Center for Immigrant Rights. The groups argue the policy “unlawfully blocks them from locating, communicating with, and providing legal services to their clients and potential clients,” according to an ACLU Massachusetts press release.

ACLU Massachusetts staff attorney Jennifer Herrmann said the absence of the online locator, a system which had been in place for 16 years, makes it near impossible for legal professionals to help their clients or find new ones.

“This is unlawful. It was implemented suddenly without any notice or legal justification, which is not permitted,” Herrmann said. “The law requires that the government provide adequate notice and explain its reasoning when making major policy changes like this. And the Trump administration did neither.”

Sarah Sherman-Stokes, a clinical professor of law and associate director of the Immigrants’ Rights and Human Trafficking Clinic at the BU School of Law, said she used the detainee locator hundreds of times over her 15 years as an immigration lawyer.

“It’s a really important tool in the toolbox to try to find someone when they’ve been detained, when they’ve been disappeared from their home or their work or off the street,” she said.

Sherman-Stokes said the government frequently moves ICE detainees away from where they were originally apprehended, separating them from family members and legal counsel and often leaving them in jurisdictions where the law is less favorable to immigrants. She said it is an intentional strategy by the Trump administration.

“It’s part of a pattern of lawlessness by ICE and this administration,” Sherman-Stokes said. “They want to make the process opaque. They want to make it difficult to find people,”

ICE did not respond to a request for comment.

The plaintiffs allege in the lawsuit the ICE policy is “arbitrary and capricious,” as well as a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act and the Freedom of Information Act.

“Arbitrary and capricious is a legal standard [for] when agencies take actions that are seemingly untethered from real policy or real articulable reasons.” Sherman-Stokes said “This policy certainly seems to satisfy both those criteria.”

Herrmann said that the Freedom of Information Act requires that government agencies proactively disclose statements of policy and interpretations adopted by an agency and not published in the Federal Register. The location of detainees is included in FOIA requirements, she said.

Earlier this week, Democrats took control of Congress in the midterm elections, flipping the previous Republican majority. Sherman-Stokes said she hopes the Democratic legislature will be a check on the Trump administration’s immigration policies.

“I really hope that the Democrats taking control of the House and the Senate will be a check on the lawlessness of this presidency and, in particular, the way that this president has carried out really, really aggressive and illegal immigration tactics,” Sherman-Stokes said.

Herrmann said the ACLU would continue in the lawsuit to ensure that immigrants can get the legal assistance they need.

“We are fortunate in this Commonwealth to be home to many immigrants who are making up our society, and those people are among those who are being hidden by the federal government as a result of this policy, to the great detriment of our communities,” Herrmann said.

title: What Democrats' midterm wins mean for ICE enforcement and Trump's deportation agenda
description:
The brutal U.S. immigration is a human rights catastrophe taking place right here on American soil.
What is happening with ICE is not about enforcing immigration law; it is about a president using the vast power of the United States against those he deems a target.
In an interview with NBC10, Stanford said ICE is a "paramilitary organization that is taking human life."
The “Boycott Ride,” scheduled for Sunday in Rittenhouse Square, has sparked ire on social media and drawn international scrutiny.
The temporary restraining order by U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan halting the work represents a major setback in President Donald Trump’s vision to remake Washington.
text:

title: Remote Immigration Judges Advance Trump's Rapid Deportations - Bloomberg Law
description:

While remote hearings became common under the Biden administration, immigration lawyers and observers say there’s less flexibility now for migrants.
Past Remote Hearings The practice of using remote judges on WebEx was considered a “game changer” during the pandemic, O’Herron said, adding that there are some “real advantages” to remote options, including rescheduling flexibility.

text:
Attorney Lilia Khordj waited with her client in a small room in the Cleveland Immigration Court where a judge more than 2,000 miles away would decide whether the client would be deported.

Judge Guy Grande, based in San Diego, appeared via remote video after Khordj and her client made the two-hour drive from Columbus. After starting the hearing over an hour late, Grande cut it short as the Cleveland court in a time zone three hours ahead of him was closing for the day.

Khordj’s client is among a wave of migrants required to appear in person at removal proceedings as the judges preside through a screen. In many cases, judges are appearing from courts in different federal circuits with separate case law on handling detention and asylum. Immigration attorneys and former judges say the practice places a heavy burden on immigrants caught up in the Trump administration’s rapid case completion and deportation strategy.

“It’s really hard to see these efforts as anything other than another strategy to get these people to a deportation faster,” said former DOJ attorney Margy O’Herron, who was also a Biden-era White House immigration adviser.

Grande, the San Diego judge, agreed to have Khordj’s client make future appearances remotely, “but I don’t really understand why that wasn’t done before,” Khordj said.

While remote hearings became common under the Biden administration, immigration lawyers and observers say there’s less flexibility now for migrants. Some judges are ordering individuals removed for not appearing in person, even as the judges or Department of Homeland Security attorneys join online.

The Justice Department’s Executive Office for Immigration Review, which encompasses the immigration courts, has worked to lower its backlog, completing nearly 974,000 cases in fiscal 2026 — a record for the office.

“Any immigration judge can hear any case at any time throughout the country to assist with caseloads, and EOIR is committed to ensuring each alien gets his day in court as efficiently as possible,” EOIR spokesperson Kathryn Mattingly said of allowing judges to preside remotely.

Past Remote Hearings

The practice of using remote judges on WebEx was considered a “game changer” during the pandemic, O’Herron said, adding that there are some “real advantages” to remote options, including rescheduling flexibility.

Remote judges have often been used amid staffing shortages, said Princeton University professor Amelia Frank-Vitale, who has studied the immigration court system for decades.

The practice expanded during President Donald Trump’s second term. EOIR has sworn in new judges each month since February for openings promoted as fully remote from “anywhere in the U.S.” or “telework eligible.”

At California’s Concord Immigration Court, four out of 21 judges are appearing in person, said Jeremiah Johnson, executive vice president of the National Association of Immigration Judges.

The situation is similar at the Federal Plaza Immigration Court in Manhattan, where several judges appear to be based in other locations, including Florida and Maryland, according to an analysis of EOIR judge bios and LinkedIn profiles.

Uneven Expectations

Remote proceedings have resulted in a patchwork of practices.

Some immigration judges require all respondents and their attorneys to appear in person. In other cases, attorneys or respondents can be remote. At times, the respondent is asked to appear even if the judge isn’t there.

In some cases, Frank-Vitale said, judges would have an immigrant ordered removed because they were not physically present.

“The variation always existed, but the stakes of that variation have become much higher,” she said, adding that immigrants also fear being detained at hearings.

Alaska-based immigration attorney Nicolas Olano said his detained clients are sometimes taken to a detention facility in Washington state. But his requests to appear via video have been denied.

“I need to represent them in that individual hearing and I can’t,” Olano said.

He fears his nondetained clients risk being arrested by immigration officials while transiting through airports to get to their hearings.

The problem compounds, advocates said, with the recent use of makeshift immigration courtrooms in other federal buildings. Immigrants, assigned to DOJ courts, are asked to appear in rooms in DHS buildings, with a remote judge on the screen. Sometimes the judge is sitting in the courthouse the migrant was originally assigned.

O’Herron said remote hearings can be fair if the administration limits some of the pressures on migrants, including removing the risk of being detained in court and giving parties an equal chance to weigh in on appearing via video.

Docket Shifting

Some judges have started to adjudicate cases at courts in other federal circuits, causing confusion on the relevant case law, lawyers and former immigration judges said. Two Cleveland judges — Monte Horton and Norman Schroth — were recently assigned to take up cases at Massachusetts’ Chelmsford Immigration Court, according to EOIR’s website.

Several judges remotely adjudicating cases in Louisiana courts are based at courts in Massachusetts and other states, said immigration lawyer Kimberly Fasking.

That poses challenges as federal circuits are split on the legality of Trump administration immigration policies, including mandatory detention without bond hearings, said Amiena Khan, former assistant chief immigration judge in New York who was fired last year.

The general rule is that the case law that applies depends on the circuit in which the notice to appear is served, O’Herron said. The judge is “going to have to get up to speed” on the “case law in that circuit.”

The learning curve can be greater for new judges hearing cases remotely, who “don’t have the ability to talk to their peers and be mentored into those decisions,” said Johnson, the judge association vice president who served at the San Francisco court until his firing last November.

Without easy access to in-person mentorship, new remote judges are more likely to succumb to pressure to rapidly close cases and issue removal orders, Johnson said.

“Judges are not given the opportunity to be deliberative anymore,” he said. “I don’t think that’s what the American people expect out of a judicial system.”

"This university has ignored that mandate. The Department will continue to challenge policies that unlawfully disadvantage American citizens," he continued.

JUSTICE DEPARTMENT SUES COLORADO OVER IN-STATE TUITION AND FINANCIAL AID FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS

The DOJ accused the university of violating federal law by "prioritizing the needs of illegal aliens over U.S. citizens in defiance of Congress’s commands."

Penn State's policy "unconstitutionally" discriminates against U.S. citizens who are not afforded the same reduced tuition rate as undocumented students, the department said.

The department seeks to enjoin the university from enforcing its policy that provides undocumented students, including illegal migrants who live in Pennsylvania, with in-state tuition rates, regardless of whether the students are lawfully in the U.S.

DOJ SUES NEW JERSEY OVER LAWS GIVING ILLEGAL ALIENS IN-STATE TUITION, SAYS CITIZENS TREATED AS 'SECOND-CLASS'

"These requirements include attending an accredited Pennsylvania high school for at least four years and graduating from an accredited Pennsylvania high school or receiving a Pennsylvania General Educational Development (GED) certificate," the school's website reads.

Democratic Congressman Robert Garcia had two words of advice for the Trump administration this week - lawyer up. After Democrats won majorities in the House and Senate, Garcia is set to become the next chair of the House Oversight Committee, so the watchdog committee. And he has promised to look into, among other things, ICE enforcement. NPR's Jasmine Garsd is here to discuss what that might look like. Hey, Jas.

KELLY: Hey. So one of the big concerns with ICE agents and ICE detention centers has been lack of oversight. What might change?

GARSD: OK. So first of all, I think it's worth mentioning that the current Congress basically gave immigration enforcement a blank check. In 2025 and 2026, Congress gave around $240 billion - that's billion with a B - to ICE and Customs and Border Patrol. Now, the incoming Congress which just got voted in could stop giving them even more money, but, you know, the truth is ICE and DHS have gotten enough funds to run mass deportation operations for the remainder of Trump's term.

There are a couple of things that could happen here. Congress could claw back that money, but, you know, the hurdle is President Trump would very likely veto that. There could also be restrictions on usage of those funds - warrant requirements, banning masks, restricting agents from going into schools, churches, hospitals. I spoke to Naureen Shah at the ACLU, who told me she thinks in order to change ICE behavior, one of the most powerful things that could happen is congressional oversight through subpoenas.

NAUREEN SHAH: ICE has to be afraid. They have to be afraid of losing their funding. They have to be afraid of being subpoenaed and asked extremely hard questions before a live audience of the American people.

KELLY: Jas, a question about facilities. You've covered the boom of the whole private detention center industry, which houses immigrant detainees. What are they saying?

title: 'My eyes opened': Latinas abandoned Republicans in droves - The 19th News
description:
SAN ANTONIO, Texas — Latino men swung back hard; Latinas swung back harder.
UnidosUS surveyed 3,000 Latino voters who cast ballots in the midterms.
Projections show that 2026 may hold the record for the largest turnout of Latino voters ever in a midterm election, though it’ll be weeks before a clearer picture emerges.
In Arizona, JoAnna Mendoza flipped a border district that decided control of the House in Republicans’ favor last cycle.
While both parties will have to contend with swing Latinas for cycles to come, in 2026, a clear majority of Latinas backed Democrats, as they’ve done for many cycles.
text:
SAN ANTONIO, Texas — Latino men swung back hard; Latinas swung back harder.

Most Latinas didn’t back President Donald Trump in 2024, but enough of them did to help usher him back into the White House. Early data from this week’s midterms suggests that many of those women came swinging back toward Democrats this cycle, taking on the role of deciders up and down the ballot, from Texas to Michigan. In places like Florida, many of them appear to have simply sat out, giving Democrats some of the best margins they’ve seen in years.

The swing didn’t come out of the blue — pun intended. Interviews with voters, as well as with experts who track Latinos, suggest that their shift to the left was fueled by intense disillusionment with Republicans, who didn’t fix the money problems that trouble them and spent the past two years rounding up their friends, neighbors and employees in immigration raids.

“I changed my mind on Trump when I realized he just likes control. He’s not about the people — he’s more like a dictator,” said Lucero Loera, 34, who lives in Round Rock, Texas, and voted for Democrats in Tuesday’s election, helping lift Democrat James Talarico to victory and in turn Democratic control of the Senate. She also backed Gina Hinojosa, who defeated incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott.

“It’s like my eyes opened.”

A post-election analysis of midterm voters by UnidosUS, a Hispanic civil rights and advocacy organization, found that 1 in 5 Latinas who backed Trump in 2024 decided to support Democrats instead, a higher share than Latino men, who also moved away from Republicans. UnidosUS surveyed 3,000 Latino voters who cast ballots in the midterms.

Latinas backed Democrats in U.S. House races at higher levels than Latino men. Within that topline victory for Democrats is the fact that Latina candidates will take up a record number of seats in Congress.

But it’s in races for the U.S. Senate where they may have made the most impact. The UnidosUS analysis found a larger than 40-point advantage for Democratic candidates for U.S. Senate among Latinas — a mix of voters who shifted loyalties or stayed home.

“It’s very clear that Latinas had a huge impact on the Michigan and Texas results,” said Gary Segura, the president of BSP Research, a Latino-owned research firm that conducted the survey.

In a strip mall on the west side of U.S. Route 281, which divides the northern suburbs of San Antonio into two congressional districts, Juliana Escudero, 42, said she simply wasn’t planning to vote.

The San Antonio resident who lives in Texas’ 23rd Congressional District previously backed Trump but said in an interview that she’s grown weary of politics. While she originally liked the business-friendly messaging coming from Trump and Abbott, the administration’s immigration crackdown has impacted the staffing agency she works for, including a worker who had a pending asylum case.

“I was on board with securing the border so long as people who were already here, who had pending cases, families, no criminal records and paid their taxes could eventually become regularized,” she said. Asked about the Democrats on the ballot, she said she didn’t want to support either Talarico or Hinojosa because she felt they were farther to the left than she was comfortable with.

Janet Murguía, the president and CEO of UnidosUS, said the data shows immigration fell far behind the economy when they asked voters what their most pressing issues were. But in every single conversation, the anger and heartbreak about the administration’s immigration crackdown showed up, along with the ways in which the administration’s enforcement was hurting people’s wallets.

Projections show that 2026 may hold the record for the largest turnout of Latino voters ever in a midterm election, though it’ll be weeks before a clearer picture emerges. Latinos have some of the lowest voter turnout rates, a challenge made particularly difficult by the fact that every election, about 1 million new Latino voters become eligible to vote. Latinas register and turnout at higher rates than Latino men.

Oriana Zapata, 37, became eligible to vote two years ago. A resident of Texas’ 23rd Congressional District, she said in a Monday interview from a Venezuelan restaurant in north San Antonio that she was backing Democrats because she felt that Republicans had shown broad rejection of immigrants in the last two years. Zapata said the one exemption is James Talarico, who went on to win the Senate race; she said she had been targeted by messaging about his views on gender that made her skeptical of him.

After polls closed, this district became a relic of a failed gerrymandering effort by Texas Republicans: Democratic Rep. Katy Padilla Stout easily trounced Republican Brandon Herrera by nine points in a district that went for Trump by 15 points. Upstream, Abbott lost his reelection bid to Texas’ first Latina governor by seven points.

Padilla Stout will join at least 26 other Latinas in the U.S. House, beating the previous record of 20 set in 2026 with some races still left to count. These women are overwhelmingly Democrats, and at least 10 will be newcomers to Congress. Their growing ranks come after voters nominated a record-breaking number of Latina House candidates — 38 — in the primaries. Latinas will make up about half of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, which will grow to a record-breaking 55 members in the 120th Congress.

In Nevada, Teresa Benitez-Thompson, a former state Assembly majority leader, flipped a district that Trump won by double digits in both 2020 and 2024. In Arizona, JoAnna Mendoza flipped a border district that decided control of the House in Republicans’ favor last cycle. All three candidates focused primarily on addressing the rising cost of living.

Franco Caliz-Aguilar, the national political director of Community Change Action, a progressive nonprofit focused on turning out infrequent voters of color that has an affiliated super PAC, said that Democrats would be making a mistake by describing the midterms’ results as a “coming home” for Latinos. Without action, Democrats could be staring at a “mirror image” of Tuesday’s results in 2028.

Caliz-Aguilar said that the intense frustration voters feel about stagnant wages and rising costs needs a solution that people can feel immediately and that Democrats can message clearly. Latinas report feeling the pain of rising costs more intensely: They have to contend with the gender wage gap, and they are also more likely to grocery shop, handle caregiving and navigate the healthcare system for their families.

“They need policies that make a difference tomorrow,” Caliz-Aguilar said. “Child tax credit expansion. Universal child care is something we hear over and over again. Direct cash assistance for folks. Is there more political imagination given last night’s results that is possible?”

Democrats will also have to contend with the administration’s immigration agenda and many voters’ desire for policies that protect some immigrants’ ability to remain in the country or reach legal status. About a quarter of Latinos ranked immigration enforcement as a top three issue in the election, with Latinas slightly more likely to say so. Among Trump regretters, it’s almost one-third.

In a social media post, Vice President J.D. Vance said he expects “any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty,” a term Republicans use to refer to a path to citizenship for immigrants without legal status to be in the country.

“I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement — by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you.”

In comments to Politico, Trump said he was open to deal-making on immigration, saying he would “consider doing whatever I think is appropriate and good for the country.” Trump also posted a picture of a red hat with the word “VETO” on Truth Social.

While both parties will have to contend with swing Latinas for cycles to come, in 2026, a clear majority of Latinas backed Democrats, as they’ve done for many cycles.

Cynthia Aguillon-Bernard has long favored Democrats but identifies as an independent. On Tuesday night, she was swaying to the music at Hinojosa’s election night party, hand to her heart. Around the venue, the campaign had handed out signs that read, “Gina Como La Gov,” a play on Selena’s “Como La Flor” record that played through the night.

Speaking of Democrats’ wins in Texas, she said: “This win is for the man and his family that have taken care of all the maintenance at our house and is detained by ICE. I think this win is for friends of our family that are afraid to go outside in their home,” she said. “Most of all, I feel like this win is for Latinas.”

text:
CARSON CITY, Nev. (KTNV) — Nevada Attorney General and Governor-elect Aaron D. Ford and a coalition of 23 states secured a legal victory blocking the federal government from imposing immigration-enforcement conditions on congressionally authorized public safety grants, including funds meant to keep law enforcement officers safe and fight crime.

District of Rhode Island Chief Judge John J. McConnell, Jr. declared the Trump administration's actions unlawful and permanently enjoined any implementation or enforcement of the conditions.

"Public safety funding is meant to protect communities, not to be used as a political bargaining chip," Ford said.

"The Trump administration unlawfully tried to force states to comply with its immigration enforcement demands by threatening critical law enforcement funding. This ruling upholds the rule of law and protects resources that help keep Nevadans safe."

The Trump administration previously declared that states would be unable to access Victims of Crime Act (VOCA) funds unless they agreed to the administration's immigration demands. The multistate coalition succeeded in getting the federal government to remove those conditions on over $1.3 billion of VOCA funds.

The U.S. Department of Justice has since applied the conditions to new grants, including funds dedicated to law enforcement and juvenile justice.

Among the affected programs is the Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Formula Grants, known as the Byrne JAG Program. For decades, regardless of which political party held power, the Byrne JAG Program has been the leading federal source of criminal justice funding to state and local governments.

Civil immigration enforcement is a federal responsibility and not a state government responsibility. The administration's attempts to coerce states conflict with core principles of American governance — the separation of powers and federalism. The actions violated laws passed by Congress as well as the Spending Clause of the U.S. Constitution.

Ford was joined in the lawsuit by the co-lead attorneys general of California, Delaware, New Jersey, Illinois and Rhode Island, as well as the attorneys general of Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia, as well as the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.

SPRINGFIELD – Today, U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, led the release of the Government Accountability Office’s (GAO) newly-completed report examining the Trump Administration’s decision to cut U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) inspection requirements of immigration detention facilities. These cuts stand in stark contrast to a massive surge in immigration detention. From April 2025 to April 2026, the average daily detained population jumped by more than 50 percent as active facilities expanded from 128 to 172. This growth was fueled by an explosion in funding, with ICE receiving over $45 billion for immigration detention in those two years alone.

With fewer inspections, there is even less accountability for ICE and its contractors, including widely documented failures to provide adequate medical care and safe and edible food and to prevent suicides. The GAO report is released after Durbin called for the GAO to expand its pending investigation of mental health care to include medical care and mismanagement of federal contracts in ICE detention facilities.

In the report, GAO outlines how detention oversight has been gutted during the second Trump Administration. The GAO examined four Department of Homeland Security (DHS) offices charged with inspecting detention facilities. The DHS Office of the Immigration Detention Ombudsman (OIDO), an independent office with statutory authority to conduct surprise inspections, has been shut down entirely. ICE’s Office of Detention Oversight (ODO) office has decreased its inspections following policy changes under this Administration—it went from inspecting larger facilities twice a year to once a year or less. Its total inspections dropped from 194 to 102 in one year. DHS now allows many smaller facilities to inspect themselves and usually tells facilities in advance when inspectors are coming. ICE justified these changes by stating few inspections would ease the obligations on facilities and would make it easier to contract with local and state partners to detain individuals. ICE Health Service Corps (IHSC), which inspects medical care in detention, has kept its process the same. The DHS Office of Inspector General (OIG) received $20 million for extra inspections.

Consistent with this Administration’s irresponsible and cruel approach to immigration policy, the GAO found ICE’s changes to detention inspections were not backed by data. ICE failed to analyze evidence, such as past inspection deficiencies or contract compliance, to assess how ICE can adequately conduct oversight over its rapidly growing detention facilities and ensure facilities comply with detention standards.

“On Tuesday, the American people overwhelmingly rejected the Trump Administration’s cruel immigration tactics—including inhumane ICE detention facilities, where people lack adequate access to food, water, and medical care,” said Durbin. “Now that the power has shifted in Congress, the Trump Administration should take immediate steps to respond to this new alarming GAO report, which found ICE has reduced inspections without assessing the impact on detained individuals.”

In the report, GAO also noted that another accountability measure recently lapsed. Since Fiscal Year 2019, appropriations language barred funding a contract with a facility after two consecutive less-than-adequate ODO ratings. That provision was left out of the FY26 DHS Appropriations Act. ICE told GAO that failing ratings now will no longer block continued funding, allowing private prison contractors like GEO and CoreCivic to fail inspections by ODO with no consequences.

In the report, GAO urges ICE to use real data to determine whether the reduced inspections are enough to keep facilities safe and compliant, and adjust its inspections based on what it finds.

text:
For nearly two years, the federal building in downtown San Diego and immigration court inside have played a key role in some of the arrests that came with President Donald Trump's mass deportations. Outside, for months, demonstrators have gathered weekly to protest that increased enforcement.

"We just continue to see abuses of power," said Jose Lopez Eguino, director of the San Diego office of Alliance of Californians for Community Empowerment. "We continue to see our communities terrorized and we're sick of it."

Lopez Eguino is one of many who have said since polls closed Tuesday that those detentions and deportations played a role in the election results handing Democrats control of the House and the Senate. Voters across the country and several exit polls indicate ICE was among the top issues this cycle, particularly for Latino voters.

"People are sick and tired of seeing this," he said. "Every day we look on the news, we look at our phones and there are families being torn apart, children screaming and crying because their parents or their siblings are being taken away from them."

On Thursday, many of the signs decrying ICE were the same that have surfaced for months. But a few were new: a large banner that proclaimed, "Democracy won," and a smaller poster that read, "There's hope."

While some protesters expressed relief, what Democrats may do to address the long-running fear and frustration is unclear.

"What I don't want to see is Democrats walk in there and be soft on the injustices that have been happening to our communities," said Alondra Alvarez, a community educator with Universidad Popular who works with people impacted by enforcement.

"I do think that there is a recognition that enforcement of the law is important, that the border should be secure and that we should do what President Trump said he was going to do, which is get rid of the violent criminals and the people that are a danger," said Rep. Scott Peters, a Democrat who represents San Diego County's 50th Congressional District. "I also think there's a recognition that these immigration laws are not working for us."

Last year, Peters introduced the Stop Excessive Force in Immigration Act, a bill to require ICE agents to wear identification and have body cameras always on. The measure would also bar face masks as well as the use of tools like flash bangs, rubber bullets and tear gas, and includes restriction around uses of force, prioritizing de-escalation.

When he introduced the measure last November, he and his colleagues were in the minority. Now, Peters said he sees a potential path forward.

"It's going to be a lot of work. And we have a lot of new people to educate, which I think we're going to do," he said. "But all across the country, we know that people are dissatisfied with the way that Trump is enforcing these laws. And I think there's going to be a market in Congress for a change."

On Fox News Thursday, former Acting Department of Homeland Security Sec. Chad Wolf, who held the role in the first Trump administration and now works for the America First Policy Institute, railed against a Democratic Congress, which will still face Trump's veto.

"What you can expect is aggressive oversight on ICE," Wolf said. "They're going to do everything in their power to try to reduce ICE's ability to do its job. ICE, like any other federal law enforcement or local or state law enforcement, need the latest tools."

When asked about the agency's plans, DHS pointed to a tweet from current Sec. Markwayne Mullin that read simply, "Deportations will continue."

On Election Day, White House Border Czar Tom Homan warned of migrants returning to the now-quiet border under Democratic control.

"We're going to lose the border if they keep pushing," Homan said on Fox News. "They are going to push to abolish ICE. You will see chaos like you have never seen before."

Those at Thursday's protest outside San Diego's federal building said they do want to abolish the agency.

"There's no way to reform ICE," Lopez Eguino said. "We need to get rid of it. We need to figure out how we protect immigrants and treat people with dignity and respect."

Peters noted many of the Democrats elected Tuesday are moderate in their ideology.

"I think moderates want to see this problem resolved," he said. "That means immigration reform that's reasonable. But it also starts with enforcing a law in a way that's humane."

If Democrats do pass Peters' measure, he said he would "dare" Trump to veto it - but its passage alone, he said he believed would place pressure.

"Even if President Trump had the veto that we couldn't override, he'd start to get the message - maybe he started getting it on Tuesday - that he's got to do things differently," Peters said.

Under Trump, Congress has allocated more than $200 billion to DHS, funding the agency through the end of his term. Peters noted that's "at a level that's higher than the United States Marines," calling it "absurd."

"They literally can't spend it fast enough. It's just too much money," he said, "so it's completely available for us to move someplace else as part of our budget authority as Congress. And I think that's what we would intend to do."

text:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection has issued an interim final rule that will establish new requirements for foreign importers of record when making entry, corresponding responsibilities for licensed customs brokers with regard to their clients, and consequences for foreign IORs and brokers that fail to comply with the new requirements.

This rule implements only some of the requirements and restrictions for IORs laid out in a June 3 executive order directing a broad tightening of customs enforcement efforts.

The rule will be effective as of Jan. 5, 2027, and comments on it are due by that date. Brokers may submit by Jan. 5 requests for delayed compliance with the new verification requirement (see below), but all brokers are expected to be in full compliance with the rule by May 6, 2027.

U.S. IORs

Under this rule a U.S. IOR is an individual who is (1) a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident or (2) an entity that is organized under the laws of the U.S., is located in the U.S., and maintains at all times (a) at least 51 percent of beneficial owner(s) who are U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents and have control of the entity, or (b) direct ownership of a significant amount of unencumbered real property in the U.S. Whether an individual or entity qualifies as a U.S. IOR is subject to verification by the appropriate Center of Excellence and Expertise director using criteria set forth in the rule.

The rule provides that qualification as a U.S. IOR must be declared at the time of filing an entry and entry summary. If an entity inaccurately declares that it qualifies as a U.S. IOR, CBP will have the ability to require live entry and discontinue immediate delivery privileges.

Foreign IORs

The new rule prohibits foreign IORs (i.e., IORs that do not meet the criteria of a U.S. IOR) from making informal or formal entry of merchandise for consumption unless (1) they themselves are validated under the Customs Trade Partnership Against Terrorism or (2) they use a CTPAT-validated and licensed customs broker.

However, CBP states that it will be monitoring informal entries filed by foreign IORs and their brokers and that if it determines that such entries present risks to the revenue, national security, or public health and safety it will take action to fully prohibit foreign IORs from using informal entry.

U.S. IORs may continue to enter goods without the need for CTPAT validation, subject to existing requirements and applicable procedures for formal entry and informal entry, and may also elect to designate a customs broker that is not CTPAT-validated.

Customs Brokers

This rule requires customs brokers to verify that a client meets the above qualifications to be considered a U.S. IOR by requesting and reviewing client records. If a broker determines during such review that the client is not a U.S. IOR it must cease filing entries on behalf of that client if the broker is not CTPAT-validated.

The rule also clarifies that a power of attorney must be executed whenever a customs broker is transacting customs business on behalf of a client, even when the broker is acting as the IOR for an entry.

CBP emphasizes that, as of Jan. 5, 2027, being a licensed customs broker alone will not be sufficient to file entry on behalf of a foreign IOR or a foreign principal on a broker’s power of attorney unless that foreign IOR is itself a CTPAT-validated IOR. Instead, customs brokers acting on behalf of a non-CTPAT-validated foreign IOR must themselves be CTPAT-validated.

The rule also enhances CBP’s enforcement options against brokers to include broader applicability of penalties under 19 USC 1592, for which a maximum penalty may be assessed at the domestic value of the merchandise, rather than just under 19 USC 1641, which sets a maximum monetary penalty of $30,000.

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's administration held secret talks with Iran on deporting Iranians even as the war there dragged on, court documents show.

The court documents unsealed Thursday show the Republican administration as recently as mid-October said it had plans to deport the Iranians through an unnamed third country, although it was unclear when it intended to do so. The judge in the case ordered the government to give the court 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country and five days' written notice before any such deportation is carried out.

READ MORE: ICE and Iran worked together to deport Iranians from U.S., newly released emails show

The documents show that the administration maintained contacts with Iranian officials during the war over the removals, specifically for submitting travel documents and figuring out "possible avenues for removal."

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

"We are at war with a country where the President of the United States has said, as recently as two or three days ago, if not yesterday, that it is essentially lawless ... A country that is an enemy of the United States, according to the current president. A country that, according to our president, murdered tens of thousands of protestors," Judge Ana Reyes said according to the Oct. 15 transcript.

READ MORE: Vance blames Iran war for GOP midterm losses

"And what you're telling me is that the United States of America is going to send individuals back to that region, facing what you and I and everyone who would ever look at this would know would be, at a minimum, a serious threat of certain death."

"Yes, your honor," Justice Department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel said. "The government is executing lawful orders of removal."

The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The development emerged from an ongoing lawsuit that alleges the Trump administration's immigration agencies have been sharing confidential information about Iranian asylum seekers with the Iranian government, violating national immigration regulations and endangering countless Iranians, court filings argue.

The new court documents show the coordination continued during the war.

READ MORE: Iranian leaders say midterm results show U.S. voters have rejected Trump's war

The lawsuit depicts a coordinated campaign between the U.S. and Iranian governments to identify Iranians in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody and pressure them to return to Iran — a marked departure from decades of diplomatic hostility between the two governments and an ongoing war. DHS has denied that it is sharing asylum application records with the Iranian government.

Hundreds of emails exchanged between U.S. immigration officials exposed how the two countries worked together to arrange for more than 100 Iranians to be flown back to Iran on three immigration flights in September and December 2025 and January 2026.

Deportations of Iranians back to their home country are historically rare, owing to the lack of diplomatic relations between the U.S. and Iran and the possible persecution they could face if they were sent to Iran.

But under the Trump administration, ICE has aggressively pushed to deport people even from countries that have typically been reluctant to take people back or with whom the U.S. has had icy or no diplomatic relations.

Sometimes that has meant sending people back to their home country but it has also meant deporting people to other countries that they have no connection with.

The Trump administration has deported people, including Iranians, to countries other than their own in an attempt to circumvent diplomatic hurdles with governments that won't take their people back. During Trump's second term, countries including El Salvador, Costa Rica and Panama have accepted noncitizens from the U.S.

In June, an Iranian woman was among the two dozen migrants the U.S. deported to the Central African Republic.

Activists abroad have expressed concern about deportees returning to Iran, whose theocracy has been cracking down on intellectuals and where the government vociferously cracks down on any dissent.

text:
Detaining immigrants has proven lucrative for the Butler County Sheriff’s Office.

Between federal stipends and salary reimbursements, the office has received more than $200,000 from Immigration and Customs Enforcement as part of a cooperation agreement with the agency, records obtained by TribLive show — and more may be on the way

Sheriff Michael Slupe told TribLive Thursday he believes the agreement has resulted in the arrests of around 150 people — and had netted his office a new Ford Expedition and a handful of “less-than-lethal” weapons.

Slupe signed a so-called 287(g) agreement with ICE last June. Since then, he’s spoken openly about many of his deputies working with ICE on immigration details, notably in Cranberry, where several people have been detained. Slupe said he’s unsure how many of those detained with the help of his office had criminal records.

The agreements give local officers greater immigration authority and incentivize departments to join by promising stipends and reimbursements for officer pay.

Documents obtained by TribLive through a Right-To-Know request show the sheriff’s office received a $100,000 vehicle stipend and a $97,500 equipment stipend — $7,500 for each of the 13 deputies — on June 18.

Less than a week later, the office purchased a $55,000 2026 Ford Expedition SUV from a Jim Shorkey dealership in White Oak, records show.

That was followed by a roughly $4,000 purchase in early August from Tech Support Screen Print, a screen printing business in Pittsburgh’s Chateau neighborhood, which Slupe said also sells less-than-lethal weapons.

Though the invoice from the screen printing business obtained by TribLive is redacted, Slupe said his office purchased a handful of Byrna rifles and pistols as well as ammunition and pepper spray.

Massachusetts-based Byrna produces look-alike guns powered by carbon dioxide that shoot nonlethal plastic balls meant to stun targets without killing them.

“Anytime you have the option to stop an action with less lethal (force), that’s preferable,” Slupe said.

So far, Slupe said his deputies are still awaiting training for how to use the weapons.

Slupe also said his office had also paid about $2,600 for two translation devices for communication with detainees who don’t speak English.

With the approval of Butler County commissioners, the sheriff’s office also purchased a $20,000 insurance policy on June 1 through Richmond National Insurance Company to cover potential liabilities related to deputies’ cooperation with ICE, according to records.

The county fronted the money for the policy before receiving the stipends later that month.

$195K pending?

While his deputies work with ICE, Slupe said they’re essentially on the federal government’s payroll.

Since November 2025, his office has received about $25,000 in salary reimbursements, which Slupe said cover deputies’ regular pay and county-paid benefits.

Much of the initial stipends of nearly $200,000 have yet to be spent, but he said he’s expecting to receive nearly that same amount again soon.

ICE offers quarterly stipends for equipment and IT resources of up to $15,000 per officer, meaning the sheriff’s office could receive another $195,000 from the federal agency, though Slupe said he’s unsure when it would arrive.

Some of those funds will go toward insurance premiums for the new liability policy, but Slupe said he’s unsure how his office will spend the rest. He mentioned the possibility of another new vehicle.

‘Blood money’

Slupe said no individual officers had earned any additional financial benefits from the deal and that ICE does not pay extra based on the number of people detained.

“There are absolutely zero quotas,” he said. “I have never been told by anyone, ‘Hey, we need to get five more people.’”

The deal with ICE, Slupe said, has proved to be a financial windfall, allowing the office to spend on equipment that would have otherwise been covered by county taxpayers.

“Not only has it been a financial benefit, it’s been a public safety benefit,” he said.

But Jaime Martinez, executive director of immigrant advocacy group Frontline Dignity, said the money should not legitimize the “terror” he says ICE has spread among immigrants in Butler County.

“How many lives would you be willing to disrupt for a new car?” Martinez said. “It’s not a justification for these agreements.”

Frontline Dignity runs frequent patrols in Cranberry and southern Butler County, which often respond to detainments and their aftermath. During one such response in late June, Martinez said volunteers found a pool of blood and single sneaker on the ground in Cranberry before ultimately locating the detained man’s family.

“I think Butler County knows better than to take blood money,” Martinez said.

Other pacts

Though cooperation agreements with ICE are fairly rare in the region, Slupe’s office is far from the only department to partner with federal immigration authorities.

In Allegheny County, agreements in Springdale and Pitcairn have resulted in detainments there. Other departments in the county like those in Glassport, Versailles and McDonald have also signed on with ICE.

The Beaver and Washington county sheriff’s offices also maintain 287(g) agreements.

Several Allegheny County municipalities have passed resolutions forbidding local officers from assisting ICE, including Oakmont, Fox Chapel, Plum and McCandless.

Allegheny County also bars its employees from cooperating with the agency, while the City of Pittsburgh prohibits ICE from staging on some of its property.

text:
Washington — President Trump seems to be reconsidering his approach to Democrats after Tuesday's massive Republican election losses and has so far made contradictory comments about how he plans to deal with them as they take control of the Senate and the House in January.

"We're going to work with the Democrats," the president told Politico as GOP defeats were beginning to stack up Tuesday night, though in a phone call with CBS News' Robert Costa before polls closed, he had said, "I have the ultimate power — it's called 'veto.'"

By Wednesday afternoon, he had merged the two approaches.

"I'll get along, probably, with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive, but I have the power of the veto," the president told reporters at the White House ballroom construction site Wednesday. On Thursday, a red hat that said "VETO" sat on the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office.

But Democrats may not be the only source of friction ahead. After two years of working in lockstep with Mr. Trump, some Republicans may prove more willing to defy the term-limited president to try to salvage their political careers.

Here's what the newly empowered congressional Democrats may have in store for Mr. Trump in 2027 for the last two years of his presidency.

Oversight and investigations

The committee chair's gavel comes with subpoena power, and Democrats plan to wield it.

"Lawyer up," warned Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the incoming chairman of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform. He has been mapping out the panel's investigative agenda for months.

New probes will focus on the Trump family's business dealings, corporate corruption, Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement actions and the Jeffrey Epstein scandal, Garcia said.

Garcia wants to know more about Donald Trump Jr.'s Bahamas wedding festivities that were partially paid for by a Russian oligarch, a $2 billion investment that Jared Kushner's private equity fund received from Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund, the Trump family's crypto ventures, companies linked to the president's sons that have received Pentagon contracts, allegations of a pay-to-play scheme and other kickbacks related to DHS contracts and White House ballroom donations.

"Folks that need to be concerned first are administration officials that have caused real harm. We're going to investigate the abuses," Garcia said at a news conference in California on Wednesday.

He singled out White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, former DHS official Corey Lewandowski and former DHS secretary Kristi Noem, as well as Trump family members, as possible targets.

"There's a lot of folks that need to understand that we are going to ask them to testify in front of the U.S. Congress," Garcia said.

He acknowledged that the Trump Justice Department is unlikely to take any enforcement action against those who don't cooperate. But he said that in the majority, Democrats will have the power to sue on behalf of the House.

"We have the power of contempt charges. And contempt charges not only go to the DOJ; there's also a civil contempt process that goes to the courts," he said.

Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, who will lead the House Judiciary Committee, has his own lengthy list of investigative targets, some of which overlap with the oversight committee, like the Justice Department's handling of the Epstein probe and Ghislaine Maxwell's transfer to a low-security prison.

Raskin also plans to scrutinize what Democrats have characterized as "slush funds" — an international initiative called the "Board of Peace;" the "anti-weaponization" fund created from a settlement of a Trump lawsuit against the IRS and Treasury Department and White House ballroom funding.

"There are private entities that we can subpoena to come in," Raskin told Punchbowl News, regarding other avenues to gather information from outside of the Trump administration.

Rep. Adam Smith of Washington, the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, said he plans to conduct "vigorous oversight" of the Defense Department.

The "illegal war against Iran is top of mind for me and the American people," Smith said in a statement Wednesday. He said he also plans to look at "sweetheart deals" and waste, fraud and abuse in government contracts.

Smith also wants to investigate the "unauthorized military strikes in the Caribbean and Latin America, the deployment of the military to U.S. cities, and the blatant and corrosive politicization of our Armed Forces and purging of the ranks based on loyalty and ideology."

Douglas Kriner, a professor in Cornell University's Government Department, said "there's always been greater investigatory activity in divided governments than when the president's party controls Congress." He said the House has always been more aggressive in its investigations than the Senate.

A White House official said that if Democrats want to "abuse their power and politicize the process of investigations, subpoenas and destroying lives, they should be reminded that we still control the federal government and all of its powers."

"As the president has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," said White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."

Not inclined to impeach Trump at this point

During the campaign, Mr. Trump often predicted he'd be impeached if Democrats took control of Congress, but for now, they've shown no sign that this is on their agenda. On Wednesday, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters, "I haven't had a single member of the House Democratic Caucus talk to me about impeachment."

Mr. Trump was impeached twice during his first term when Democrats controlled the House. Both efforts ended without a conviction in the Senate, which requires a two-thirds majority vote.

Even those on the far left, like Rep.-elect Melat Kiros of Colorado, who is among the contingent of democratic socialists joining Congress next year, told CBS News in a recent interview that the party should focus on legislation that could make a material difference in the lives of working-class people.

"I'm not convinced that there is a path forward for impeaching the president that would lead to removal," she said.

Asked whether he would support impeaching the president, Rep.-elect Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania, another democratic socialist, told CBS News that the question was "too broad" for him to answer.

Some Democratic leaders like Raskin agree there are more important issues to address than pursuing impeachment, even though they believe that Mr. Trump has committed impeachable offenses. Raskin was the lead House manager for Mr. Trump's second impeachment.

The president also perceives that there's currently little appetite for a third try.

"Not even a little bit," Mr. Trump responded when asked if he was worried about being impeached again. "I think it would destroy the Democrat Party if they did that. 'Cause impeachment for no reason — what, for having a successful country? Our country is more successful now than at any time in its history."

Taking back power of the purse

Democrats will also be taking back Congress' power of the purse from Mr. Trump, who often bypassed the Senate and the House, and Republicans in the Capitol, who usually went along with the president's budget priorities. But their much slimmer House majority often slowed down the process.

Democratic Rep. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, who's expected to lead the House Appropriations Committee, said she plans to use "what tools are available" to rein in the Trump administration.

In a recent interview, DeLauro said she wants to address cost-of-living issues but also said, "I will fight Donald Trump and the Cabinet secretaries as well."

"I'm going to hold the Trump administration accountable for the corruption," she said. "I'm going to rein in corruption at the highest level of government. I would do that through appropriations."

"We will build in guardrails in the appropriation bills," DeLauro added.

Asked whether she would consider zeroing out funding to enforce accountability, DeLauro said all options "will be reviewed."

Although congressional Democrats plan to ratchet up the pressure on the Trump administration, they know they'll need to work with Republicans on major legislation, like funding the government because of the Senate filibuster. The majority of measures need to reach a 60-vote threshold of support in the Senate to overcome a filibuster.

With a few exceptions like the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, "most of what Congress has done in the first two years of the Trump administration has required bipartisan support because it's had to overcome the filibuster," said Molly Reynolds, vice president and director of governance studies at the Brookings Institution. "So, in that sense, we would still be looking at bipartisan legislating."

Kriner suggested Democrats may try to use the appropriations process, limitation riders and other tools at their disposal to influence what Mr. Trump's agencies can and can't do. And more than once, the White House Office of Management and Budget has unilaterally made spending decisions about funds that were already appropriated by Congress. The OMB has tried to make the case, Kriner said, that presidents have exclusive powers under Article II to decide how money is spent.

"That's been the central front of an institutional battle over the first two years of the Trump administration, and it has really big, lasting implications for what the balance of power across the branches is going to look like," Kriner said.

In contrast with the White House's pugnacious tone, Mr. Trump has been more conciliatory and said he may work with Democrats.

"My message is congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country," the president told CBS News senior White House correspondent Weijia Jiang on Tuesday night.

What will happen to Trump nominees?

Democratic control of the Senate will make it difficult for the president to get his nominees confirmed.

Mr. Trump has repeatedly said he doesn't plan to fire Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. But he also told ABC News' Jonathan Karl on Wednesday that it would be easier to confirm a new defense secretary before the new Congress is seated in January.

The president will likely have to rely on acting officials for roles that need to be filled, unless he nominates candidates who can win bipartisan support.

Power of the pen

The president has relied on executive authority for much of his second-term agenda, even under the unified control of government he enjoyed during his first two years in office.

Brandon Rottinghaus, political science professor at the University of Houston, said, "That's been his M.O. He likes it as a streamlined way to pursue his objectives in a way that aren't checked typically by Congress."

Rottinghaus noted that President Barack Obama increasingly relied on executive actions after Republicans won back the House in 2010, especially on his immigration priorities, many of which were challenged in court and rolled back by the Trump administration.

"Legislative constraints will encourage presidential unilateralism, but the courts will definitely limit those kinds of actions," Rottinghaus said.

The president picked up his pen Thursday to sign an executive order designating the Oval Office and Cabinet Room national landmarks, saying future presidents won't be able to make major changes. But a future president could also sign a new executive order to undo it.

Trump's relationship with Republicans

Before the elections, most Republicans in Congress supported, defended and voted for Mr. Trump's priorities. Now, Mr. Trump is looking at what Rottinghaus called a "ticking clock."

"The last two years are going to be the hardest of his political career," Rottinghaus said. "His leverage over members of Congress, especially Republicans, will diminish as lawmakers think about their own political futures rather than the president's."

"Republicans are going to have to figure out a way forward," he continued. "You know, they're going to have to figure out a way forward around Donald Trump."

text:
MARY LOUISE KELLY, HOST:

Democratic Congressman Robert Garcia had two words of advice for the Trump administration this week - lawyer up. After Democrats won majorities in the House and Senate, Garcia is set to become the next chair of the House Oversight Committee, so the watchdog committee. And he has promised to look into, among other things, ICE enforcement. NPR's Jasmine Garsd is here to discuss what that might look like. Hey, Jas.

JASMINE GARSD, BYLINE: Hi.

KELLY: Hey. So one of the big concerns with ICE agents and ICE detention centers has been lack of oversight. What might change?

GARSD: OK. So first of all, I think it's worth mentioning that the current Congress basically gave immigration enforcement a blank check. In 2025 and 2026, Congress gave around $240 billion - that's billion with a B - to ICE and Customs and Border Patrol. Now, the incoming Congress which just got voted in could stop giving them even more money, but, you know, the truth is ICE and DHS have gotten enough funds to run mass deportation operations for the remainder of Trump's term.

There are a couple of things that could happen here. Congress could claw back that money, but, you know, the hurdle is President Trump would very likely veto that. There could also be restrictions on usage of those funds - warrant requirements, banning masks, restricting agents from going into schools, churches, hospitals. I spoke to Naureen Shah at the ACLU, who told me she thinks in order to change ICE behavior, one of the most powerful things that could happen is congressional oversight through subpoenas.

NAUREEN SHAH: ICE has to be afraid. They have to be afraid of losing their funding. They have to be afraid of being subpoenaed and asked extremely hard questions before a live audience of the American people.

KELLY: Jas, a question about facilities. You've covered the boom of the whole private detention center industry, which houses immigrant detainees. What are they saying?

GARSD: So the Trump administration has spent billions of that money given by Congress to expand ICE detention facilities, many of which have been accused of having dire, even deadly, conditions. I mean, we've seen a historic amount of deaths in ICE detention. I tune into every quarterly investors call for the two main contractors for ICE detention centers. That's GEO Group and CoreCivic. And this morning, I listened in on the CoreCivic call, and almost every question asked was about this blue wave. Here's an exchange between CoreCivic President Lucibeth Mayberry and several investors asking how will the result of midterms affect ICE operations?

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

LUCIBETH MAYBERRY: You've seen them continue to enter into contracts. They also, you know, have, again, began increasing enforcement activities and growing the number. They have the secure funding to do so. You know, we would urge the, you know, ICE administration to move quickly.

GARSD: So she's basically saying ICE has the funding, but they should hurry up and purchase space. And I think that statement is this moment in a nutshell.

KELLY: And what's the Trump administration saying about this moment?

GARSD: So yesterday, U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin simply tweeted, quote, "deportations will continue." On the other hand, in a post on X, JD Vance wrote that he thinks the big loss this week is due to voters' concerns over economy, inflation, the war. He left out immigration enforcement. He said he is open to changing enforcement tactics by focusing more on businesses that hire undocumented workers, but he says immigration amnesty is not the solution.

KELLY: NPR's Jasmine Garsd, thank you for joining us.

GARSD: Thanks for having me. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

Harmeet Dhillon stepped down as head of the Department of Justice's (DOJ) Civil Rights Division after Democrats' sweeping midterm victories, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced on Thursday. "Today, I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led the Civil Rights Division with conviction the past 18 months," Blanche wrote on X. "She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor," he added. "The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors." Dhillon, a longtime ally of President Donald Trump, was confirmed by the Senate in April 2025 to lead the division, which enforces federal civil rights laws. During her tenure, the division shifted its priorities toward issues, including religious liberty and Second Amendment rights, while also pursuing cases involving voter rolls, immigration, and alleged antisemitism on college campuses. The division also saw departures among career attorneys, followed by recruitment of lawyers with backgrounds in conservative advocacy. "Serving my country as AAG for Civil Rights has been the honor of a lifetime. We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women and girls' sports, and so much more," Dhillon wrote on X. "I want to thank President Trump for giving me this opportunity," she added. "I look forward to what’s next!" Dhillon's departure makes her the first senior DOJ official reported to be leaving after the election, as the administration prepares for a change in congressional control. Bloomberg Law reported that other political appointees could also leave before the end of the year.
