text:
Erin Daly said the anxiety was already building at the start of summer break. That’s when some of her students told her they were “going into hiding” or said they wouldn’t be allowed to play outside.

“‘Getting caught’ and ‘rounded up’ were words that my students were using amongst themselves in conversations,” Daly said.

Then came the first week of school, and the Immigration and Customs Enforcement operation that sent shockwaves through the city of Danbury, where two-thirds of K-12 students are Latino. One story in particular grabbed the attention of students and teachers: Agents had approached a bus stop to detain parents dropping off their kids.

Daly is a third grade teacher and the president of NEA-Danbury, the district’s teachers union. She said after the ICE raids, one of her students refused to stand for the Pledge of Allegiance.

“I asked him why, and he said … ‘The flag does not keep me safe, and I’m not doing it anymore,’” Daly recalled. “It unleashed a huge assortment of emotion in my class from my other students.” Half the class, she said, was in tears.

“I’ll tell you one thing,” she said. “That bus stop incident from the first week of school traumatized so many of our kids, and I’m hearing that from all of my colleagues.”

“I’ve had students that have demonstrated a lot of negative behaviors in the classroom that they ordinarily wouldn’t have, or that they didn’t demonstrate in younger grades,” she added.

When asked for comment on those detentions, a representative for ICE shared a link to a statement released on Sept. 11, roughly two weeks after the Danbury arrests. The statement said agents with ICE’s Boston field office had arrested “118 illegal aliens,” of which “numerous have been charged with crimes.” It listed five specific individuals alongside their pending criminal charges or previous convictions.

The agency representative, who responded from a general email address and did not provide their name, did not say whether ICE is detaining green card holders or what individuals with legal residency can do to avoid being detained by agents.

NEA-Danbury Vice President Julian Schafer, who teaches high school social studies, said students’ opinions of ICE have changed markedly since the August enforcement operation. Last year, he said, a fair number of his students expressed the belief that ICE was focused on removing dangerous criminals from the country.

“I think the blinds on that were ripped off this first week of school,” Schafer said. “It was clear mass enforcement — you know, parents being taken from a bus stop.”

On Sept. 2, Danbury teachers, advocates and city leaders held a rally alongside U.S. Sens. Richard Blumenthal and Chris Murphy to condemn ICE and show support for the city’s immigrant community. Schafer was one of the speakers.

In his speech, he recounted how some of his students had seen ICE agents making arrests out the windows of their buses. A video of Schafer’s speech posted on Facebook drew over 100 comments, some defending ICE’s actions.

“Well, if they’re here legally, then these families have nothing to fear,” one user wrote.

“When laws getting enforced scares people, it implies that they know that they have been violating the law,” another wrote.

In early October, a group of masked protesters appeared outside Danbury police headquarters holding a sign reading “Keep New England White.” Daly described them as a “white nationalist neo-Nazi group.”

“Another level of hate being brought into our community,” she said in a text message.

The Connecticut Mirror spoke with several teachers in the Danbury area, and none expressed support for the scale of ICE arrests taking place under the Trump administration.

Schafer said he worries the detentions could potentially hurt Danbury’s tax base, which the city relies on to fund local services — including schools. “When, let’s say, an immigrant family is renting an apartment or a home, they’re paying a landlord property taxes through their rent,” Schafer said. “I’ve seen the local economy … struggle in the wake of these deportations because folks are not out patronizing local businesses.”

Outside Danbury, the impact of the late August ICE raids is less clear. In Windham, in Eastern Connecticut — which also has a majority-Latino student body — attendance during the first 10 days of school was actually 2% higher than the same period last year, according to District Superintendent Iris Gomero.

“The trends that I’m seeing is that our students are coming to school,” Gomero said. Those are “very intentional efforts that are happening from across the district. And it starts with students knowing that they’re going to be safe in our schools.”

That safety, Gomero said, comes in part through ensuring students and parents know the school’s policies around who is and is not allowed in the building.

“They know that if someone was to show up at our doors, that there’s a process and a protocol in place. That we would ask for ID, we would ask for judiciary subpoenas,” Gomero said. “And if that is not the case, then … we wouldn’t allow them to have access to our students.”

About 20 minutes west of Danbury via I-84 is Brewster, a New York town of fewer than 3,000 residents with a large Latino population. The proximity of the two municipalities means some people work in one and live in the other — as is the case for Tom Mullane, a Brewster social studies teacher and Danbury resident.

When immigration enforcement agents first started showing up in August, Mullane said, one of his close friends became afraid to leave the house, worried that the color of her skin could put her at risk of arrest.

Mullane said his friend is a Mexican citizen with permanent legal status in the United States. In the past, Mullane said, she was a visible participant in community events in Danbury, but ICE’s actions made her too scared to even shop for groceries alone.

The atmosphere in Brewster was entirely different. Although more than half of the students are Hispanic or Latino, Mullane said ICE wasn’t on their minds at the start of the school year. Instead, everyone’s attention was on something decidedly ordinary: The district’s new class schedule.

Below the surface, there are signs of disruption. Shannon Riley — a colleague of Mullane’s who also happens to be chair of the Brookfield Democratic Town Committee in Connecticut — said there are students in Brewster the district has yet to see this year.

“We’ve reached out to find out where they are and haven’t gotten any information,” Riley said. “They either have picked up and moved or they’re just afraid and don’t trust us to protect their identities.”

Mullane said he’s aware of a couple of isolated immigration cases. He’s written a letter of support for one student and talked to another whose relative was deported. And he feels there’s a sharp political divide in the community, as evidenced by opinions his students have expressed.

Mullane said he and his colleagues have become skilled in moderating political conversations when they occur in the classroom. But ICE is one topic he’s not sure they can manage.

“I feel bad saying this, but I really, I’ve avoided it,” Mullane said. “I’m worried that [these conversations are] going to go badly, even though I know that I facilitate them well.”

And the relative calm of the moment may be fragile.

“If ICE does in Brewster what they just did in Danbury, call me back and we’ll be having a very different conversation,” Mullane said.

text:
A coalition of 24 attorneys general and two governors says proposed changes to the census could exclude more than 600,000 New Jersey residents and undermine the accuracy of population counts.

New Jersey could lose political representation in Congress and millions of dollars in federal funding under proposed changes to the 2030 U.S. Census that would exclude hundreds of thousands of immigrants from the state’s population count, according to Attorney General Jennifer Davenport and a coalition of state officials.

Davenport is co-leading a coalition of 24 attorneys general and two governors opposing the Trump administration’s proposed changes to how the federal government counts residents and collects demographic information.

In a 39-page letter submitted to the U.S. Department of Commerce on Monday, Nov. 2, the coalition warned that the changes would violate the Constitution, distort population numbers, and undermine the ability of state and local governments to plan for public services.

The coalition estimates that roughly 16.1 million people nationwide could be excluded from the census, including at least 600,000 New Jersey residents, or more than 6% of the state’s population. The New Jersey figure is based on estimates of the state’s undocumented immigrant population in 2023 and does not include all other noncitizens who could be excluded.

“Everyone counts in New Jersey, just as the Constitution requires. The proposed census rule ignores that constitutional mandate and would undercount our population,” Davenport said in a statement. “This would lead to the loss of an untold amount of federal funding for critical services and programs that touch all of our lives and our communities, including for vital public safety initiatives.”

The census, conducted every 10 years, determines how many seats each state receives in the U.S. House of Representatives. Its population figures also help determine how federal funding is distributed to states and communities for education, transportation, health care, infrastructure, and other public services.

Changes to the count could have consequences for New Jersey that extend well beyond the 2030 Census, affecting congressional representation and government funding throughout the following decade.

Who would be excluded from the census?

Under the proposal published by the U.S. Census Bureau on Sept. 10, only U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents, commonly known as green card holders, would be included in the population count for congressional representation.

Millions of other immigrants living in the United States would be excluded, including people with work, student, or family visas and immigrants who have lived in the country for years without permanent resident status.

The administration argues that the Constitution’s requirement to count people for congressional representation should apply to those with “sufficient ties or allegiance to the United States.” In its proposed rule, the Census Bureau maintains that its interpretation would better fulfill the constitutional purpose of the census and improve the accuracy of population data.

The attorneys general dispute that interpretation. The 14th Amendment requires congressional seats to be apportioned according to the “whole number of persons in each State,” a standard the coalition says includes residents regardless of citizenship or immigration status. The coalition also argues that the proposal would violate the federal Census Act, which requires the government to determine each state’s total population for congressional apportionment.

According to the letter, no previous decennial census has excluded residents solely because of their immigration status.

The consequences would not be evenly distributed across the country. States with larger immigrant populations, including New Jersey, California, and New York, could lose congressional representation relative to states with smaller immigrant populations.

Because Electoral College votes are partly determined by the number of congressional seats each state receives, changes to population counts could also affect presidential elections.

Federal funding and local services at risk

The coalition warned that excluding immigrants from the population count could reduce federal funding without reducing the demand for government services.

States and municipalities use census figures to determine where schools, hospitals, public transportation, emergency services, and other resources are needed. Immigrants who are excluded from the census would still live in their communities, use roads and public services, and send their children to school.

New Jersey’s Office of New Americans, for example, uses census information to assess the need for refugee resettlement programs and services that help immigrants integrate into their communities.

Inaccurate population counts could also complicate the process of redrawing legislative and local government districts, which must meet constitutional standards for equal representation.

The coalition did not estimate how much federal funding New Jersey could lose under the proposal.

Changes to how residency is determined

The administration is also proposing to change how the census determines where people live.

Since the first census in 1790, the federal government has counted people at their usual residence, meaning the place where they live and sleep most of the time.

The proposed rules would instead determine residency based on where a person lawfully spends the greatest number of days between Jan. 3 and April 1 of the census year, using tax records as evidence of residency.

The attorneys general warned that the new approach could count people in states or communities where they do not ordinarily live.

For example, someone who spends the winter at a vacation home could be counted there rather than at their permanent residence. A person who moves to another state shortly before Census Day on April 1 could be counted at their former address.

The coalition also raised concerns about using tax documents to determine residency. College students may be listed as dependents at their parents’ homes, military personnel may file taxes in states where they no longer live, and some taxpayers use business addresses or post office boxes.

The letter argues that the Census Bureau has not adequately explained how it would resolve conflicting information or test the new system before 2030.

Eliminating race and ethnicity questions

Another proposed change would eliminate questions about race and ethnicity from the decennial census and prohibit questions about sexual orientation.

Race has been included in the census since 1790. Sexual orientation has not been included in the traditional decennial census, but the proposed rule would prohibit its inclusion in future population-counting questionnaires.

The administration argues that such questions are unnecessary for the census’s primary constitutional purpose of counting residents for congressional representation and could discourage participation.

The attorneys general counter that demographic information is essential for enforcing civil rights laws, identifying disparities in public services, and evaluating government programs.

For example, New Jersey used demographic information from the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey to develop its 2025 Direct Care Workforce Strategic Plan, which examined the racial, ethnic, and immigration characteristics of workers who care for older adults and people with disabilities.

The coalition warned that eliminating detailed demographic information from the census could weaken the data used to evaluate whether workforce policies are reaching the populations they are intended to serve.

The attorneys general also argued that other federal surveys cannot fully replace the detailed demographic information collected through the decennial census, particularly for smaller communities.

Coalition calls for withdrawal

The proposed changes have not been finalized. The Census Bureau accepted public comments through Nov. 2. The coalition is urging the Census Bureau to withdraw the proposal rather than proceed with changes. The federal government has not yet issued a final rule.

In addition to New Jersey, the coalition includes attorneys general from Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia, along with the governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania.

text:
SALINAS, Calif. —

The County of Monterey is demanding that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement stop using county property as a staging area for civil immigration enforcement, citing reported vehicle activity at several facilities and concerns about safety and access to services.

In a cease-and-desist letter dated Thursday, County Counsel Susan Blitch said ICE vehicles and personnel had been seen this week and last week at Natividad Medical Center, the Monterey County Jail, the Salinas Regional Soccer Complex and Juvenile Hall.

ICE agents were also reportedly seen outside the Monterey County Jail on Thursday.

The letter says vehicles were seen congregating in county parking lots and driveways, parking in red zones, blocking traffic and pedestrian access, and blocking employee parking at Natividad.

The county also said the reported activity created risks for employees and the public and was especially troubling when it could interrupt access to medical care.

The county demands that DHS and ICE immediately:

Cease any unauthorized use of County parking lots or other County property as a staging area, processing location or operating base for civil immigration enforcement activities.

Comply with all posted parking restrictions.

Comply with all applicable traffic laws and operate vehicles safely while on County property.

Refrain from conducting activities on County property in a manner or location that interferes with, intimidates or impedes individuals from seeking vital County services, particularly medical care.

Monterey County supervisors adopted a policy in September prohibiting the use of county property for ICE operations. The policy does not restrict lawful judicial warrants or criminal law enforcement.

The letter says ICE vehicles’ operations forced the jail to temporarily shut down last week. The Sheriff’s Office previously said the jail resumed normal operations after a lockdown that began as protesters gathered amid reports of federal immigration agents near the facility.

The county said it reserves its legal rights and may take action to protect county property, employees, the public and access to services if the conduct continues.

Monterey County Supervisors Wendy Root Askew and Luis Alejo addressed the cease-and-desist letter in social media posts Thursday.

“Today, I can say with confidence that the county is doing everything in our power to de-escalate the dangerous situation that immigration agents are creating in our community. Our County Counsel just sent this cease-and-desist letter to DHS,” Askew said.

Alejo said the county was demanding an immediate end to the unauthorized use of county property for immigration enforcement operations.

“Today, the County of Monterey sent a cease-and-desist letter to ICE demanding an immediate end to the unauthorized use of county parking lots, driveways and other property to stage or conduct civil immigration enforcement operations,” Alejo said.

“The letter cites ICE activity at four county sites in Salinas: Natividad Medical Center, the Monterey County Jail, the Salinas Regional Soccer Complex and Juvenile Hall. The county reported that ICE vehicles blocked access to employee parking at Natividad and that ICE operations forced a temporary shutdown at the County Jail.

“The county is demanding that ICE follow posted parking restrictions and traffic laws, drive safely on county property, and stop any activity on county property that intimidates people or interferes with access to essential county services.

“Everyone in Monterey County should be able to seek medical care without fear or obstruction. The County of Monterey stands with our immigrant workers and families and the county employees who serve them.”

description:

However, DHS said these detainers were not honored, and the individuals were released from jail.
In certain cases, individuals who face ICE detainers but are released from jail may go on to commit other crimes.

text:
By Naveen Athrappully

Contributing Writer

Almost 24,000 illegal immigrants with criminal convictions or charges have been released into communities since Jan. 20, 2025, due to California’s refusal to honor Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainers, the Department of Homeland Security said.

“There are more than 81,000 criminal charges or convictions associated with these non-honored detainers,” the DHS said in a Monday statement.

This includes 3,295 burglaries, 1,097 assaults, 1,088 drug trafficking charges, 169 homicides, and 147 sexual assaults.

An ICE detainer asks a law enforcement agency to notify ICE before releasing a removable illegal immigrant from any prison or confinement facility, or to hold an illegal immigrant up to 48 hours past their scheduled release so DHS has time to take custody of the individual.

ICE typically issues such detainers in instances where an illegal immigrant has been convicted of crimes by a court or if they pose a public or national security threat.

Some of the ICE detainers in California include an El Salvador national who has been convicted of cruelty to a child and murder, a Cuban convicted of second-degree murder, an Armenian convicted of voluntary manslaughter, and a Libyan convicted of assault with a firearm on a person.

ICE had filed detainers for these individuals in 2025 or 2026. However, DHS said these detainers were not honored, and the individuals were released from jail.

“Sanctuary politicians have not only refused to cooperate with federal law enforcement to target and arrest the worst of the worst — but they’ve released nearly 24,000 criminal illegal aliens onto the streets of California to terrorize innocent Americans,” DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in the statement.

In California, state and local resources must not assist immigration enforcement activities unless they’re lawfully required to do so, according to guidance issued by California Attorney General Rob Bonta in July.

The guidance asks agencies to limit the collection, retention and disclosure of information that could help identify or apprehend people without lawful immigration status.

“Where there is no legal obligation to comply with a request from immigration authorities, agencies should require appropriate legal process — such as a judicial warrant, judicial subpoena, or court order — before complying,” the guidance said.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom justified his state’s sanctuary policies in a January podcast with conservative commentator Ben Shapiro. Newsom said that California does cooperate with federal immigration under certain circumstances, claiming that the state has coordinated more than 10,000 prisoner transfers. Newsom said he disagreed with calls from some Democrats to abolish ICE.

“California has cooperated with more ICE transfers probably than any other state in the country. And I vetoed multiple pieces of legislation that have come from my Legislature to stop the ability for the state of California to do that,” Newsom said.

In certain cases, individuals who face ICE detainers but are released from jail may go on to commit other crimes.

In June, an illegal immigrant from El Salvador was charged with murdering a veteran in Utah. ICE had previously lodged detainers for this illegal immigrant twice in California. But on both occasions, the state refused to honor the requests and released the individual, DHS said in a July 20 statement.

In addition to California, DHS has also criticized New York state for allegedly failing to comply with ICE detainers.

In an Oct. 9 statement, the department said New York did not honor 14,916 immigration detainers issued by ICE between Jan. 20, 2025, and Sept. 14, 2026. These detainers were associated with 47,750 criminal charges and convictions.

“Sanctuary politicians create an environment for criminal activity to thrive, not for American citizens to be safe. President Trump made it clear that he would restore law and order in our cities and in our states. When you have sanctuary cities and politicians, you endanger the safety of the public,” Mullin said in the statement.

text:
Amnesty International has urged Thailand to offer two Uyghur men sanctuary in a safe third country, warning that deporting them to China would endanger their lives and violate international law.

Secretary-General Agnes Callamard called on the Thai government to halt any plans to return the men, provide access to lawyers of their choice and find a safe third-country solution, saying their forced return would breach international law.

"Thai authorities must immediately halt any plans to forcibly return these two Uyghur men to China, where they face a real risk of torture, arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance," Ms Callamard said.

She warned Thailand against repeating its February 2025 deportation of 40 Uyghur men, whose whereabouts and well-being remain unknown despite subsequent visits by Thai representatives to China's Xinjiang region.

The two men are among five Uyghurs remaining in Thailand from a group of more than 300 detained without charge on March 13, 2014, after fleeing persecution and discrimination in Xinjiang.

On Oct 21, the two were released from prison under a royal pardon and transferred to Bangkok's Immigration Detention Centre. Amnesty said they had since been denied access to their lawyers, civil society organisations and the National Human Rights Commission of Thailand.

Both men have told their legal representatives that they fear for their lives if returned to China and do not consent to deportation. They have spent more than 12 years in Thai detention.

Ms Callamard said diplomatic assurances from Beijing could not override Thailand's obligation not to return anyone to a country where they face a real risk of torture or other serious human rights violations.

Amnesty also cited Thailand's obligations under the Convention against Torture and Article 13 of the Prevention and Suppression of Torture and Enforced Disappearance Act, which prohibits deportation where there are substantial grounds to believe a person would face torture, ill-treatment or enforced disappearance.

The organisation said its 2021 report documented crimes against humanity against Uyghurs and other Muslim ethnic groups in Xinjiang.

text:
Chicago – Attorney General Kwame Raoul secured an important legal victory that protects Congressionally-authorized public safety grants, including grants intended to fight crime and keep law enforcement officers safe.

In August, Raoul co-led a coalition of attorneys general in filing a lawsuit challenging the Trump administration’s attempt to impose illegal immigration-enforcement conditions on public safety funding. On Wednesday, the District of Rhode Island Chief Judge John J. McConnell Jr. declared the Trump administration’s actions unlawful and permanently enjoined any implementation or enforcement of these illegal conditions.

“By targeting these funds, the Trump administration threatened to harm state and local law enforcement and put public safety at risk,” Raoul said. “This funding has no relationship to civil immigration enforcement, and I am pleased that the court ruled these conditions unlawful. I will continue to fight to protect public safety funding from overreach by this administration.”

Among the affected programs is the Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Formula Grants, known as the Byrne JAG Program. For decades, regardless of which political party held power, the Byrne JAG Program has been the leading federal source of criminal justice funding to state and local governments. Congress directed the U.S. Department of Justice to distribute funds based on a state’s population and violent crime rate, not the immigration priorities of the executive branch. The program provides crucial support for law enforcement, including funding for equipment and training. Over the last four fiscal years, Illinois has received a total of more than $25 million in law enforcement funds through this federal program.

This win comes after Raoul co-led a coalition of attorneys general that succeeded in getting the federal government to remove similar conditions on over $1.3 billion of Victims of Crime Act (VOCA) grants last year. Raoul also co-led a coalition that successfully blocked similar conditions on billions of dollars in annual U.S. Department of Transportation grants last year.

In July, Raoul co-led a coalition in filing a lawsuit challenging the administration’s attempt to impose unlawful conditions on billions of dollars in federal funds that Congress appropriated for states to use in preparing for and responding to emergencies and natural disasters, including acts of terrorism. Raoul filed this lawsuit after co-leading a coalition that successfully defended the same category of funding from unlawful conditions in 2025.

Civil immigration enforcement is a federal responsibility and not a state government responsibility. The Trump administration’s unlawful attempts to coerce states into doing its bidding conflict with core principles of American governance – the separation of powers and federalism. The administration’s actions violated laws passed by Congress as well as the Spending Clause of the U.S. Constitution.

Attorney General Raoul led the lawsuit along with California Attorney General Rob Bonta, Delaware Attorney General Kathy Jennings, New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport and Rhode Island Attorney General Peter F. Neronha. They were joined by the attorneys general of Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Hawaii, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Vermont, Virginia, Washington and Wisconsin, as well as the commonwealth of Pennsylvania.

text:
Now that we’ve sobered up from our celebratory shots and pre-rolls, it’s time to cast a sharp eye on our local and national governments.

As a nation, the tremendous feat of tipping the scales in favor of progressives, the working class, and immigrants may have been the easier part of establishing the possibilities of change. Now we need to hold our elected officials to keeping the promises they’ve made to us, the ones that influenced us to mark their names on our ballots.

Tuesday’s election resulted in a deep blue-shaded shift across the country. We saw historically red states flip, and a progressive candidate was elected as L.A.’s first Asian mayor. This week’s elections also brought the country’s first Black and Native women governors into office. This is the same optimism that New Yorkers probably tasted when they elected Mamdani.

If these politicians are truly working in the best interests of their constituents, we’ll see the quick defunding and absolute abolishment of ICE, as well as better support for small businesses, working families, and improved resources for the homeless community.

In other news, ICE’s abuses continue.

Looking northward, last Friday, a 23-year-old Berkeley student and asylum seeker from Colombia named Paula Valentina Albornoz Hernandez was detained by ICE at San Francisco International Airport.

The young woman, who escaped “severe gender-based violence” in her home country, was about to visit Portland with her boyfriend when an ICE agent in plain clothes began interrogating her. AP reports that Hernandez’s asylum application is pending and that she currently has a valid work permit.

In August, we highlighted the Turkish chef behind Ararat Kebab in Culver City in our street kebabs guide. Sadly, he was recently detained by ICE. West Los Respuesta Rapida, a West L.A. rapid response group, helped get the truck towed to a “safe place,” and says they’re in touch with the only support systems he has in the U.S.

L.A. cannot keep suffering like this, lest we lose everything that makes L.A. the city we love: its people. Even though it has now been revealed that ICE was quietly ordered not to conduct any raids on Election Day, Aisha Wallace-Palomares was out in the streets ready to document any potential ICE activity at the polls.

Here’s to collective hope, a feeling that many of us have forgotten since Trump’s second term began. Here is to the encouraging development that a lot of younger, newer leaders are being given a chance to run things. Here’s to the collective pressure we need to put on our elected officials.

L.A. TACO will be here beside our city, observing and reporting on whether change is truly on the horizon.

title: 'We will not be intimidated': 3 anti-ICE protesters plead not guilty to federal charges - VTDigger
authors: Alan J. Keays, Emma White, Charlotte Oliver, Waterbury Record
description:
BURLINGTON — Three people have denied federal charges stemming from demonstrations where they allegedly blocked doors at a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement surveillance facility in Williston.
The filing of the federal charges is the latest prosecutorial turn following many anti-ICE protests and demonstrations in Vermont.
Vermont Attorney General Charity Clark, who also has the authority to bring state criminal charges in Chittenden County, has since filed trespass-related charges against protesters stemming from demonstrations at the White Cap facility.
Appel, the attorney for the three people who appeared in federal court Thursday, told reporters outside the courtroom that it is extremely rare for prosecutors to bring federal charges in such cases.

text:
BURLINGTON — Three people have denied federal charges stemming from demonstrations where they allegedly blocked doors at a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement surveillance facility in Williston.

Peter Booth, 58, of Jericho; Henry Prensky, 80, of Burlington; and Sherri Wormser, 57, of Colchester, appeared Thursday in federal court in Burlington for their arraignments on misdemeanor charges.

Attorney Robert Appel, representing all three, entered not guilty pleas on their behalf, and they were each released on a condition that they not violate any federal, state or local laws.

All three are charged with obstructing access to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center at the White Cap Business Park in Williston during anti-ICE demonstrations earlier this year.

VTDigger has previously reported that, according to federal records, information at that facility is reviewed and collected from publicly available sources, such as social media, and assists ICE officers with investigations.

The U.S. attorney’s office in Vermont filed the charges in September against the three defendants as well as two other people — Lexington Kennedy, 22, of New York City, and Roan Wade, 23, of Red Hook, New York — in connection with the anti-ICE demonstrations in Williston.

Kennedy and Wade are to be arraigned on similar misdemeanor charges as the three arraigned Thursday.

According to charging documents, Booth, Prensky, Wormser, Kennedy and Wade went into the atrium of the White Cap building Feb. 9 and blocked the doors between the atrium and the federal facility with their bodies. They ignored orders to move, according to the documents.

Then on May 14, the documents say, Booth and Prensky blocked the doors again. Kennedy and Wade are charged with similar conduct on July 24, according to the documents.

By blocking the doors to the federal property, the defendants obstructed its “usual use, enjoyment and access,” according to the documents.

Each offense carries up to 30 days in prison and up to a $5,000 fine.

Appel, speaking to reporters after the hearing, said he was told by a prosecutor to expect an offer to resolve the cases that did not include jail time. Appel added that if he does receive a plea offer, he is obligated to present it to his client for their consideration.

Booth, Prensky and Wormser read a joint statement outside the federal courthouse to a group of about 30 supporters.

“The purpose of these prosecutions is to intimidate,” Wormser said, adding, “We will not be intimidated.”

Activists say they plan to continue protesting ICE’s presence in Vermont. Organizers have announced a mock funeral procession Friday starting at the Williston facility in remembrance of people who have died in ICE custody since the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term in January 2025. The event will be followed by a sit-in, according to a press release.

The filing of the federal charges is the latest prosecutorial turn following many anti-ICE protests and demonstrations in Vermont.

Chittenden County State’s Attorney Sarah George has declined repeatedly to press state charges against anti-ICE protesters after their arrests at demonstrations in the county, contending that it didn’t serve justice to prosecute them.

Vermont Attorney General Charity Clark, who also has the authority to bring state criminal charges in Chittenden County, has since filed trespass-related charges against protesters stemming from demonstrations at the White Cap facility.

Appel, the attorney for the three people who appeared in federal court Thursday, told reporters outside the courtroom that it is extremely rare for prosecutors to bring federal charges in such cases. He said that he would seek to have the charges thrown out on several grounds, including that they violated his clients’ First Amendment rights.

“A potential problem I see is that this is not a federal facility,” added Appel, a former head of the Vermont Human Rights Commission. “It’s rented space in a public building that offers a variety of other services.”

Assistant U.S. Attorney Nathanael Burris, the prosecutor, requested a condition of release prohibiting the defendants from coming “within 50 feet of federal facilities or property occupied by the United States Department of Homeland Security” in Vermont, without prior court approval.

Magistrate Judge Kevin Doyle said he wouldn’t impose that restriction, adding that he was concerned the request was too broad and could result in violations for being at airports or ports of entry where Homeland Security may be located as well.

text:
The legal battle over a Nicaraguan immigrant deported from Minnesota to a potentially dangerous third country in Africa is escalating, as the federal government fights a judge's mandate to bring him back to the United States. Meanwhile, community advocates are rallying to demand his immediate return.

Sent to Africa

What we know:

The U.S. government had granted Kenis Lopez Gonzalez legal protection to live and work in Minnesota so he would not face torture in his home country of Nicaragua. He had lived in Shakopee, operated a construction company, and possessed a valid state driver’s license and work permit at the time of his deportation.

According to court records, Lopez Gonzalez was arrested outside his home in January during Operation Metro Surge. After being shuffled between several immigration detention centers for months, ICE deported him to the Central African Republic (CAR), a country that agreed to accept what are known as "third country" deportees from the United States.

The U.S. State Department currently maintains a Level 4 "Do not travel" advisory for the CAR, warning that the country suffers from a severe lack of government control and that foreigners are frequently targeted for violence and kidnappings. His legal team reports that Lopez Gonzalez is currently stranded in a guarded building in the capital city of Bangui where he relies on an international humanitarian group for "basic survival."

On October 30, U.S. District Court Judge Jeffrey Bryan ruled that the government likely violated federal regulations and constitutional due process by arbitrarily detaining and deporting Lopez Gonzalez. The judge ordered the government to immediately return him to Minnesota.

Government appeal

The other side:

The Trump administration is pushing back aggressively against the judge's mandate. Earlier this week, federal attorneys filed an emergency motion requesting an immediate stay to halt the return order. The government is appealing the ruling to the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals.

In their court filings, attorneys argue that judicial intervention in this case irreparably harms the government by interfering with U.S. foreign policy and delicate diplomatic negotiations with foreign sovereign nations.

Furthermore, the government claims the District Court's decision conflicts with actions taken by the U.S. Supreme Court. Attorneys noted that the Supreme Court has already paused a similar class-action lawsuit regarding third-country deportations, arguing that this precedent should squarely control and pause Lopez Gonzalez's case.

Advocates Demand Action

What's next:

As the government fights the order, grassroots organizations are stepping in to rally for Lopez Gonzalez's safe return. The Workers Circle and Centro de Trabajadores Unidos en la Lucha (CTUL)—of which Lopez Gonzalez is a member-- have scheduled a Friday news conference to call for his immediate return.

Judge Bryan has yet to issue a follow-up ruling on whether he will pause his return orders to give the Eighth Circuit time to respond. Stay with FOX 9 for the latest developments in the case.

As President Donald Trump’s administration prepares for a flurry of congressional investigations into shootings by immigration agents and the Jeffrey Epstein files, the top official in charge of the United States Department of Justice’s civil rights division has resigned.

US Attorney General Todd Blanche on Thursday confirmed Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon’s departure in a post on social media.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

list 1 of 3Former US Justice Department staff says civil rights division ‘destroyed’

list 2 of 3Ex-US Attorney General Pam Bondi testifies in Epstein files probe

list 3 of 3US Justice Department denies whistleblower claims on anti-Semitism probes

end of list

“Today, I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon,” Blanche wrote on X. “She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor.”

A top Trump ally, Dhillon was confirmed to her role in April 2025 and has overseen a dramatic overhaul of the Justice Department’s civil rights division, which is tasked with enforcing anti-discrimination laws. Hundreds of former Justice Department officials penned a letter last December decrying the “destruction” of the agency division under Trump.

Dhillon is the first high-ranking official to resign from the Trump administration since US Democrats swept both chambers of the US Congress in the country’s pivotal midterm elections on Tuesday.

Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, who will likely become the new chair of the powerful House of Representatives Committee on Oversight and Accountability, pledged on Wednesday to take on four major investigations, including abuses of power by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents and the Epstein files.

Dhillon reportedly told her staff earlier this year that her office, which has typically been charged with investigating law enforcement killings by police officers, would not be looking into the fatal shootings of two US citizens – Renee Good and Alex Pretti – who were gunned down by ICE agents in Minneapolis.

In May, Garcia accused the administration of continuing to shield Trump from scrutiny related to unreleased documents tied to the Epstein investigation

During a closed-door hearing in which Blanche’s predecessor, Pam Bondi, was asked by lawmakers about the case, the California Democrat Garcia alleged Dhillon repeatedly intervened to block questions about the president’s connection to the release of the files.

The Justice Department referred Al Jazeera to Blanche’s social media post when asked when Dhillon submitted her resignation. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

text:
More than 10 people were apprehended on the morning of Nov. 5 as federal agents conducted an immigration operation with the assistance of nearby agencies, a local official said.

At 7:47 a.m. that day, the Putnam County Sheriff’s Office released a Facebook statement advising people of a heavy law enforcement presence due to a traffic stop 17 minutes earlier in the Round Lake Park neighborhood, which is near the intersection of Silver Lake Drive and State Road 19 in Palatka.

At 3:30 p.m., however, the sheriff’s office updated its Facebook post to say there had been a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operation at a construction site near that area.

“Due to the proximity to a school and the possibility one individual was armed with a gun a modified lockdown was (triggered) at Palatka Intermediate School for several hours,” sheriff’s office officials said in the updated post.

While ICE has not released information about its operation, the sheriff’s office post stated that the county agency, as well as the Palatka Police Department and Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, assisted the feds with a “mutual aid request to assist in locating the individuals who ran.”

The sheriff’s office’s post didn’t list exactly where the ICE operation took place, but a video posted on Facebook shows law enforcement officials leading at least 13 handcuffed people from the construction site of Palatka Primary School on Kelly Smith Road.

In a text message to the Daily News, Superintendent Rick Surrency said he was alerted of the operation at about 8 a.m. Nov. 5.

Surrency said he spoke with the construction manager and learned construction was halted for three to four hours.

While the construction manager is in charge of the goings-on at the site, Surrency said, local law enforcement agencies and the Putnam County School District must adhere to state mandates to assist federal agents when required.

“I’m not really worried about these operations at our construction sites because our construction managers are responsible for the workers who are on the site,” he said Nov. 5. “My reaction about today is that I know law enforcement needs to do their job, and as a school district, we will cooperate in any way that we are required.”

There have been numerous ICE operations in Putnam County. Surrency said immigration agents conducted a raid at a South Putnam construction site last year but that “it created no issues.”

Allison Waters-Merritt, the sheriff’s office’s public information officer, said ICE was in Putnam County on Nov. 4 and received assistance from the Florida Highway Patrol. She did not know how many operations took place that day, but she said the sheriff’s office helped with one stop in the area of Point of Woods Trail and S.R. 19 in Palatka.

text:
Muslim civil rights groups’ advocacy and legal services for Floridians are suspended in the state while they appeal

November 5, 2026 2:25 pm

Media Contact

125 Broad Street

18th Floor

New York, NY 10004

United States

TALLAHASSEE, Fla. — The Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) and its Florida chapter, CAIR-Florida, will appeal a Wednesday night ruling by the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida that denies their request to reverse Florida officials’ “terrorist” designation of the two civil rights organizations. According to Chief Judge Allen C. Winsor, the plaintiffs are unlikely to succeed at this stage on their claims that the designations under HB 1471, a new and unprecedented state law, violate their due process and First Amendment rights. However, the judge issued a narrow form of preliminary relief, holding that Florida prosecutors cannot enforce the law’s penalties against plaintiffs, their employees, or third parties with respect to the provision of legal services to the groups.

While Chief Judge Winsor’s ruling does not resolve the case, address all claims in it, or make factual findings about Florida officials’ allegations against the Muslim civil rights groups, which the groups maintain are baseless, the designation takes effect today, November 5. As a result, CAIR and CAIR-Florida are forced to shut down their advocacy and operations in the state.

“Florida’s new law has profoundly disturbing parallels to authoritarian states, in which political leaders silence and punish dissent without due process,” said Hiba Rahim, executive director of CAIR-Florida, before the shutdown went into effect. “Governor DeSantis and other officials have unilaterally branded Muslim nonprofits as ‘terrorist’ with devastating consequences for our rights, our supporters, and the communities we serve. CAIR-Florida categorically rejects Florida officials’ baseless designation of us. Nevertheless, we are heartbroken that we have no choice but to close our doors to protect our staff and people of all faiths who support our work. Years ago, when Alabama banned the NAACP from operating in the state, the U.S. Supreme Court ultimately issued a landmark decision protecting every American’s freedom of association. We trust that the courts in our case, too, will ultimately uphold the fundamental rights we are entitled to as Americans and the constitutional freedoms that protect every one of us.”

The impact on the Floridian communities CAIR and CAIR-Florida serve will be immense. CAIR-Florida provides a range of pro bono legal services to Florida residents, including those who suﬀer government and workplace discrimination in violation of their civil rights, as well as those navigating the immigration system.

As the ACLU explained in court last month, CAIR and CAIR-Florida’s devastating designation under the new Florida law is unjustified. Neither group has ever been charged, let alone convicted of, any crime. If Florida tried to do so, it would fail. The reason is simple: neither CAIR nor CAIR-Florida is engaged in terrorist activity, and the state would be unable to prove its case to a jury in a court of law.

“Today’s ruling is deeply disappointing and we are appealing it. Our clients’ challenge to Governor DeSantis’s grave abuse of authority continues,” said Ashley Gorski, senior counsel with the ACLU’s National Security Project. “Today’s decision upholds state officials’ sweeping power to punish American organizations they brand as ‘terrorist,’ without due process and in violation of the First Amendment. Florida officials have been relentless in seeking to silence our clients’ civil rights work and advocacy, damaging not only them but also their community. We cannot allow this dangerous and sweeping censorship regime to stand.”

Under HB 1471, five Florida executive officials have the power to designate and debilitate U.S. groups — including nonprofits engaged in First Amendment-protected advocacy — without filing charges, initiating judicial proceedings, proving their case beyond a reasonable doubt, submitting the case to a jury, or complying with any of the other required constitutional protections of the criminal legal system. Once a designation becomes effective, an organization’s lawful, constitutionally protected speech and association are immediately rendered illegal and impossible. An elaborate set of prohibitions makes it a serious crime for the targeted American organization to do virtually anything in the state, and for others to work for or otherwise actively associate with or support the designated group. The consequences of violating these prohibitions are severe, including up to life imprisonment.

According to Chief Judge Winsor, while the groups did not succeed in demonstrating that their freedom of association had been unconstitutionally restricted or that the designation regime was an unlawful “prior restraint” on speech, the state’s attempt to criminalize the provision of legal advice to CAIR and CAIR-Florida was a content-based restriction of speech that likely violated the First Amendment. “The State has no meaningful interest in denying Plaintiffs’ legal counsel,” the court said.

Concerning due process, the court recognized that Florida’s new designation regime is “novel—and perhaps unprecedented,” but said that the plaintiffs had not demonstrated that the state-level appeal procedures were constitutionally inadequate. The court also held that the plaintiffs did not show that the designation was a form of criminal punishment, as opposed to a civil remedy.

“Today, for the first time in over twenty years, Florida Muslims cannot call their community’s leading civil rights organization for help if they experience a hate crime at their mosque, illegal discrimination in the workplace, violent bullying in school, or any other acts of bigotry,” said Edward Ahmed Mitchell, National Deputy Director at CAIR. “The Constitution’s guarantees of free speech and due process apply to every inch of our nation, including Florida. The unprecedented notion that Governor DeSantis has the power to punish an American civil rights organization for its speech and unilaterally force the closure of its doors without due process is an affront to the Constitution. We look forward to appealing this initial ruling so that we can protect the rights of everyone in the State of Florida. Although this is a tragic day for the people of Florida, our struggle to protect the U.S. Constitution is just beginning and we are confident that the rule of law will ultimately prevail, God willing.”

“We are dismayed by this ruling,” said Scott McCoy, deputy legal director, Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC). “A law that allows officials unjustly to brand a civil rights nonprofit with such a grievous label and expose it, and anyone who supports it, to life in prison with no hearing and no trial, threatens every Floridian’s constitutional rights. Our commitment to CAIR, CAIR-Florida and the communities they serve has not changed, and we will continue fighting this unconstitutional law throughout this case and on appeal.”

“The court’s decision at least recognizes that an organization cannot be prosecuted for participating in its own legal defense, contrary to the state’s dystopian law,” said Daniel Tilley, legal director of the ACLU of Florida. “CAIR-FL has already been forced to shut its doors in Florida, cutting off Floridian Muslims and others who relied on its services. No nonprofit engaged in First Amendment-protected activity should face this kind of harm without due process. We stand with CAIR and CAIR-FL and will appeal this decision. Our commitment to challenging this dangerous and arbitrary designation has not wavered.”

On Wednesday night, the defendants also stipulated that they would not prosecute (a) employees, board members, and third parties for their good-faith and reasonable involvement in the groups’ two legal challenges to Florida officials’ designations, or (b) good-faith and reasonable actions undertaken to comply with state and federal legal obligations. As a result, these legal and compliance activities may continue as the litigation moves forward.

CAIR and CAIR-Florida are represented by the ACLU, ACLU of Florida, the SPLC, and Bondurant Mixson & Elmore LLP.
