description: After Democrats' sweeping House and Senate victories, the party is laying out how it plans to wield power, while President Trump and Republicans react to their midterm losses.
text:
The U.S. Senate race in Mississippi remains a toss-up between incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democrat Scott Colom, with Colom leading by fewer than 2,000 votes.

According to Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson , there are approximately 3,600 outstanding mail ballots and an unknown number of affidavit ballots, or provisional ballots, from voters whose eligibility needs to be confirmed. Absentee ballots must be received within five business days, while affidavit ballots must be processed within the 10-day window that counties have to certify results, which ends Nov 13.

Both parties are keeping a close eye on the process. CBS News has confirmed the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has deployed lawyers and resources to the state to monitor the count.

"I'm confident that ultimately Mississippi has decided to go in a new direction," Colum told reporters after greeting campaign volunteers Thursday morning in Jackson.

The National Republican Senatorial Committee and Hyde-Smith campaign filed a request for all counties to separate and preserve all affidavit ballots. The Colom campaign called the move a "desperate stunt."  His counsel also sent a new letter to Mississippi's 82 counties asking them to respect election procedures.

Hyde-Smith predicted that she will represent Mississippi for another six-year term, posting on X : "We believe thousands of votes remain to be counted from dozens of Republican counties, and we are confident those votes will reinforce her path to victory."

At a news conference Thursday, Mississippi Republican Party Chair Mike Hurst insisted the election "is far from being over" and noted the state party has attorneys and observers throughout the state to ensure all legally cast ballots are counted.

Mississippi does not allow recounts, so a winner will be decided based on a plurality of votes.

Democrats won control of the House of Representatives by picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red. The party's wins ranged from suburban areas in the northeastern United States to areas of South Texas that were once viewed as increasingly GOP-friendly.

So far, 42 districts have shifted to Democrats and two have shifted to Republicans. Winners in dozens of races have yet to be projected.

Read more here .

GOP Rep. Anna Paulina Luna narrowly won her race in Florida's 13th District, CBS News projected. With 99% of the votes counted, Luna was leading by less than one point.

She faced Democrat Leela Gray.

Democrat Cait Conley defeated two-term Republican Rep. Mike Lawler, winning a highly competitive seat in New York's Hudson Valley region, CBS News projected.

Lawler's loss is another setback for Republicans. CBS News has projected that Democrats will take control of the House in January with a wide majority.

Lawler called Conley to concede Tuesday.

Read more here .

Rep. Ted Lieu of California announced his bid for Democratic Caucus chair in a dear colleague letter on Thursday.

"I am now running for Chair of the Caucus because I want to work with all of you to seize the opportunity the American people just gave us. If we do this right, we can build an enduring majority, one that will win not just the next one or two election cycles, but many more," he said.

House Democrats are on pace to win 256 seats, according to the latest CBS News estimate.

It's quite an increase from the 214 seats they hold in the current Congress.

The estimate includes several races that CBS News has not yet projected.

GOP Rep. Richard Hudson, the chair of the GOP's House campaign arm, lost to Democrat Richard Ojeda in North Carolina's 9th District, CBS News projected.

Hudson conceded the race on Wednesday.

Ojeda was previously a state senator in West Virginia, and in the last decade ran unsuccessfully for the House, Senate and president before moving to North Carolina.

Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker defeated GOP Rep. Mike Turner in Ohio's 10th District, CBS News projected.

Turner has represented the district since 2003 and won reelection in 2024 by more than 18 points.

Widespread Republican losses in the midterm elections are roiling the GOP, prompting soul-searching over what went wrong and a brewing blame-game that's expected to heat up as the party looks toward the next election.

From House and Senate races to governors' mansions, Republicans saw striking losses, both in battlegrounds and in places where the party saw significant support just two years ago. The victories dramatically shifted the balance of power in Washington, delivering Democrats a sizable majority in the House far beyond what was expected heading into Election Day, as well as a Senate majority larger than what the GOP has enjoyed for the last two years.

As Republicans process the results, including some GOP officials who have ambitions of their own in 2028, they're offering frank assessments of the shortcomings — and laying the groundwork for where the party heads next.

Read more here .

Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa gave her first press conference since Democrats' stunning wins in the state on Tuesday, with every statewide seat flipping to Democrats.

"This is a transition for the whole state of Texas," Hinojosa said as she announced members of a bipartisan transition team.

"This is not about being a Democratic administration, I'm not going to be the governor just for Democrats, I'm going to be the governor for all the people of Texas," Hinojosa said.

Hinojosa said Gov. Greg Abbott, who she defeated on Tuesday, is being "gracious" and said they are both committed to a "smooth transition."

When asked about Republicans at the state Capitol who may try to undermine her power, she said "the people of Texas have spoken." Democrats are on track to have a majority in the state House of Representatives, but Republicans will continue to have a majority in the state Senate.

L.A. Mayor Karen Bass released a statement on Thursday morning conceding to Nithya Raman, saying she called her to congratulate her on the victory.

"While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken. I have called Councilmember Nithya Raman to congratulate her on her victory, and I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition," Bass wrote.

Bass thanked her supporters and other leaders who helped during her campaign. She added that she will continue to "ensure the promise of a better life belongs to all of us."

Democratic Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez won a third term in Washington's 3rd Congressional District, CBS News projected.

Gluesenkamp Perez's victory, in a district President Trump has won three times, comes as she's flexed her independence over party loyalty. Democrats will take control of the House of Representatives in January, with stunning wins across the country .

The congresswoman beat Republican state Sen. John Braun to win reelection in the rural district in the southwestern corner of the state. Braun, the top Republican in the Washington state Senate, was a more mainstream Republican than Gluesenkamp Perez's prior opponent, far-right conservative Joe Kent, who went on to become Mr. Trump's counterterrorism chief before resigning in protest over the Iran war. But Braun, who was endorsed by Mr. Trump, also distanced himself from the president on some issues, including on tariffs, the Iran war and affirming that Joe Biden won the 2020 election.

Read more here .

Democratic Rep. Joe Neguse of Colorado on Wednesday announced his bid for assistant speaker when Democrats take the House majority in January.

"With our decisive and overwhelming victory this week, it is more important than ever for the House Democratic Caucus to be unified in the 120th Congress, and to repay the faith that the American people have put in us to lower costs, end corruption, and deliver for working families. To that end, and as we embark on that road together, I write to respectfully request your support for Assistant Speaker," he wrote in a letter to his Democratic colleagues on Thursday.

"If elected Assistant Speaker, my goals would be straight-forward — to prioritize direct member services for every member of our diverse and talented caucus, and to assist Speaker Jeffries and our incredible Democratic Leadership team," he said.

The leadership hierarchy could be a point of tension as both Neguse and Rep. Ted Lieu of California seek to claim the No. 4 spot. Neguse currently holds the No. 5 spot in the minority as assistant Democratic leader. A source familiar with the matter told CBS News that assistant speaker is the No. 4 spot in the majority.

Lieu, who currently holds the No. 4 spot in the minority as Democratic Caucus vice chair, will run for Caucus chair. Another source familiar with the matter told CBS News that the leadership hierarchy will be the same as it is now — with Lieu as No. 4 and Neguse as No. 5.

Sen.-elect Annie Andrews told CNN on Thursday that she has spoken to Republican Sen. Tiim Scott, the chair of Senate Republicans' campaign arm, and they scheduled a longer call for next week. Andrews did not say if Scott apologized for calling her "Trany Annie," but said she is focused on working "productively" with the senior senator from South Carolina moving forward. On the campaign trail, Darline Graham called Andrews "batshit crazy."

"You know, I understand politics is a dirty business, and name calling is sometimes part of it," Andrews said on CNN. "But it's not really about my hurt feelings or the way that they operated in the campaign. It's about Sen. Tim Scott and I finding a way to work productively together. And I really do have a lot of hope that we can do that."

Andrews also addressed reporting that she had internal polling showing she was winning, but declined to share it publicly.

"We were on track to win and we didn't want anything to disrupt the path that we were on," Andrews said. "And we knew if we kept showing up everywhere, talking to local media, talking about the issues, like I said, in addition to those issues, the data center issue that became really hot at the end of the race, we knew we could bring this across the finish line, and we didn't want this to become a national race because it's not about national politics."

Progressive Democrat Nithya Raman, a democratic socialist, defeated incumbent Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass in the mayoral race, CBS News projects.

Read more at CBS News Los Angeles .

Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general in charge of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, resigned on Thursday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said.

"Today, I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led the Civil Rights Division with conviction the past 18 months," Blanche wrote in a post on X . "She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor. The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors."

Dhillon oversaw a mass exodus from the Civil Rights Division last year, with more than 75% of its staff departing. She upended many of the division's traditional priorities that focused on combating discrimination against some of the nation's most vulnerable and historically marginalized groups.

Read more here .

President Trump is scheduled to attend the Army-Navy game, one of the longest rivalries in college football, U.S. officials told CBS News.

The stands at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on Dec. 12 will be filled with active-duty troops and veterans.

Mr. Trump has made an appearance at the game several times as commander-in-chief, including last year. The game is known for its military flyovers and patriotism.

Read more here.

House Democratic Whip Katherine Clark has launched her bid for majority leader in the next Congress.

"Today with pride in what we've achieved and confidence in what we will deliver, I ask for your support," Clark wrote in a letter to fellow Democrats obtained by CBS News.

The Massachusetts Democrat pledged to make affordability a top priority, give rank-and-file members a "seat at the table" and harness the party's "collective power."

If elected by her caucus, Clark would become the first woman to serve as House majority leader.

Rep. Erin Houchin of Indiana is challenging Rep. Lisa McClain of Michigan for the role of GOP conference chair in the next Congress.

In a letter to colleagues on Thursday, she wrote, "The road back to a Republican House Majority runs through our message and our ability to communicate it effectively. The American people are asking for something different. Our Conference should be willing to do the same."

On Wednesday, McClain released a list of 35 Republicans who are backing her to remain as conference chair. She was elected to the leadership position in 2024.

"We can spend the next two years licking our wounds and waiting for the political winds to shift, or we can get off the mat and go on the offensive. I know which path I'm taking," McClain said in a statement.

As Alaska continues to count its ballots cast in the midterms, President Trump posted on Truth Social that he believes votes for retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan and Republican candidate Gerald Heikes should be given to Sen. Dan Sullivan, a Republican who is running for reelection.

"The vote totals for the Fake Dan Sullivan, plus the other 'slug' that the Dems put on the Ballot, should be immediately given to the REAL Dan Sullivan, and the Election is over - He easily wins. There is no other fair solution!" Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social.

CBS News has rated the Alaska Senate race a toss-up.

Alaska uses ranked-choice voting , where voters rank candidates in order of preference, instead of selecting a single candidate. Under the system, if no candidate is ranked as the top choice for more than 50% of voters, the count goes to a second round. The candidate with the least amount of votes is eliminated, and votes from that candidate's supporters are redistributed to their second pick.

The process continues until a candidate wins a majority.

Days before the election, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit and asked a federal judge to block certification of the Alaska Senate election if Sullivan, the incumbent, lost. But a judge tossed out the suit on procedural grounds. The Justice Department has appealed.

ABC News' Jon Karl posted on X on Thursday morning that he had spoken to President Trump, who told him "I have every intention" of keeping Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Karl said Mr. Trump said "I get these calls, you know, about him. I don't understand why." But Karl said Mr. Trump also acknowledged that it would be easier to get a new defense secretary confirmed by the Senate before the Democratic majority takes over in January.

Multiple sources told CBS News on Wednesday that Mr. Trump was asking advisers if Hegseth should stay in his job. Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, publicly blamed the Iran war for the GOP's losses on Tuesday.

Outgoing Republican Sen. John Cornyn, who lost a primary earlier this year to Attorney General Ken Paxton, wrote an op-ed in the Wall Street Journal criticizing Republicans for their decisive losses in the midterms.

Cornyn wrote that an "epic blame game had begun" before the polls even closed, but he writes that "both sides miss the point" because "this week's beat-down wasn't only foreseeable, it was foreseen — because our party forgot four basic rules of coalition politics."

Cornyn said that Republicans shrunk their coalition after making gains with Hispanic voters in 2024, noting that some Republicans obsessed over "RINOs." He said Texas Republican Bo French "poisoned the well even further with blatant bigotry against Indian-Americans."

Cornyn also outlined other mistakes he feels the GOP made: the Republican candidates weren't likeable enough, and the Trump administration didn't follow through on its promises.

But ultimately, Cornyn wrote, "character and integrity still matter."

"Pre-election polls showed that corruption had surged toward the top of voter anxieties, thanks to flawed midterm candidates and a parade of unsavory headlines out of Washington," Cornyn said. "Voters won't trust Republicans to cut fraud and scams out of government programs until we cut them out of our own ranks. Party leaders have to stop excusing the inexcusable and police our side of the aisle—or voters will continue to police it for us."

As President Trump prepares for the final two years of his presidency, he is expected to devote more attention to his presidential library, which has become a growing destination for money from companies and allies, according to current and former advisers who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

"He undoubtedly recognizes that the library development season opens now, and he will go for it," said a senior administration official. A second administration official said that in this lame-duck period Mr. Trump will focus on "all things he can control, which means: Building."

With Democrats taking control of Congress in January after a sweeping victory in the November elections, lawmakers have pledged investigations into the library's finances.

Read more here .

House Democrats will start 2027 with a sizable majority, but their exact margin isn't clear, as votes are still being counted in key races in Maine, Montana, Florida, Alaska and elsewhere.

Here's how many House seats CBS News projects for each party:

CBS News still rates two Senate races as toss-ups: Alaska and Mississippi.

The Alaska race between GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola is still tight, and vote-counting could take some time , partly due to the state's ranked-choice system. The race was shaken up last week by allegations that Peltola-linked operatives helped recruit a candidate with the same first and last name as Sullivan — which Peltola's campaign denied.

The Mississippi race between GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde Smith and Democrat Scott Colom wasn't expected to be competitive, but  is razor-thin. State officials say thousands of ballots still need to be counted, including outstanding absentee ballots that aren't due for a few more days and "affidavit" ballots from voters whose eligibility needs to be confirmed.

Here's where control of the Senate stands:

Democrats won control of the House of Representatives on Tuesday by flipping more than two dozen Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red. The party's wins ranged from suburban areas in the northeastern United States to areas of South Texas that were once viewed as increasingly GOP-friendly.

Read more here on the districts that are changing hands.

Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' Congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House. That effort was rebuffed on Tuesday night as the GOP was on track to lose all of the districts it tried to gerrymander.

There were several reasons that states undertook what had previously been a rare practice of mid-decade redistricting. Republican efforts started when President Trump ordered Texas lawmakers to redraw their map to net up to five seats for the GOP.

But despite the all-out effort, Democrats won control of the House on Tuesday, with CBS News estimating Democrats could end up with 251 to 268 House seats.

Read more here .

Republicans have begun trying to pick up the pieces from Tuesday's midterms, with top GOP voices pitching themselves for leadership roles and offering theories on why the party lost.

House Speaker Mike Johnson announced on a call with his staff that he won't run for minority leader next year, a source familiar with the matter told CBS News .

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise announced he plans to run for Republican leader. He told his colleagues : "We will need to be honest with ourselves about what happened."

House Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan also threw his hat in the ring, calling it a "staggering day for our Conference." He said he's "battle-tested" after brawling with Democrats on investigations.

Others offered diagnoses on what went wrong. Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, whose state shifted hard toward Democrats, called the results an "ass-kicking" and a "Watergate-level repudiation."

On his podcast, Cruz argued his party didn't address a "real economic disconnect" and that many GOP politicians "seem like they didn't understand or they didn't care" about the cost of living.

In what could be a looming intraparty debate, Vice President JD Vance said the "reason we lost is the war." He said many Trump 2024 voters flipped to Democrats in order to end the Iran war, address cost-of-living issues, "Put America First" and change the U.S.-Israel relationship.

The likely presidential contender wrote that "everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."

(The president's son, Donald Trump Jr., reacted to Vance's post with "💯💯💯.")

Former Republican National Committee chairwoman Ronna McDaniel told CBS News' "The Takeout with Major Garrett" that Tuesday's results were a "red rebellion" that she linked to people's frustrations with the economy. She said the GOP needs to do some "soul-searching."

"You don't win Texas, you don't win Kansas, you don't win South Carolina without Republican voters actually crossing over and voting for the Democrats," she said.

President Trump's first public appearance since the midterms was at the construction site for his White House ballroom, where he lauded the contractors and signed a steel beam.

In remarks to reporters, Mr. Trump again blamed Republican candidates for the party's massive losses Tuesday night, saying there was so much "love" at his rallies.

"If I was on the ballot, we would have won," he said. "But they just — you couldn't transfer that love. There was such love at those rallies, it was incredible. And we weren't able to transfer the love to candidates."

He also said it's "largely true" that the GOP lost the House and Senate because of the Iran war's impact on energy prices, agreeing with Vice President JD Vance, but he argued it was worthwhile, saying: "If I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again."

"You have no choice; you have to do it. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon or everything that you see here some day might not exist," the president said.

President Trump has been asking advisers around him and on the phone whether Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should stay in his job, following Republicans' catastrophic losses Tuesday night, multiple sources familiar with the matter told CBS News on Wednesday.

Some White House aides have predicted some of the blame for GOP midterm losses will be trained on Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command, and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, who both played big roles in guidance on the Iran war.

One source told CBS News that GOP Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is being floated as a possible replacement for Hegseth, arguing he could go through Senate confirmation in the lame-duck period before Democrats take control of Congress.

Still, other sources said Mr. Trump hasn't decided to replace Hegseth.

White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement that the president "has full confidence in Secretary Hegseth." Asked if he is considering replacing Hegseth, Mr. Trump told reporters: "No, I think he's doing a very good job."

Read more here .

Rep. Robert Garcia of California, who will chair the House Oversight Committee next Congress, laid out four areas where the panel will focus its investigative efforts.

The overarching investigations include the Trump family's business dealings, corporate corruption, actions of the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and the Jeffrey Epstein scandal.

"I think folks that need to be concerned first are administration officials that have caused real harm. We're going to investigate the abuses," Garcia said at a news conference Wednesday, singling out Stephen Miller, Corey Lewandowski, Kristi Noem and Trump family members.

Garcia acknowledged the Justice Department is unlikely to prosecute people who refuse to cooperate, but said House Democrats could sue in civil court.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, meanwhile, called the midterms a "generational remake of the Senate map," but said his party's most important task is to respond to the mandate from voters by "prov[ing] ourselves worthy of their trust."

Previewing the party's plans starting next year, the minority leader said: "Whenever Trump defies the will of the American people or the law, we will launch investigations, take him to court, and entangle him in legislative razor wire."

Many congressional Democrats are likely to be enthusiastic about investigating the Trump administration. But one moderate incoming Democratic senator, Adam Hamilton of Kansas, told CBS News he wants to spend more time on cost-of-living and other issues than investigations or impeachments, saying: "I do not want to spend the next two years in trials."

Asked about the potential for Democrat-led investigations, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said: "As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."

Democrat James Talarico on Wednesday said his win over Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race delivered a message to Elon Musk, who spent more than $150 million to boost Paxton's candidacy: "Texas is not for sale."

Hours after his projected win over Paxton, Talarico told "CBS Mornings" that his victory is an opportunity to get big money out of politics "for good."

"The people of Texas delivered a crystal-clear message to the world's first trillionaire: Texas is not for sale," Talarico said. "The power in this state, in this country, belongs to the people and we've got to make sure it stays that way."

Read more here .

text:
Voters delivered Democrats decisive control of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate in the 2026 midterm elections, giving years of oversight interest a path to investigative action. When the 120th Congress convenes on January 3, 2027, the incoming majority will have the power to compel document productions and testimony in pursuit of inquiries into the Trump Administration, companies, other organizations and individuals. Those drawn into these inquiries can face significant reputational, legal and financial consequences well before any future legislative risks.

For private companies, Democratic control of the U.S. Congress will have several immediate and longer-term implications:

Existing Inquiries Will Gain Force. Companies should expect renewed or expanded document and testimony requests, backed by the incoming majority's authority to hold hearings and issue subpoenas.

Corporate Relationships with the Administration Will Face Increased Scrutiny. Government contracts, waivers, regulatory approvals, loans and policy changes may become subjects of investigation, bringing companies' communications with administration officials and the benefits they received into focus.

Companies May Become Sources of Evidence When Their Conduct Is Not the Focus. Where executive branch agencies resist or delay disclosure, investigators may turn to private parties for corresponding emails, messages, meeting notes and other records concerning government decisions.

Likely Investigative Priorities and Committees to Watch

Long before the midterm elections, Democratic members and oversight staff laid the groundwork for a return to the majority. The election now gives that work a path to compulsory process and other committee action. Affordability and scrutiny of the relationship between private interests and government decisions will drive much of the agenda, while leadership choices will help determine which inquiries move first and how aggressively they proceed.

Reps. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) at the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) at the House Committee on the Judiciary and Frank Pallone Jr. (D-N.J.) at the House Committee on Energy and Commerce are positioned to advance inquiries they have helped develop from the minority. Other gavels remain contested. At the House Committee on Financial Services, Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.) faces challenges from Reps. Bill Foster (D-Ill.) and Sean Casten (D-Ill.), with implications for the committee's approach to financial regulation, digital assets, housing and consumer protection.

Senate leadership choices are also interconnected. Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) is positioned to succeed retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.) at the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, while Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) is positioned to lead its Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. An anticipated move by Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) to the Senate Committee on the Judiciary following the retirement of Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) could open the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works gavel to Sens. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) or Ed Markey (D-Mass.), depending on other leadership selections.

At the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) is positioned to chair, although Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) has also been discussed as a contender; his prior chairmanship does not automatically restore his seniority under Democratic Conference rules. These selections remain subject to party processes and organizational decisions and will help determine which inquiries receive sustained attention.

Not all oversight efforts will be exclusively partisan. China, healthcare and consumer prices, energy costs, artificial intelligence (AI) and data centers are likely to attract bipartisan interest and potential cooperation. The following chart maps the principal areas of anticipated scrutiny and committees positioned to pursue them.

The incoming majority could also create select committees or dedicated subcommittees to pursue particular priorities. Recent Congresses have used these bodies to investigate the coronavirus pandemic and competition with China. Affordability or AI could provide a focus for a similar effort in the 120th Congress, creating additional avenues for scrutiny of private companies.

Considerations for Organizations Facing or Preparing for Congressional Scrutiny

The change in control warrants a fresh assessment by organizations already responding to congressional inquiries and those anticipating future scrutiny. Prior correspondence and staff reports offer useful indicators of likely priorities. Organizations should review outstanding requests, commitments and submissions and assess applicable preservation obligations – including where they have received preservation letters – as well as prepare for expanding document demands or witness testimony.

Leaders of legal, government affairs, communications and relevant businesses should establish response objectives, identify relevant records and personnel, and confirm procedures for escalating inquiries. Counsel should help structure this work to preserve applicable privileges and work-product protections, recognizing that congressional committees may challenge those protections.

Response decisions should account for parallel litigation, enforcement matters, government contracts and pending approvals. Meeting a committee's information needs while protecting sensitive information requires procedural and political judgment alongside litigation, regulatory and communications experience. Organizations should revisit their strategies as committee priorities become clearer and inquiries develop.

How Holland & Knight Can Help

Holland & Knight's nationally recognized Congressional Investigations Team helps organizations prepare for scrutiny and respond to active investigations, including document requests. subpoenas, investigative interviews and hearings. Our attorneys work with Holland & Knight public policy professionals and colleagues across white collar defense, litigation and regulatory practices to develop strategies tailored to each organization's circumstances.

We also offer a fixed-fee congressional investigations readiness assessment to identify potential vulnerabilities, evaluate response capabilities and establish practical steps for managing an inquiry. For more information, please contact the authors.

It is not designed to be, and should not be used as, the sole source of information when analyzing and resolving a legal problem, and it should not be substituted for legal advice, which relies on a specific factual analysis. Moreover, the laws of each jurisdiction are different and are constantly changing. This information is not intended to create, and receipt of it does not constitute, an attorney-client relationship. text:
Where a petitioner who was denied bond in immigration court has requested habeas corpus relief, the petitioner should be released because the government has not proven by clear and convincing evidence that the petitioner poses a danger to the community or proven by a preponderance of the evidence that he poses a flight risk.

“… The Court previously ordered the government to provide Petitioner with a bond hearing in immigration court that complies with due process standards as explicated by the First Circuit in Hernandez-Lara v. Lyons, 10 F.4th 19 (1st Cir. 2021). …

“Here, the Immigration Judge commendably found facts tending to suggest that Petitioner does not present a risk of flight but no contrary facts specifically addressed the risk of flight save for concluding that Petitioner is an alien who the Immigration Judge has found dangerous and concluding that the BIA is unlikely to reverse such finding. This is tantamount to a ruling of law that all such petitioners must be detained. Absent any actual finding of fact specifically addressed to the risk of flight issue, such ruling violates Hernandez-Lara and is arbitrary and capricious. It is set aside as violative of Petitioner’s right to due process. …

“The Petitioner having been denied a bond hearing that comports with due process, he is ordered released forthwith on terms sufficient to secure his attendance at further immigration hearings.”

Hernandez-Arevalo v. Blanche, et al. (Lawyers Weekly No. 02-579-26) (10 pages) (Young, J.) (Civil Action No. 26-13891-WGY) (Oct. 29, 2026).

text:
The midterm election’s “blue wave” has changed the political landscape in Washington, particularly when it comes to the hot topic of immigration. With Democrats in control of both houses of Congress beginning in January, Catholic immigration advocates have an opportunity to play offense on this crucial issue, rather than scrambling to block punitive policy initiatives.

In assessing what the Catholic community, including the U.S. bishops, should pursue, a long-term strategy is required—one that should extend beyond the presidential election in 2028. Any “overreach” in the near term could create a backlash at the ballot box in 2028 and jeopardize the church’s ultimate goal of humane and comprehensive immigration reform.

The election results were the product of several issues (most prominently the high cost of living), of which immigration was only one. To interpret the outcome as some sort of mandate on the passage of positive immigration reform would be a mistake. Nevertheless, the excesses of Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in the administration’s mass deportation campaign did seem to play a part in electing the new Congress, especially among Latino voters and other voters of color, who, according to early estimates, turned out in high numbers.

However, President Trump still maintains control over immigration policy and will certainly use his veto power to defeat any immigration legislation that runs counter to his mass deportation agenda. As such, Catholic immigration advocates should pursue immigration priorities that have at least some bipartisan support in Congress, if only to raise the profile of these issues for a future time when they can become law.

A sound immigration agenda the church could pursue for the new Congress would feature three priorities.

First, we need oversight and accountability for ICE. With the majority, the Democrats have the power of the gavel and the purse and can use them to ensure that ICE conducts enforcement in concert with legal norms. They can hold oversight hearings that require ICE to explain its enforcement actions, including the shootings of both U.S. citizens and immigrants.

Second, issues of specific importance to the church can be highlighted, including limits on the pastoral access to detainees, the separation of families, the detention and deportation of pregnant women, children and the disabled, and the weakening of asylum protections at the border. The new Congress could require reforms to enforcement through the appropriations process, conditioning any new funding for the Department of Homeland Security on their implementation. A statement signed by 20 Catholic bishops in February provides a blueprint for possible reforms to immigration enforcement.

Finally, advocates of immigration reform can pursue the passage of legislation that has bipartisan support. Legislation that could, realistically, be passed by both chambers of Congress would help draw attention to important immigration issues, even if it were vetoed by the president.

For example, the American Dream and Promise Act, introduced in the current Congress, provides a path to citizenship to undocumented youth who entered the country as children, known as Dreamers, and members of groups that had Temporary Protected Status before it was stripped away by the Trump administration, including Haitians and Afghans. These are groups who most Americans believe should not be sent back to their home countries.

The church could also push for passage of the Religious Workforce Protection Act, legislation that would facilitate the permanent status of foreign-born pastoral workers, including Catholic priests and religious, who have legally entered and worked in the United States.

For the long term, we need to lay the groundwork for humane immigration reform. Advocates may first need to spend time convincing Democrats to back positive immigration reform, as opponents have been successful over the past 10 years in pushing the debate in a more restrictionist direction. And any passage of a comprehensive immigration reform bill, including a path to citizenship for the undocumented, would certainly be met with a veto by President Trump (and the bill might be severely weakened during the legislative process at any rate). Passing a humane and fair immigration reform bill requires a president—either Democratic or Republican—who is willing to spend political capital on its passage.

In the meantime, Catholic immigration advocates should pursue a more prudent path and join with labor and business leaders to push for congressional hearings that highlight how mass deportations have hurt the nation, both economically and socially, and reveal how the current legal immigration system is severely broken and needs repair.

Advocates should also work to shape public opinion among the Catholic faithful. Catholic IMMpact (the Catholic Immigrant Prophetic Action Project), an initiative of the Catholic-based Center for Migration Studies of New York and Hope Border Institute, was launched to help (arch)dioceses educate Catholics and prepare them for the immigration reform debate that is to come.

Catholic leaders should also hold internal discussions about what a successful immigration reform bill might look like and what concessions are inevitable. For example, advocates may face the decision of whether to accept a form of legal status for the undocumented that does not include a pathway to full citizenship. They should keep in mind that in past immigration reform debates, the “perfect” bill has been the enemy of the good.

The Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign has revealed the ugly underbelly of the U.S. immigration system and how it can undermine human dignity and violate human rights. It has also taught us that the removal of hard-working immigrants and their families can harm the U.S. economy and weaken the social fabric of local communities. These lessons provide hope that out of the darkness of the current period of mass deportation a dawn of opportunity may emerge to pass humane immigration reform legislation, for which the church must be patient yet prepared.

text:
The Justice Department filed a lawsuit on Thursday against Pennsylvania State University over its policy of giving in-state tuition to illegal immigrants.

The DOJ alleged that Penn State violated "federal law by prioritizing the needs of illegal aliens over U.S. citizens in defiance of Congress’s commands."

The university's policy allegedly "grants in-state tuition to illegal aliens while denying reduced tuition to U.S. citizens," the DOJ said. "This policy unconstitutionally discriminates against U.S. citizens who are not afforded the same reduced tuition rate, in direct conflict with federal law."

The lawsuit seeks to enjoin Penn State from enforcing the policy and "from enacting any new tuition policies that favor undocumented students over U.S. citizens," according to the DOJ.

“The Department of Justice today continues its efforts to ensure that no state law or university policy gives preferential treatment to illegal aliens over our Nation’s own citizens,” Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward, Jr., said in a statement. “Congress long ago made clear that states, through their public universities, cannot give reduced tuition to illegal aliens not available to all Americans.”

With Thursday's lawsuit, the DOJ has filed 27 total complaints against states and Washington, D.C., over in-state tuition for illegal immigrants. Of the 27 lawsuits, six of them — involving Texas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nebraska, Illinois, and Kansas — had resulted in favorable court orders permanently blocking and declaring unconstitutional the challenged provisions. Other cases remained pending.

According to Penn State's website, "Undocumented students, with or without [Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals], can be eligible for in-state tuition if they meet Penn State’s residency requirements. These requirements include attending an accredited Pennsylvania high school for at least four years and graduating from an accredited Pennsylvania high school or receiving a Pennsylvania General Educational Development (GED) certificate."

Under the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, which is codified as 8 U.S.C. 1623, a person who is not lawfully present in the United States cannot receive a postsecondary education benefit based on state residency unless U.S. citizens are eligible for a benefit of at least the same amount, duration, and scope regardless of whether they live in that state.

Supporters of in-state tuition policies for illegal immigrants counter that many recipients have lived and attended school in their states for years, that expanding access to higher education can increase graduates' earning potential and tax contributions, and that denying resident tuition can make college financially inaccessible.

text:
Where a habeas corpus petitioner has challenged his detention following the revocation of his release, his petition should be granted because the government revoked his release without complying with the applicable legal requirements.

“This is a habeas petition that concerns a noncitizen’s challenge to his detention following the revocation of his release. Petitioner … is a citizen of Brazil who illegally entered the United States in 2021, was ordered removed, and was released on an order of supervision. He was on supervision for more than five years without apparent incident.

“In September 2026, he was arrested and his release was revoked. In revoking his release, the government failed to comply with its own procedural regulations. Because those regulations are intended to provide notice to the arrestee and a meaningful opportunity to be heard, the failure of the government to follow them violated [the petitioner]’s right to due process of law. The Court will therefore grant the petition and order [the petitioner]’s release and return to supervision.

“The Court recognizes that the government may have the authority to re-arrest [the petitioner], and if the government complies with its regulations before revoking his release, [the petitioner] will likely receive the due process to which he is entitled. Nonetheless, the government cannot simply ignore the law, and if it does, it must live with the consequences. For his part, [the petitioner] contends that he plans to file a motion to reopen his removal proceedings and stay his removal. The Court cannot, however, base any part of its ruling on that representation. Instead, the Court will issue its ruling based on the circumstances as they now exist, without regard to possible future events. And because the government revoked [the petitioner]’s release without complying with the applicable legal requirements, it will be ordered to release him from custody pending further developments. …

“In short, nothing in the revocation notice puts [the petitioner] on notice of the ‘reasons for revocation,’ as the regulation requires, and that would permit him to meaningfully contest his revocation during his informal interview. 8 C.F.R. §241.4(l)(1). …

“… Because ICE violated its own regulations and thereby impaired [the petitioner]’s right to due process, the revocation of his [Order of Supervision (OSUP)] is invalid and his detention is unlawful. …

“For the foregoing reasons, the petition for writ of habeas corpus is granted. Respondents shall release [the petitioner] no later than 5:00 p.m. local time on October 23, 2026. …”

Modolo v. Wesling, et al. (Lawyers Weekly No. 02-574-26) (8 pages) (Saylor, J.) (Civil Action No. 26-14411-FDS) (Oct. 22, 2026).

text:
The Trump administration held secret talks with Iran on deporting Iranians even as the war there dragged on, court documents obtained by the Associated Press show.

The court documents unsealed on Thursday show the Republican administration as recently as mid-October said it had plans to deport the Iranians through an unnamed third country, although it was unclear when it intended to do so.

The judge in the case ordered the government to give the court 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country and five days’ written notice before any such deportation is carried out.

“We are at war with a country where the president of the United States has said, as recently as two or three days ago, if not yesterday, that it is essentially lawless … A country that is an enemy of the United States, according to the current president. A country that, according to our president, murdered tens of thousands of protestors,” the judge, Ana Reyes, said according to the 15 October transcript that has now been unsealed.

“And what you’re telling me is that the United States of America is going to send individuals back to that region, facing what you and I and everyone who would ever look at this would know would be, at a minimum, a serious threat of certain death.”

“Yes, your honor,” justice department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel said. “The government is executing lawful orders of removal.”

Georgiev-Remmel told the court there was no specific date set to carry out any removals. A legal group representing Iranians held by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) said a dozen Iranian detainees had been given notice over the past week that they would be deported to Iran. The legal group, the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund, brought the lawsuit in which the transcript was released.

The court documents show that the administration maintained contacts with Iranian officials during the war over the removals, specifically for submitting travel documents and figuring out “possible avenues for removal”.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), ICE’s parent agency, and the state department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The development emerged from an ongoing lawsuit that alleges the Trump administration’s immigration agencies have been sharing confidential information about Iranian asylum seekers with the Iranian government, violating national immigration regulations and endangering countless Iranians, court filings argue.

The Iranian American Legal Defense Fund said on Thursday at least 12 Iranian detainees have been contacted by the Iranian Interest Section, an Iranian representative office in the Pakistani embassy in Washington that handles consular affairs, in the past week and notified of an upcoming deportation flight to Iran through Pakistan. The group did not say when the deportation would occur.

One of those detainees attempted suicide once he learned he might be returned to Iran, according to Yasmine Chubin, the executive director of the organization. He was one of two people who were subsequently moved across state lines to a detention center in Texas, where detainees are often relocated immediately preceding a removal.

None of the detainees who have been contacted have been provided any information in writing from immigration authorities, the legal group said.

Activists abroad have expressed concern about deportees returning to Iran, whose theocracy has been cracking down on intellectuals and where the government vociferously cracks down on any dissent.

The lawsuit depicts a coordinated campaign between the US and Iranian governments to identify Iranians in ICE custody and pressure them to return to Iran – a marked departure from decades of diplomatic hostility between the two governments. The DHS has denied that it is sharing asylum application records with the Iranian government.

Hundreds of emails exchanged between US immigration officials exposed how the two countries worked together to arrange for more than 100 Iranians to be flown back to Iran on three immigration flights in September and December 2025 and January 2026.

During the 15 October hearing, Reyes warned government attorneys that she would initiate contempt proceedings if the administration violated her order to give the court advance notice of any planned deportation flights.

“We are talking about sending individuals in our care and custody to a country that we have bombed and we may continue bombing, and is a declared enemy of this country,” Reyes said.

In a court filing on Wednesday, the justice department said the judge’s order effectively served as an injunction against the government “given the possibility of sanctions and contempt dangling overhead”.

Deportations of Iranians back to their home country are historically rare, owing to the lack of diplomatic relations between the US and Iran and the possible persecution they could face there.

But under the Trump administration, which is carrying out a broad immigration crackdown, ICE has aggressively pushed to deport people even from countries that have typically been reluctant to take people back or with whom the US has had icy or no diplomatic relations.

Sometimes that has meant sending people back to their home country, but it has also meant deporting people to other countries they have no connection with.

name: Policy
title: What a Democratic Congress Means for Oversight in 2027 | Morrison Foerster
authors: Carlos Felipe Uriarte, Kimberly Hamm, Joseph Charles Folio III
description:
Democrats’ Oversight Agenda Voter sentiment will shape Democrats’ oversight agenda in 2027.
Key committees: House Energy and Commerce Committee, House and Senate Judiciary Committees, Senate Banking Committee, and Senate Finance Committee Federal power and civil liberties.
Key committees: House Oversight Committee, House Judiciary Committee, House Natural Resources Committee, and Senate Finance Committee The Pentagon, national security, foreign donations, and foreign business.
Key committees: House Foreign Affairs Committee, House Armed Services Committee, House Intelligence Committee, and Senate Armed Services Committee AI and data centers.
Key committees: House Energy and Commerce Committee, Senate Banking Committee, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and Senate Commerce Committee Takeaway: Expect Democratic investigations into alleged corruption paired with legislative reform proposals.
text:
Democrats will control both chambers of Congress in 2027 following a sweeping midterm election victory on Tuesday. While votes are still being counted in several states, Democrats are on track to hold at least 54 Senate seats and a House majority of more than 250 seats, the largest in nearly two decades.

Within hours of the results, the incoming chairs of two of the most powerful investigative congressional committees signaled what comes next: “Lawyer up.” and “Subpoenas.”

Key takeaways

Investigations will be wide-ranging and move quickly, driven by four issues: affordability, federal power and civil liberties, alleged corruption, and national security. Against this backdrop, artificial intelligence (AI) and data centers will feature prominently in investigations across committees and chambers.

Parallel investigations will multiply, as Congress, state attorneys general, and potentially the Trump administration act on the same issues.

Subpoenas may be ubiquitous, but litigation could be selective. Democrats have threatened the robust use of subpoenas, but enforcement is challenging and accommodations are the preferred method of resolution.

The clock is already running. Letters can arrive now, and subpoenas are likely early next year.

“Lawyer Up”: The Signal Is Clear

On election night, House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform Ranking Member Robert Garcia (D-CA) issued a two-word statement: “Lawyer up.”

This message follows Democratic committee leaders’ 2026 preview of their investigative agenda, sending hundreds of letters requesting records and information from the Trump administration and private parties alike. Representative Jamie Raskin (D-MD), in line to chair the House Judiciary Committee, has been meeting with House Democratic leadership to divide the oversight work among committees and expects to spend November and December setting priorities for public hearings.

Takeaway: Democrats are in the minority until the 120th Congress convenes on January 3, 2027, but incoming chairs can send letters and preservation requests now. Subpoenas are likely early next year, once committees organize and adopt their rules. How a company responds to an informal request today will shape the record later, and declining to engage is rarely a sound strategy.

Democrats’ Oversight Agenda

Voter sentiment will shape Democrats’ oversight agenda in 2027. On key concerns that dominated the exit polls, Democrats spent 2026 sending the letters that will become 2027 investigations.

Affordability, market power, and consumer protection. Three in four voters said the economy is in bad shape, and at least 85% were concerned about the cost of gas, food, utilities, and healthcare. Expect scrutiny of pricing practices, drug-pricing arrangements, energy costs, the impact of tariffs on consumers, and industries Democrats argue are raising costs or shifting risk onto consumers.

Key committees: House Energy and Commerce Committee, House and Senate Judiciary Committees, Senate Banking Committee, and Senate Finance Committee

Federal power and civil liberties. A majority of voters said immigration enforcement has gone too far. Democrats are poised to investigate the administration’s immigration enforcement and deportation efforts, as well as government contractors and companies whose products and services may have been used to support the administration’s immigration enforcement actions.

Key committees: House Oversight Committee, House Judiciary Committee, House Homeland Security Committee, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee and its Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations

Corporate engagement with the Trump administration and Trump family members. About nine in 10 voters called corruption a major factor contributing to their vote, and both parties will want to demonstrate to voters they can be trusted to address the issue. Democrats will attempt to tie this concern to Trump family businesses, donations to Trump-aligned projects, and corporate interactions with the administration. Expect probes into corporate donations, government financial support of certain industries, government contracts, and corporate ties to Trump family-aligned businesses or industries.

Key committees: House Oversight Committee, House Judiciary Committee, House Natural Resources Committee, and Senate Finance Committee

The Pentagon, national security, foreign donations, and foreign business. Nearly two-thirds of voters (63%) were opposed to military action in Iran. Ranking Member Gregory Meeks (D-NY), in line to chair the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has promised investigations into the administration’s Iran war decision-making, as well as Venezuela operations and military strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific. These probes include inquiries into energy companies, government contractors, and financial services companies. Democrats have also highlighted possible national security risks of foreign donations to Trump-aligned projects, foreign investment in sensitive technology, and foreign business entanglements with Trump family businesses.

Key committees: House Foreign Affairs Committee, House Armed Services Committee, House Intelligence Committee, and Senate Armed Services Committee

AI and data centers. Three in four voters (76%) oppose a data center in their community, and 57% believe AI will do more harm than good. Expect committees across Congress to hold hearings with technology and AI leaders, along with scrutiny of data-center energy costs and chip exports.

Key committees: House Energy and Commerce Committee, Senate Banking Committee, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and Senate Commerce Committee

Takeaway: Expect Democratic investigations into alleged corruption paired with legislative reform proposals. AI cuts across all four issues, and with comprehensive legislation unlikely, congressional action will shift toward hearings and other oversight requests.

Parallel Investigations

Congress rarely investigates alone. Democrats flipped attorney general offices in Texas, Georgia, Iowa, and Kansas. Texas elected its first Democratic attorney general since 1994, who has pledged a focus on consumer protection and anti-corruption. These offices join states such as California and New York that already lead multistate litigation. Meanwhile, the administration may want to show that it is protecting consumers too, with the Federal Trade Commission and Department of Justice (DOJ) pursuing visible enforcement of their own, including partnering with state attorneys general.

With Democrats in the majority, expect committee reports to serve as road maps for state attorneys general, and potentially as source material for plaintiffs’ attorneys.

What this means for companies:

Be prepared for multi-front fights with Congress, state, and federal authorities. While congressional committees in the past may have simply referred concerns of misconduct to state or federal authorities, or declined to press agencies about open criminal investigations, companies are unlikely to see such restraint next Congress.

Assume anything produced to Congress will become public. Committees control their own records and can release documents, quote them at hearings, or publish them in reports. Caution should be observed if committees demand copies of records provided to state or federal authorities.

Be mindful of privilege concerns. Committees do not consider themselves bound by attorney-client privilege or work-product protection, but in practice accommodations can be reached.

Keep one fact record. Inconsistent statements across forums become the story and criminal false-statement liability extends to congressional inquiries.

Democrats’ Subpoena Authority

On election night, President Trump had a simple message: “VETO.” Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden (D-OR) posted his own one-word message: “Subpoenas.”

Despite the confrontational rhetoric, expect both the administration and a Democratic Congress to pick and choose their battles, with accommodations reached on both sides.

The White House has added legal staff to prepare for oversight and a recent DOJ Office of Legal Counsel opinion suggests the administration may assert executive privilege over certain presidential communications with private parties. But contesting every request across dozens of committees would consume time and capital the administration will need elsewhere in its final two years.

Despite the focus on potential subpoenas next Congress, the use of congressional subpoenas is now a commonplace occurrence. Since 2021, nearly 600 subpoenas have been issued by congressional committees, but Congress has brought just three civil enforcement actions during that time. Document demands and subpoenas may be broadly worded to seek “any and all” documents, but narrowed responses are typically negotiated. Litigation risks for House committees mean negotiation is the preferred resolution.

Why understanding subpoena threats and litigation matters:

The threat of a subpoena no longer carries the weight it once did. Subpoenas are common and rarely enforced, through litigation or criminal contempt of Congress.

The legal arguments shape leverage. Legislative purpose, pertinence, breadth, burden, and constitutional defenses all bear on how much room a company has to negotiate scope.

Companies may be caught in the middle. If the White House asserts privilege over its communications with a company, the company should consider its exposure on each side as it considers whether to produce, withhold, or seek an accommodation.

Congress will enforce subpoenas selectively. Committees will choose the strongest candidates for litigation – subpoenas narrowly written, with a clear legislative purpose, seeking clearly non-privileged materials, and in support of an investigation with a compelling narrative. Criminal contempt requires a DOJ prosecution, which rarely follows when Congress is led by the opposing party.

Takeaway: Expect widespread subpoena threats, but behind-the-scenes negotiations to resolve disputes. Disputes that reach court will be chosen carefully to win and to set precedent. Knowing which category a matter falls into should shape strategy from the first letter.

Looking Ahead: Key Dates

November 10, 2026: Republican leadership elections to take place.

November 18-19, 2026: House Democratic leadership elections to take place. Senate Democrats hold leadership elections in December.

December 11, 2026: Government funding expires, an early signal of how each side will approach the 120th Congress.

January 3, 2027: The 120th Congress convenes, and the House adopts its rules package.

January 2027: Committees set organizational meetings and finalize internal rules.

Early 2027: The first subpoenas are possible, along with opening hearings.

We will continue to monitor developments as the new Congress takes shape. For questions, please contact the Congressional Investigations team.

Alec Bartishevich, a Policy Advisor in our Washington, D.C. office, contributed to this alert.

text:
A private prison company that has raked in billions by selling immigration detention centers to the Trump administration wants the government to “move quickly” on more deals, days after a Democratic landslide in the midterms.

CoreCivic has sold four detention centers to the Department of Homeland Security this year for $2.2 billion and has been touting plans for future sales. But its new CEO faced questions Thursday during an earnings call from investors wanting to know if that would continue under Democratic control of Congress starting in January.

“We can’t predict what will happen one way or the other on timing or really on whether they will happen at all,” CEO Lucibeth Mayberry said of the negotiations for additional sales. “We would urge the ICE administration to move quickly. They have a need for capacity. We have the capacity. There’s no reason to wait.”

Mayberry, who took over as the head of CoreCivic in September, emphasized that Congress had given DHS billions for immigration detention — $45 billion in 2025 and $31 billion last year — available through fiscal year 2029. She said she saw no reason DHS wouldn’t continue entering into contracts until that funding is gone.

Trending

But the massive cash influx Congress gave to Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and the contracts with CoreCivic and its main competitor, Geo Group, are set to come under scrutiny once Democrats take back the gavel.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington), the ranking member of the House Judiciary subcommittee dealing with immigration, said the heads of the companies can expect to be called to testify. She’s been closely tracking immigrants’ deaths in detention.

“The gravy train is over,” Jayapal said.

And Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Connecticut) is seeking to chair the House Appropriations Committee, saying the party must “claw back” billions of dollars Republicans gave to ICE and Border Patrol outside of the regular appropriations process.

Geo Group is expecting to sell four detention centers to DHS by the end of the year, but those sales won’t materialize if the company can’t secure long-term agreements to manage the daily operations, CEO George Zoley told investors Thursday.

The company announced last month the sale of a complex of more than 2,600 beds in Adelanto, California, to ICE for $950 million and a new 10-year contract to run the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Washington, that will generate $140 million in annual revenue.

The day before the election, Geo Group announced another 10-year contract to manage a 2,329-bed detention center in Big Spring, Texas, though it does not own the land.

CoreCivic acknowledges in its quarterly reports that its contracts with ICE can be terminated. “We can provide no assurance that we will continue to manage these facilities in the future, or that the terms of the management agreements will remain the same,” the most recent report states.

The detention center sales have already raised questions about federal waste and how the federal government is agreeing to pay hundreds of millions of dollars for detention centers that, in most cases, ICE was already using.

For example, ICE paid more than $495 million for a vacant 1,600-bed lockup in Appleton, Minnesota, that CoreCivic had offered to the state government for $75 million a year prior, an investigation from KARE 11 found.

Both companies and the Trump administration have said the value is calculated based on how much it would take to replace the buildings, adjusted depreciation and land value, among other factors.

“Why are both of those things happening in the order that they’re happening in?” Jayapal said of the sales and long-term management agreements. “It seems like somebody is making a lot of profit off of these sales and purchases, and we need to understand that.”

text:
BANGKOK—Two Uyghur men held in Thailand for more than a decade are pleading to not be sent back to China, fearing abuse or torture.

Human rights activists and some Thai politicians warn the men could be sent to China following their release from prison in late October.

Uyghurs are a Turkic, majority Muslim ethnic group native to Xinjiang in China’s northwest. After decades of conflict with Beijing over discrimination and suppression of their cultural identity, the Chinese government launched a brutal crackdown on them that some Western governments have called a genocide.

The two men were among more than 300 Uyghurs fleeing China detained by Thai authorities in 2014 near the Malaysian border. China has consistently pushed for their return, saying they were terrorists.

The two men, ages 26 and 35, told the Office of the National Human Rights Commission on Wednesday that they do not want to be sent back to China, according to a source with direct knowledge of the meeting who requested anonymity for fear of retribution. They made the same plea in a letter published last week.

In response to the concerns, Thailand said Wednesday that China must make a formal extradition request if it wants the two Uyghur men returned.

National Security Council chief Chaipruak Doungprapat said the courts would decide on whether to deport the two, unlike the case of 40 Uyghur men sent back to China last year, and that the men would be able to defend themselves. A ruling in their favor could allow them to resettle in another country.

“But if the court rules against them, they will be extradited according to the treaty. This is the judicial process,” he said.

China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Mao Ning didn’t comment on whether China had sent an extradition request.

“China and Thailand’s cooperation in combating cross-border crimes, including illegal immigration, is in accordance with the laws of both countries, as well as international law and international practice,” Mao said Wednesday.

Of the group of more than 300 Uyghurs detained over a decade ago, Thailand sent mostly women and children from the group to Turkey. In 2015, Thailand deported 109 to China against their will, prompting an international outcry. The Thai embassy in Turkey was ransacked in protest.

In February 2025, Thailand sent back another 40 despite pleas from the men themselves, Thai lawmakers and U.N. officials not to.

Today that fear is front and center for the two men.

“Every time we are worrying from China to take back us,” one of the Uyghur men wrote in English in the letter shared by Kannavee Suebsang, a former lawmaker and founder of the Peace Rights Foundation, a human rights group that represents them. “We aren’t terrorist,” he wrote.

Sasinan Thamnithinan, a lawmaker from the opposition People’s Party, said Thailand is obligated by both domestic and international law to ensure that no individual is returned to a country where they could face torture or inhumane treatment.

“Maintaining international relations is important, but it must not take precedence over human rights and the rule of law. No one should be sent back to face danger simply because the government wants to end a problem,” Sasinan said in a statement Tuesday.

Up until the very last moments before the previous group was deported, the Thai government denied they would be sending the men to China.

The Thai government said the men had signed forms in Chinese to return voluntarily. China then took select Thai media groups on an official tour, but they did not have independent access to speak to the individuals who were returned.

Thailand’s Office of the National Human Rights Commission said last year that Thai officials involved failed to provide evidence that the men consented to be sent back or an assurance of the group’s safety upon their return.

“The assertion that the Uyghurs returned voluntarily remains a one-sided claim ... despite reports assessing human rights concerns in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, which document instances of torture and cruel treatment against the Uyghur population,” the office said in a statement.

Kannavee said he made official attempts while still in office to determine what happened to the 40 men but received no reply. He said Thailand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and others also attempted to follow up. The ministry declined to comment.

text:
The Trump administration said during a court hearing that it has been making plans to deport Iranian immigrants back to Iran while the U.S. is at war with that country, earning a rebuke from a federal judge, court documents show.

According to an unsealed transcript of a hearing held on Oct. 15, a Justice Department attorney disclosed in federal court that the Trump administration was making plans to deport Iranian nationals to Iran through third countries.

The hearing was part of a lawsuit brought by the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund against the Trump administration alleging that the government is sharing confidential information about Iranian asylum seekers with the Iranian government.

During a heated two-hour hearing, U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes blasted government lawyers after learning that Department of Homeland Security officials were working on removal logistics to send individuals back to Iran.

"Your Honor, one of the questions that you had asked is whether there are any planned removals to Iran," said DOJ attorney Dimitar Georgiev. "The answer in August was no. Today that answer has changed and it is yes".

"I'm sorry, I just want to make sure I understand this correctly," Judge Reyes said. "We are going to remove people in our custody to a country with which we are at war?"

"We are at war with a country, where the president of the United States has said as recently as two or three days ago, if not yesterday, that it is essentially lawless ... and what you're telling me is that the United States of America is going to send individuals back to that region facing what you and I and everyone who would ever look at this would know would be at a minimum a serious threat of certain death?" Reyes said.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment from ABC News.

The transcript shows the U.S. government has been holding talks and coordinating with representatives of the Iranian government to arrange removals.

According to court documents, the Iranian Interest Section in Washington, D.C., sent officials to U.S. detention centers to meet with detainees. Iranian detainees in California and Arizona were offered meetings with officials, but they refused and no meetings took place, according to the transcript.

During the hearing, Georgiev said the U.S. will "facilitate the travel" of the Iranian detainees to a third country and that the government of Iran will facilitate the travel from the third country into Iran.

Judge Reyes ordered the government to provide at least five days' advance notice before any individual is "placed on a transport vehicle or plane bound for removal," and 24 hours' notice of any finalized removal plan.

"If anything happens that violates either of those two orders, I will hold every single person associated with violating it. I will start contempt proceedings," Reyes said.

"We are talking about sending individuals in our care and custody to a country that we have bombed and we may continue bombing, and is a declared enemy of this country," the judge said. "It is like saying we have individuals in 1942 in this country that we are going to send back to Nazi Germany. That is the equivalent of what you are telling me."

description:
The 2026 midterms have opened a door, as voters made clear that rising health care costs and threats to their coverage demand action.
What we do next will determine whether that opening becomes meaningful change for people who need health care.
